News.title: Woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband speaks out as abusers found guilty
News.content:
A woman who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband has said she will "never feel completely safe" after four men were found guilty of sexually abusing her, in the first trial of its kind in England.

Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said: "The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."

Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire. He invited men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to the couple's home without her knowledge.

On Thursday, Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.

Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".

On the steps outside the court, she said: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to."

News.title: Tens of thousands of UK fridges secured from hackers in secret nationwide operation
News.content:
A behind the scenes cyber-security operation has taken place to secure tens of thousands of fridges and freezers at major UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums from hackers, the BBC has learned.

Recent waves of cyber-attacks in Europe have seen tonnes of food spoiled at hundreds of stores, causing millions of pounds of damage.

France has blamed Iran for one of the waves of attacks that impacted its supermarkets, a claim Tehran denies.

It was thought the UK had largely escaped such hacks as the British refrigeration industry relies on different devices but there was in fact a potential vulnerability the sector has been rushing to fix.

In late October, security researchers discovered a major flaw that, if found by hackers, could have led to even worse damage to the UK.

Since then, researchers, IT teams and the National Cyber Security Centre have been working around the clock to warn dozens of companies.

The BBC has not reported on the large-scale, secretive operation until now to reduce the chances of hackers causing harm if they found the vulnerability.

News.title: UK-EU mobility scheme to benefit up to 200,000 young people a year, BBC understands
News.content:
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.

The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.

The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.

A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.

The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.

In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.

Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.

Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.

The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.

Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.

"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.

"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.

"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."

Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.

The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.

News.title: Bowen: Myanmar genocide verdict is historic and could have far-reaching implications
News.content:
The undoubted joy and relief felt by Rohingyas in the camps in Bangladesh will not deliver them an immediate improvement in the miserable and dangerous living conditions they have been forced to endure for almost a decade.

The court has no mechanism to enforce its rulings, but it has told Myanmar to make reparations to the Rohingyas.

That will not be easy. Hundreds of villages have been razed to the ground, and the Myanmar government is unlikely quietly to accept the verdict of the court.

The UK, as the so-called "pen holder" on the UN Security Council with responsibility for diplomacy around the Myanmar issue, put out a statement saying it was "determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimesâ¦ we must ensure the Court's ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity".

It has called for an urgent session of the Security Council, is expelling Myanmar's defence attachÃ© in London and has promised other measures in the coming days.

Not much might be possible at the UN. A tough resolution against Myanmar could be vetoed by either China or Russia, or both.

Other rumblings have come from the Trump Administration about the case. Without waiting for the ICJ's verdict, former US President Joe Biden's administration declared in 2022 that the Myanmar military committed genocide against the Rohingya people.

But Mike Waltz, the current US ambassador to the UN, warned the court last month not to "lower the legal threshold for proving genocide".

Waltz said he was speaking out to protect "American and allied soldiers" but his post has been widely interpreted as support for Israel's defence at the ICJ.

He condemned what he called the "leftist, global, antisemitic agenda" of the international community, singling out Navi Pillay, this year's recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize, who was one of the judges in the Myanmar case.

She led a UN independent international commission that reported a year ago that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip.

News.title: Watch: What did Trump, Xi and Putin get out of their historic meeting?
News.content:
Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have concluded their historic 90 minutes of trilateral talks by issuing a "joint declaration of peace", but what did each leader actually get out of the meeting?

The highly anticipated meeting of three of the world's global superpowers held in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, marked the first time that the three had met together.

The BBC's Russia editor, China correspondent and North America correspondent got together to discuss the outcome of the meeting.

Read more about the historic meeting in Shenzhen.

News.title: Massive hope for pancreatic cancer pill after trial saw tumours vanish
News.content:
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US. It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS, external, found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.

Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.

Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."

He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."

There are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease in Britain each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.

Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.

Symptoms can include, external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

News.title: Next round of BBC cuts will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns
News.content:
Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.

The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its Â£500m target.

In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures would be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.

The BBC welcomed the report, saying it had "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".

The NAO report, external also said the BBC's current measures were expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."

The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.

News.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
News.content:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

News.title: Covid inquiry report: key findings on testing, tracing and 'the pingdemic'
News.content:
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.

Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.

NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.

In the end, more than Â£30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.

Once established, it was effective.

But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

News.title: England fined for fans' anti-Catholic chants in Spain
News.content:
England have been punished by Uefa following anti-Catholic chanting from the away fans during their Nations League victory in Spain.

European football's governing body have fined the Football Association Â£12,572 (15,000 euros) and imposed a suspended one-match ban for England away supporters.

BBC Sport understands the charge of 'racist and/or discriminatory behaviour' relates to chants that were deemed anti-Catholic and anti-Irish.

A further offence within the next two years would mean a ban on away fans is enforced.

There had been concerns of the prospect of racist chanting from Spain fans before the game in Madrid with England boss Thomas Tuchel stating he would remind his players of Uefa's anti-racism protocol before the fixture.

Tuchel stressed he didn't expect any incidents, but the visit was England's first to the Spanish capital since a notorious 2004 encounter at the Bernabeu was overshadowed by racist chanting directed at their players.

That led to a firm response from Spain head coach Luis de la Fuente, who said: "What I'd tell you, and you can tell Thomas, is that in Spain, there's no racism.

"Just like that, crystal clear. Just like in England, there's no racism in Spain. We aren't racist, any of us."

England won the match 3-2 to end Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and top League A Group 3.

News.title: Tourist jailed for damaging Belfast's Big Fish
News.content:
A man has been jailed for five months after causing an estimated Â£10,000 worth of damage to Belfast's Big Fish sculpture.

Peter Smith, 44, of no fixed abode, admitted criminal damage and possessing items with intent to damage property.

He is believed to have used a hatchet, a hammer and a sledgehammer to smash ceramic tiles around the sculpture's left eye.

District Judge Francis Rafferty told Belfast Magistrates' Court: "I regard it as a targeted attack, but it remains unexplained."

Police were called to Donegall Quay shortly after midnight on 20 September. A witness saw Smith striking the sculpture with a long-handled object and detained him until officers arrived.

Smith was carrying a hammer and a small hatchet in his backpack and officers later found a sledgehammer in nearby bushes.

Defence barrister Garrett O'Kane said Smith was visiting Belfast from England and that he had a psychiatric disorder following a car crash four years earlier in which two of his sons were killed.

O'Kane said Smith told him that he had found the tools and used them to attack the sculpture.

The court heard that plans for repairing the sculpture remain unclear.

News.title: Attempted murder arrest after councillor stabbed
News.content:
A councillor has been seriously injured after being stabbed while undertaking his duties in Bradford.

Bradford Moor councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:04 GMT on Manse Street, according to the deputy leader of Your Bradford Independent Group, councillor Ishtiaq Ahmed.

West Yorkshire Police said a 32-year-old man had been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder and was being held in custody.

The force added there was "no information to suggest that this is a politically motivated incident at this time".

Ali is believed to have been injured on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to the nearby Manse Street where emergency services attended, according to police.

A force spokesperson previously said the suspect had climbed on to the roof of a property on Thornbury Avenue following the incident and was later brought down.

News.title: Flag injunction case 'spiralling out of control'
News.content:
The co-founder of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours has said an interim injunction banning him and others from putting flags on lamp-posts in Birmingham is "spiralling out of control", as he learned the case could go to trial.

The High Court granted Birmingham City Council the order on Wednesday against Ryan Bridge and others, after thousands of union jacks and St George's flags were put up across the city.

The council argued that they posed a hazard on lamp-posts, signs and other highway structures, and fuelled community tensions.

On Thursday, Bridge attended another hearing where he was told the injunction had come into force and would be in place until a trial or further court order.

The 45-year-old heard that if the council sought a permanent injunction, the case could involve at least three to four days of evidence.

He said: "It's spiralling out of control, isn't it?" and added that he did not "want to exploit any more of the public purse and the council's money".

Bridge, from Blackwell, near Bromsgrove in Worcestershire, said he stopped putting up flags in Birmingham when he first heard about the injunction.

He said the other defendants in the case, which include six other named individuals and "persons unknown" who may put up flags, thought the case was "done".

News.title: Badenoch defends amputee marathon runners claim in benefits cut row
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has defended her suggestion that because double amputees run marathons more disabled people should work instead of claiming benefits.

Badenoch had used the example when setting out her party's plans to cut welfare spending by Â£36bn a year.

Her comments were criticised by Paralympian Richard Whitehead, who accused her of "weaponising" his sporting success, while Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the Tory leader's words "crass and insensitive".

But in an interview with the BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Badenoch stood by the remarks, insisting that "if people even with significant problems can work, then those who have ADHD and mild anxiety should go to work".

Asked if she accepted the comments were insensitive, Badenoch said: "No, no, no. I do not accept it. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense. I will speak the truth, and I will say what I believe is common sense.

"What I know is that if people can work, then we should encourage them to work."

Badenoch acknowledged she had used "extreme examples to illustrate things", but added: "If someone can do that, then yes, your condition of ADHD or anxiety is mild."

"I will say things as they are. People may disagree with things that I say, and that's fine, this is a free country, people are free to disagree, but they know where I'm coming from," she said.

"I start from first principles: If you can work, you should work, and the Conservative Party is going to help you get a job."

News.title: Glampsite owner appeals £135k bill after blocking neighbours from using their driveway
News.content:
A glampsite owner is challenging a court order to pay Â£135,000 in legal costs after she tried to block her neighbours from parking their car in their own garden.

Carol Esteban told her neighbours Neil and Nadine Gould that their right to use their shared driveway ended opposite their front door, which would block them from their parking space.

Both sides accused the other of trespassing, while Esteban was accused of using "boulders" to block the couple's access to the shared track.

The Goulds sued Esteban in 2025 and won a High Court ruling enabling them to drive far enough along the track to turn off into their parking space. But Esteban has now appealed that ruling.

In the ruling in July 2025, Judge Milwyn Jarman explained how the Goulds' detached cottage, Cwmtawe Villa, Abercrave, near Swansea, was completely surrounded by land attached to Cwmtawe Farm, where Esteban runs her glamping site, which was set over 60 acres of ancient woodland with their own individual hot tubs.

The properties were once all held by the same owner, but the house was sold off in 1949, with documents relating to that transaction now lost.

However, a 1964 conveyancing document stated the owners of Cwmtawe Villa could enjoy an "easement" - granting them the right to use a track owned by the farm to access their house on foot or with vehicles.

But a missing letter on a map attached to the document sparked the row over how far along the track the easement ends.

Esteban argued that a thick hedge had surrounded the villa at the time the right of way was granted and that it would have "made no sense" for the right of way to entitle the owners to go any further than the gap in the hedge by the front door.

But Jarman rejected Esteban's argument, and said her assertion "has the potential to lead to impracticability, if not absurdity".

He concluded that the claimants were entitled to a declaration that their vehicular right of way extends to the space at the north side of the villa, where they currently park their vehicles.

Esteban was also handed a Â£135,000 costs bill.

News.title: Irish government denies 'foot-dragging' over Omagh Bombing Inquiry
News.content:
The Irish government has denied "foot-dragging" over the Omagh Bombing Inquiry, following calls from some victims' families for the Republic of Ireland to hold its own investigation.

The inquiry is examining whether the attack on 15 August 1998, in which 29 people including a woman pregnant with twins were killed, could have been prevented.

Jim O'Callaghan, the Irish government's justice minister, said they were fully cooperating with the inquiry and if there remained unanswered questions "we will certainly look at that".

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant earlier said it was "almost inconceivable" that Ireland would not hold its own inquiry into the bombing.

They were speaking as ministers met on Thursday in Dublin for the British Irish Intergovernmental Conference.

O'Callaghan said the Irish government was "doing a huge amount" in relation to the legacy of the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

"I don't believe the Irish government is foot-dragging," he said in response to questions from reporters during a press conference.

"If at the end of this Omagh inquiry there are questions that need to be answered, we will certainly look at that.

"But there are really significant problems that will arise in terms of having a parallel inquiry at the same time."

News.title: Asia shares drop on AI worries, echoing Wall Street's decline despite the strong Anthropic debut
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Asian shares dropped in trading early Friday as a wide selloff hits issues related to artificial intelligence and computer chips.

Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 shed 4.5% in morning trading to 56,775.04. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 dropped 1.6% to 8,594.10. South Korea's Kospi shed 4.5% to 4,905.20. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell nearly 2.0% to 22,393.93, while the Shanghai Composite lost 1.7% to 3,515.87.

The AI-related stocks dipping in the region included Advantest Corp. and SoftBank Group Corp. in Tokyo, as well as Samsung Electronics Co. in South Korea and Tencent in China.

Worries that the AI boom may be over have been hanging over global markets for some time, despite the strong debut Thursday of Anthropic's stocks on Wall Street.

On Wall Street, benchmarks declined, with the S&P 500 dropping 2% for a sixth straight loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101 points, or 2.2%, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3%.

The S&P 500 jumped as much as 1.3% after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold shares of its stock at $83 apiece in its initial public offering. Its price quickly surged above $115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. Anthropic later pared its gain and finished the day at $97.17, still up 17.1%.

Anthropic’s IPO appeared to demonstrate faith remained among investors in the AI revolution. The industry needed a boost following sharp recent drops for AI-related stocks on worries their prices shot too high in the frenzy around the technology.

Nvidia erased its early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 3.3%. The sudden resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO added to the damage. He was one of AI’s biggest evangelists and helped build interest in the industry while using some of Nvidia’s massive profits to further fund its growth.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 147.80 points to 7,175.83. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1,101.11 to 49,097.06, and the Nasdaq composite sank 550.69 to 23,879.20.

In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 5.04% from 5.07% Wednesday.

In energy trading, benchmark U.S. crude rose 0.38% to $83.53 a barrel. Brent crude, the international standard, edged up 0.40% to $92.35 a barrel.

In currency trading, the U.S. dollar slipped to 159.22 Japanese yen from 159.60 yen. The euro cost $1.0970, inching down from $1.0973.

___

AP Business Writer Stan Choe contributed to this report.

News.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya people, UN’s top court rules
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled, the first time a state has ever been found guilty of the crime.

Gambia brought the case in 2019, arguing that Myanmar’s military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Muslim Rohingya from Buddhist-majority Myanmar amounted to genocide.

"The court finds that Myanmar's security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh," presiding judge Yuji Iwasawa said.

On Thursday, judge Iwasawa said the actions by Myanmar’s security forces showed the “intention to destroy” a substantial part of the Muslim minority population, meeting the legal threshold for genocide.

open image in gallery Rohingya refugees watch the International Court of Justice ruling ( AFP/Getty )

Judges voted by 9 votes to 6 that the state of Myanmar was guilty.

It is only the third time in the ICJ’s history that the court has issued a judgment on a genocide case and marks the first time a state has been found guilty.

It is the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled genocide had been committed, with courts previously recognising the 1994 Rwanda genocide, the 1995 Srebrenica killings in Bosnia, and atrocities by Cambodia's Khmer Rouge in the late 1970s as such.

In Bangladesh, many of the 1.2 million Rohingya who have been stuck in the Cox's Bazar refugee settlement, followed the judgment closely as it was read on Thursday morning.

The Rohingya have been stuck in the settlement since 2017, when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a clearance campaign in northern Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group.

open image in gallery Myanmar's Union Minister for the Ministry of the President's Office Ko Ko Hlaing attends a hearing on the day the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ( Reuters )

Judges found that Myanmar's military carried out mass executions of men and boys, committed widespread rape against women, and burned or razed hundreds of villages during so-called clearance operations.

The military actively spread hate speech targeting the Rohingya population, they said.

“Myanmar knew or should have known of a serious risk of acts of genocide being committed... during the 2017 clearance operations,” judge Iwasawa said.

He said Myanmar had carried out “destruction of evidence”, by burning and disposing of bodies, and destroying sites where the “clearance operations” had taken place.

During the Myanmar trial, survivors recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. As part of its case, Gambia has asked the court to order Myanmar to pay reparations and ensure the safe return of Rohingya refugees.

open image in gallery Rohingya refugees watched on as the verdict was read out on Thursday morning ( AFP/Getty )

The Rohingya refugees now endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Judge Iwasawa said Myanmar must "facilitate the safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohinghya displaced as a result of Myamar's wrongful acts”.

Human Rights Watch said the ruling marks the “long-awaited recognition” of Rohingya suffering, adding that it provides a “significant precedent for victims of genocide, and other grave crimes, across the world in their own quest for justice”.

The case has implications for other genocide cases, such as South Africa's 2023 case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, giving clues on how the 15-member bench assesses state responsibility.

open image in gallery The judgment was delivered on Thursday morning ( Reuters )

Both Israel and Myanmar deny genocide and say their forces have responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups.

Crucially, for judges to establish genocide under the 1948 convention, the court must find that there was an intent to destroy a protected group, either in whole or in part, a threshold that was met in the Myanmar case.

The UK’s all-party parliamentary group on Burma said the ruling “must serve to mobilise the international community to do everything it can to protect the Rohingya, and the entire population of Myanmar, from continued violations of international law by the Myanmar military”.

It called on the British government to resume “regular rounds of sanctions” against the military and to significantly boost aid to Rohingya refugees.

open image in gallery (File photo) Rohingya siblings fleeing violence hold one another as they cross the Naf River along the Bangladesh-Myanmar border in Palong Khali in 2017 ( Reuters )

The court’s rulings are final and legally binding, but it has no effective way to enforce it beyond reporting noncompliance to the UN Security Council.

In 2007, the court said that Serbia “violated the obligation to prevent genocide” in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when Bosnian Serb forces murdered some 8,000 mostly Muslim men and boys in the Bosnian town.

Judges at The Hague-based court have also been asked to weigh in on other allegations of genocide.

Beyond South Africa’s case against Israel, Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia.

Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

News.title: White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The White House has named a new national cyber director after a series of widespread service outages disrupted life and unnerved many Americans.

Kirsten Davies, chief information officer at the Defense Department, will fill the role, according to social media posts by several members of Trump's cabinet. She will replace Sean Cairncross as the administration's top cybersecurity official.

“Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected,” Davis wrote in a post on X. “Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future.”

Trump faced a groundswell of criticism as Americans grappled with a cascade of service outages that snarled travel, cut off work, limited bank access and disrupted classified communications.

Even staunch Trump allies accused the administration of lying to Americans or hiding information about the true cause of the disruptions. Over the past week, Microsoft, Chase Bank, air traffic control and the National Security Agency have all been affected.

Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there’s “zero” information that the technical failures are related to each other or to a malign actor.

The White House made the change as Trump returned from a three-day trip to Asia, where he downplayed the episodes, declaring that “things like that happen.”

“She has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth wrote in a post on X congratulating Davies.

News.title: Warming has gotten so out of hand, nations call for sucking carbon out of air somehow
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

For the first time, United Nations climate talks are likely to conclude that the world will have to suck heat-trapping gases out of the air as well as cut carbon pollution because society has failed to keep Earth out of the warming danger zone.

Doing that will cost tens of trillions of dollars and rely on still unproven technology, but it's the best the globe can hope for because it is now inevitable that the world will blow beyond the safe temperature threshold set by the 2015 Paris climate agreement and confirmed by subsequent scientific reports, scientists and United Nations officials said.

Earlier this year, a United Nations annual report acknowledged it's certain that the planet will breach the Paris threshold of keeping long-term warming below 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) since the mid 1800s. While that key temperature threshold is measured over a couple decades, short-term warning signs continue to mount. October's global average temperature set a record for highest above pre-industrial times for any month of the year, at 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) higher, said scientists at Berkeley Earth, who also predict that 2026 will pass 2024 as the hottest year on record.

The U.N. climate negotiations, known as COP31, are scheduled to end Friday in Turkey, though they rarely finish on time.

Early drafts of the end-of-conference communique acknowledge that the world has failed at preventing 1.5 degrees of warming, will enter a period of decades of temperatures in a more dangerous zone and then somehow bend the curve back down below 1.5. Doing that requires sharp cuts in carbon dioxide emissions and the removal of carbon from the atmosphere, according to the drafts. Carbon dioxide emitted from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas traps heat in the atmosphere and causes the planet to warm.

“Carbon removal is the magic eraser we’re left with when we’ve busted the world’s carbon budget, such as the 1.5C target,” Stanford University climate scientist and emissions tracker Rob Jackson said in an email. “Is carbon dioxide removal feasible technically? Yes. Is it likely to happen at the billion-ton scale needed to make a difference? No.”

Hundreds of billions of tons must be removed

The world needs to remove 320 billion metric tons (350 billion tons) of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere this century to bend the curve back down, United Nations Environment Programme Director Inger Andersen said at the climate conference this week. That's eight years' worth of global emissions, she said.

Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather calculated that it costs about $22 trillion to reduce global temperatures by every tenth of a degree Celsius (.18 degrees Fahrenheit) through carbon removal. Even if the world were to peak at two or three tenths of a degree Celsius (.36 to .54 degrees Fahrenheit) above the Paris threshold — the most optimistic scenario — it would cost $44 to $66 trillion by 2100 to get back underneath the threshold, Hausfather said.

Planting more trees would not remove anywhere near enough carbon, experts said. In the past decade, increased tree planting and other nature-based solutions removed, at most, 2 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide, Andersen said.

So what's needed are mechanical methods, such as huge devices resembling giant fans that suck carbon out of the air, some of which are being tested at pilot scale. This nascent technology currently removes as much carbon dioxide in a year as fossil fuel burning plants put in the air every half hour, said Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany. And the current hope is that it could scale up to 5 billion metric tons by 2050, he said.

This type of carbon removal is different than carbon capture and storage technology that some industries use to prevent their own pollution from escaping into the air. The climate talks are also likely to encourage more of that type of carbon capture.

Pollution cuts first and foremost, then removal

The world will need to remove massive amounts of carbon dioxide, “but there’s not much point of thinking about that until we have deep emission reductions,” Climate Analytics CEO Bill Hare said at the conference. That's because unless policies around the world change, the world is heading for at least 2.7 degrees Celsius of warming by 2100, and there's no way the world can remove enough carbon from the air to compensate for that, he said.

Still, the world has to seriously consider carbon removal “because there really are no good outcomes above 1.5 degrees, ” Andersen said, noting that warming is already causing stronger heat waves, droughts, floods and extreme storms.

She and others said carbon removal - sometimes called negative emissions - is not a replacement for steep emission cuts, but rather an addition to them.

“We need deep emission reductions. That is, and will always remain, the most important tool at our disposal,” said Denmark's environment minister Samira Nawa. That's why Denmark is aiming for a 110% reduction of emissions, going beyond net zero emissions to putting 10% less carbon in the air than what oceans and forests naturally take out.

Denmark and Ethiopia, the chair of next year's climate talks, are leading a newly formed coalition called the Group of Negative Emitters, or GONE.

Balancing bad news and hope

Officials, analysts and scientists say humans have put the planet in a tough spot. Because society has not heeded years of calls for steep emissions cuts, they say the planet is essentially stuck with relying on carbon removal.

“This is something I don’t think everyone has internalized yet. If you’re a champion of 1.5 degrees C, then you’re also a champion of reaching net-negative emissions," said World Resources Institute's global climate and economics director Melanie Robinson.

Even though he pointed out the difficulties in carbon removal, Rockström said, "we must keep this as our safe landing temperature, now that we fully understand how dangerous it is to exceed 1.5°C."

News.title: Nations still seeking deeper fossil fuel cuts as annual UN climate change summit enters final day
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Negotiators entering the final day of this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey are seeking meaningful commitments to address global warming amid warnings that only drastic cuts in fossil fuel emissions can avert its most catastrophic effects.

Friday marks the official end of the two-week annual summit, which has so far largely failed to advance any big ideas to move away from fossil fuels — mainly coal, oil and gas — which are contributing to more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters.

A goal introduced this year to increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably from renewable energy, also would allow the use of coal and other fossil fuels.

And leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable countries that contributed little to the problem — say a U.N. fund to help them recover from climate disasters and adapt to a warmer world is not nearly large enough.

Top-emitting nations did not participate directly in this year's summit, complicating efforts. That includes the United States, the world’s second-largest polluter after China and the largest polluter historically, which is absent for the second year in a row.

A report last week by the independent nonprofit Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years. That means the world is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Without drastic reductions beyond what countries already have promised, the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said. ___

Delgado reported from Bangkok. Associated Press reporter Tammy Webber contributed from Fenton, Michigan. ___

News.title: Opening practice session at Las Vegas Grand Prix washed out
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Formula One’s opening session in Las Vegas ended without a wheel being turned in anger amid a Sin City practice washout.

Following persistent rain in Nevada, 17 of the grid’s 22 drivers completed a reconnaissance lap – gingerly navigating their way round the 3.8-mile circuit – before returning to their respective garages without setting a time.

Four-time world champion Max Verstappen reported the street venue – which runs along the famous Las Vegas Strip – was like an “ice rink”.

The drivers took to the circuit one-by-one, in an apparent orchestrated bid to provide some on-track action across the one-hour session for the frustrated fans.

The Las Vegas GP is the sole event on the calendar that the sport’s American owners’ Liberty Media promotes itself.

But with dry conditions forecast for the remainder of the weekend here – and the risk of sustaining damage outweighing the need to rack up meaningless wet-weather data – they will be nervously braced for a second effective no-show in the day’s other session which is due to begin at 8pm local time (4am Friday GMT).

There is, however, some hope that the conditions will improve by then.

The race here is already an effective dead-rubber after Kimi Antonelli secured the world championship in Mexico last month. Antonelli’s Mercedes team have also wrapped up the constructors’ title.

News.title: MAGA favorability is at a disastrous low as former Trump backers flee the movement
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Public support for the Make America Great Again movement has dropped to its lowest net favorability rating on record, leading high-profile allies to distance themselves from the brand.

Among those pulling back is tech billionaire Elon Musk, who recently rejected the MAGA label after losing nearly $500 million backing candidates aligned with President Donald Trump in the 2026 midterm elections.

Speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit, Musk said he felt “foolish” for spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the midterm races.

“American elections are not just about money,” Musk said.

During the same summit appearance, Musk sought to separate himself from the movement altogether.

open image in gallery Prominent allies of President Donald Trump are beginning to distance themselves from his Make America Great Again movement after polling data showed public support for the brand dropping to a record low ( Getty Images )

“I’m not MAGA,” Musk told The New York Times. “Well, at least I’m not, like, I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m, like — if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies of the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

Trump addressed Musk’s remarks on Thursday in a phone interview with NBC News while returning from a trip to Asia, calling the SpaceX and Tesla CEO “a friend of mine” with “very good intentions.”

“MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well,” Trump told NBC News, noting that Musk “was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”

The comments mark a shift for Musk, who previously led the administration's Department of Government Efficiency — overseeing major reductions across federal agencies — and appeared alongside Trump at the 2025 Conservative Political Action Conference, where he held a chainsaw onstage.

During a broadcast segment featuring footage from the DealBook Summit, CNN host John Berman pointed out the contrast between Musk’s recent remarks and his past support.

“I mean, he’s basically wearing a MAGA hat here!” Berman said. “So, why might he be saying now he’s not that way?”

open image in gallery Tech billionaire Elon Musk says he feels ‘foolish’ after spending nearly $500 million on Trump-backed midterm candidates, distancing himself from the movement as its net favorability drops to 41 points underwater ( Getty Images )

CNN senior data reporter Harry Enten attributed Musk’s pivot to declining public sentiment toward the movement, which he said reached its lowest net favorability rating on record in October 2026 polling at 41 percentage points underwater, including a net rating of minus 61 points among independent voters.

“I’m not the puppet!'” Enten said on air. “Why is he taking the ball and trying to run to the other side of the field? I’ll tell you why he’s taking the ball and trying to run to the other side of the field! MAGA’s Lowest net favorability rating ever, ever, ever, ever! In October of 2026, the latest poll we have available, 41 points underwater! Forty-one points! My goodness gracious.”

Enten added: “Down there in the Gulf of Mexico! With independents, it’s -61 points. No wonder he doesn’t want to be associated with MAGA! It is a brand that is failing amongst the American public. We saw it in the 2026 midterm elections. We saw it in those races that Elon Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars in. Simply put, he’s a businessman. He knows MAGA at this point is failing amongst the American public, and that’s why he wants to take his ball and go home.”

The polling slump coincides with broader challenges for the White House, with Trump's overall approval rating sitting between 32 percent and 38.3 percent, as reported by The New York Times.

News.title: Trump’s DOJ is backing down on election fraud cases
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

After mounting dozens of “voter fraud” prosecutions in the weeks before midterm elections, Donald Trump’s Department of Justice has quietly dissolved legal battles that potentially threatened thousands of eligible ballots, court records show.

On Thursday, the Justice Department moved to effectively dismiss its lawsuit challenging election results in Alaska, where government attorneys accused Democrats of conspiring to recruit a candidate with a similar name to the incumbent Republican.

On Tuesday, the Justice Department dropped its lawsuit demanding California purge alleged noncitizens from its voter rolls after facing uphill legal battles in federal court. And on Wednesday, the Justice Department also threw in the towel in a legal battle over the government’s attempts to perform door-to-door interrogations to root out suspected fraudulent voters.

Nearly 200 noncitizens were accused of voter fraud-related crimes in the weeks before midterm election day, charges announced in high-profile press conferences and amplified across the administration’s social media platforms. Officials had promised hundreds more were coming.

But those dockets have largely gone cold, and prosecutors have brought only one new fraud-related case since November 3, according to a review from The Washington Post.

open image in gallery The Department of Justice, steered by Attorney General Todd Blanche, has pulled out of several high-profile legal battles seeking to challenge results in 2026 midterm elections and appears to have slowed the pace of fraud-related prosecutions ( AP )

The administration’s retreat follows sweeping Republican losses in midterm elections that will tilt the balance of power in Congress to Democratic control in January, a seismic rebuke to the Trump administration that will likely derail his final two years in office.

The withdrawal also follows the government’s routine losses in federal courtrooms over the administration’s attempts to seize unredacted voter rolls and threaten thousands of ballots cast in California and Washington state.

Asked whether the Justice Department discovered any new evidence of widespread fraud in the aftermath of midterms, Attorney General Todd Blanche told reporters last week that the agency was still engaged in a legal battle over results in the Alaska Senate race.

But the Justice Department on Thursday asked a federal appeals court to hold the case as moot and open the door for dismissing it altogether.

Government attorneys had tried to convince federal judges to block the certification of that election if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan lost. A federal judge tossed the case November 1, and Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the winner in the race on Tuesday.

“There are hundreds of ongoing criminal investigations into fraud associated with voting and elections, and those aren’t stopping because November came and went,” Blanche told reporters last week. “We will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly and that wasn’t expected to start or stop no matter what the results of the election were.”

open image in gallery Democrat Mary Peltola was declared the winner in Alaska’s Senate race after DOJ officials accused Democrats of conspiring to dilute votes for Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan by recruiting a similarly named challenger. Government attorneys moved to dismiss the lawsuit November 19 ( Getty )

The Justice Department has not formally ended its challenge in Washington, but a federal judge Thursday blocked the government from pressuring Washington election officials to set aside ballots cast by voters who are accused of being noncitizens.

That 14-day restraining order expired this week, nearly two weeks after Election Day and after the state certified its results, making any future attempt from the Trump administration to interfere in this year’s election outcome virtually impossible.

In California, the administration’s demands that the state set aside ballots sent to more than 20,000 alleged noncitizens was blocked in court after state officials warned that the Justice Department’s list was riddled with errors and could end up disenfranchising thousands of eligible voters.

That legal battle stalled at the Supreme Court, which refused to take up the case one day before Election Day.

In a two-sentence court filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department said it is dropping its appeal.

open image in gallery The Justice Department has also ended its defense of an ‘Unlawful Voter Initiative’ with Homeland Security to investigate alleged noncitizen voters ( AFP/Getty )

The next day, the Justice Department also indicated it is ending its defense of an “Unlawful Voter Initiative” that sought to gather large amounts of data to generate a list of suspected fraudulent voters.

In August, the Department of Homeland Security rolled out a program that paved the way for a “surge” of door-to-door investigations and arrests based on potentially faulty data without enough time for state officials or voters to correct any registration errors, according to court filings.

A federal judge earlier this year warned that even under the “best conditions,” there is a “high likelihood of error in review because there is no federal database containing citizenship status of U.S. residents.”

In October, a federal appeals court agreed.

“In an operation ostensibly focused on past voter fraud, the government could have aggressively pursued its campaign against non-citizen voting well before these elections commenced,” appeals court judges wrote.

A brief appeals court notice Tuesday noted that the government is ending its appeal.

“This was one more desperate attempt by the Trump administration to interfere in the midterm elections, and the courts have again said no,” Benjamin R. Farley, supervisory counsel for Democracy Defense at the National Immigration Law Center, which was leading the legal fight, said in a statement last month.

Those losses also followed more than two dozen failed attempts from the Justice Department to seize state voter data, which a federal judge in Pennsylvania condemned as a “fishing expedition” that appeared designed “for potential weaponization in future elections.”

The latest retreat also follows the departure of now-former Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, who steered the Justice Department’s election investigations. She resigned from the role two days after Election Day.

The Justice Department has charged nearly 300 people in voter fraud-related cases since returning to the White House, including 197 people in 26 states within the last 11 weeks, an agency spokesperson told The Independent.

That pace has appeared to slow down, raising questions about the agency’s abilities in the aftermath as the administration hemorrhages prosecutors, though the Justice Department disputes that characterization.

“The Department’s focus on noncitizen voting did not begin or end with Election Day,” Justice Department spokeswoman Kiersten Pels told The Independent.

“In the weeks before the election, we prioritized bringing these cases to deter illegal voting and to make clear that voting by noncitizens carries serious criminal consequences,” she added. “The increase in charges and announcements you describe reflects that effort. It doesn’t indicate a change in priorities.”

The investigations are ongoing, she said.

“There are hundreds of ongoing criminal investigations into fraud associated with voting and elections, and they did not stop when the election ended,” Pels added.

News.title: Anthropic achieves $2tn valuation as shares soar
News.content:
Anthropic has surged to a $2tn (£1.5tn) valuation as the Claude-maker defied a tech sell-off with a record-breaking float.

Shares in the Silicon Valley AI lab soared as high as $111.50 in opening trading on the Nasdaq exchange in New York on Thursday. The stock traded up around a third on its initial price of $83, before falling back to $97 per share at close.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 closed 2.3pc lower, with investors cashing-in on the excitement, analysts say.

Dow Jones ended the session 2.2pc lower, while the S&P 500 closed down 2pc.

The AI lab raised a record $107bn in the stock market listing, smashing a previous $86bn record set by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June.

Many investors had been concerned about the backdrop to the blockbuster listing after a Chinese spying scandal engulfed US chip giant Nvidia and Jensen Huang, its former chief executive.

Nvidia is a major investor in Anthropic, but it has suffered a $900bn share price wide-out since Mr Huang admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an alleged Chinese spy earlier this month.

The US midterm elections, meanwhile, wiped trillions of dollars from the stock market earlier this month over concerns about a Democrat-led crackdown on AI companies and data centres.

Anthropic is likely to emerge as a bellwether for the wider AI industry. The AI giant plans to spend more than $1tn on technology infrastructure to power its digital chatbot and its pursuit of superintelligence, which its founders claim could lead to unprecedented growth and an “age of miracles”.

The float also sees Anthropic leap ahead of its main rival, ChatGPT-developer OpenAI, which is plotting its own trillion-dollar float next year.

The deal cements the status of Anthropic’s seven founders, including chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela, and British policy boss Jack Clark, as multi-billionaires.

The seven were worth around $19bn at the initial float price, which valued Anthropic at $1.4tn late on Wednesday, but could be worth as much as $26bn based on its latest valuation.

It also catapults Mr Clark, a 37-year-old former journalist from Brighton, into the ranks of the richest Britons.

Anthropic was founded just six years ago with a promise that it would pursue superintelligent AI while focusing on safety. It was launched after Mr Amodei quit OpenAI amid a bitter split over its approach to safety with founder Sam Altman.

The company’s founders have been deeply concerned about the potential risks of AI, including that an uncontrollable future AI system could spell disaster for humanity.

Mr Amodei said on Thursday that AI carried “real risks” but that the company would be “obsessed with safety”.

Anthropic launched its Claude AI as a helpful chatbot in 2023, but it has since found widespread use among businesses for coding or acting as an AI “agent”, a kind of digital co-worker.

The company reported revenues from its AI tool of around $33bn in the first nine months of the year, although it lost $104bn.

The deal also mints nearly all of Anthropic’s staff as millionaires. Private market data company Hill estimated that, at its initial float price, some 5,100 out of its 5,300 staff would become overnight millionaires. Some 580 will have fortunes of more than $100m.

It will provide a stunning return for many of Anthropic’s early investors, who include Ashton Kutcher, the actor, and Jaan Tallinn, the founder of Skype.

XTX Ventures, a fund launched by British billionaire trader Alex Gerko, is also set for significant gains after a $10m investment in Anthropic three years ago.

Dan Ives, a technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, said after trading began that the deal would help “restore some investor confidence” that the “AI revolution” is not waning.

However, Joe Maher, an analyst at Capital Economics, warned the deal may not be enough to “save the AI trade” as stocks fell on Thursday.

Elsewhere, a short-seller report targeting AMD, a chip company led by Lisa Hsu, the cousin of Nvidia chief Mr Huang, prompted an 8pc share price fall. The report claimed AMD had deeper ties to China than widely believed.

An AMD spokesman said the report “misrepresents” its business practices.

As the float got underway, there were protests outside the Nasdaq exchange, with several anti-AI demonstrators arrested.

In recent months, Anthropic’s own researchers have warned of the risk of an AI disaster that could destroy humanity. One suggested the risk was as high as 10pc.

The protests in New York called for a “a freeze to reckless AI development and destruction”.

News.title: Myanmar guilty of genocide, International Court of Justice rules
News.content:
Myanmar’s military junta has been found guilty of committing genocide in a ruling that could have implications for Israel and its war on Gaza.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, the UN’s highest court, said Myanmar had systematically attempted to destroy the Muslim minority Rohingya population. It is the first time in its 81-year history that the ICJ has found a state guilty of genocide.

The 2017 attacks led to one of the largest movements of people in modern history, with hundreds of thousands fleeing violence across the border to Bangladesh. The court said the attacks constituted more than an attempt to contain unrest in the region through military means.

The judges said: “The execution of Rohingya men and boys in some locations, the widespread sexual violence, the targeting of children and babies, the methodical burning of villages, and attacks on fleeing civilians are not consistent with an intent to conduct counterinsurgency operations.”

The judges ruled by nine votes to six that it had been genocide.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”

Inflation increased in October as a result of surging fuel prices for motorists.

The average price of petrol rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October to 174.7p, the highest level since August 2022.

The ONS said diesel rose by 7p to 199.5p per litre last month – the highest since records began in 1996.

News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” added the ASA, who launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

Voy said the ads were retracted while the investigation was underway, adding that they will not run them again.

Dr Earim Chaudry, Chief Medical Officer at Voy, said: “Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance”.

News.title: Saucepan racks, fitted sheets and dehumidifiers: Your tricks for drying laundry in winter
News.content:
As temperatures drop and laundry piles up, drying clothes indoors can become a headache. But when Laura de Barra gave her verdict on the best heated clothes airers, Telegraph readers had a lot to say. So, we asked you what works in your homes.

While some of you have relied on heated airers for years, others have found a standard clothes horse or an overhead airer paired with a dehumidifier preferable. Several of you argue that you can’t beat the efficiency of a tumble dryer.

Here are your tried and tested tips...

Heated airers

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.



After seeing a review for the Lakeland heated airer printed in The Telegraph in 2008, Clive Ruffle, 67, from Surrey, felt enticed to buy one. “It had a price offer and a coupon to send to the newspaper,” he recalls.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

The options to fold the airer away flat and use only half of it, where one side is folded down, are the two major features that attracted Clive to the product.

“The drying speed is good, and we’ve never felt frustrated by it,” he says. “The heated bars are very effective and if we choose to heat, clothes are usually done in the day. They take a bit longer without the heater.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

For a more affordable option, Caroline Morrell, 65, from Greater Manchester, recommends buying a tiered Minky heated clothes airer, which she uses with a Beldray cover.
