The Premier League has confirmed next season will begin on Friday 13 August and finish on 21 May. It said players would have 75 “clear days” of break at the end of the current season.

Sports.title: Thomas Frank admits he has a point to prove after taking reins at Crystal Palace
Sports.content:
Thomas Frank has admitted he has a point to prove on his return to management as he aims to steer Crystal Palace away from relegation trouble after taking over from Pierre Sage.

The Dane was confirmed as manager on Monday with Palace at the bottom of the table after 10 matches having conceded 24 goals – the most in the Premier League. They face a crucial trip to Coventry on Saturday and Frank said he had been “surprised about how good it feels” after returning to work for the first time since being sacked by ­Tottenham in February.

The 53-year-old spent most of the intervening period travelling, working as a pundit at the World Cup and taking in trips to Japan, Australia and his native Denmark, where he was visiting friends and family when he received the SOS call from Palace last week. Frank previously spent seven years in charge of Brentford but left Spurs after just eight months with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history. He believes he has learned from that experience.

“I think you’ve all got an ego,” he said. “Some are better at controlling it than others. For me, it’s not the critics. It’s more what I can bring myself, what I can learn, what I can prove, how I can get better. I think that’s the big thing.

“In this world there’s a lot of clever people out there. But they only know a 10th of the truth. And that’s a 10th of the truth at Brentford and a 10th of the truth at Tottenham. That’s just the way it is – if you can’t handle that as a coach or a player or whatever, then you shouldn’t be in this business. I’m just very happy to be back in the game, very happy to be in a fantastic club, at Palace, where you walk in the door and you just feel the energy. You feel the people. It just feels good.”

Frank said he is planning to pick Roy Hodgson’s brains in the coming days after recalling a conversation they had when the former England and Palace manager was still at Selhurst Park.

“I was thinking, does it ever go away? The worry, do you get more relaxed about everything?” he asked Hodgson. “‘No chance, it’s impossible.’ I thought it would have been a little bit easier with age and experience. But in a way can’t help ourselves. I know what I want and the direction we should go in.”

Justin Cochrane – one of Thomas Tuchel’s assistants for England – has joined as first-team coach and took his first session with Palace on Monday less than 24 hours after the Nations League victory over Spain in Madrid. He is expected to be joined on Palace’s backroom staff by Bernardo Cueva, with Frank confirming that a deal with Chelsea is “very close” for the Mexican. Both worked with Frank at Brentford, where he spent almost nine years as an assistant and then manager. He is also hoping to add Andreas Georgson from Tottenham, who has been credited for his prowess on set-pieces: an area that Palace have struggled with for some time.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But asked whether he will be judged on the perception that his success at Brentford was based on the model that has allowed his successor, Keith Andrews, to thrive since taking over, Frank was not impressed. “Put it this way, I think it was pretty important in terms of building that model,” he said.

Sports.title: Socceroos’ future looks bright as Australia stun Argentina in U17 World Cup
Sports.content:
Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon has demonstrated why he’s one of the most exciting talents in Australian football, leading the Joeys to a shock 2-0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style.

The brilliant young winger had his shot deflected for an own goal on the hour and then produced an audaciously cheeky finish 11 minutes later to seal the opening-day win on Friday (AEDT) as Carl Veart’s side announced their return to the global boys’ competition for the first time in seven years.

Against one of the powerhouse football nations, Australia had their backs to the wall, having to make 31 clearances as Argentina enjoyed two-thirds of the possession and 22 shots on goal. But the Joeys fought back after the break, spearheaded by Akon, who hailed their second-half heist as “amazing”.

The 17-year-old livewire provided the real star quality, and it was soon evident why the Sky Blues had wanted to keep him in Australia for their A-League Men campaign instead of releasing him for the tournament; a decision that triggered widespread backlash before being reversed.

Allow Instagram content? This article includes content provided by Instagram . We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'. Allow and continue

Akon caused havoc from the start down the right flank, his neat through ball in the fifth minute almost resulting in a goal for Central Coast Mariners’ Luke Becvinovski.

The teenage sensation then struck after the break following another dangerous foray down the right that ended with his shot across goal deflecting off the hapless Alvaro Guich and into the net.

In the 71st minute, Mariners midfielder Oli O’Carroll expertly picked off an Argentina attack before Brisbane’s Emmett Shaw released Akon with a slide-rule left-foot pass, the winger going on to dummy the goalkeeper before slotting into an empty net.

View image in fullscreen Australia opened their U17 World Cup account with a famous win over Argentina. Photograph: Álex Caparrós/FIFA/Getty Images

It only got worse for Argentina when substitute Benjamin Vallejos got sent off for a reckless challenge in stoppage time.

But it wasn’t all about Akon, a considerable talent who’s already made his national U23 bow. At the other end, Charlie Wilson-Papps, the young goalkeeper who’s on the books at Brighton and Hove Albion, made half-a-dozen fine saves and kept a clean sheet.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Football Desk Australia 

“I do it for my teammates, I do it for my family at home, so to make them proud is is the most important thing,” said Akon as he clutched the player-of-the-match trophy afterwards.

Akon’s only worry came with the video checking of his goal. “Ah, that was nerve-racking, man,” he said. “Because at 1-0, it was a very scary game. So to be able to seal it like that, the coach was telling me it was a goal.

“The first goal? It wasn’t really my goal, but I just wanted to do the Tim Cahill, start off the tournament like that. So, yeah, the knee side had to come with it.

“Now, the group, we’re really confident, really confident in our ability, and I think that showed today.”

Next up on Sunday for the Joeys will be Denmark, who lost 4-0 to Mozambique in their Group C opener on Thursday.

Sports.title: What it's really like to kill a fellow athlete - and the terrible grief 'you carry for the rest of your life': The cursed band of haunted sportsmen reveal the nightmares that never leave them
Sports.content:
Towards the end of the Australian summer of 2014-15, as the country prepared to host the Cricket World Cup, I took a flight from Sydney to Hobart, Tasmania, to watch a Sheffield Shield game between Tasmania and New South Wales at the Bellerive Oval, a beautiful ground perched on the banks of the Derwent River.

Australian sport was still in shock. A few months earlier, Australia's Test opener, Phillip Hughes, had died after he was struck on the side of his neck by a short ball from a young bowler called Sean Abbott in a game between New South Wales and South Australia at the Sydney Cricket Ground.

Hughes was treated at the ground for 40 minutes and then taken by ambulance to St Vincent's Hospital in nearby Darlinghurst in a critical condition. 'Feeling for Phil Hughes after being hit,' former Australia Test cricketer Dean Jones wrote on Twitter. 'He is not in a good way! Stay strong Sean Abbott. Not your fault, young man.'

The impact of the ball had compressed a vein in Hughes' neck and when it split, it caused a catastrophic bleed on the brain. Hughes had emergency surgery and was placed in an induced coma. He never regained consciousness and passed away two days later.

Hughes was a popular, talented, gutsy cricketer with three Test centuries already under his belt. A small guy with the heart of a lion. He was 25 years old. Cricket mourned a terrible tragedy – some called it the sport's saddest day and the agony of Hughes' family was hard to bear. But there was something else. There was an awareness that two tragedies were playing out in front of us.

Hughes was lost but the man who had bowled the delivery that felled him had been left behind, desolate and distraught. Many thought Sean Abbott, who was 22, would never play cricket again. That he would not be able to find the strength. But that was why I had flown to Tasmania. Because Abbott had found the strength.

Phil Hughes was the golden boy of Australian cricket in 2014, with three Test centuries already to his name, when he was hit by a ball bowled by Sean Abbott and died

Abbott visiting the Sydney hospital where Hughes was in a coma that he would never wake from, having suffered a catastrophic bleed on the brain

That February afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I sat among a smattering of spectators who watched Abbott walk to the top of his mark. His team-mates shouted encouragement to him. They were willing him on with everything they had and Abbott bowled his heart out.

'Beautifully bowled, Abbo,' one of the NSW fielders shouted after one ball to former Test opener Ed Cowan. 'That's a beauty, Seanie,' another yelled after the fifth ball of his first over, when Cowan jerked his head out of the way of a short delivery so fast he fell over. Only one wicket fell that afternoon. Abbott took it.

It was one of the bravest sporting performances I have ever witnessed. Because even though cricket had voiced its support for Abbott, the sport could not protect him from his thoughts and from the knowledge he had become one of a cursed band of sportsmen who have unwittingly caused the death of an opponent during a contest.

Sometimes, tragedy in sport is not just the tragedy of the player who dies; it is the tragedy of the opponent who must live the nightmare of what he has done over and over again in his mind. To those that it has befallen, they say it is a grief that never leaves them.

That grief, that sense of a double tragedy, was brought sharply back into focus earlier this month when Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono. The accident happened in the final minutes of a game in Spain's Segunda Division, when Owono hurtled out of his goal and collided with De Miguel in the centre circle. He was shown a red card for the foul.

There was an outpouring of grief for De Miguel. I was among those who observed a minute's silence for him before the Barcelona-Aston Villa Champions League tie at the Nou Camp the next evening. Tributes continue to be paid to him. Owono, meanwhile, has become a pariah. It is said that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house.

Owono does not appear to have had the same sympathy extended to him that Abbott benefited from. His challenge on De Miguel, a striker who had had a peripatetic career in Spain's lower leagues, was reckless and cavalier. For him, the struggle with guilt and responsibility and public judgment is only just beginning.

FC Andorra will play their first home game since the tragedy against Leganes on Friday night but when they run out at the Encamp Stadium, a neat little ground beside a babbling river, the Valira d'Orient, and in the shadow of the mountains that make Andorra such a popular ski resort, Owono will not be there.

Earlier this month Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died in hospital the day after a sickening collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono

Owono has become a pariah. It is said that the 25-year-old rarely leaves his house

The goalkeeper, who has 47 caps for Equatorial Guinea, was given the maximum sentence of a 12-match ban by the Spanish Football Federation.

Tenerife manager Alvaro Cervera suggested Owono's ban 'might feel light' to all those mourning the striker, who was 30 years old, while FC Andorra owner Gerard Pique, the former Barcelona and Spain centre back, said the maximum sanction 'puts him (Owono) in a situation he does not deserve, because he is not to blame for all of this having happened'.

No one knows whether Owono will feel able to return to football when his ban ends. Footage circulated of him in an on-field argument moments before the clash with De Miguel, and it was used to suggest that he was in an unstable state of mind.

Some have pressed for him to be charged with manslaughter. His Instagram account was deactivated after it was deluged with abuse, including messages which branded him 'a murderer'. It has been reported that his brother, who is also a footballer, has been the victim of abuse because of his association with Owono.

Owono has only communicated through a statement released by his club. 'These are the most difficult days of my life,' he wrote. 'I struggle to find the words, and I find it very hard to ​process what has happened. I feel enormous pain at the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and all the people who loved him. I know there will be many questions to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.'

I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies. His brother, Dermot, took his own life. He lost his daughter, Danika, to cancer when she was just 33, in 2019. And in 1982, three years before he won the world featherweight title at Loftus Road, he nearly quit boxing altogether.

In the 12th fight of his professional career, McGuigan fought a Nigerian boxer called Young Ali at the World Sporting Club in Mayfair. He still remembers the clink of cutlery coming from the diners who were sitting ringside that night. That sound still takes him back.

McGuigan still remembers the sequence of punches that put Young Ali down in the sixth round of the fight. He saw his opponent's eyes roll back in his head and a feeling of dread washed over him. Young Ali, just 21, fell into a coma from which he never emerged and died five months later.

I spoke to the great British fighter Barry McGuigan (right) about Owono this week. McGuigan has suffered his share of tragedies

'There was the horror of that and we sat and we waited and we prayed that he would be better and he never got better,' McGuigan told me. 'I didn't know whether I wanted to continue boxing. I thought: "If I can do this to somebody…"'

He shuddered when he talked about Owono. 'Other tragedies happen and other terrible things happen,' he said. 'Life is a struggle. Something like that, you never leave it behind you.

'It is something invisible and it depends how emotionally vulnerable he is. He may never be the same again but I hope he is able to overcome it.'

There are others out there in sport, still trying to overcome it. Think of Matt Petgrave, the Sheffield Steelers ice-hockey player who was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after his skate fatally cut the neck of Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson in an Elite Ice Hockey League match at Sheffield Arena in October 2023.

Think of Jochen Mass, the Formula One driver, who spent years blaming himself for the death of Gilles Villeneuve during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix at Zolder in 1982, because he slowed and moved to the right in front of Villeneuve. The Ferrari ran into the back of Mass and flipped in grotesque cartwheels across the track.

Think of Matthias Behr, the German fencer who killed his opponent, Vladimir Smirnov, at the 1982 World Fencing Championships in Rome when Behr's foil blade broke during a match, penetrated the Ukrainian fencer's mask and pierced his eye.

Think of Gary Cully, the Irish fighter, who learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves, had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August.

'What a character and a gent,' Cully wrote in tribute to Reeves. 'It's never been nothing but love between us champ, can't really believe I'm writing this but RIP brother.'

Nottingham Panthers' Adam Johnson died in October 2023 when opponent Matt Petgrave's skate cut his neck during a match

Gary Cully (left), the Irish fighter, learned this week that his last opponent, Lee Reeves (right), had died after spending three months in a coma following their bout in Dublin in August

Dr Victor Thompson, a prominent UK clinical sports psychologist, has studied the effect on competitors of being involved in the death of a rival.

'The biggest thing a player will have had to absorb normally is bad performance,' Dr Thompson says. 'Now he has to absorb the fact that he was involved in somebody dying. He will be trying to work out was it his fault? Is he to blame? And all of that, because the emotions are so high, gets associated with playing the sport in question.

'So when Sean Abbott thought about going out there again, when he thought about putting his pads on, or putting his kit on and being around team-mates or the smell of the cricket bat – it'll all be associated to that very traumatic day.'

University of North Carolina academic John M Silva III argued that aggression in sport is defined in two categories: hostile aggression and instrumental aggression. Hostile is when the main aim is to cause harm or injury to your opponent. Instrumental is aggression for a purpose, perhaps ball recovery or to sow doubt in an opponent’s mind.

The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy. Whether forgiveness is extended to or opprobrium visited on the competitor who has caused the death of another.

That interpretation was used against Petgrave, who was notorious for having a bad disciplinary record on the ice. Some likened the action which fatally injured Johnson to a kung-fu kick and drew a link between it and some of his past behaviour. He was mercilessly trolled on social media. Team-mates, and many ice hockey fans, leapt to his defence and said any suggestion his action was deliberate was fanciful. They said his unusual action in lifting his left skate high was a direct result of being knocked off balance by a collision.

Petgrave could not return to ice hockey immediately even if he had wanted to. It was a full 18 months before the Crown Prosecution Service and South Yorkshire Police decided there was no realistic prospect of conviction for manslaughter and that no criminal charges should be brought against the 34-year-old Canadian.

In the intervening period, Petgrave's family set up a crowdfunding page, pointing out that he was unable to work or to return home until the CPS had decided whether to press charges. The page raised nearly £20,000 from well-wishers.

The interpretation of a player's actions at a time of high stress, frustration or adversarial combat is often central to the reaction to a sporting tragedy - as it was for Petgrave

Petgrave did receive widespread support from inside his sport, with a standing ovation at his Sheffield side's next home match, while he was beginning 18 months under investigation

'This has been the most painful and overwhelming period of our lives,' a message from Petgrave's family said at the bottom of the page. 'Watching someone I love go through this has been incredibly difficult.

'Despite everything, we are doing our best to stay strong, and the support and kindness from so many people have been a source of strength. We continue to recognise the heartbreaking nature of this situation, and our thoughts remain with everyone affected. We hold on to hope that this will soon come to an end.'

Petgrave now plies his trade in the minor league ECHL for the Indy Fuel, a team based in Fishers, Indiana. He is an ever-present this season, playing opponents like the Wheeling Nailers, the Greenville Swamp Rabbits, the Kalamazoo Wings and the Bloomington Bison.

'We understand the responsibility that comes with the great support we receive from this community,' Sean Hallett, CEO of Hallett Sports, which owns the Fuel, said when they hired Petgrave. 'We are confident he will be a positive addition to our team and our city.'

I wrote to the Fuel, asking if there was any chance of speaking to Petgrave. They did not respond. The reticence is understandable and, in many ways, laudable. Players involved in this kind of tragedy are preoccupied with respect for the victims' families and the sensitivities that come with such terrible grief. There is nothing they can say or do to make it better.

Sometimes, it is the other way round. Sometimes, it is the family of a lost loved one who find a way to ease the pain of a sportsman eaten up by shame for inadvertently causing the death of a competitor.

Mass, who died last year, blamed himself for the sickening crash that killed the most exciting, charismatic, talented, electrifying driver in Formula One. As Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track until he came to rest in the catch-fencing by the side of the circuit. He died of catastrophic injuries later that evening, aged 32.

Mass was absolved of responsibility. It was a tragic accident. Villeneuve was running hot after a disagreement with his team-mate Didier Pironi and was pushing even his own boundaries. There were any number of extenuating circumstances but Mass still blamed himself. He retired from the sport the same season.

As Gilles Villeneuve's Ferrari cartwheeled across the track, breaking into pieces, he was flung clear of the wreckage still strapped to his seat, catapulting across the track

Despite being absolved of responsibility, Jochen Mass (pictured in 2019) blamed himself for the accident and retired from the sport the same year

It was years later when he felt a tap on the shoulder as he was sitting on a plane. He looked up to see Villeneuve's son, Jacques, the 1997 F1 world champion, standing over him.

'I felt so guilty about what had happened and then suddenly, there was Jacques,' Mass recalled. 'He said: "Jochen, our family – we never blamed you. It was a racing incident – just a wrong decision by the two of you."'

All the shame that Mass felt ebbed away. He found his own peace just as Behr found redemption by sheltering the grandchildren of Smirnov and his widow, Emma, at his home in Germany to protect them from the Russian invasion of Ukraine.

Behr, tortured by guilt about the accident that killed Smirnov, had written to Emma 30 years ago but the letter was lost. When he did not receive a reply, he was convinced that Smirnov's widow blamed him for killing her husband.

They finally met when a television documentary crew brought them together and Emma reassured Behr that she had never held him responsible. Behr has suffered from depression and suicidal thoughts because of flashbacks to the fatal accident.

'They are always there,' Behr said later. 'Even if I go into a liquor store and see vodka with the Smirnoff label on it, the thoughts of what happened immediately come back to me. But now that I am playing a part in the lives of Vladimir's grandchildren, it has come full circle for me. It was a gift for me. I can finally give something back.'

Maybe Abbott has been trying to give something back all these years, too. Perhaps the fine career he has had is his tribute to Hughes. He has represented Australia in one-day and Twenty20 cricket and is the all-time leading wicket-taker in the Big Bash League. He has represented Surrey in English cricket and was part of Australia's World Cup winning squad in 2023.

Many had worried that Abbott would not play again after Hughes' death. Not your fault, young man. Easy to say, harder to grasp amid the grief and the disbelief. But there was an outpouring of support for him, including from Hughes' family.

Perhaps the fine career 2023 World Cup winner Sean Abbott (bottom right) has had is his tribute to Hughes

That afternoon at the Bellerive Oval, I asked him about the day's play as he came off. He said he was happy with how it had gone. Afterwards, I sat in the stand with Abbott's team-mate Nathan Lyon, the Australia spinner, who spoke movingly about Hughes and about Abbott. At the end of the interview I thanked him for making the time to speak to me in such difficult circumstances. 'Too easy, mate,' he said.

Except it wasn't too easy. Inside, Lyon and the rest of Australian cricket were still in agony. Later that day, Lyon complained to Cricket Australia that he had not been expecting to be asked about Hughes. He was upset about my questions. I had made a misjudgment. Things were still too raw.

Lyon was comfortable talking about Abbott, though. 'The way Sean has carried himself through the whole incident, well, credit goes to him,' Lyon said. 'He is a very impressive bloke. I've got a lot of time for him. He will do anything to help anyone out. He always puts mates first. He always has your back. He is a typical good mate. I'm proud to call him a mate.

'I think (Abbott not playing again) went through the minds of a few of us. But natural instinct will come over and you do what you do best and if that's play cricket, you go out and play cricket. It's about being around your mates and the mates who are there with him now, they're the guys who are going to get him through it.'

Abbott has never spoken about the tragedy. He gave written evidence in January 2016 to the inquest into Hughes' death.

'I saw him start to sway and I ran to the other end of the pitch and I held the right side of his head with my left hand,' Abbott wrote. 'I remained on the field until Phillip was placed on the medicab and then returned to the changing room. Once in the changing room I felt confused and upset, I had a headache, people kept coming up to me but I cannot recall what they said.'

Much of the inquest was dominated by suggestions that Hughes had been subjected to a barrage of short balls and sledging. The inquest heard that Abbott's bowling partner, Doug Bollinger, had said to Hughes 'I'm going to kill you' at one stage during the game. Bollinger denied that accusation. Abbott was exonerated of any responsibility for the tragedy that unfolded.

Only rarely are there glimpses of the impact that Hughes' death has had on him. At a tribute to Hughes on the tenth anniversary of his death, Abbott broke down and wept at the end of the minute's silence at the SCG. One of his team-mates put an arm around his shoulders to try to comfort him.

Abbott at Hughes' funeral in his hometown of Macksville, Australia, in 2014

'The difficulty with boxing is that you are in this sport to hurt your opponent,' says McGuigan. 'Nobody believes - or wants to believe - that it is going to do lasting damage'

McGuigan says the pain never quite goes away. 'I had a love-hate relationship with boxing,' he says. 'The difficulty with boxing is that you are in this sport to hurt your opponent. Nobody believes – or wants to believe – that it is going to do lasting damage.

'After Young Ali died, I had to make a very serious decision about whether to carry on or not. I refocused and tried to make it a goal to win the world title and think about him when I achieved it. And the night I won the world title, I told Harry Carpenter through my tears that I was dedicating the fight to Young Ali.

'What happened in Tenerife looked like a terrible accident. Jesus de Miguel did not see him coming and he had no chance to brace for the impact. The outcome is the same as the outcome I had to deal with.

'I hope the goalkeeper will be able to come to terms with it. Sometimes, you can't. Sometimes, you are never quite the same, emotionally or mentally. It is the burden you carry for the rest of your life.'

Sports.title: 'He was his twin's carer from the word go': Will Joseph's parents reveal astonishing backstory of new England hero who's deaf in one ear, their Twickenham tears seeing his five tries against Japan and why he thought he'd never win another cap
Sports.content:
To truly understand the making of England's new try-scoring superstar Will Joseph you must begin with his twin brother, Alex.

Alex has learning difficulties and epilepsy so Will – or William as he is to his mother, Philippa – had to learn how to muck in from an early age.

It goes some of the way to explaining why their father, Ivan, had a tear in his eye after watching Will score five tries at Twickenham in England's victory over Japan last Saturday.

'William has been Alex's carer from the word go,' Philippa tells me on the phone this week. 'As far as William's living memory goes, he's always been there and looked after Alex. He's a humble, kind person because his default has always been to make sure Alex is OK.

'During breaktimes at primary school, Will would spend half of the time getting Alex's coat on or off,' adds Ivan.

'He didn't get much of a break himself. That nurturing means he has always put others before himself. That's shaped him into the person we see today.'

Will Joseph touches down spectacularly during his dazzling five-try performance against Japan last weekend at Twickenham

(From left), Will Joseph with his sister Hannah and brothers Alex and Jonathan

Will is the latest sporting success story in the Joseph family. His sister, Hannah, plays netball for England and their eldest brother, Jonathan, the former centre, won 54 Test caps and toured New Zealand with the British & Irish Lions.

Will and Jonathan are identikit players despite the 11-year age gap. Both stand 6ft tall, have similar jawlines, cover centre and wing and they have the same hop and glide across the pitch. As of last Saturday, they have both scored Test hat-tricks for England.

'It's quite interesting how they've ended up in the same place when their journeys have been quite different,' explains Philippa. 'With Jonathan, we lived in a small house in Derby without much space. William grew up in the south when we were 10 or 15 years further on and much more established as a family.

'Both William and Jonathan played a lot of tennis. As the first-born, Jonathan would have all the kit, the big Wilson bag, and I'd be there watching with two little boys in the pushchair. Everything was set up for him to succeed.

'Because of the family dynamic with Alex, William pretty much had to get on with it himself. He couldn't be needy, he had to fit in. He had very, very different parenting.'

As a youngster, Jonathan was often chasing a rugby ball down the touchlines at Derby RFC, where Ivan played until he was 40. Will spent his youth following his brother's career. He flew out to Italy with the family to watch Jonathan play alongside a host of future Test stars for England in the Under 18s World Cup.

'William grew up around these kinds of people, having rugby balls thrown at him in all directions,' says Philippa. 'We used to have these parallel sofas in the lounge. Hannah would be lying on one sofa, Jonathan on the other, and they would launch balls at each other while they watched TV.

'William would be in the middle of it all, 14 months old, running around in a nappy trying to catch this funny-shaped ball.

'The family were obsessed with sport so it was just the norm for William,' says his mum Philippa

Joseph puts the hard work in during England training at Pennyhill Park

'The family were obsessed with sport so it was just the norm for William. Because of Jonathan, he spent a lot of his younger years with friends and family at Twickenham, chatting to famous rugby players.

'When he joined George Ford in England camp, he said, 'It's so weird because I just remember coming out to watch you playing for England Under 18s in Italy when I was at primary school'.'

Like Jonathan, William was enrolled at the famous rugby breeding ground of Millfield School in Somerset. From the age of 13, he was mentored by London Irish academy coach James Lightfoot-Brown, who is now his club coach at Gloucester.

'I played with JJ a couple of times in the London Irish academy and I couldn't believe the obvious physical similarities,' says Lightfoot-Brown. 'Knowing what JJ had done, we had a great opportunity to mould Will's game around that.

'His family were incredibly supportive. They had a little camper van that they'd all travel down to training in. They had a lot of love and care for London Irish because of what JJ had been through there.'

Yet for all of their physical similarities, the siblings have contrasting personalities. 'When Jonathan was growing up, he had an air of confidence,' says Ivan. 'I wouldn't call it arrogance, but he feared nobody. He thought he could beat anybody.

'Generally speaking, Will is quite a humble individual. But there was one occasion around 2016, when he was 11 or 12 and Jonathan was playing for Bath. We were in the marquee behind the stand, with some fellow Bath supporters, and J had a good game.

'Will always carried a ball around with him, just like J did, and this lady, an estate agent, asked him: 'Do you think you'll be as good as your brother when you grow up?' He responded: 'I'll be better than him.'

'As a kid Will (left) was asked: 'Do you think you'll be as good as your brother when you grow up?' He responded: 'I'll be better than him''

Joseph earned a surprise England call-up from Eddie Jones as an apprentice in 2022. He was capped against Australia a week before his 20th birthday

'Will always appeared humble and meek and mild, but that showed me there was a burning fire in there. His confidence is internalised. He has a lot of inner strength.'

Will excelled through age-group rugby. He broke into the London Irish first team as a teenager, earning a surprise England call-up from Eddie Jones as an apprentice in 2022. He was capped against Australia a week before his 20th birthday but the following season his club were declared bankrupt.

'Will was on a really positive trajectory at London Irish,' says Lightfoot-Brown. 'If the club hadn't gone under, we would have seen him excelling in an England shirt far sooner.

'I've seen him do some things on rugby pitches that other people simply aren't capable of. From the Wellington Under 15s festival, where he could just run around everyone, to some of the moments he had for London Irish.

'We had Will and Henry Arundell coming off the bench and ripping up games. It was frightening. He's so fast but he's not just someone who can run with the ball. He's a 13 who can play on the wing at a very high level.'

Will moved to Harlequins after London Irish went bankrupt, although he struggled to break into the team. He suffered setbacks – including becoming deaf in his left ear – and eventually relocated to Gloucester with his team-mate and house-mate, Will Trenholm.

'He's needed to be resilient because he's gone through a hard time,' says back-rower Trenholm. 'He nearly got a hearing aid because of a problem with his ear. It happened during a pool session at Quins. He came out of the water and his ear just wouldn't pop.

Joseph has been one of the PREM's standout performers with Gloucester this season

Joseph takes his time to score the second of his five tries against Japan on Saturday

'He thought he had liquid in it and it was a bit quieter for the first few days. It got worse over time so he went to the doctors. They tried to sort it out but it got slowly worse to the point where he's now deaf in his left ear.

'If you watch his post-match interviews after the Japan game, you can see that he has to lean in with his right ear. The answer he gave to the second question had nothing to do with the question they asked!

'Sometimes you have to repeat the call to him on the pitch. He'll have to run up and double check. He obviously prefers being on the left wing. I asked him if it affected his balance at all. It did at the start but he's adapted to it brilliantly. He doesn't really think about it too much now.'

Will has been one of the PREM's standout performers this season with Gloucester, who have been the surprise package and sit second through five rounds after finishing eighth last year. He has wowed team-mates with his ability to light up the pitch, second only to Immanuel Feyi-Waboso for defenders beaten per carry.

'The way he moves just reminds me of JJ... I keep thinking JJ's outside of me!' says England centre Henry Slade, who has now played Test rugby alongside both Joseph brothers.

'I know JJ really well. I played for a number of years with him. It's cool that I'm getting to do it with his brother now. The way they move is so similar, both of them are such incredible athletes.

'Will's very, very fast – winger speed so really, really quick. He's an incredible talent, we've just got to get him the ball and let him do some damage.'

Will with his family, most of whom were at Twickenham last weekend to cheer him on

'Will is humble and kind because his default has always been to make sure his brother Alex is OK. That's shaped him into the person we see today'

Borthwick wants 'fire' from England against All Blacks Steve Borthwick has urged his England stars to 'bring the fire' in Saturday's crunch Nations Championship clash with a wounded New Zealand. After impressive wins over Australia and Japan, the national team face their toughest challenge of the autumn so far with the All Blacks next up. Dave Rennie's side are reeling after a first loss to Wales in 73 years, but have recalled their big guns for the visit to Twickenham. England head coach Borthwick has vowed his team will be bang up for the test after he named George Furbank and Seb Atkinson in a strong starting XV. 'I see the players bring fire and pride when they're wearing their club shirts,' Borthwick said. 'I want them to bring that in an England shirt. I've been really pleased with how the players have started the games. 'Emotion is a key part. I sense the players are physically ready to go, but also mentally. These last couple of weekends, the players have produced performances that have made their families proud and the England fans proud. 'We want to make sure we put out that level of performance this weekend. We know it's going to be a fierce encounter and we know what a quality side New Zealand are.' Full-back Furbank, centre Atkinson and flanker Ollie Chessum have all been recalled for the All Blacks after missing the hammering of Japan due to injury. So too is No 10 Fin Smith, who is back to lead the team. Borthwick's XV this weekend is the same as that which put 45 points on Australia, except for Will Joseph who replaces the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the wing after scoring five times against Japan. New Zealand have global superstars Will Jordan, Jordie Barrett, Damian McKenzie and Codie Taylor back for England after they missed their shock loss in Cardiff. In November last year, England produced one of their impressive performances under Borthwick to beat the All Blacks 33-19. Now, the task is to produce a repeat. A big New Zealand response is expected. Of the 47 past meetings between the two teams, England have won just nine. 'It would be disingenuous for me say that when the team's playing New Zealand, the players don't feel the excitement every rugby fan feels,' Borthwick said. 'They are an incredible team. They have such a rich history and the games between England and New Zealand have been quite tight between the two teams over the last few years now. We came out on the right side a year ago and we came out on the wrong side the year before that, on three occasions. The players are super excited, as are the fans. 'That's always the case in games like this. I've looked at their (New Zealand's) last number of games closely. 'What I think they've done this week is name a team of experience with as many caps they could. That's the changes they've made. They're a very different team. It's a very different proposition of a team this week.' By Alex Bywater

Apart from Alex, the whole family were at Twickenham to watch Will's breakthrough appearance last weekend. 'Alex stayed at home with a carer,' says Ivan. 'He's not that much into rugby. Music is what makes Alex tick.

'He's a big Michael Jackson fan, and he always listens to music. So that's his thing. He's aware of rugby. He says, 'My brother plays for England' but it doesn't rock his boat, as it were.'

Philippa adds: 'Alex had uncontrolled seizures until about six months ago. We're now going through a phase where we've got really good control. For the first time in about four years, he's able to do things that he enjoys doing.

'We take Alex to these daytime nightclubs. There was a Michael Jackson tribute event in Oxford recently. As a good brother, William did his bit and came along. We all try to support each other and they all do their bit to support Alex.

'Until the rugby took off, that's what we were doing on Saturday afternoons. Now we're coming along to support William playing for England. What he's achieved is quite remarkable. I'm overwhelmed with pride.'

'It feels like deja vu, to a certain extent,' says Ivan. 'Because we've gone through all of this with Jonathan, we know what's coming. For Will, it feels like time has been suspended for four years since his first cap. He pointed out that the bedrooms at Pennyhill Park haven't changed much.

'I was close to tears after the game on Saturday. I've seen him slouched on the sofa, watching the game on TV, wishing that he could be out there. Four years between Tests is a long time.

Will celebrates with his father Ivan and sister Hannah at Twickenham last weekend. 'I was close to tears after the game,' says Ivan

'A lot has happened during that time. He didn't know if his time would come again. It's been one thing after another for Will. He's had to quietly build himself back up.

'Two years ago, I was diagnosed with early-onset Parkinson's. It's a shortage of dopamine in the brain but the medication I'm on is basically compensating for that. My life hasn't changed significantly and watching Will's success brings me great pleasure.'

Pride is the overwhelming feeling in the Joseph family. For so much of his life, Will has been the one looking out for others. Now, after all of the challenges, it is his turn to enjoy his moment in the spotlight.

And in English rugby, the spotlight doesn't shine much brighter than this Saturday when the All Blacks come to Twickenham.

Sports.title: Inside the deadly world of bodybuilding: Athletes dying at an alarming rate, rampant drug use and why thousands still risk everything in fatal obsession with the perfect body
Sports.content:
We're at the Vaillant, a mid-sized arena in Derby. It’s the Sunday before last and a bronzed man with a grey beard is discussing his new identity.

His name is Jake Bourne and he’s 48, three years removed from the 26 he spent in the military. First, he was in the parachute regiment and then he worked in intelligence, serving in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya, Kosovo and Sierra Leone. ‘Some interesting stuff,’ he tells me, while snacking on a small rice cake.

In a couple of hours, he’ll head away from this corridor by the toilets and onto the stage, where he will compete in the men’s physique category of the UK Open, an amateur bodybuilding contest run by the Physical Culture Association (PCA).

This has been part of his life since 2024 and it has dominated his thoughts in the past 16 weeks of hard preparations. If today goes well, he’ll win his pro card, so he talks about discipline, sacrifice and sustaining himself on chicken and a bit of rice to make it happen.

Bourne is an intense guy, but likeable and honest enough to list his other ingredients – doses of testosterone and human growth hormone. In this realm, it is often the case that anything goes, including the kind of performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) banned in conventional sport.

But bodybuilding isn’t conventional. And whatever he tries, Bourne is still unhappy with his legs. ‘They are so used to working under load in the military that I can’t push them hard enough to grow,’ he adds. Everyone in this corridor has something similar to say. For Harry Taylor, a personal trainer who competes clean, it’s his ‘love handles’, and Kyle Davies, another ‘natural’, isn’t getting what he wants from his pecs.

Competitors strike a pose for bodybuilding's UK Open, which took place this month in Derby

Jake Bourne (left) has been bodybuilding since 2024 after 26 years in the military, while Harry Taylor (right) wants to get rid of his 'love handles'

To Tom Reynolds, who has ‘enhanced’ himself with peptides and other substances, it’s his ‘extended gut’, which he ascribes to cocaine and alcohol addictions in his younger years.

He says bodybuilding improved his life, mimicking the sentiment of Phil Vickery, a 2003 Rugby World Cup winner for England who has been struggling with brain injury. He wasn’t in Derby but strongly dislikes his glutes. Of the 150 or so competitors in this arena, each has a problem to fix.

But there’s an edge to it and it’s darker than two coats of tan. Because what about deeper issues, like overloaded hearts, kidneys and livers? What about the tragedy that happened 55 miles away a few weeks ago? And what about the role drugs might play in a terrifying trend?

Daily Mail Sport has spoken to dozens of athletes, event organisers, medical experts and the author of a landmark study to explore the extremities of an extreme sport. What we found was a warm community filled with good and intelligent people. But it is also a place where the protagonists are dying at a truly astonishing rate. In this space of thongs and flexes, serious questions need to be posed.

The initial assumption of at least one witness was that Mateusz Chmura had fainted last month. In a sport where athletes want a dryer, more toned appearance, dehydration is common, so there wasn’t an immediate assumption of the worst when he collapsed on stage at the PCA’s British Finals in Telford.

But it rapidly became apparent on Sunday, October 18 that the situation was far more severe for Chmura, a newlywed from Wakefield who had made his amateur debut a fortnight earlier.

Within moments, he received CPR from an attending paramedic. He was then airlifted to New Cross Hospital in Wolverhampton.

While that was unfolding, a crowd of several hundred was ushered from the hall of the Telford International Centre. A statement from the PCA a day later, on what would have been Chmura’s 34th birthday, announced he had died.

Mateusz Chmura died at the age of 33 after collapsing on stage at an event in Telford

Chmura was a newlywed from Wakefield who had made his amateur debut a fortnight earlier (Source: Instagram/mateusz.chmura.92)

‘It was horrible,’ says Nick, a 40-year-old bodybuilder and coach who was present in the arena and declines to give his surname. ‘I’d never known anything like it to happen in the UK. We all went outside for a couple of hours and a decision was made to continue the event, but I believe he was still alive at that point. If he had died on stage, it would have been cancelled.’

A formal cause of death has not been publicised by Chmura’s family. Nor is it known if he was using any performance-enhancing substances in a sport where they are not banned in many categories and legal to possess under UK law.

But the events of October 18 do blend into an established pattern. And the figures make for shocking reading.

A study published last year by the European Heart Journal tracked 20,286 amateur and professional male bodybuilders from databases belonging to the International Federation of Bodybuilding and Fitness (IFBB) and MuscleMemory.org, following the criteria that they had competed in at least one of 730 events between 2005 and 2020. Within that sample, 121 deaths were recorded at an average age of 45.

Some involved suicide, homicide or vehicle accidents, and many lacked quantifiable data. But 46 fatalities fell into the largest category of ‘sudden cardiac deaths’ (SCD) and 11 of those occurred within one year of the athlete’s last competition. Drilling further, the study said one bodybuilder collapsed on stage, two suffered SCD during training and four athletes did so less than a week after an official event.

Discoveries from the pinnacle of professional bodybuilding were the most eye-catching. The ‘open’ category of Mr Olympia was won seven times by a steroid-infused Arnold Schwarzenegger and is sanctioned by the IFBB Pro League (a separate organisation to the IFBB), with prizes of up to £450,000.

It’s where the best want to be. It’s also where the study found seven deaths from just 100 competitors. The average age was 36.

Daily Mail Sport consulted the lead author of the study, Dr Marco Vecchiato, a specialist in sports and exercise medicine, to discuss the scenario. Among the details he shared was a troubling admission – none of the sport’s many federations, leagues or athletes had been in contact to better understand his research.

Bodybuilding has a warm community filled with good and intelligent people. But it is also a place where the protagonists are dying at a truly astonishing rate

The ‘open’ category of Mr Olympia was won seven times by a steroid-infused Arnold Schwarzenegger. It’s also where a study found seven deaths from just 100 competitors

‘My personal impression is that the study has generated considerable media attention,’ says Dr Vecchiato. ‘Its impact on practical measures to protect athletes has been less apparent.’

Dr Vecchiato has continued to monitor mortality in bodybuilding beyond 2020 for an updated report in 2027 and confirmed the subsequent number of deaths is ‘substantial’, involving both men and women.

That might include the case of Neil Currey, an Englishman who contested the men’s classic physique at Mr Olympia in 2022 and died a year later, aged 34. His parents were clear on why – in a written statement to the inquest, they said their ‘firm belief’ was that his use of steroids was responsible.

The study isn’t alone in exploring this trend. A detailed story in BoxLife Magazine claimed there were as many as 56 fatalities worldwide in 2025. Even without cataloguing the consequences that fall short of death, these numbers would indicate bodybuilding is one of the most dangerous sporting pursuits on the planet.

Naturally, a significant conversation here will discuss the rampant use of performance-enhancing drugs – Dr Vecchiato’s study found ‘at least’ 19 of the 121 deceased carried evidence of PED use. On the ground level of the sport, in places like this hall in Derby, there is a level of cognitive dissonance on that front, among even the more knowledgeable practitioners.

It’s a space where Nick, our coach and competitor from earlier, will comfortably share with me that he might ‘blast and cruise’ on testosterone. That can mean ticking over on anywhere between 125-150ml of testosterone per week, he says, and then upping the dose for competitions with oral compounds that add a couple of hundred extra millilitres.

A point to add here – Nick is not some shadowy figure. He was very pleasant, actually. And open about the entire operation – the testosterone is relatively cheap at £50 for a bottle that can last 12 weeks, and his growth hormone is dearer at £300 for a month.

‘I know guys who have gone IFBB Pro and take nothing – they have great genetics,’ he says. ‘But you’ve got to be sensible (if you do use drugs). Some just go silly with it. Around competition time, it is usually diuretic use (removing excess fluids) that can cause them problems. I get my blood work done, heart scans, but some don’t. If you’re not getting your heart checked, something serious can happen.’

Neil Currey, who contested the men’s classic physique at Mr Olympia in 2022 and died a year later aged 34. His parents had a ‘firm belief’ that his use of steroids was responsible

To talk to Nick is to hear a man who is significantly better informed than a layman and isn’t blindly following a coach’s advice.

But, aside from legal questions about the supply of substances that are prescription-only in the UK, not to mention health concerns about what might be contained in black-market equivalents, can there be a sensible approach, especially if no medical need has been diagnosed?

Perhaps inadvertently, Nick answers that himself several hours later, when he tells me his plan is to only do one more year on his drug cycles because he is mindful of potential heart complications down the line.

On these high wires, bodybuilders exist in vast numbers. And, as experts have explained in the course of researching this article, it is easy overlook one salient fact – the sport places more stress on the body than most, even before you supercharge the fuel.

One England-based source contacted by Daily Mail Sport remains convinced her brother took no performance-enhancing drugs prior to his death following a stroke last year. He was in his mid-twenties and training hard for his first competition as an amateur; a doctor shared with the family his belief that the strain of workouts was influential.

We spoke to multiple bodybuilders who claim to be clean. But it has long been known that substances are endemic in the sport, including events reserved for ‘naturals’ on the global calendar. Daily Mail Sport studied the most recent testing figures compiled by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and discovered a remarkable statistic: of 1,217 samples collected on behalf of the Madrid-based IFBB in 2024, 162 returned adverse findings.

That's a fail rate of 13 per cent, more than four times greater than the next highest among 39 sports that supplied more than 1,000 samples. WADA deemed the IBFF non-compliant in 2022 and confirmed that status is ongoing. The IFBB told me they are ‘committed’ to clean sport and ‘actively working to resolve’ their non-compliance.

That bodybuilding shares a symbiotic relationship with performance-enhancing drugs is no surprise. But it is only recently that the wider risks of the sport have been quantified by a peer-reviewed fatality toll. The existence of which begs a pair of key questions: why do it? And should the Wild West do more to make itself safer?

‹ Slide me › Phil Vickery was a Rugby World Cup-winning prop for England in 2003 before turning his hand to bodybuilding in retirement (swipe for transformation)

The ‘why’ is easier is to answer. According to the aspiring cast of amateurs in Derby, it’s an obsession rooted closer to perceptions of improvement rather than money.

For those who might win a PCA pro card, the prizes at the subsequent PCA World Championships in Spain were listed at £2,500. That’s far more indicative of the landscape than the rewards at Mr Olympia.

As Bourne puts it: ‘You want to see what you can do. Push yourself. It becomes a bug.’

Some of his subsequent equivocations around drug use contain kernels of truth.

‘My caveat would be that people come back after a stressful day at work and won't exercise, might have four cans of lager,’ he says. ‘I take a bit of testosterone, a bit of growth hormone, but I don't drink, my food is measured and clean. I do my blood work every six weeks, my blood pressure each morning. I know what's going on in my body. We're going to identify problems in our health much sooner than somebody that's doing what is socially acceptable.’

It’s an interesting perspective but hardly bulletproof. Dr Vecchiato directed us to a Danish study in 2025 that found ‘steroid exposure was associated with approximately three times the risk of myocardial infarction, almost nine times the risk of cardiomyopathy and more than three times the risk of heart failure’.

He has serious misgivings about the level of understanding among bodybuilders around what they are taking.

‘There are important gaps in knowledge particularly about lifetime exposure, repeated combinations, newer compounds and outcomes after people stop using them,’ he says.

Tom Reynolds, who has ‘enhanced’ himself with peptides and other substances, is targeting his ‘extended gut’, which he ascribes to cocaine and alcohol addictions in his younger years

Dr Vecchiato believes three areas need addressing urgently. First is an independent registry of deaths in bodybuilding, and secondly an education programme in gyms. His third objective is fascinating – a ‘structured pre-participation medical assessment’ including family medical history, substance disclosures and physical examination.

The latter is common in other sports – think of the medicals required for a boxing licence. As with much in bodybuilding, the picture is far less clear.

The PCA, for instance, require competitors to sign a waiver with their entry fee (£70 for Derby) that declares ‘to the best of their knowledge’ that they are fit and well. They also have to notify organisers of any medical conditions or prescribed medication, while remaining ‘responsible for decisions concerning their personal preparation’.

Those disclosures can trigger a refusal of entry, but the PCA did not respond to a Daily Mail Sport request for more detail.

One question asked if a bodybuilder would be required to supply proof of a professional health assessment, and another enquired how many would-be participants had been refused entry in the past 12 months.

As the waiver on the PCA website stated it was ‘effective’ from October 30, 12 days after Chmura’s passing, we also asked if there was an earlier version. No answers were forthcoming.

Similar questions were sent to the IFBB, the separate IFBB Pro League, which sanctions Mr Olympia, and the US-based National Physique Committee to ask if their athletes are required to supply proof of having undergone a professional health assessment prior to competing.

Only the IFBB replied, stating the health of their athletes is a ‘fundamental priority’ and supported by their medical commission, but they do not require a ‘specific medical examination certificate’.

Chmura's passing is the latest entry in the sport's catalogue of tragedy (Source: Instagram/mateusz.chmura.92)

At the PCA in Derby, Bourne would go on to win his pro card. Beaming a grin on stage with a glistening tan that will take a full two weeks to wash off, he is satisfied with his sacrifices. By exercising his free will, he is making strides.

Meanwhile, the organisation’s owner, Ryan Alexander, would later tell me that Chmura’s death was the first since their formation 10 years ago, and that they have a medical team and defibrillator at their shows.

‘The safety of our athletes is paramount,’ Alexander said. ‘When we find out (the cause of Chmura’s death), if there’s something that needs to be reviewed additionally, that's of course something we would do.’

For now, the detail of Chmura’s passing is unknown. But one fact is inescapable - this extreme sport has become dangerously familiar with tragedy and remains some distance short of a solution.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino's first Man United training session is LEAKED ahead of Liverpool clash: Drone over Carrington captures 12 MINUTES of footage in major security breach
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino's first Man United training session is LEAKED ahead of Liverpool clash: Drone over Carrington captures 12 MINUTES of footage in major security breach

Manchester United have fallen victim to a security breach after footage of Mauricio Pochettino’s first training session as head coach was leaked online.

The 12-minute video taken by a drone hovering over the club’s Carrington training complex on Thursday clearly shows Pochettino and his coaching staff working with the players.

United have refused to comment.

The incident is a major embarrassment for United on Pochettino’s first full day in charge after the club paid £10million to buy the Argentine and his staff out of their contracts with the US Soccer Federation.

His first game is against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, although it’s unclear how much United’s bitter rivals would be able to benefit from the video.

United regularly use their own drones to film training sessions, but put up signs six years ago banning the use of them near the training ground in case they could reveal top-secret information to their opponents.

Mauricio Pochettino's first Man United training session has been leaked on YouTube

Footage of the session was captured from a drone close to Carrington and uploaded online

Man United players were captured during a drill under the gaze of Pochettino's coaching staff

The footage was posted on YouTube by an account called CC Overview which insists that the airspace over Carrington is unrestricted and the drone was operating legally within Civil Aviation Authority rules.

It said that the video was taken half an hour into Pochettino’s training session and clearly shows the 54-year-old instructing the United squad along with his coaching team of No.2 Jesus Perez, first-team coach Miguel D’Agostino, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, his son and fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya.

Pochettino only flew into Manchester on Wednesday with D’Agostino, Tuya and analyst Alec Scott after taking charge of his last game as US coach against Haiti in Cincinnati.

They caught a private jet provided by United after the game and he went straight to Carrington after landing in the UK shortly before noon.

Perez, Jimenez and Sebastiano Pochettino have been at the training ground since the weekend after being given permission by the US Soccer Federation to leave after the first-leg against Haiti in Miami.

Pochettino addressed the Man United's internal media team for the first time on Thursday, outlining how he plans to drag this underperforming squad up the table.

'The culture is the most important,' Pochettino explained.

'Create the habits, the principles, and I think that is what we want to create.

The breach comes as Man United prepare for a daunting trip to Anfield on Sunday afternoon

The 12 minutes of drone footage captured Pochettino and his staff coaching across two training pitches at Carrington

Man United installed signs in 2018 warning that the use of drones over Carrington was 'strictly prohibited' and would be reported for prosecution

'We need to [be] looking forward and to find a way to create the best habits and the culture that makes us to be close to winning every single game.'

'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure.'

Pochettino has stressed he is focused on the potential of his squad, rather than their present position in the Premier League.

'It's a mistake to see the [current] situation. We need to see the potential of this club,' a defiant Pochettino added.

'Of course, the circumstances are the circumstances, and we need to be responsible for the circumstances. But at the same time, we need to understand that it's a game and, to connect with the game, we need to feel free.

'The players need to express their talent. We need to create the environment and the platform for the players to perform. That is the most important thing and that is our priority now – it's to work with them and try to take the pressure [off].

'Pressure needs to bring energy, responsibility needs to bring energy. Because if not, it's too heavy to put all that pressure and responsibility on your back.

'When you connect with the game, you connect through your talent and when you feel freedom, when you feel happy, when you want to play for your team-mates, when you want to play for your family, when you want to play for your club, your fans.

'That is what we need to create all together and I think we have an amazing staff - we were talking a lot today. Then [we need to] settle all the principles and the ideas and to create our own philosophy and start from zero.

'I think with the power of this club and the fans supporting us, I think we will get in the place that we deserve to be.'

Sports.title: Andriy Shevchenko hits back at explosive Mykhailo Mudryk claims in blame game over doping case: Ukraine chief accuses £89m star's camp of asking official to falsely take blame for positive drugs test
Sports.content:
Andriy Shevchenko hits back at explosive Mykhailo Mudryk claims in blame game over doping case: Ukraine chief accuses £89m star's camp of asking official to falsely take blame for positive drugs test

Andriy Shevchenko has accused Mykhailo Mudryk's representatives of trying to persuade the Ukrainian FA to find someone to falsely take the blame for the winger's failed drugs test.

Mudryk, now on loan at Tottenham from Chelsea, was suspended for 20 months between November 2024 and July 2026 after testing positive for banned substance meldonium in October 2024.

In an interview, Mudryk blamed the Ukrainian FA (UAF), claiming the substance entered his body while on international duty.

'This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that's Ukraine,' he said.

But Shevchenko, president of the UAF, described the accusations as 'baseless slander'. Shevchenko added: 'His representatives repeatedly approached the UAF with a proposal to find an employee who would falsely take responsibility for the meldonium found in his doping sample,' he told Tribuna. 'Such a proposal contradicts the principles of our work.'

Shevchenko said investigations had failed to establish how the substance entered Mudryk's system. He added that national team staff complied with Chelsea's request not to give Mudryk medication, and that two of his personal specialists were allowed at training camps.

Mykhailo Mudryk (left) has been accused of 'baseless slander' by Ukraine FA (UAF) president Andriy Shevchenko after he blamed his failed drugs test on the national team's setup

'If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it,' Shevchenko said, demanding a public retraction and apology otherwise.

Mudryk's representatives have been approached for comment.

The 25-year-old was initially handed a four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'.

In a bombshell two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel, Mudryk laid the blame for his situation with the Ukraine national team - something Shevchenko vehemently denies.

'Loud statements have been made about the UAF and the Ukrainian national team. This is baseless slander against our people, who do their work honestly and professionally,' the UAF president, who also played for Chelsea during his time, said in a statement to The Athletic.

'After Mykhailo became a Chelsea player, the club sent a letter to the UAF requesting that he not be given any medication during national team training camps,' he continued.

'The national team staff complied with this request. Head coach Serhiy Rebrov also approved for Mykhailo to have two of his personal specialists work with him at the training camps. These were the exact people who monitored his regimen and recovery, and helped him with his daily routine.

Mudryk has won 28 caps for Ukraine but is yet to represent them since his ban was overturned

'The UAF completed all necessary checks in this case. We provided Mudryk's representatives with the information they requested and remained in contact with those working on the case.

'I know the people who have worked with the national team for many years. I trust them, because throughout all this time there have been no incidents in the team that could make anyone doubt their professionalism. If Mykhailo has evidence to back up his words, let him provide it. If no such evidence exists, I expect him to publicly retract his accusations and apologise to the people whose honesty and professionalism he has called into question.'

In his interview, Mudryk - who is yet to add to his 28 caps for his country since returning from his ban - laid the blame at Ukraine's door.

'I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It's a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe,' the winger said.

'This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that's Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

'I was at home and Chelsea's management came to see me and they said we needed to talk. Then they say you've returned a positive doping test and now you're facing a ban.

'You can't believe it's true. You can't believe this is happening to you. If I'd ever taken anything anywhere, I'd have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

He is currently on loan at Tottenham from Chelsea but has only played once so far this season

'At least I'd have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that's the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

'Otherwise there'd be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don't hear them.

'At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you're falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You're flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don't wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.'

Mudryk, who joined Chelsea for £89million from Shakhtar Donetsk, has only made one substitute appearance for Tottenham so far this season due to an ankle injury.

Sports.title: Donald Trump pardons disgraced MLB legend Pete Rose two years on from death
Sports.content:
Donald Trump pardons disgraced MLB legend Pete Rose two years on from death

Baseball's hit king Pete Rose has been posthumously pardoned by Donald Trump a year after being reinstated by Major League Baseball, according to a Thursday afternoon post on the President's social media platform.

'I have just given a Complete and Total Pardon to the Late, Great Pete Rose, a true Baseball SUPERSTAR & LEGEND, whose record of 4,256 Hits in a Season will never be broken,' Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Of course, Trump was wrong about Rose's hit total, which was 4,256 for his entire 17-year career and not just a single season.

The President stopped short of explaining why he was pardoning Rose, who pleaded guilty in 1990 to felony counts of filing false federal income tax returns and underreporting more than $300,000 in income. Rose ultimately served five months in a minimum security prison and was required to perform 1,000 hours of community service.

Instead, Trump focused on the lifetime ban Rose received for betting on baseball in violation of one of the game's oldest rules. Rose ultimately admitted to gambling on baseball in 2004, although he insisted he never bet against the Cincinnati Reds, whom he was managing prior to his lifetime ban.

Trump then listed Rose's considerable accomplishments as a player for the Reds, Philadelphia Phillies and Montreal Expos before referencing Roger Clemens, the former Boston Red Sox, Toronto Blue Jays and New York Yankees ace who has been denied entry into Cooperstown after facing accusations of steroid use.

Rose points his bat at a group of photographers prior to a spring training game in 1989

In 2024, Rose died in Las Vegas at 83 without ever being enshrined in the Baseball Hall of Fame. However, in 2025, commissioner Rob Manfred removed Rose from the ineligible list

Trump failed to mention what, exactly, he was pardoning Rose for. However, Rose did plead guilty in 1990 to several counts of federal tax crimes. He did serve five months in prison

'In addition, Pete played 3,562 career games (Highest Ever!), had 1,314 Runs batted in, 160 Home Runs, a.303 Batting Average, was a 17x All-Star, 3x World Series Champion, NL MVP, World Series MVP, NL Rookie of the Year, 2x Recipient of the Gold Glove Award, Silver Slugger Award, Roberto Clemente Award, 3x NL batting champion and, just like the Great Roger Clemens, who won 354 games, was treated terribly by Major League Baseball in not allowing him to go into the Baseball Hall of Fame,' Trump wrote. 'Politics, I guess!'

In 2024, Rose died in Las Vegas at 83 without ever being enshrined in the Baseball Hall of Fame. However, in 2025, commissioner Rob Manfred removed Rose and 16 others from the permanently ineligible list, thereby creating an opportunity for their induction into Cooperstown.

So while Trump's Truth Social was framed as a significant step towards Rose's enshrinement, the decision is now in the hands of Hall-of-Fame voters, many of whom have opposed Charlie Hustle's candidacy or decades.

Trump previously signaled plans to pardon Rose last year, writing on Truth Social 'shouldn't have been gambling on baseball, but only bet on HIS TEAM WINNING.'

But even if that was the case – something that's difficult to know for sure – many Rose critics insist the specifics of the bets are immaterial.

'Betting on one's own team gives rise to the ultimate conflict of interest in which the individual player/bettor places his personal financial interest above the interests of the team,' read a section of the Dowd Report, which described Rose's transgressions as Reds manager.

Trump has repeatedly brought up Pete Rose's Hall-of-Fame candidacy while in office

Rose played in a record 3,562 career games with the Reds, Phillies and Expos (pictured)

Baseball commissioner A. Bartlett Giamatti announced Rose's lifetime ban on August 24, 1989

Rose accepted his lifetime ban in 1989.

The following season, under new manager Lou Piniella, the underdog Reds swept the favored Oakland Athletics in the World Series.

Rose's gambling problem didn't end with his lifetime ban from baseball. Two decades before his death last year, baseball's all-time hit king was averaging $1,000 wagers per game with Mathew Bowyer, the convicted California bookmaker arrested in 2023.

Ultimately Bowyer was forced to cut Rose off due to his worsening habit.

'Rose just loved the action,' Bowyer told the New York Post in 2025. 'He was absolutely compulsive. No question.’

As well as his betting scandal, Rose was also accused of having an improper sexual relationship with a minor in the 1970s when he was in his early 30s. The woman, identified in a 2017 court filing as Jane Doe, said she was 14 or 15 at the time.

Asked about the alleged affair in 2022, Rose told a female baseball writer for The Philadelphia Inquirer that 'it was 55 years ago, babe.'

Sports.title: Have Portugal found Cristiano Ronaldo's replacement? Ex-Man City star Carlos Forbs impressed Erling Haaland and stunned Wales this week in No 7 shirt - just over a year after being brutally axed via WHATSAPP
Sports.content:
As far as auditions to replace Cristiano Ronaldo go, Carlos Forbs' couldn't have gone much better.

His winner against Wales on Tuesday certainly looked and felt like a Ronaldo goal, especially from early in the former Manchester United star's career.

Right flank. Dribbling at pace. Ben Davies back-tracking. A quick flap inside with the left boot. Shoot. Goal. He only needed 11 minutes since coming on to change the game - and potentially his career trajectory.

Portugal's No7 later insisted he did not feel the 'weight' of the shirt, but the jersey is pregnant with meaning. Ronaldo wore No 7 for the national team for 20 years, inheriting it from the legendary Luis Figo. Its next permanent incumbent matters deeply in the Portuguese footballing psyche.

Forbs has not inherited it full-time yet, as a source within the Portugal camp has confirmed to Daily Mail Sport. He appears locked in a battle with Rafael Leao, who was supposed to have it this international break until he missed out through injury.

But now Forbs - a chap who went to school in Leeds and was praised by Erling Haaland while at Manchester City - is the name on fans' lips.

Carlos Forbs is gunning to be Portugal's new full-time No7 after Cristiano Ronaldo's retirement - and his audition against Wales went swimmingly

Ronaldo held the shirt for 20 years, having inherited it from the legendary Luis Figo

They are already calling him 'CF7' and media outlets across the world hailed the 22-year-old, a relative unknown for plays for Club Brugge. 'The new national hero,' is how leading Portuguese outlet O Jogo described him. No pressure, kid.

His form is attracting attention on British shores. Rangers were interested in him over the summer, as were Lyon. Daily Mail Sport has been unable to verify recent reports that the likes of Arsenal, Aston Villa, Everton and Newcastle are keen.

But it would be no surprise to see him in the Premier League one day. Stardom has long felt like it might be on the cards for Forbs. Born in Sintra to Bissau-Guinean parents, he started off playing futsal and was picked up by Sporting Lisbon's academy, just like Ronaldo. His family left for England when he was just 11, and it wasn't long before Manchester City came calling.

The attacker spent eight years in the City academy and was considered a gem. In 2022-23 he was named Premier League 2 player of the season after a stunning campaign which saw him score 29 goals and provide 18 assists in all competitions.

He had a knack of scoring hat-tricks - not a bad habit to adopt. In one match he scored four against Manchester United like it was child's play. It felt like nothing could go wrong for the winger, who copied Ronaldo's lesser-known 'nap' celebration to mock the Red Devils. A player who looked up to the likes of Raheem Sterling and Phil Foden didn't look far off joining them in the first team.

He was rewarded with chances to train alongside Pep Guardiola's seniors, and Kyle Walker and Bernardo Silva were noted as being particularly welcoming. Erling Haaland was impressed with him. Watching a montage including the youngster's goals, he said: 'Is that Carlos? I've been training a lot with these guys. Carlos is good.'

But a debut never came due to the competition at City and in 2023, yearning for opportunities to play in the big-time, he moved to Ajax in a £17million deal.

'I didn’t have to leave, but in the summer, clubs came along where I knew I had more prospects,' he told AD in October 2023, while he was still known as Carlos Borges.

Forbs, previously known as Carlos Borges, was a gem in Manchester City's academy but never got a first-team debut
