According to The Guardian, Sullivan repeatedly shouted 'let Tommy fight him' while Robinson's entourage – referred to by the YouTuber as 'Tommy's boys' – were permitted to enter the ring to face off with Deen and Co.

He added: 'What is that nonsense? You think I would want them to have a bare-knuckle fight for free, not to just face off and hype up the next event?'

🚨MUST SEE: Hstikkytokky has OFFICIALLY SOLD AWAY his UNHINGED PROMOTIONS COMPANY…



He goes on to apologise to all fans and every supporter 😳



HS: “I’ve had message from police and the boxing commission, I am no longer able to host @UnhingedEvents pic.twitter.com/6EopqIhyMr — KickClipz (@Kickclipzfeed) November 8, 2026

Chairs were hurled and punches were thrown as the event descended into absolute chaos

HSTikkyTokky appeared on Louis Theroux's Inside the Manosphere documentary this year

Sources have told Daily Mail Sport influencer events such as Saturday's Unhinged 003 tend to take place without authorisation from any official boxing body.

HSTikkyTokky had promoted the event as a 'proper scrap between two of the most chaotic names in the internet scene', with British rappers Russ Millions and Kirky set to headline a card that was ultimately abandoned before their bout could take place.

After initially hinting that a potential bout between Robinson and Deen had been in the works for next month, Sullivan appeared crestfallen on a later video as he called an end to Unhinged Promotions, claiming they had been shut down from operating 'worldwide'.

'I've had a lot of messages from police around the world, message from the boxing commission... I am not allowed to put an Unhinged event on anymore after Tommy Robinson riots at Kilkenny last night,' he said on his channel.

'Obviously it's massively disappointing, I wanted to grow the company Unhinged Promotions, I wanted to make it massive and huge and take over the world but the risks that have come in play from the decisions some of my staff have made has now led to us having to cancel any future event. We won't be back, but I will sure be supporting some of the other promotions around the world.

'I just want to apologise to the internet. I didn't want to ever have to put on events that risked the safety of people that came to support. I'm super sorry and I won't be doing an event again. I wish I could, but I'm not allowed to now.'

In case the message wasn't already clear, he stated again: 'There is no venue around the world that will take me, there is literally nothing I can do. I feel cornered, I feel lost, I feel gutted. I feel jobless, this was my passion, my desire, my life.

'Now it's been taken away from me over something that was meant to be a light-hearted promotion for the next event. I'm gutted and I want to say again, sorry to everyone.'

Sullivan's self-pitying demeanour offered a stark contrast to the buoyant figure he immediately cut after the chaotic event, which he claimed went 'absolutely brilliantly'. Footage from earlier in the night had shown him being hit by a glass bottle thrown from the crowd while he stood in the ring.

Thrilled that Unhinged's third event had trended globally on social media platforms as a result of the riots, he said: 'I think it went absolutely brilliantly. Listen it was controversial as f*** but please tell me other promotion on their third event is trending globally on Twitter like this, has generated over 200 million views across TikTok, Twitter and Instagram.

'So everyone who's hating, you're clearly still watching. The fights were absolutely brilliant up until the venue got closed down.

'I'm gutted that we didn't get to see the final three fights but s*** happens. I totally hold accountability for misjudging the amount of security that was needed and the types of people that were coming. I misjudged that.

'But what I won't listen to is that wasn't a f***ing great night of entertainment. It was huge. Every single person is watching what I do. Every single person likes to talk about what I do because I'm the number one at what I do.'

Robinson was holding a copy of his book, The Grooming Gang Cover-Up, as he entered the ring

Robinson, who is on bail before his sentencing in December, said 'Muslims have been raping our country for 100 years' as he riled up the crowd with inflammatory remarks about Islam

Irish mobster Paul Flaherty just KNOCKED OUT a boxer at HSTikkyTokky’s Unhinged boxing press conference 😳 pic.twitter.com/NHVJFG10Ij — vxdeo (@vxdeo) September 17, 2026

Sullivan has seen other boxing events shut down in the past. In January, he complained that 'hundreds' of complainants had called the local council and police to cancel a show in Basildon, saying that one of his fighters was a 'convicted child predator'.

The mayor of Kilkenny called the scenes this weekend 'absolutely disgraceful'. Andrew McGuinness said on local radio station KCLR: 'I am absolutely disgusted Kilkenny was used as a backdrop for such a horrendously managed event.

'They are grooming young people to behave in a way that's absolutely disgraceful. They have no respect for themselves, no respect for other people and particularly no respect for women.

'They groom thousands of people into going to these events. The fact there were minors and teenagers at the event is just absolutely appalling.'

Sports.title: F1 Las Vegas GP: Rain drowns out FP1
Sports.content:
"If we're on a track like Vegas and it rains, honestly, I think we're in trouble," Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson predicted after sampling this year's rain tyres in Brazil.

His comments reflected the general mood in the paddock as the Pirelli tyres are difficult to bring up to temperature, especially at a circuit with low corner speeds and glacial temperatures like the 6km street circuit in the gambling haven.

Lawson's comments proved relevant as the heavens opened up intermittently in Nevada on Thursday morning, and more rain arrived right before the start of FP1 at 4:30 pm local time.

With little rain expected for the remainder of the weekend, it naturally led to an action-starved session, leaving fans forking out the event's eye-watering ticket prices to look for action at the blackjack tables instead.

Venturing out on the low-grip surface, with the walls looming large, felt like a gamble, too. But as if intent to at least offer the home fans something, Sergio Perez of US-owned team Cadillac was first to brave the conditions on full wet tyres for an exploratory lap. He was later joined by Haas duo Rafael Camara and Ryo Hirakawa, the latter completing a rookie FP1 session instead of Oliver Bearman.

The second Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas also explored the inclement conditions, celebrating his 2027 confirmation with a huge tank slapper on his one lap, showing the two US-owned teams certainly couldn't be accused of not chipping in.

Sergio Perez, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

While TV audiences and punters intent on analysing lap times and long runs were also left wanting, FP1 actually became one of the most picturesque sessions of the year. The Las Vegas Boulevard is photogenic at the best of times, but the rain further drowned the Strip in neon-tinted reflections, hues Hunter S. Thompson would have approved of.

"Amazing, it's a lovely Strip," gawked Ferrari reserve driver Dino Beganovic as he replaced Lewis Hamilton for the session.

"Enjoy the sightseeing... but we'll box this lap, please," came the perfunctory reply from Ferrari.

Beganovic may as well have enjoyed it, as staying tucking inside the garage was not an option to begin with for the Swedish-Bosnian driver. For any of the teams' four mandatory rookie FP1 sessions to count, drivers must at least leave the garage once.

It explains why all three rookie runners went out, including Jak Crawford who deputised for Fernando Alonso at Aston Martin, though they will be ruing the lack of actual mileage the rare opportunity was able to provide.

As world champion Kimi Antonelli reported aquaplaning, several more tenured drivers had close shaves with the walls. Alex Albon went straight at Turn 11 at the end of the Strip , while Audi's Nico Hulkenberg also locked up at the drenched left-hander.

"It's almost like an ice rink," reported Red Bull's Max Verstappen, The Dutchman a rather cool admirer of street circuits at the best of times.

Eventually, all but five drivers sampled the conditions, with the four cars from McLaren and Racing Bulls thinking better of it, and Aston's Lance Stroll also not feeling particularly motivated.

Camara and Alpine duo Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto were the only three drivers to venture out twice, with the Argentine nearly reliving the scenes of his high-speed qualifying shunt in 2024 for Williams as he momentarily lost control over his car on the straight.

For the avoidance of doubt, no laptimes were recorded.

Sports.title: Nike joins F1 as apparel partner
Sports.content:
Athletic apparel giant Nike has joined F1 as its official partner and uniform supplier, taking over from Puma at the start of 2027.

As was long rumoured, Nike will start supplying F1 personnel with apparel and footwear from the start of next season, a partnership that also extends to F1 Academy, which had both been using Puma kit until this year.

The athletic company will also come up with F1-inspired retail collections, the first of which will go on sale on Friday and be centred around the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

"Nike will bring new energy to the pinnacle of motorsport through capsule collections with a focus on style, performance, and lifestyle including footwear, apparel, and accessories, as well as performance innovations, and race-weekend experiences for the next generation of athletes and fans," the announcement promised.

"Fans will get a first look on 20 November, when the limited Las Vegas Grand Prix x Nike capsule collection drops at the F1 Hub and Nike Las Vegas stores.

Nike CEO Elliott Hill said: "Formula 1 is driven by competition, speed and a constant push to innovate. That’s an athlete mindset, and it’s one we share at Nike. Together, we have an incredible opportunity to bring new energy to the sport, serve its athletes and inspire fans around the world.”

Sports.title: FIA to phase in full-time F1 stewards from 2027
Sports.content:
The consistency of stewards’ decisions has been a topic of discussion in the Formula 1 paddock for years. While the complexity of the sporting regulations and racing guidelines is one factor, another question keeps coming up: would a permanent panel of stewards improve consistency?

From 2027, the FIA will take a step in that direction. The governing body announced on Thursday that it will gradually move towards full-time stewards, with the first phase beginning in 2027.

The intention is to recruit a panel of 12 to 15 full-time stewards, although that number will only be reached over time. The first full-time stewards will be recruited during the 2027 season, who will be joined at each race by the usual part-time stewards and a driver’s steward, whose specialist knowledge and perspective as a former racing driver will remain part of the process.

The main objective is to improve the consistency of decisions, although according to the FIA, the initiative goes beyond that. By making the role full-time, these stewards can also be deployed outside race weekends, for example “to identify emerging trends and areas requiring regulatory clarification” and to train FIA officials.

That would allow for shortcomings in the sporting regulations and racing guidelines used by stewards to be addressed more effectively. The aim is therefore not only to improve consistency during races, but also to make the rules and guidelines themselves more robust in the first place.

Start action Photo by: Clive Rose / Getty Images

This move is in line with what FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has been advocating for some time: further professionalisation of the stewarding panel. The FIA believes moving beyond the current voluntary, rotating system will help improve continuity and consistency.

And that is precisely one of the key areas the FIA wants to improve, while emphasising that the move also complements the FIA Remote Operations Centre, which recently opened at Biggin Hill.

“This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport. The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport,” Ben Sulayem said.

“This development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships.”

The FIA is now setting up the recruitment process for the phased introduction in 2027, with plans to expand the group in 2028 and subsequent years until it reaches the target of 12 to 15 full-time stewards.

Sports.title: Hamilton insists there are no "trust" problems at Ferrari
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has insisted there are zero “trust” problems at Ferrari despite him overruling strategic calls becoming a repeated occurrence across recent Formula 1 grands prix.

The seven-time world champion has ignored calls to pit in two of the last four rounds - Singapore and Brazil - with both backfiring on the Scuderia driver.

In Singapore he elected to keep track position under a virtual safety car, but on worn tyres he dropped from podium contention to sixth late on - for which he apologised afterwards.

Then in Brazil last time out, Hamilton stayed on slicks despite the rain intensifying and this led to a late spin at the final corner before pitting the following lap to eventually finish ninth.

Those instances came amid talk of fractious relations down at Ferrari but ahead of this weekend’s Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton confirmed all is well - particularly with his new-for-2026 race engineer Carlo Santi.

“It’s definitely not a trust thing, we’re constantly working on our communication,” said the 41-year-old.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"It's been a lot better this year. Carlo has done an amazing job and those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed.

“I got the call right at the last minute. We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."

This year has been much improved for Hamilton, who is fourth in the standings with three rounds remaining, currently on 261 points compared to his total of 156 in 2025.

His first year in Ferrari colours was certainly underwhelming, but there have still been signs of improvement in 2026 despite it being a significant jump from last season.

Not only is that in reference to the strategic calls, but also his connection with team-mate Charles Leclerc, clashing on a few occasions and most notably in Mexico three weeks ago.

It cost Ferrari the win and Hamilton subsequently criticised Leclerc’s “do or die” attitude, before suggesting in Sao Paulo that the Monegasque races him harder than he does with other drivers.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Yuri Cortez / AFP via Getty Images

That led to an hour-long meeting between both Scuderia drivers plus team boss Fred Vasseur and Hamilton and Leclerc are now confident that the issue has been resolved.

“Charles is a great driver,” said Hamilton. “The detail we went into about stuff like that, in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear, we understand each other, we understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team.

“So I don't feel like that will be a problem moving forward. I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does for me either.”

The talk surrounding the Mexico clash was naturally high, but Leclerc reckons that is a consequence of driving for Ferrari and all focus is now on securing runner-up in the constructors’ standings.

“Everything has been taken out of proportion,” said Leclerc. “I'm kind of used to it now, driving for Ferrari for so many years. But things are very often taken out of proportion.

“The goal is not always to agree and that will never happen. We can have different opinions and that was the case, for example, in Mexico.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

“But just the fact of speaking eased all tensions and we were completely fine with it. It's not that we had to speak for an hour, even though it ended up lasting an hour, just because we had a good time.

“We started speaking about many other things in trying to bring the team and to help the team go forward.

“But the discussion about the tension was like maybe five or 10 minutes and then the air was clean and that's it.”

Ferrari heads into the Vegas race 95 points ahead of third-placed Red Bull and 142 behind Mercedes, who clinched its ninth title at Interlagos.

Sports.title: Who has the best F1 power unit: Red Bull or Mercedes? Russell shares interesting theory
Sports.content:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix promises to be an interesting challenge for Formula 1 teams in several respects, arguably even more so than in previous years. With the 2026 cars producing less downforce and relying on active aerodynamics, getting temperature into the Pirelli tyres – and, given the long straights, keeping it there – promises to be even more difficult than before.

According to newly crowned world champion Kimi Antonelli, this factor will determine who gets to lift the Las Vegas GP winners' trophy on Saturday night, although another aspect should not be underestimated either: energy management.

During a weekend in which much of the discussion has centred on the return of V8 engines, the reality remains that the 2026 power units have significant limitations, many of which will be exposed again in Las Vegas.

Verstappen described the simulator work as “painful”, a sentiment echoed by other drivers. Clipping is once again expected to play a major role on the long straight, with Antonelli also warning about the return of “yo-yo racing”.

Although that is hardly good news in itself, it does raise an interesting question: who currently has the best power unit at these energy-poor circuits?

At the beginning of this year, the answer was clearly Mercedes, while efficiency on the electrical side of the power unit was still a weakness for Red Bull. Although the newcomer from Milton Keynes has not received an ADUO token and has therefore been unable to make hardware changes, it has made significant progress in terms of efficiency and learning how to optimise its power unit for each circuit.

Nevertheless, Verstappen still points to Mercedes as the benchmark at an energy-poor track like Las Vegas.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

“In Baku, we were probably not the strongest in that regard. I hope that it will be a little bit better here, but I think Mercedes is normally the strongest on that side, with maximising that.”

When Autoport subsequently put those comments to Russell, the Mercedes driver offered a nuanced reply. According to him, it is not so easy to distinguish between the internal combustion engine and the electrical components, and the picture from the beginning of this year is not necessarily valid.

“I do think we've probably got the most efficient electrical management, but I think it's unfair sometimes to separate the two things,” Russell said. “You've got to develop a car and a power unit and a battery deployment setup that all contribute to one another.”

And it is precisely in this respect that different manufacturers and teams make different compromises, according to Russell.

“You can compromise the ICE to give you more, and vice versa. And you can compromise your aero package to give you more power. We could achieve more power from the engine, but we would have to take a sacrifice with the aerodynamics.”

When Russell takes all those factors into account, however, his conclusion is clear: “On the whole, I think Red Bull, on the power unit side, are the team to beat right now. So I just look at that as over the course of a lap and not distinguishing between ICE and battery.”

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

An interesting point is that, according to Russell, the picture from the beginning of this year is no longer valid for two reasons. Firstly, the competition – particularly Red Bull – has made progress in extracting performance from its power unit, but secondly, Russell says the drag levels of the W17 have changed, particularly following the upgrade in Malaysia.

“I think earlier this year, we had an exceptionally efficient car. With our previous package, we were considerably faster than the other Mercedes power unit cars on the straights,” he said.

“Since we brought the new package, we've added drag to the car. And I think that has kind of scuppered people's views a bit on what's power and what's drag. As I said, you can't just draw a line in the sand and say, it's battery, it's ICE, it's chassis.”

The additional drag mentioned by Russell could potentially be a handicap in Vegas, but it is precisely in this area that his team-mate Antonelli also sees a positive for Mercedes: “I think Red Bull is going to be very strong this weekend. However, I think we're the only one who has a set of wings that is slightly less downforce-wise, so a bit less drag. Let's see if we're going to use it here, but definitely it's going to be very interesting.”

At Monza – another energy-poor circuit – Antonelli produced a particularly memorable recovery drive, his most emotional F1 win to date, but he expects the opposition in Vegas to be stronger than it was at his home race.

“I think our power unit has been very strong on the electrical side, obviously also on the combustion, but the electrical side has been very strong. I think we're probably the most efficient ones in terms of electrical power and efficiency,” Antonelli said.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

“However, Red Bull, they have a very strong power unit as well, and their car is very efficient on the straight, especially with the Macarena wing they have.

“I think our main competitor will be Red Bull this weekend, probably McLaren as well. And let’s see how Ferrari will do here. This track is an outlier, so it’s definitely going to be interesting.”

All the problems with energy management and the 2026 power units are painful to watch, but in a sense, Vegas does provide an interesting benchmark for determining who leads the way at energy-poor circuits – with one crucial caveat, as Antonelli rightly points out: tyre temperature could overshadow everything in Sin City.

Sports.title: Honda reveals key F1 power unit change for 2027
Sports.content:
Immediately after the Brazilian Grand Prix, Honda was still unable to fully explain Lance Stroll's DNF. The Canadian was forced to retire for the 14th time, equalling the all-time record for the most retirements in a single Formula 1 season.

Ahead of the race weekend in Las Vegas, Honda has gathered more information about the battery failure, with chief engineer Shintaro Orihara explaining when asked by Autosport about the problem: "After Brazil, we have done some inspection on the battery and we found, as expected, what happened.

"It's a kind of expected issue. We thought we applied a countermeasure for Brazil, but that was not enough to prevent a battery issue from happening.

"Then for this event, we brought another countermeasure to get better reliability. I can't explain the exact details of it, but after the Brazilian GP, we did the inspection and found out what happened."

The Japanese engineer immediately added that he was not sure whether the additional measure introduced for Las Vegas would be enough to prevent a repeat of the problem.

"The countermeasure we brought to this event will probably, how to say, not fully prevent it. We still need to get a complete picture and understanding."

Orihara also revealed that the battery will be one of the areas Honda changes for next year. The Sakura-based manufacturer will no longer rely solely on countermeasures, instead seeking to address the problem more fundamentally.

Shintaro Orihara, Honda Racing Corporation Trackside General Manager and Chief Engineer Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

"But for 2027, we will update the structure inside the battery to have better reliability. We're still working on it in Sakura, but they realised that they need to improve reliability of battery for next year.

"And we need to keep bringing countermeasures for this year as well, to have good reliability and to accumulate more mileage on the car."

The word 'structure' could theoretically refer to several aspects, but when asked for clarification, Honda confirmed that it concerns "the internal structure of the energy store to increase robustness and overall reliability".

The need for this change had already become apparent before Stroll's retirement in Brazil, although Orihara explained that the lessons learned from the latest failure can still be used to improve the 2027 power unit.

"For our 2027 battery, we developed another structure, but we can still learn something from this year's issue to improve our reliability," he said.

"So it was not directly leading [to the change for 2027], but in some areas, we can learn from this year's reliability. That's why we keep bringing countermeasures to improve our reliability. That will help us for next year as well."

Previous combustion breakthroughs no longer work under 2026 rules

While the battery change is primarily intended to improve reliability, Honda's focus in terms of outright performance remains on the internal combustion engine.

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing, Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

Orihara has already explained in an interview with Autosport that improving energy management or efficiency is of little use if the ICE is significantly lacking in outright power, which is why that remains the key focus for 2027.

The chief engineer acknowledged in Las Vegas that combustion works somewhat differently under the current regulations than it did previously, meaning Honda could no longer use some of the tried-and-tested solutions from the previous cycle. This initially sent the manufacturer down the wrong path.

"Under the previous regulations, we found what we call rapid combustion. That gave us a lot of performance under those regulations," Orihara admitted.

"We started our development for this year, so for this regulation, with the rapid combustion as well, but then we realised that we needed to improve combustion further beyond the rapid combustion.

"Still now, we are on the way to overcome rapid combustion. That is what we are focusing on now and for the future. Rapid combustion gave us good performance, but sometimes it's challenging to manage the combustion itself.

"The main difference under this regulation is that we no longer have a cylinder pressure sensor. Under this regulation, we need to find some other combustion style to get more performance and that's an area we are working on to improve."

Finally, Orihara acknowledged that Honda's outright peak power is at the required level at times, but that controlling it and delivering it consistently remains particularly challenging.

"If we have good control, we can keep that peak power in a wider range. But if we don't have good control, we just get peak power, but without that wider range, there’s less torque delivery or torque accuracy. So yes, we need to improve combustion control and combustion performance under this regulation."

Sports.title: Why Verstappen's ideal F1 rules would make some circuits off-limits
Sports.content:
Although the FIA's announcement was only online for five minutes, there is no doubt in the paddock that V8 engines will return to Formula 1. An agreement in principle has been reached on a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 with a smaller electrical component, which is set to be introduced in 2030 rather than 2031.

Max Verstappen is one of the biggest critics of the current regulations and therefore one of the strongest advocates for change. He welcomes F1’s future plans, but says it is too early to tell whether they could keep him in the series for longer.

"I don’t know. For sure it’s better, but I cannot tell you now what I will do after 2030. But for the sport itself, it’s a good choice," he said.

The contract Verstappen signed ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort runs until the end of 2030, meaning he will get a taste of the new regulations regardless. Alongside the V8 engines, the new rules are also expected to include a further reduction in car weight.

When Autosport asked Verstappen whether the plans for 2030 are what he himself would have come up with if he were writing the rules, the Dutchman made it clear that this is not entirely the case.

"No, but that’s also because [with my plans] you would not be allowed to race at some tracks because it would be too loud! If it is up to me, then I would take the turbo off. And I would get rid of the [electrical] power. Well, maybe you can use it as a push-to-pass, but not too much on the battery side anymore. But then on some tracks you are not allowed to race," Verstappen said, referring to the noise restrictions that many circuits face nowadays.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images

For street tracks in major cities, this would logically be an even bigger problem.

Verstappen added: "Fuel consumption also goes up a lot without the turbo, so you would need a bigger tank if you don’t want to do refuelling during the races. So then, of course, I understand that you want to have a turbo."

Besides this practical argument, retaining the turbo was also important from a political perspective, for example to keep Audi and Honda on board.

With all those factors in mind, Verstappen does see this compromise as an important step in the right direction for F1.

"If it’s fully up to me, then of course I would go back to a V10 or whatever. That sounds even better, but I know that’s not something realistic.

"But this is good. This is for sure in the right direction. But again, it’s not confirmed yet, so I guess there are a few things that they still need to agree on."

Nevertheless, this agreement in principle does seem to indicate that F1 and the FIA have taken drivers' complaints about clipping, super clipping and other issues with the 2026 power units seriously when considering the future.

Verstappen agrees, but also believes that even F1's leading figures realise things cannot continue as they are, even if they would never admit that publicly: "It’s probably a combination of maybe listening to our advice, but also realising that what we have now is not what you want! So yeah, it’s probably a bit of a combination."

Sports.title: Alonso won't stay for V8 return: "F1 has lost 16 years of pure racing"
Sports.content:
Although the FIA's formal confirmation on Tuesday was only online for a few minutes before being temporarily taken down again, it is clear to everyone in the paddock that V8 engines will return to Formula 1.

The agreement in principle involves a 2.1-litre turbocharged V8 – with the turbo being particularly important for Audi and Honda – and a significantly smaller electrical component. The target for its introduction is 2030, which would be a year earlier than initially planned.

Read Also: Formula 1 The factors behind the abortive 2030 F1 rules announcement

It is largely what the drivers have been pushing for, which explains the positive reactions in the Las Vegas paddock during the media day.

Fernando Alonso, however, stressed to media including Autosport that the V8 return will come too late for him. The Spaniard is currently 45 and, perhaps unsurprisingly, has no intention of remaining in the pinnacle of motorsport for another four years: "No, I will not be around for the new V8. 100%."

When it was pointed out that Alonso has surprised people in the paddock before, for example with his F1 comeback in 2021, he laughed: "Yeah, I have surprised myself in the past as well! But this time I think it's the good one. When I stop, it will be the moment, also the moment to try different things.

"It's still a long way ahead, [the V8 return], but I think it will be enough [for me before that]."

Alonso does find it frustrating, in a sense, that he will have to bow out under a set of regulations that he, like many other drivers, is far from fond of: "Yes, it's frustrating that we didn't have it in 2014 already. From 2014 to 2030 or 2031, so that means 16 years or 17 years of pure racing are lost."

Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

While Alonso will no longer be competing in F1 by then, he still has his sights set on other racing categories. Even after retiring from F1, Alonso intends to continue racing for a long time.

In January 2027, he will make an appearance at the Dakar Rally, but he is also leaving the door open to other iconic races once his F1 career comes to an end.

"Dakar was on my mind. Le Mans is on my mind, the Indy 500 is on my mind," the Aston Martin driver said.

"I love competing and I love competing in race cars in which you have power when you go on throttle, and in which you have deceleration when you brake. Those are the things that we miss now in Formula 1.

"Obviously, if I continue in Formula 1, that will always be my priority and it's difficult to put things together or to combine different programs. Dakar, because it's in January, it fits a little bit better, but even that had to come with a few coincidences."

That Alonso would like to return to endurance races such as Le Mans is no surprise – he would even like to do so alongside Max Verstappen – but his mention of the Indy 500 is somewhat more unexpected.

After his last attempt in 2020, the Spaniard did not seem particularly keen on another appearance at The Greatest Spectacle in Racing at the Brickyard, but with a new IndyCar chassis on the way, his opinion could change.

"Yeah, I don't know. They will change cars soon. There's a new car coming for 2028, I think, so yeah, I don't know," he said. "I may consider it one day. It’s not in my short-term plans and not on my mind now, but I cannot say no to it 100%."

Fernando Alonso, Arrow McLaren SP Chevrolet Photo by: Michael L. Levitt / Motorsport Images

Sports.title: FIA to introduce full-time stewards to Formula 1 during 2027 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA has announced it will begin introducing full-time stewards to formula 1 during the 2027 season.

The sport’s governing body said its new programme “aims to establish a department of 12-15 full-time stewards over coming years.” It expects the change will “bring even greater levels of consistency and dedication to race officiating.”

The FIA currently selects between four and five stewards per race weekend, at least one of which is a former grand prix driver. The identities of the stewards change from race to race, though many stewards attend multiple races per season.

The full-time stewards will also help develop future regulations and train new FIA officials.

The FIA will begin recruiting its first cohort of full-time stewards which will work alongside its existing representatives to begin with. It expects to introduce a “small number” of full-time stewards next year and expand the practice in 2028.

The move is the latest in a series of changes to FIA officiating. The governing body recently inaugurated its Remote Operations Centre at Formula One Management’s broadcasting facility at Biggin Hill in the UK, which supports the on-site race control staff.

“This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport,” said FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem. “The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One world championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport.

“Following the milestone opening of the new FIA Remote Operations Centre and strengthening of officiating development through initiatives such as the FIA High Performance Programme, this development will help to build greater expertise and continuity within our stewarding structure, strengthening our ability to review and improve regulations, support the development of future officials and ensure the highest standards of consistent officiating across all our championships.”

Sports.title: Video: FIA reveals how Formula 1 race control takes decisions during an event | Brief
Sports.content:
The FIA has published a new video providing insight into how decisions are taken in race control during grands prix.

Formula 1 race director Rui Marques, Safety Car driver Bernd Schneider and others explain how the race control systems at the track work alongside the recently-introduced Remote Operations Centre.

One common misconception the video highlights is that race control is responsible for taking penalty calls. This is not the case: decision on whether drivers should be penalised, and how, are handled separately by the stewards.

However race control is responsible for supplying the stewards with information they need to make calls during grands prix.

“As we need to review something, we go into replay mode and then we can track and drop certain cameras and show it to the race director or deputy race director, or to the sporting director,” explains video operator Richard Serschen. “Then they will have a deeper look and of course maybe they ask ‘can we have another angle, can we maybe have an onboard camera?’

“If this needs to be provided then to the stewards room – because in the stewards’ room we also have a video operator – I can then clip and file everything up together in a couple of seconds and then this is sent to the steward’s room that they have the same images.”

Sports.title: The five-way fight for second is close – but no one cares about ‘winning’ it | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli may have clinched the world championship with four rounds to spare but there’s a close, five-way fight over second place.

But unlike in the constructors’ championship, which determines how much prize money each team receives, the final ranking in the drivers’ title fight matters little to the competitors. None of the drivers competing for the runner-up spot expressed much interest in taking it.

Outgoing world champion Lando Norris made it clear his priority is getting McLaren back up to third place in the constructors’ championship ahead of Red Bull. His former title rival Max Verstappen is eyeing the same goal and made it clear he doesn’t care if he holds on to second place in the drivers’ standings.

“I only care about staying in [third] with the team,” he said. “That’s the goal of the team and of course that becomes my goal.

“For me I don’t have any satisfaction in being second or third or [fourth] because that’s not what you’re here for. Of course, once you have won championships you probably just don’t really care, right, because it doesn’t get remembered anyway to be in that place. At least not for me.

“But for sure for us in this season, I think we can be very proud of the progression that we made as a team. I think that’s way more important than when we finish in the drivers’ championship, to be honest.”

Verstappen’s fellow multiple world champion Lewis Hamilton said “the constructors’ championship is the main focus” for him and second place in the drivers’ title isn’t a priority.

“It’d be nice to finish it [second], but you want to finish first,” he said. “So the main focus is making sure we solidify second in the constructors for the team, because I think that’s something that everybody, it means a huge amount to everyone at the factory, but especially to me also.

“So that’s what we’re working towards. Then if we’re able to do well and keep in the battle, in the fight, in these last few races, maybe we can climb back up from fourth and hopefully be in the top three.”

Charles Leclerc, whose best championship finish is second place in 2022, gave a similar view.

“I don’t think that it’s something that we are obsessed about, to be honest. I mean, P2 is always better than P3, and I would lie if I say I completely don’t care. But I would also lie to say that it is what I absolutely want.

“My main focus at the moment is to try and win races, and the natural result of winning races will hopefully be the second place in the drivers’ championship. But it’s not something that I’m obsessed about.”

Antonelli has said he’s prepared to help Russell to secure second place in the championship for him. But Russell, whose best championship finish is fourth in 2022 and 2025, is not concerned with his finishing position after missing his chance to win the title this year.

Sports.title: People in the team are asking why my 2027 deal hasn’t been announced – Bearman | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Oliver Bearman is “disappointed” Haas has not yet officially confirmed he will drive for them again in 2027.

Haas announced last month Rafael Camara , who like Bearman is a Ferrari junior driver, will occupy one of their seats next year. However it is yet to name his team mate.

Bearman, who has been a full-time Haas driver since the start of last season, said he has been asked by some team members why no new deal has been announced.

“It’s certainly a bit disappointing when you have people within the team questioning why you haven’t been announced yet and things like that,” he said. “It’s certainly not ideal, not only for them but also for myself.

“From a mental side, I wouldn’t say it’s the best to be standing here at round 20-something without any confirmation. So we’re working on it and all I can say is that I’m a bit disappointed that I’m standing here without anything to tell you because there’s no excuses for that.”

Bearman said it is “not true” to suggest there is a problem with his new deal for next year, “but things have dragged on a lot and I don’t like that.”

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu made an unexpected change to the team’s line-up when he dropped Bearman’s previous team mate, Esteban Ocon, during the Mexican Grand Prix three weeks ago. That led to Camara joining the team early. Haas has not yet confirmed whether Camara will continue to drive for them in the final two rounds.

Besides Haas, Mercedes and Audi are the only teams yet to officially confirm their drivers for next season, but both are expected to continue with their current line-ups.

Bearman still expects the team will confirm his contract for next season. “It’s just a difficult situation,” he said. “I don’t think there’s any excuse to be standing here at this stage without anything to tell you, and that’s shown by the fact that I’m the only guy who hasn’t been announced for next year.

“Even if I can tell you that – touch wood – I’m going to be driving for Haas next year, the fact it’s not official is just disappointing.”

Sports.title: Sainz won’t tolerate “being a test driver on grand prix weekends” for long | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Carlos Sainz Jnr is experiencing a dissatisfying end to his second season at Williams as the team focuses on testing developments for next season.

Having finished on the podium in two grands prix for the team last season, this year Sainz is languishing in 18th place in the championship. He said the team is focused less on competing in the races and more on solving the problems with its car.

“We’re basically evaluating a lot of our correlation, wind tunnel, CFD to track,” said Sainz. “We’ve had a lot of issues with this year’s car, not so much in terms of actual correlation, but just bringing performance to the track hasn’t been easy for us.

“We are just not quick enough. We’re slow, I think, as a team in general. We’ve struggled to understand these new regs and we’re doing everything possible to change the set-up, challenge a few things that come to the track, make sure we can give the factory the best possible feedback to know how to develop next year’s car.”

The team has only scored one point in the last 13 rounds. Sainz admitted they have little chance to add to their haul of 12 points over the final races.

“Right now, we are one second off [Racing Bulls], who are finishing P9 and P10 when the top four are not having any issues. They are taking the P9 and P10, which is two and one points on the board, and that’s one second off for us. So the chances of points really are very, very small.

“This track maybe offers a little bit more hope, but the reality is that we’d rather invest that time in becoming a test driver and testing for the team than actually doing anything else.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

However he admitted he doesn’t find it enjoyable arriving at races knowing he won’t be racing properly. “I don’t like being a test driver on race weekends,” said Sainz.

“I honestly enjoy going testing. Probably not many drivers enjoy testing, but I actually enjoy testing. I enjoy trying different set-ups, trying different things in the simulator. It is true that I like investing my time on that, and I always feel like I learn a lot from it, and I enjoy that side of Formula 1 and racing.

“But it is true that when it comes to going to a race weekend, I don’t look forward to testing. I look forward to winning and fighting for good results and this year there’s been none of that.”

Sainz extended his contract to drive for Williams earlier this year. However he made it clear he expects the team to be more competitive in the future.

“[For] one year I can take it in the chin. I think it’s been an extremely tough year, but I feel like I’ve dealt with it with patience and with good spirit. I’ve driven well this year, which probably has helped that and my motivation quite a bit.

“But it is true that I don’t foresee many more years like this, because going into race weekends without even having a chance to score a point is extremely frustrating.

“I’ve been very lucky in my career that in these 11 years I’ve always had a car to score points. Even my three years in Toro Rosso, I had a car that could get into a top 10. My years in Renault, years in McLaren, midfield cars were always on that level where Liam [Lawson] and [Racing Bulls] are, always top of the midfield, which, for the battles that you fight, actually there is satisfaction from scoring those points.

“But then it has been my first-ever season where not even with a perfect race, perfect execution, you get to score a point, and that is extremely frustrating. But we’re doing the best we can to get out of that situation for next year.”

Sports.title: Russell explains why he chose not to use Mercedes’ turbo upgrade in Las Vegas | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell said he was involved in the decision not to use the power unit upgrade his team mate will have this weekend.

Mercedes is introducing a revision to its power unit made under the FIA’s Additional Development Upgrade Opportunity regulations. It allows them to bring a performance upgrade to reduce their deficit to leading design, which the FIA determined is Red Bull-Ford’s.

But while Andrea Kimi Antonelli will use the new turbo design this weekend, Russell will not. He has already used five turbos this year, exceeding his maximum allocation for the season, while Antonelli has used three, one less than the maximum.

Russell said the team gave him the chance to influence the decision and he felt avoiding a penalty was more beneficial than gaining the performance benefit from the new part. “The performance benefit it brings is not huge, it is just a step in the direction as a team we want to take,” he said.

“We’re obviously lucky with Mercedes that there’s eight drivers running the power unit. I think five or six of them are taking the turbo. The two or three who aren’t, including myself, it’s just because it would mean a back-of-grid penalty.

“Vegas is a track I’ve gone well at in the past, I enjoy it here and I was very much involved in the decision. They said ‘if you want to take it, you can take it, if you don’t, you don’t’.

“I was happy not to because I want to fight for the victory and I think we can do it with or without it.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Antonelli, who will take the new turbo, said the team “don’t expect any major performance gain” from the new turbo. “It will just improve some of the features that we’ve been struggling with.”

“It’s mostly to improve the feeling whilst driving. There will be a slight performance gain but we’re talking less than a tenth [of a second]. It’s mostly to improve the feeling with the driving because obviously the power unit has been very different this season compared to previous seasons.

“Drive-ability hasn’t been the best at times. So this turbo should improve that and hopefully it will make just the feeling of driving even better.”

Sports.title: Beating Red Bull to third place matters, says Norris: “It’s a hell of a lot of money” | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris says claiming third place in the constructors’ championship matters “a huge amount” to McLaren because of the extra prize money it begins.

McLaren won the constructors’ championship in the last two seasons but lost the crown to Mercedes this year. They dropped to fourth place behind Red Bull two rounds ago and lie 17 points behind them with three rounds remaining.

Norris said the extra money the team would earn for finishing third makes this the goal for him and team mate Oscar Piastri in the remaining rounds.

“It’s a lot of money for the whole team, for every individual in the team,” he said. “So, as always, there’s a lot of natural pressure on me and Oscar to go out and perform well, to bring points back to the team and have two cars up there.”

Some of the extra money for finishing higher in the championship will go to McLaren’s staff as bonuses, said Norris.

“You always talk about points and constructor points and all of these things, and it’s very important, but I think you often do forget the extras, the bonuses that come with it,” he said. “Not for me, but for all the members of the team.

“It’s a hell of a lot of money from P4 to P3. All the team members that work every day also get their bonuses at the end of the year, so they want it just as much as anyone.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“Obviously, then it is me going out and driving, and they rely upon me and Oscar to go out and do a good job so, I don’t know, simple things they can buy their kids cooler presents or presents or whatever it might be, and move into the new house or whatever it is. So it obviously means a lot.”

McLaren face an added complication this weekend as Piastri will take a grid penalty for a power unit parts change.

“Oscar’s taking a nice penalty this weekend, so he’s coming from the back of the grid – hopefully not even at the back, the middle of the pack,” said Norris. “But we just need consistent results.

“We need to make sure we’re there. Plenty of things can still be happening and have been happening through the races, so we need two cars up there fighting for points.”

Norris won the last race in Brazil but McLaren gained no ground on Red Bull as Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar finished on the podium while Piastri was sixth.

“Max is doing a good job and Red Bull are doing a good job,” said Norris. “Isack did a good job last weekend, so we’ve got a tough fight, but we’re up for it.”

Sports.title: Andy Hiraoka Signs With Zuffa, Moves to Welterweight
Sports.content:
Andy Hiraoka has signed a multi-fight deal with Zuffa Boxing and will move up to welterweight, the promotion announced. The Japanese southpaw enters the 147-pound division after pushing WBA light welterweight champion Gary Antuanne Russell hard enough in February to make a case that he deserved the decision.

Hiraoka (24-1, 19 KOs) went into that fight unbeaten and left with three scorecards that made Russell’s first title defense look comfortable. The Nevada commission recorded scores of 116-111 twice and 117-110 for Russell. Those margins were hard to square with what Hiraoka did in the second half, when he began hurting Russell to the body and forced the champion to give ground.

Russell had the better of the first five rounds in Las Vegas. He got his combinations off first and built a 60-36 edge in punches landed over that stretch, according to CompuBox. Hiraoka had landed only one body punch through five rounds. In the seventh alone, he landed 20. Once he started getting through downstairs, Russell had to spend more time fighting off his back foot.

Hiraoka landed 76 power punches to Russell’s 59 over the last six rounds. There were rounds in that stretch where Russell was still busy enough to give the judges a choice, but Hiraoka was landing the shots that changed how the fight was being fought. If you gave him one or two of the closer early rounds and most of the second half, you could get to a Hiraoka win. The point he lost for low blows in the 10th made his case harder, especially on a card where he was already giving away early rounds.

That fight against Russell put Hiraoka on the map in a way none of his domestic bouts in Japan ever could. Most guys who lose a decision on a big stage walk away with their stock dented, but Hiraoka actually raised his value because of how he broke Russell down in the second half.

You don’t often see a 140-pounder punish a champion to the ribs and liver like that, especially someone as physically strong as Russell. Watching Russell go from firing crisp combinations in the first five rounds to literally running out of room and looking desperate to survive down the stretch told the whole story. If not for that slow start and the point deduction in the 10th, Hiraoka walks out of Las Vegas with the WBA belt.

Before this signing, he was completely stuck in neutral. Fighting in Japan under Ohashi Promotions kept him off the radar for casual fans and made it almost impossible to lure top American or British names into the ring with him. Nobody wanted the risk for a low-profile payday.

“I feel like he was down on the scorecards and knew it, so he tried to pick up the intensity,” said Russell after the fight, as reported by The Ring. Hiraoka’s attack held up deep into the fight. He landed 13 power punches in the 12th, his second-highest total of the night, and finished just two behind Russell in power punches landed overall.

The move to 147 raises a question about how quickly Hiraoka can get that body attack going against bigger men. He found his way into the Russell fight by stepping close enough to hit the body after spending much of the opening rounds at a distance where Russell could get off first. A welterweight who can make him pay on the way in would put that adjustment to a different test.

Zuffa’s announcement named neither a debut date nor an opponent. The first opponent will tell us how much the promotion took from the Russell fight. A durable welterweight who can make Hiraoka work beyond the opening rounds would show whether the pressure he put on a champion at 140 comes with him to 147.

Sports.title: Senate Passes Ali Revival Act by Unanimous Consent
Sports.content:
The U.S. Senate passed the Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act by unanimous consent Thursday, moving Zuffa Boxing’s league model a step closer to federal recognition. The bill would let leagues stage fights between boxers they sign and run their own title systems alongside the traditional sanctioning bodies.

The Senate Press Gallery confirmed that H.R. 4624 passed with a substitute amendment from Sens. Ted Cruz of Texas and Jacky Rosen of Nevada. The House, which passed an earlier version, must agree to the Senate’s changes before the bill can go to the president.

The bill’s biggest change is the creation of a legal path for Unified Boxing Organizations. Under the published Cruz–Rosen amendment, a league would match fighters under contract to it and could run its own rankings. It could also recognize titles and rankings from an independent organization. Fighters could choose to sign with a league or continue working with traditional promoters.

For Zuffa, the benefit is in the matchmaking. If two contenders are on the same roster, the league can put them together without first having to negotiate with a rival promoter. That could help keep a division moving when the best available opponents are already signed. The model is less helpful when the opponent fans want fights for somebody else. The league still needs enough depth in each division to make the fights it wants to sell.

For a boxer, the question is what happens when the league has the belt he wants and controls who gets the next shot. A contender can climb the rankings and still depend on the same company for a date, an opponent and a purse. The amendment addresses some of that leverage. It would generally cap promotional agreements at six years, limit a boxer’s first professional promotional agreement to three and allow talks with other promoters or leagues during the final 90 days of a deal. A boxer could sign a new agreement once the existing one expires.

The published amendment would also set a $200 minimum for each round a boxer participates in, covering traditional promoters as well as leagues. It would require at least $50,000 in medical coverage for injuries sustained during a bout and $15,000 in accidental death coverage. The leagues would also have to carry insurance for injuries sustained while training for a covered bout and use an independent third party to administer drug testing.

The test for Zuffa is whether it can sign enough contenders to make its belts worth chasing. A league can build a title fight from its own roster, but a belt is only as valuable as the competition behind it. For a fighter weighing a multi-year deal, the decisions that count are who he can fight, how often he gets booked and what he can earn by moving up.

Sports.title: De La Hoya Says WBA Cleared Teofimo Lopez for Ryan Garcia
Sports.content:
Oscar De La Hoya says the WBA is giving Teofimo Lopez an exemption to fight Ryan Garcia before mandatory challenger Jack Catterall. The proposed February 6 welterweight unification could put Eddie Hearn’s threat to sue the WBA to the test if the association confirms that Lopez can keep his title and fight Garcia first.

“It has already been worked out,” said De La Hoya on Fight Hub TV when asked whether the Catterall mandatory could hold up the fight. “The WBA has already ruled on it. They’re giving an exemption to Teofimo Lopez because he is the world champion and this will be a unification.”

De La Hoya called it an exemption and gave no details of the ruling or its terms. The WBA’s November 11 public decision reaffirmed that Lopez must defend his Super title against Catterall and gave the camps 10 calendar days to reach an agreement or propose another solution. Either side could request a purse bid if talks failed.

The same decision said the WBA can consider a unification under its special permit rule. Mike Coppinger reported on November 14 that the WBA had informed the parties that Lopez could apply for a permit to face Garcia, the WBC champion. De La Hoya’s account goes a step further. He says the WBA has made its decision, though the association has yet to publicly confirm that it has granted an exemption.

“I would sue them immediately,” said Hearn on Inside the Ring last week when asked what he would do if the WBA ruled against him. The Matchroom promoter has argued that Catterall was already owed a shot at the Super title before Lopez took it from Rolando Romero. Catterall holds the WBA’s Regular belt and earned the right to challenge for the top title by beating Shakhram Giyasov.

If the WBA confirms De La Hoya’s account, the terms of the exemption could determine how long Catterall has to wait. A written ruling could spell out whether Catterall gets the winner and when that defense would be due. Hearn has been pressing for Catterall to get his shot first. If he follows through on his threat, the WBA’s November order and the terms of any exemption would both come into play.

De La Hoya said Las Vegas and New York were under consideration and that a few details remained to be worked out for February 6. He also said he had never spoken to Floyd Mayweather about making a fight with Garcia. Later in the interview, De La Hoya said he believed the Lopez deal was close. For Catterall, the immediate question is what the WBA will put in writing about the title shot it ordered.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Refuses To Admit Ryan Garcia Exposed His Style
Sports.content:
Devin Haney is still trying to convince fans he knows how to beat Ryan Garcia in a rematch, yet he refuses to admit what actually happened in their first fight. During his appearance on Club Shay Shay, Haney kept falling back on the same old excuse about Garcia’s left hook, calling them “PED punches.”

“It’s boxing. You get caught,” said Haney on Club Shay Shay. “But those PED punches … they were a little different.” Later, when asked whether he’d ever felt that kind of power in the division, he went right back to the positive drug test again.

Ostarine does not make a fighter drop his right hand every time he throws a jab. That was Haney’s biggest problem all night. He kept stepping forward behind his jab, ducking his head, and lunging in to clinch with his right glove down at his chest. Garcia saw that bad habit from a mile away and timed him with left hooks over the top. You do not need banned substances to hit a guy whose chin is sitting wide open.

Haney boasted about getting off the canvas three times, saying it proves he can take a punch. He also broke down what Conor Benn did wrong when Benn walked into Garcia’s shots. It is funny how Haney can spot another fighter’s mistakes from ringside, yet he still refuses to look in the mirror and fix his own. Until he admits his style is tailor-made for Garcia’s left hook, a rematch will end the exact same way.

Before Haney even thinks about fixing his mistakes for Garcia, he’s got to deal with IBF welterweight champ Liam Paro on December 19. You can tell Haney wants that Garcia rematch badly because the first fight wrecked his reputation with fans and killed his leverage at the negotiating table.

Looking past Paro is a massive mistake, though. If Haney loses that unification fight, he isn’t getting near a Garcia rematch anytime soon unless he’s willing to walk in coming off a loss, and you know the purse split would be totally against him in that spot.

Sports.title: Canelo Alvarez Given WBC Green Light for Willy Hutchinson, Will Eddy Reynoso Block It?
Sports.content:
Canelo Alvarez has a clear path back to 175 pounds if he wants it. WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman told Sky Sports on Thursday that the sanctioning body would approve a fight between Canelo and WBC light heavyweight champion Willy Hutchinson as Hutchinson’s first title defense.

The WBC discussed Hutchinson’s mandatory status at its convention in Acapulco, but Sulaiman confirmed the organization left the division without an official ruling. Without a mandatory challenger ordered, the Scottish fighter could move directly from his November 7 decision win over Joshua Buatsi into a bout with Canelo.

The next move is with Canelo, who reclaimed the WBC super middleweight belt by outpointing Christian Mbilli on October 31.

“It would certainly be approved, champion against champion,” Sulaiman said to Sky Sports regarding a potential Canelo move back up to light heavyweight.

The real issue may not be the WBC, however, but trainer Eddy Reynoso. Once Reynoso scouts the Buatsi tape and sees Hutchinson’s length, lateral movement, and busy jab, he could easily decide the stylistic headache outweighs the reward of another belt at 175.

Moving up to face Hutchinson would certainly be courageous on Canelo’s part, yet there is a big difference between courage and plain common sense. Behind the scenes, it would be no surprise to see Reynoso steer Canelo toward safer, more lucrative waters at 168 against someone like Hamzah Sheeraz, defending his newly reclaimed title against a big UK draw rather than spending 12 frustrating rounds trying to track down Hutchinson.

Hutchinson’s win over Buatsi showed why he would be a problem fight for Canelo. He used his footwork to create space for counters and banked early rounds before Buatsi’s pressure and body work began to close the distance. Two judges scored the bout 115-113, proving Hutchinson can be made uncomfortable when forced to defend on the inside. For Canelo, the main question is whether he can apply steady pressure early enough to keep Hutchinson from building a large lead.

In past losses to Dmitry Bivol and Terence Crawford, Canelo struggled against fighters who controlled distance and refused to stand in front of him. Bivol used a jab to dictate the distance and fired combinations whenever Canelo stood behind his high guard. Crawford frequently changed angles, made Canelo miss, and countered before Canelo could move his feet. Hutchinson utilizes a similar formula. He scores with a sharp jab, follows up with quick combinations, and moves out of range before Canelo can return fire.

Against Mbilli in Riyadh, Canelo benefited from an opponent who marched forward and offered steady counterpunching opportunities. Hutchinson would force Canelo to be the aggressor, slip the initial shot, and exit before the second punch comes. Canelo carries the heavier power when he closes the distance, yet Hutchinson is capable of winning rounds on activity and movement while Canelo looks for a single opening. Allowing Hutchinson to control the early tempo would leave Canelo chasing the fight by the midpoint.

Canelo previously captured a light heavyweight title by stopping Sergey Kovalev in 2019 before dropping a decision to Bivol in his only other appearance at 175. Buatsi provided a workable blueprint for getting to Hutchinson through sustained forward pressure and targeted body shots. Canelo possesses the tools to execute that same game plan, provided he starts fast and stays committed even when Hutchinson makes him miss.

Sports.title: Simon Jordan Tells Eddie Hearn To Shut His Gob Over Fury vs. Joshua Undercard
Sports.content:
Simon Jordan is dead right to tell Eddie Hearn to shut his gob about the Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua undercard. Hearn has been running around bellyaching that the December 11 bill at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff is weak, even though he and Frank Warren spent years failing to make the main event happen themselves.

“If Eddie Hearn pops up telling you he could do an undercard that’s better, that’s fabulous, but you couldn’t make the main event. So sit down and shut up,” Jordan said on talkSPORT Boxing. “You and Frank [Warren], with respect, had years to make this fight.”

Now that somebody else finally got Fury and Joshua across the finish line, Hearn wants to act like he has all the answers for the undercard. The truth is, Hearn has no vision and no clue what fans actually want to see. Looking at the fights he floated to iFL TV, fans should be glad he is not running the show.

Hearn bragged to iFL TV that Joe Cordina had agreed to terms to face Manny Pacquiao, who turns 48 in December, and also wanted to throw Cordina in with WBO lightweight champion Abdullah Mason. Putting a Welsh two-time titleholder like Cordina on the card might please the local Cardiff crowd, as Jordan noted, but it does nothing for fans watching in the U.S. and Canada, and regular Brits barely care either. Zuffa got it right by leaving him off the show.

Giving a 34-year-old Cordina an undeserved title shot against Mason makes zero sense anyway. Cordina has not fought a good opponent since his eighth-round blowout loss to Anthony Cacace back in May 2024. That was ages ago, and beating Jaret Gonzalez Quiroz and Gabriel Flores Jr. since then does not earn him a shot at Mason.

Dragging a 47-year-old Pacquiao out to face Cordina is even worse. Pacquiao’s name might trick a few casual American fans into glancing at the poster, but nobody in North America is paying to watch Cordina. He was never a draw in America even when he held a belt at super featherweight.

The rest of Hearn’s matchmaking ideas are just as weak. Wanting Dave Allen to face Andy Ruiz Jr. or sticking Pacquiao in with Jack Catterall, Conah Walker, or Lewis Crocker sounds like a desperate attempt to unload Matchroom fighters onto a giant pay-per-view stage.

Jordan is dead right that the organizers need real fights before Fury and Joshua make their ring walks around 1 a.m., because fans shelling out big money deserve better than cheap filler. Hearn whining from the sidelines while pitching washed-up legends and domestic mismatches just proves Zuffa was smart to ignore him.

Sports.title: Low WBO Bid Would Expose Shakur Stevenson Real Value
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson needs to vacate his WBO light welterweight title right now before the November 30 purse bid exposes what promoters actually think he is worth. WBO president Gustavo Olivieri ordered the bid for 11 a.m. Atlantic time (10 a.m. ET) at WBO headquarters in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and the organization plans to stream the entire thing live on social media for his mandatory defense against Raymond Muratalla.

If a live-streamed WBO purse bid comes back at $3 million or $3.5 million, every promoter in boxing gets hard proof that Shakur’s open-market value is a fraction of what he demands.

Those last three paydays on Turki Alalshikh cards against Josh Padley, William Zepeda, and Teofimo Lopez clearly warped Stevenson’s view of his own drawing power. He started acting like a Canelo Alvarez-level attraction, even reportedly walking away from a $7 million offer from Zuffa Boxing to fight Jose Valenzuela because he wanted $15 million.

If $7 million was too low for Valenzuela, Stevenson is obviously not taking $3 million to $3.2 million from a purse bid to risk his unbeaten record against a heavy-handed puncher like Muratalla (25-0, 17 KOs). None of his last three opponents he’s beaten hit as hard as Muratalla, who gave up his IBF lightweight belt to chase this shot at 140 pounds.

By dropping the WBO strap before November 30, Stevenson can control the story, pretend he is moving on to bigger fights against Devin Haney or Gervonta Davis, and avoid the embarrassment of watching a low bid go viral. That leaves Muratalla waiting for the WBO to work down its top 15 rankings to find a contender willing to fight him for the vacant title.

An ultra-low winning bid on November 30th brands Shakur as a non-draw without Saudi money. Rival fighters like Devin Haney, Ryan Garcia, and Gervonta Davis already use Stevenson’s defensive style and ticket-selling history against him in negotiations. A low winning bid hands them ammunition to demand an 80-20 or 75-25 split in their favor whenever talks start, arguing that Stevenson cannot generate revenue unless Turki Alalshikh is writing the check.

Sports.title: Matchroom Weighs Quick Teremoana Return After Ahio Fight
Sports.content:
Matchroom is considering a quick return for Teremoana Teremoana after his second-round stoppage of Hemi Ahio. Promoter Frank Smith said the team would decide within 24 to 48 hours whether to get him out again soon. Petar Milas looks like a sensible next opponent if Matchroom wants to move Teremoana up a level and give him a chance to get some rounds in.

Teremoana called for a shot at Australian heavyweight champion Ivan Ivić, saying he’d heard he was the mandatory challenger. Smith said Matchroom had already made Ivić several offers for what he called “really good money,” and the champion hadn’t taken the fight. With several Matchroom cards coming up, there’s little reason to build the next date around an opponent Smith says has already passed.

“If he wanted to get out quickly again, that’s something we are looking at right now,” said Smith after the Ahio fight. He said he wanted to give Teremoana time to rest after the fight and the training camp before making a decision.

Milas is ranked one place above Teremoana on the IBF list discussed here. That’s the kind of incremental move that makes sense on a short turnaround. Guido Vianello would be a tougher option, while Efe Ajagba or Justis Huni would represent a bigger jump. Milas is a matchmaking option, and Smith gave no indication that Matchroom had approached him.

Teremoana said he’d leave the opponent to his team. He also said he wanted Ahio to get up after the second knockdown because he wanted more ring time. That gives Matchroom a clear brief if it brings him back quickly. Find someone who can extend him past the early rounds and make him work for a win.

The bigger question is whether Teremoana’s team is trying to manufacture an artificial fighter designed to make a big killing without ever facing anyone dangerous. If this is all just artifice to build a hype job and create a pseudo star, we won’t see a true step up in opposition for his next fight.

Some fans believe Matchroom ran that exact same play with Anthony Joshua, who was matched carefully through much of his career and made massive money without beating high-level opposition. Once Joshua finally stepped in against the real thing, he lost to Oleksandr Usyk and Daniel Dubois.

If that is the blueprint for Teremoana, it could be a long time before he faces a genuinely good opponent, and by the time it happens, there will likely be huge money on the line.

Ghana News.title: Drugs war: GACL boss flags threat from compromised officers
Ghana News.content:
The fight against drug trafficking at Ghana’s airports could be undermined by the very personnel assigned to detect it, the Managing Director of the Ghana Airports Company Limited (GACL), Yvonne Nana Afriyie Opare, has warned.

She said sophisticated scanners and other screening equipment would offer little protection if officers operating them colluded with traffickers or allowed suspicious consignments to pass unchecked.

“If you have a scanner which is efficient and there is a person who is operating the scanner who is compromised, then that’s also a gap,” she told Parliament’s Public Administration and State Interests Committee on Thursday, November 19.

Her warning comes against the backdrop of a series of drug interceptions linked to Ghana, including cases that have raised questions about how narcotics are moved through the country’s transport hubs.

To strengthen detection at the airports, GACL has funded the acquisition of 10 sniffer dogs for the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC). The dogs are expected to be imported from Europe and deployed to support the Commission’s narcotics detection operations.

Ms Opare said payment had been made to NACOC during the week, describing the intervention as part of efforts to close security loopholes and address the threat of insider involvement in drug trafficking.

“We’ve just this week made a payment to the Narcotics Control Commission for 10 sniffer dogs to be imported, I believe, from Europe, to help with making sure that we are sealing these gaps that exist in our airports and also insider threat,” she said.

The concern is not merely theoretical. In October, the Director-General of NACOC, Brigadier General Maxwell Obuba Mantey, told Parliament that some airport personnel allegedly used their positions to help suspected traffickers bypass established screening procedures.

He also disclosed that investigators had encountered a case involving a suspected trafficker who had acquired a personal scanner, raising concerns about the methods being adopted to evade detection.

The scale of the challenge has also been reflected in recent interceptions. On November 16, NACOC announced the arrest of a 58-year-old passenger at the Accra International Airport who was allegedly found to have swallowed 58 pellets suspected to contain cocaine while preparing to travel to India.

In another case, Lebanese authorities arrested a Syrian national at Beirut’s Rafic Hariri International Airport on October 31 after allegedly finding 46.7 kilogrammes of cocaine in luggage brought from Accra. The seizure prompted renewed scrutiny of Ghana’s airport security and anti-narcotics enforcement arrangements.

A JoyNews Research tally published in October recorded 28 drug seizures between March 2025 and September 22, 2026, including 11 cocaine cases. The tally covered seizures made in Ghana and overseas interceptions involving consignments that had left or passed through the country.

Ms Opare said GACL was working with NACOC, the Bureau of National Intelligence and National Security to reinforce security at the terminals.

She stressed that the response must combine reliable technology with alert and trustworthy personnel, adding that staff training was continuing to improve vigilance and prevent insider threats.

“It’s a work in progress,” she said.

Ghana News.title: White House national cyber director Cairncross leaving his post
Ghana News.content:
Sean Cairncross, National Cyber Director at the White House

White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, a White House official ‌said Thursday, marking the latest departure from the Trump administration after Republican losses in this month's midterm elections.

Cairncross, who leads the Office ​of the National Cyber Director that coordinates cybersecurity ​policy and strategy across the federal government, did not ⁠want to serve another two years and was leaving now ​to give the White House time to secure Senate confirmation for ​his successor before Democrats take control of Congress in January, Axios reported earlier.

Cairncross' departure was amicable, Axios reported.

President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost its majority ​in the Senate and House of Representatives in this month's US ​midterm elections.

The news of the departure comes after tech outages that have ‌hit ⁠US air travel, banking and national security systems in recent days.

The Trump administration has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the ​series of disruptions to ​critical systems ⁠over the past week was not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Top US officials have repeatedly said the outages are separate ​and unrelated to any cyberattacks.

Cairncross was an executive at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need ⁠to ​be confirmed by the US Senate, which ​will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.
