Ghana News.title: Businesses could face higher tax costs despite no new taxes in 2027 Budget – Deloitte warns
Ghana News.content:
Deloitte Ghana has cautioned businesses that the absence of new taxes in the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy does not mean tax costs will remain unchanged but could witness an increase in the effective tax cost due to a series of tax policy and administration reforms.

In its analysis of the 2027 Budget Statement of the Government of Ghana, the professional services firm said that while the government did not introduce any new headline taxes or increase existing rates, the budget contains measures that could reshape the tax landscape and increase compliance obligations for businesses.

"The proposed modernisation of tax laws, rationalisation of customs concessions, and improvement in the value-for-money of the exemptions regime may have an impact on the effective tax cost of businesses," Deloitte stated in its analysis.

The report further explained that businesses should not equate stable tax rates with a stable tax environment.

According to Deloitte, changes to customs concessions, tax exemptions, incentives and technology-driven enforcement could materially affect tax liabilities, cash flow and compliance requirements.

The report based these developments on the government’s decision to target an ambitious domestic revenue of 17.7% of GDP in 2027, up from a provisional domestic revenue-to-GDP ratio of 13.7% as of October 2026.

Unveiling Deloitte’s highlights of the 2027 budget, Daniel Owusu, Country Managing Partner of Deloitte Ghana, reinforced the need for businesses to look beyond tax rates and assess the broader implications of the Budget's tax reform agenda on operations, investments and compliance obligations.

He further urged businesses to take advantage of tax incentives announced to spur growth.

Modernisation of tax laws

The government has completed the review of the Income Tax Act, 2015 (Act 896), with a new Income Tax Bill expected in 2027, but plans to review the Revenue Administration Act, Stamp Duty Act and Communications Service Tax Act were also announced.

These reforms are expected to introduce new rules for digital services, virtual assets, crypto transactions and multinational businesses.

Deloitte said the changes will strengthen Ghana's tax system and address gaps in existing tax laws. Businesses involved in digital or cross-border activities should monitor the reforms and assess their impact on tax compliance and reporting obligations.

Rationalisation of customs concessions

The government plans to review the concessionary import duty regime under Chapter 98 of Ghana's Customs Tariff Schedule as part of a broader review of customs concessions.

Deloitte expects the changes to tighten eligibility requirements and increase compliance monitoring for businesses benefiting from these concessions.

While the reforms may improve transparency and reduce disputes, some businesses could lose concessions that currently lower their import costs. Deloitte therefore advises importers of agricultural equipment, pharmaceuticals, textile inputs and other concessionary goods to assess the potential impact on their costs and supply chains.

Implementation of excise reforms

Deloitte expects the Ghana Revenue Authority (GRA) to increase compliance monitoring in the beverage sector as it seeks to meet revenue targets. Manufacturers, importers, distributors and retailers are likely to face closer scrutiny.

The increased focus follows the implementation of the Excise Act, 2026 (Act 1180), which introduced new excise rates for beer and stout and a hybrid excise regime for wines and spirits. The reforms are expected to generate an additional GH¢2.6 billion in revenue. Deloitte therefore advises affected businesses to review their pricing, production plans and margins to remain compliant and competitive

Improving value for money of tax exemptions

The government’s decision to increase scrutiny over tax exemptions and evaluate whether incentives generate sufficient returns through investment, job creation, local value addition and economic growth. The review aligns with the objectives of the Exemptions Act, 2022 (Act 1083), and could result in tougher requirements for accessing and retaining tax incentives.

Based on the above, businesses seeking tax exemptions should therefore strengthen business cases for proposed investments and provide evidence showing alignment with the government's economic development and employment objectives.

Implementation of the medium-term revenue strategy

Deloitte noted that proposed reforms to the Stamp Duty Act, Communications Service Tax, taxation of digital services and debt-to-equity rules form part of Government's broader revenue strategy, indicating that tax reforms will continue beyond 2027.

The firm therefore encourages businesses to adopt a long-term approach to tax planning and closely monitor future policy developments.

Ghana News.title: Trump’s $15 billion defamation case against New York Times may proceed, judge rules
Ghana News.content:
A ​federal judge on Thursday said President Donald Trump's $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and book ‌publisher Penguin Random House may proceed, a victory for Trump in his legal campaign against media companies he accuses of treating him unfairly.

Trump has filed several lawsuits against media companies since 2024, alleging they defamed him or fraudulently misled the public with false coverage. His critics have denounced the ​lawsuits as attacks on the free press.

Thursday's ruling came a week after another federal judge said Trump's defamation lawsuit against ​the BBC over a misleadingly edited clip may proceed. The BBC has denied liability for defamation.

The lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House cited a book about Trump by two New York ​Times reporters and what it characterised as "false, malicious, defamatory, and disparaging" articles that he says were aimed at sabotaging his chances ​in the 2024 presidential election, which he won. Trump seeks at least $15 billion in damages.

US District Judge Steven Merryday in Tampa, Florida, said Trump's complaint plausibly alleged that statements in a Times article by Peter Baker and a book by journalists Susanne Craig and Russ Buettner that accused ​Trump of "planning and perpetrating complex crimes" were “based on incomplete, minimal information." The judge dismissed Trump's claims over a Times article about ​his work on the reality TV show "The Apprentice."

The Times and Penguin have denied defaming Trump and said in a court filing that his ‌case is ⁠legally flawed and aimed at scoring political points.

A Times spokesman said in a statement that Trump's lawsuit had no legal merit and was "a baseless attack on The Times and the rights of the free and independent press in this country.”

A spokesman for Trump's personal legal team praised the ruling and said the defendants "will now have to answer for intentionally and maliciously defaming President ​Trump."

A Penguin Random House spokesperson ​said in a statement that ⁠it stands by the book and its authors and is confident the case will be fully dismissed.

The lawsuit against the Times and Penguin concerned two articles and a book that cast doubt on Trump's origin story as a savvy businessman who rose in the real estate and entertainment industries.

Trump ⁠cited more than two dozen statements from Times articles by the three journalists and a book by Craig and Buettner titled "Lucky Loser: How Donald Trump Squandered His Father’s Fortune and Created the Illusion of Success."

They include assertions about Trump’s role in creating his hit reality TV show “The Apprentice,” his inheritance from his father, his business ventures, and his upbringing in New York City.

The Times and Penguin said in a motion to dismiss that Trump's lawsuit failed to explain how the statements were defamatory and included subjective ​opinions that cannot be proven true or false.

Ghana News.title: Accused child sex predator Thomas Markle ruled competent to face trial
Ghana News.content:
A U.S. judge in Florida on Thursday declared Thomas Markle, the ​estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan ‌Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal charge filed in court earlier this month accusing him of being a ​child sexual predator.

Agreeing with the findings of ​a court-appointed forensic psychiatrist, US Magistrate Judge ⁠Lindsay Griffin ruled that the 82-year-old father-in-law of ​Prince Harry was mentally fit to understand the proceedings ​against him and to properly assist in his own defense.

He was charged November 5 in a criminal complaint with a ​single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse ​images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the ‌material ⁠in question, including two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of ​undress, was found ​in two ⁠Los Angeles storage units.

Commenting on the case at the time of his arrest ​on November 6 at an assisted-living ​center ⁠in Florida, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle had "targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through ⁠his ​criminal actions."

Ghana News.title: GACL buys 10 sniffer dogs to tighten airport security
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana Airports Company Limited (GACL) is stepping up efforts to close security loopholes at the country’s airports, with the acquisition of 10 sniffer dogs to help detect narcotics and deter drug trafficking.

The dogs, which are expected to be brought in from Europe, will be deployed by the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) to support screening and security operations at the airports.

Managing Director of GACL, Yvonne Nana Afriyie Opare, disclosed this when she appeared before Parliament’s Public Administration and State Interests Committee on Thursday, November 19.

She said the company had paid NACOC for the dogs during the week as part of a broader response to weaknesses in airport security, particularly the threat posed by insiders who might facilitate the movement of prohibited substances.

Ms Opare said even the most sophisticated screening equipment could be rendered ineffective if the officers responsible for operating it were compromised.

“If you have a scanner which is efficient and there is a person who is operating the scanner who is compromised, then that’s also a gap,” she said.

She explained that airport security required more than investment in technology, stressing the need to strengthen personnel integrity and vigilance alongside the use of detection equipment.

GACL is also working with NACOC, the Bureau of National Intelligence and National Security to improve security arrangements at the terminals.

The company, she added, is continuing to train its staff to sharpen their vigilance and help identify and prevent insider threats.

“It’s a work in progress,” she said.

Ghana News.title: MPs clash over claims of unemployed doctors in Ghana
Ghana News.content:
A disagreement has emerged in Parliament over the employment prospects of newly qualified doctors, with the Majority insisting that all eligible medical practitioners have been offered jobs, while a Minority MP says some remain without public-sector appointments.

The Chairman of Parliament’s Health Committee, Dr Mark Kurt Nawaane, dismissed claims of unemployment among doctors, arguing that some practitioners had turned down postings to deprived communities.

He told the House that the Ministry of Health had the necessary authority to recruit doctors without first securing financial clearance and that those who had rejected their postings could still report for duty if they reconsidered.

“Mr Speaker, I want to state as a fact that there’s no unemployment among doctors in Ghana. And currently, as we speak, the Minister of Health does not need any financial clearance to employ doctors,” he said.

Dr Nawaane maintained that the challenge was not a shortage of available positions but the reluctance of some doctors to accept appointments in less-developed parts of the country.

However, his position was challenged by the Akim Oda MP and member of the Health Committee, Alexander Akwasi Acquah, who said some doctors who had completed medical school and their housemanship were still waiting for public-sector jobs.

He said private health facilities were taking on some of the affected practitioners, even though many would prefer appointments in government hospitals and other public health institutions.

“Doctors who have completed medical school, having finished their house jobs, are home. It is the private facilities that are absorbing them. It is the private sector that is absorbing them. It is not their wish to remain with the private sector. They should be offered employment,” he argued.

The contrasting accounts have brought into focus questions about the availability and distribution of medical personnel, particularly whether recruitment opportunities are sufficient and whether postings to underserved areas are attractive enough to draw qualified practitioners.

While Dr Nawaane maintains that doctors have been offered appointments, Mr Acquah says the experience of some newly qualified practitioners points to gaps in public-sector recruitment.

The debate leaves key questions for the Ministry of Health, including how many doctors have received postings, how many have declined them and how many remain eligible but have yet to secure public-sector appointments.

Ghana News.title: Ringleader pleads guilty to $100 million US jewellery heist
Ghana News.content:
The ringleader in a spate of truck burglaries pleaded guilty on Thursday to a federal robbery charge for his role in stealing roughly $100 million ​worth of jewellery from an armoured vehicle five years ago in California, considered ‌the largest such heist in US history, prosecutors said.

Carlos Victor Mestanza Cercado, 33, an Ecuadorean national arrested two years ago in Panama during a layover on a flight from Guatemala to his home country, was one ​of seven men indicted on charges of robbing a Brink's truck at a ​highway rest stop north of Los Angeles on July 11, 2022.

The armoured vehicle ⁠was plundered while carrying 73 sacks of precious gems and fine jewellery from a ​major exhibition in the San Francisco Bay Area to a Southern California storage facility.

Mestanza and his ​accomplices followed the jewellery shipment in multiple vehicles for 300 miles (480 km), coordinating by cellphone, then broke into the armoured truck while it was parked at a rural Kern County rest stop and fled with 24 bags of treasure, authorities said.

The stolen collection of ​fine gold, diamonds, rubies, emeralds and luxury watches were valued at approximately $100 million, marking the largest US ‌jewelry heist ⁠on record, according to the US Attorney's Office in Los Angeles.

Under an agreement with prosecutors signed earlier this month, Mestanza pleaded guilty to one count of interference with commerce by robbery, a felony punishable by up to 20 years in prison, in exchange for prosecutors dropping several other charges he faced. Sentencing ⁠was set for April 15.

In addition to the jewellery heist, Mestanza admitted to taking part with his co-defendants in the highway robberies of ​electronics being shipped by several trucks in March 2022. A statement ​from the ⁠U.S. Attorney's Office in Los Angeles announcing his guilty plea described Mestanza as "the lead defendant in the case."

Three of Mestanza's co-defendants are scheduled for trial in federal court in Los Angeles in March 2027. ​Two others remain at large, and a seventh accused ​member of their gang has been deported.

Court documents do not make clear whether any of the stolen jewellery from the heist was ever recovered.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
World.content:
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.

The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.

Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.

“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.

What was the pledge?

In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.

Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.



A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.

About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.

A wider retreat

During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.

The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.

Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.

Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

World.title: Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration
World.content:
Three top Democrats called Trump’s dealings with law firms a case of ‘official coercion’ and pledged investigations.

Share Democrats say law firm gave $11.8m in free services to Trump administration on social media

Democrats in the United States say their investigation has revealed that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis provided at least $11.8m in free legal work to President Donald Trump’s administration.

On Thursday, Representative Jamie Raskin, Senator Richard Blumenthal and Senator Adam Schiff released a statement calling the sum evidence of Trump’s “unprecedented official coercion of major law firms”.

Since Trump returned to the White House for a second term, he has issued executive orders seeking to bar certain law firms from receiving security clearances and government contracts.

His administration has also threatened law firms with workplace discrimination investigations. Those orders and probes have led some of the firms to enter into settlements with the Trump administration, offering millions of dollars in free services.

“We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood,” the three Democrats said in the statement, citing the $11.8m in services.

They proceeded to request records from nine other law firms, in an effort to determine if they too had done free work on behalf of the Trump administration.

“Since April 2025, the lawmakers have repeatedly demanded answers about the ten firms’ dubious multimillion-dollar deals with President Trump,” the statement said.

“However, to date, the vast majority of the firms still have yet to provide any substantive answers or turn over a single responsive document.”



Midterm shift

The three Democrats involved in Thursday’s statement include lawmakers poised to take leadership roles in investigations during the upcoming 120th Congress.

The Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.

That will give the party power over Congress’s ability to oversee investigations and issue subpoenas. The new Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3.

Raskin is currently the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee. Blumenthal, meanwhile, is the ranking member of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

Schiff, for his part, gained fame for leading Trump’s first impeachment trial in 2020, over allegations that the president abused his power by seeking Ukraine’s help for his first re-election bid. Trump has previously called for Schiff’s prosecution.

The three Democrats say they received information about Kirkland & Ellis’s free services for the Trump administration two days after the midterm race.

Some $4m in services was reportedly offered to the Department of Commerce. Another $2.2m went to the Department of Defense, and $1.6m was dedicated to the US Postal Service.

Kirkland & Ellis also reportedly gave $2m in services to the US International Development Finance Corporation, an agency that provides loans and development assistance to overseas projects.

The Democrats also said $1.8m went to an “investment entity negotiated between the Trump Administration and Japan to create a $550 billion slush fund”.

Law firms cut deals

In 2025, Kirkland & Ellis agreed to settle with the Trump administration after the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) opened an investigation into the law firm’s employment practices.

It accused Kirkland & Ellis of embracing diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI), a slogan for building greater opportunities for under-represented groups in education and the workplace.

The Trump administration, however, has characterised DEI as illegal discrimination, disadvantaging men and white people.

“The EEOC is prepared to root out discrimination anywhere it may rear its head, including in our nation’s elite law firms,” the commission’s acting chair said at the time.

In a Truth Social post on April 11, 2025, Trump revealed that Kirkland & Ellis had pledged $125m in free services. He also indicated that the EEOC would halt its investigation as a result.

Other law firms likewise entered into agreements to avoid the consequences of Trump’s executive actions or employment-related probes.



Estimates indicate that they collectively pledged nearly $1bn in pro bono services.

The handful of law firms that fought Trump’s executive orders, however, won their cases, with judges ruling the president’s actions to be unconstitutional.

In the case involving the law firm Perkins Coie, Judge Beryl Howell said the executive order against it was an “overt attempt to suppress and punish certain viewpoints”.

Fears of corruption

The Democrats in Thursday’s statement highlighted other concerns with the agreements.

The deals, they said, were announced on Truth Social, Trump’s social media platform. That made “the President the sole judge of whether those firms were complying with their obligations – putting these firms at the political mercy of the Administration”.

The Democrats also warned that law firms like Kirkland & Ellis might be dissuaded from taking on certain clients, for fear of upsetting Trump.

“For people and communities who rely on pro bono lawyers to defend their rights, that could mean facing the full power and intensifying fury of the federal government alone,” they said.

In a November letter obtained by the Reuters news agency, Kirkland said it began negotiating with the Trump administration after rival firm Skadden reached its own deal in March 2025.

It added that its White House agreement has had “little impact” on its pro bono work, telling lawmakers that the firm “still devotes substantial pro bono resources to interests that could be considered ‘progressive'”.

The law firm is represented by prominent Washington litigator Beth Wilkinson of Wilkinson Stekloff. She did not immediately respond to Reuters’s request for comment.

World.title: ‘Completely messed up everything’: Malawi’s fuel crisis causes chaos
World.content:
Blantyre, Malawi – Finding fuel in Malawi has become a daily struggle, with motorists spending hours, sometimes entire nights, waiting for tankers that may never arrive.

As shortages persist, filling stations across the country have become flashpoints for frustration and violence as motorists compete for dwindling supplies.

Ken Mhango, 40, a car flipper in Blantyre, recently drove to a nearby filling station after a friend told him a fuel tanker was on its way. He had gone several days without fuel.

Twelve people were already waiting when he arrived, but the situation soon turned chaotic.

“Minibus drivers and motorcycle taxi operators started arriving and jumping queues. They were so reckless they didn’t care if they bumped your vehicle. A scuffle erupted and I saw others, especially women, desperately trying to keep their place in the queue. It took me four hours to get 20 litres but others spent the night in the queue,” he told Al Jazeera.

Violence at filling stations

The scramble for petrol has increasingly turned violent in Malawi’s cities and towns. Although the Malawi Energy Regulatory Authority publishes daily schedules indicating which filling stations are expected to receive fuel, motorists say uncertainty over deliveries makes it difficult to plan their journeys.

Videos of confrontations have circulated on social media, including footage appearing to show people attacking a man at a filling station. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the circumstances surrounding the incident.



The mayor of Blantyre has also been sued for assault following an incident at a fuel queue, while an attendant was killed after being struck by a vehicle during a commotion at a filling station, according to local media reports.

Purchases are reportedly rationed to 20 litres (5.3 gallons) a day, while motorists sometimes pay attendants for an additional five litres, Mhango said.

“The whole chaos that this has created is hectic. It is very hectic and it has created an atmosphere of uncertainty. This is happening when money is scarce, you have to make sure that you plan properly to survive,” he said.

On another occasion, Mhango arrived at Nyabadwe filling station in Blantyre at 5pm after joining a convoy of motorists searching for fuel. The tanker arrived at 9pm, and did not leave until 1am.

“My schedule has been completely altered. Now commuting is no longer a norm but a luxury. I have two parcels in town but I can’t even manage to go and get them,” he said.

Unable to find sufficient supplies at filling stations, Mhango turned to the black market. He paid 30,000 Malawian kwacha (about $17.31) for two litres of petrol for his father. On another occasion, he suspected fuel bought for his garage had been mixed with water after an engine malfunctioned.

“The crisis has completely changed and messed up everything. As a businessperson who deals with vehicles at my garage, people are no longer bringing their vehicles any more because of lack of fuel. And we can’t take our equipment to follow the client,” he said.

He added that his business was unlikely to meet its monthly targets, forcing him to consider docking the salaries of employees who assist him.

Black market dangers

Selling fuel without the required permits is illegal in Malawi, but shortages have created opportunities for vendors to sell petrol at inflated prices.

Motorists who need to travel for work, business or medical care are increasingly turning to informal sellers despite the high prices and safety risks.

According to GlobalPetrolPrices, petrol in Malawi costs about $3.24 per litre, more than double the global average of approximately $1.52.

The informal trade has also proved deadly. Authorities have stepped up arrests of illegal vendors, while fires and explosions caused by unsafe fuel storage have killed people.

Earlier this year, petrol vendors and motorcycle taxi operators protested in Lilongwe after a suspected black market fuel seller was burned alive in an explosion following a police chase, local media reported.



Malawi’s Nation newspaper has documented at least six deaths from fuel explosions this year, including incidents involving families and children.

Calls for accountability

The shortages, alongside foreign-exchange problems and electricity blackouts, have fuelled demands for government accountability.

The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC) planned nationwide demonstrations on November 17, calling for the resignation of the energy minister over persistent fuel shortages and power cuts.

The protests were postponed after police said they could not provide adequate security because officers were committed to a governing-party parade scheduled for the same day.

Michael Kaiyatsa, HRDC chairperson, told Al Jazeera that the decision reflected “genuine concerns about public safety”, rather than a retreat from the coalition’s demands.

He described the fuel situation as “heartbreaking”, saying its effects extended beyond transport and commerce to people’s access to essential services.

“It affects access to healthcare, education, food, employment and other essential services; ultimately this is a human rights issue,” he said.

“People are struggling to get their children to school. We have small-scale businesses that are losing money. We have employees that are failing to get to work, and ordinary motorists that are spending hours and sometimes entire days just looking for fuel.”

Kaiyatsa said the shortages were pushing people to buy fuel on the black market, not necessarily because they wanted to break the law but because they were trying to meet their daily needs.

“We must therefore be clear that this is the responsibility of the government to ensure that fuel is normalised,” he said.

While acknowledging the dangers of illegal fuel trading, he said law enforcement must respect human rights and due process.

“We have seen tragic incidents recently involving explosions and fires resulting from petrol being kept in homes. These incidents are serious public safety concerns. However, our position is that law enforcement must be exercised within the confines of the law with respect to human rights, proportionality and due process,” he said.

Livelihoods on the line

In a statement issued hours before the planned demonstrations, the Ministry of Energy acknowledged the difficulties caused by the shortages but rejected accusations of government inaction, saying interventions were under way to restore fuel supplies.

“The current fuel supply challenges are largely attributable to a combination of financial, foreign exchange and logistical constraints affecting the country’s capacity to consistently import petroleum products,” the statement said.

For motorcycle taxi operator Tadala Kachingwe in Limbe, the shortage has meant dwindling earnings and depleted savings. He said he could no longer set aside money to buy relish for his wife in the morning.

“The business has been affected because previously, when fuel was available, I could have some savings but now it’s impossible,” he told Al Jazeera.



Getting his motorcycle into a filling station has also become difficult, with minibuses blocking the entrances.

“I have no idea which queue I should be joining because the minibuses have blocked off all sides of entry into the filling station. I will need to pay caller boys to sneak this motorcycle into that filling station,” he said.

World.title: El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term
World.content:
The Salvadoran president has won popularity at home and abroad through a crime crackdown that has granted the state enormous power.

Share El Salvador’s Bukele expected to formalise bid for third presidential term on social media

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele is set to formally register his candidacy for his country’s upcoming presidential race, as he seeks a third consecutive term.

Thursday was the registration deadline for the election, which is slated for February 28, 2027.

The 45-year-old president has been widely expected to seek re-election, a move that would further consolidate his party’s leadership in the Central American country.

Bukele is the founder and leader of the Nuevas Ideas party, which controls El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly by a wide margin.

While El Salvador’s constitution previously prohibited presidents from seeking immediate re-election, the Supreme Court overturned that rule in 2021, paving the way for Bukele to run for a second term in 2024.

Then, in 2025, the Legislative Assembly passed a constitutional amendment allowing Bukele to seek a third term. The amendment also extended the length of a presidential term from five to six years.

Bukele secured his party’s nomination for the 2027 race in July. He is expected to return to the ballot alongside his current vice president, Felix Ulloa.

Bukele’s time in office has been defined by a crackdown on criminal gangs that has won him massive popularity at home and turned him into an icon for the political right across Latin America.

In 2022, his government announced a so-called state of emergency to address high levels of crime in the country.

It empowered the police to make sweeping arrests, but it also heralded the suspension of key civil liberties. Some people were detained without charge. Mass trials have been carried out, with hundreds of defendants being sentenced at a time.



More than 1 percent of the country’s population is estimated to have been arrested as a result, with little due process for those seeking to contest their guilt, according to human rights groups.

Advocates also warn that rights abuses, torture and poor conditions are systematic in Salvadoran prisons.

The state of emergency has been extended for years, although it was initially intended as a temporary measure and the government claims El Salvador’s gangs have been all but dismantled.

The United States Treasury has also accused Bukele’s government of negotiating with the gangs in secret, offering incentives to help lower crime.

But experts say human rights activists and members of the news media have seen their ability to monitor abuses and corruption in the country hampered under Bukele.

Some, like human rights lawyer Ruth Lopez, have allegedly been detained for their work without access to legal support. She has spent more than a year in “incommunicado detention”, according to the group Amnesty International.

Under Bukele, El Salvador has also passed a Foreign Agents Law that allows the government to restrict civil society groups that receive funding from abroad.

Those efforts have prompted allegations that Bukele has weaponised the state against his critics.

But those concerns have done little to dent his popularity, and Bukele is considered the clear favourite to win the election.

A handful of candidates, including Maytee Iraheta of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance and Rafael Aguirre of the left-wing Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front, are also set to contest the presidency.

World.title: Four bodies recovered after Senegal boat capsizes amid migration surge
World.content:
Four bodies have been recovered after a migrant boat capsized off Senegal’s coast, as authorities continue searching for survivors amid fears that the death toll could rise significantly.

Boubacar Seye, president of the nonprofit Horizons Sans Frontieres, confirmed the latest death toll to the Reuters news agency on Thursday, a day after the vessel capsized near the coastal town of Yenne, south of Dakar.

A local official said at least 50 people were aboard the boat, which struck a rock while migrants were being transferred from smaller fishing vessels to a larger wooden pirogue.

The number of people still missing remains unclear.

Canary Islands

The incident comes amid an intensifying wave of attempted Atlantic crossings from West Africa to Spain’s Canary Islands, with migrant boats being intercepted or rescued almost daily.

New figures from Spain’s Interior Ministry show that 24,364 migrants reached the Canary Islands between January 1 and November 15, compared with 14,690 during the same period last year, an increase of nearly two-thirds.

The ministry had recorded just 13,327 arrivals by the end of October, meaning 11,037 people reached the archipelago in the first 15 days of November alone.

The surge has persisted despite extensive maritime operations. Senegal’s navy said it had rescued or intercepted 1,424 people on November 16 and 17, including passengers aboard nine fishing boats, according to the Senegalese Press Agency (APS).



Cheikh Sadibou Senghor, head of Senegal’s National Division for Combating Migrant Smuggling, said authorities had intercepted 6,889 people in operations linked to irregular migration, prevented 107 departures and dismantled 88 smuggling networks between January and November, APS reported.

Just days before the boat capsized, authorities announced the dismantling of a suspected migrant-smuggling network in Yenne itself, arresting 14 people and seizing two boats, three engines and 12.5 million CFA francs ($22,000), according to APS.

Nearly 600 dead

The United Nations refugee agency said nearly 600 people had died trying to reach the Canary Islands from West Africa so far this year, highlighting the dangers of the increasingly busy migration route.

As authorities struggle to contain the surge, Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has called for greater efforts to improve employment opportunities for young people.

At a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Faye requested a detailed assessment of the challenges facing efforts to curb irregular migration, according to a government statement cited by Reuters.

But Seye warned that tougher enforcement measures alone would not prevent further tragedies.

“We need to wake up to the gravity of the situation. The strategy deployed until now is not working,” he told Reuters.

“We need to fix the root causes of this problem.”

World.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
World.content:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

World.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
World.content:
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

World.title: Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority, top UN court rules
World.content:
Myanmar has been found guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority by the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The verdict marks the first time a state has ever been found to have committed genocide by an international court.

Yuji Iwasawa, president of the UN's top court, said Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and engaged in "extensive destruction of evidence" to hide its crimes.

A military crackdown in 2017 killed thousands of Rohingya and forced more than 700,000 to flee Buddhist-majority Myanmar, formerly known as Burma. Myanmar denied the claims against it, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups.

World.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
World.content:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.

"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.

Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.

Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.

In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.

Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."

But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".

Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".

Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.

Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.

Zelensky and the three European leaders â Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron â were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."

The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".

"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.

He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.

World.title: Trump, Putin and Xi release 'peace declaration' after historic meeting
World.content:
US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping have issued a "joint declaration of peace" following historic trilateral talks.

The three leaders met for 90 minutes in China's south-eastern city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

While the presidents have previously had one-on-one meetings, these are their first trilateral talks.

In the declaration, they said "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and that the countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum. They also said they were "committed to reform the UN" to respond more effectively to global challenges.

Thursday's statement also flagged the issue of immunity enjoyed by state officials and said "they agreed that the International Criminal Court and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction".

Trump praised the trilateral meeting calling it "a great and highly consequential trip", in a social media post while flying back to Washington on Air Force One.

In the same post, the president announced he would host a news conference to talk about the trip on Friday at the White House.

While in China, Trump met Putin ahead of the trilateral, in their first meeting since August 2025, where the US president greeted his Russian counterpart as his "friend".

He also spoke with Xi in a separate conversation, describing the pair's relationship as "very special".

Beyond the warmth and shared niceties, however, the three men had different goals and motivations for the sit-down.

World.title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
World.content:
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.

World.title: Fiona the hippo dies after swallowing a hat at Cincinnati Zoo
World.content:
"We are in shock at the moment," Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn't anymore."

Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.

"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.

While she seemed fine at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system.

An ultrasound before her death showed the hat passing through Fiona's small intestine. A zookeeper said surgery was not an option for full-grown hippos and "our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own".

The zoo also tried a different approach to attempt to get the hat to pass by encouraging Fiona to stand on a vibration plate platform borrowed from a local horse farm.

"Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn't fight anymore," Jenike said.

Fiona was born premature at the Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.

World.title: Judge finds Thomas Markle mentally fit to stand trial on child abuse charges
World.content:
A judge in Florida has declared Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, to be mentally competent to stand trial for possessing indecent images of children.

The hearing came after an evaluation by a court-appointed psychiatrist conducted on Prince Harry's 82-year-old father-in-law.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was ordered to stay in jail pending trial earlier this month after allegedly removing a location monitoring device.

The FBI arrested Markle on 6 November at an elderly care home that specialises in dementia. His arrest came after a search of a storage unit he had allegedly rented in Los Angeles uncovered the abuse material.

Markle appeared in court in Tampa in a wheelchair, and his lawyers did not dispute the court-appointed psychiatrist's finding that he is mentally competent to understand the nature and consequences of the charge against him.

His next court hearing is scheduled for early December, but any trial is expected to take place in California, where the federal charge was filed.

Inside the storage units in Los Angeles the FBI says agents found about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades.

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

On Monday, police in the Philippines asked prosecutors to charge Markle with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.

Last month, police there obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.

World.title: Police detain five over disappearance of five-year-old boy
World.content:
The Police Command in Cross River State has apprehended five people over suspected involvement in the disappearance of a five-year-old boy in Adim community, Biase Local Government Area of the state.

Sunday Eitokpah, the police spokesperson in Cross River, disclosed this in a statement to reporters in Calabar on Thursday.

Mr Eitokpah, an assistant superintendent of police, said the child, a nursery school pupil in Adim, reportedly left home for school on Monday but had not returned.

He said the child’s father reported the incident to the police at about 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday after the family could not trace his whereabouts.

The police spokesperson said personnel from the command visited the community and began investigations that led to the detention of five suspects.

Mr Eitokpah further said the suspects have been handed over to the Violence Crime Response Unit for further investigation to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

He said the Commissioner of Police in the state, Ajo Ordue, directed a thorough investigation into the matter and ordered intensified efforts to locate the missing child.
