Questions subsequently emerged about the vessel’s cargo, movements, possible activities, and the circumstances surrounding its initial presence along Liberia’s coastline.

Although allegations and speculation about possible contraband circulated during the incident, no publicly established findings have confirmed those allegations.

Following diplomatic and security engagements between Monrovia and Abidjan, the vessel was returned to Liberia in late August, reportedly arriving on August 27 under the command of the Liberian Coast Guard.

Its return was expected to provide Liberian authorities an opportunity to conduct a comprehensive investigation and publicly account for the circumstances surrounding its interception.

Instead, the vessel and its seven crew members remained under state custody, with no comprehensive public account of the investigation’s findings.

The prolonged detention eventually prompted the vessel’s management and the seven crew members to seek judicial intervention through a habeas corpus petition.

The petition challenged the legality of their continued confinement and resulted in Judge Banwon’s order directing their release by Wednesday afternoon.

The Ministry’s failure to meet that deadline, followed by the continued detention of the vessel and crew on Thursday, has now triggered the issuance of a contempt summons against the Attorney-General.

For the seven crew members, the case represents months of uncertainty and detention aboard a vessel whose presence in Liberian waters has remained shrouded in unanswered questions.

The Attorney-General will have an opportunity to explain the Ministry’s position and show cause why contempt proceedings should not proceed.

The country’s chief legal officer has now been summoned to answer before that same court.

The IB Atlantic IV controversy has therefore entered a new phase, one in which the government is not only being asked to explain a mysterious vessel, but also to account for its continued detention of the ship and its crew after a judicial order for their release.

All eyes are now on the Temple of Justice on Friday, November 20, when Cllr. Betty Lamin-Blamo is expected to appear before Criminal Court ‘A’ and answer the court’s summons.

World.title: Liberia: 23 Years After the Guns Fell Silent, Opposition Arrests and Prosecutions Test Liberia’s Post-War Bargain
World.content:
Monrovia – In 2003, a group of Liberian women nearly gave up on the peace talks in Accra because they had no money. Leymah Gbowee told a gathering in Monrovia this week that a US$10,000 grant from the African Women’s Development Fund kept them going. To women who had buried husbands, sons and neighbors, she said, it felt like a million dollars.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The war they were trying to end had reached every corner of the country. There was “not a single home in this country that had not been touched by the war,” Gbowee recalled. An estimated 250,000 Liberians died between 1989 and 2003.



Also speaking at Monday’s gathering was former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, who led the country out of those ashes. Sirleaf, who turned 88 last month, delivered a warning. Twenty-three years of unbroken peace, she said, could be undone if Liberia’s leaders fail to build unity, inclusion and equal opportunity.

She did not name President Joseph Boakai or any case. But her words land at a tense moment. A former House speaker faces a retrial over the burning of the Capitol. A former vice president sits in Monrovia Central Prison awaiting a drug trial. And the main opposition party says the justice system has been turned into a weapon against it. Critics fear the government’s approach, whatever its legal merits, could chip away at the fragile consensus that has held Liberia together since 2003.

“Peace is not enough”

Sirleaf spoke at the West African Women Peacebuilding Convening, hosted by the Gbowee Peace Foundation Africa. Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti was also on the program.



She traced Liberia’s unraveling to the April 1980 coup that toppled President William R. Tolbert, Jr. From there, she said, the country lost not only its peace but almost everything it had built. She urged Liberians to celebrate 23 years without war, then warned that peace alone was not enough. It had to be matched by unity, inclusion and equal opportunity, and those in power, she said, should beware.

She also told the women in the room that their work was unfinished. “Women brought the peace, now women must help keep the peace,” she said.

Coded as it was, the message was not hard to read in Monrovia. Exclusion, a sense that the state belonged to one group, was a thread that ran through the grievances of 1980 and the wars that followed.

A warning from someone who knows the cost

Few Liberians are better placed to issue such a warning, and few carry more of the history it touches. Sirleaf took office in January 2006, little more than two years after the Accra peace agreement ended 14 years of civil war. She inherited a country with no electricity grid, gutted ministries, disarmed but restless ex-fighters and roughly 15,000 UN peacekeepers on the ground.

Over 12 years, she oversaw two elections, debt relief, the UN mission’s drawdown and, in 2018, the first peaceful transfer of power from one elected Liberian president to another in decades. The 2011 Nobel Peace Prize she shared with Gbowee recognized that work.

Her record is not without question marks.

In 2009, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission recommended that she be barred from public office for her early support of Charles Taylor, a recommendation the Supreme Court later held unconstitutional. Critics also accused her government of nepotism and of letting corruption take root.

But on the narrow point she raised this week, her experience is hard to dismiss. Her government kept rivals inside the tent, including some who had fought on opposite sides of the war. The peace she managed was built on the idea that no group should feel it had been pushed outside the system.

The cases

The former speaker. J. Fonati Koffa was Speaker of the House when a fire tore through the Capitol Building’s joint chambers on December 18, 2024, at the height of a bitter fight over his removal. In 2025, a special grand jury handed down a 63-count indictment against him and 13 others, including sitting lawmakers, on charges ranging from arson to attempted murder.

FrontPageAfrica’s own reading of that indictment found no direct evidence tying Koffa to the planning or execution of the fire, only hearsay and links through his staff. Koffa resigned the speakership in May 2025. On January 2, 2026, the trial judge dissolved the jury, citing alleged juror misconduct. In August, the Supreme Court rejected Koffa’s petition and cleared the way for a retrial. Nearly two years after the fire, he still has no verdict.

The former vice president. On August 19, Jewel Howard-Taylor was on her way to catch a flight to Accra, where she was due to give a keynote speech, when authorities stopped her at Roberts International Airport. Prosecutors charged her with drug trafficking and money laundering tied to the cocaine network behind Liberia’s largest drug busts. They allege she accepted payments and met members of the network in Dubai. She denies the charges.

On September 24, Criminal Court “C” denied her bail. The 63-year-old former senator, who lost her son Philip in January, has been held at Monrovia Central Prison since. Reports say the leaders of Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire and Rwanda privately questioned the circumstances of her arrest. Former President George Weah has called her detention political persecution.

The others. Former Finance Minister Samuel Tweah was acquitted by a jury in May in a US$6.2 million corruption case. Last week, former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah and others were sentenced to 10 years over Saudi-donated rice. In August 2025, police helped carry out a court-ordered eviction that ended with the demolition of the CDC’s Congo Town headquarters. And Weah himself now faces unconfirmed talk of being called in for questioning, which the government has dismissed.

The government’s case

The Boakai administration rejects the charge of persecution. Officials argue that a government elected on a promise to fight corruption and impunity cannot exempt people because they belong to the opposition. The Unity Party has pointed to the drug crackdown as proof that the law is being applied evenly.

Boakai made the point bluntly after the CDC headquarters was torn down. “The law is the law,” he told reporters, insisting the police were enforcing a court ruling, not a political decision.

The record is not one-sided. Juries have acquitted as well as convicted. Tweah walked free, and two defendants in the rice case were sent for retrial after jurors could not agree.

Kemayah’s conviction came after a full trial, and he keeps his right to appeal. The cocaine seizures were real, and the pressure on Liberia to confront trafficking is coming from its own citizens and its foreign partners alike.

The opposition, for its part, has not always backed its claims of selective prosecution with evidence. But perception matters in a country where the line between political defeat and personal danger was once very thin.

Why critics fear for the peace

The worry is less about any single case than about the pattern, and about what it tells the losers of Liberia’s elections. Since 2003, the country’s peace has rested on an unwritten bargain: you can lose power without losing your freedom, your property or your life.

The CDC says it kept its side of that bargain. Its leaders like to point out that the party conceded the 2023 election when Weah lost by a razor-thin margin. “We conceded the election peacefully with a margin of just 17,000 votes,” Janga Kowo, then the party’s secretary-general, told supporters in June 2025, warning that the government had crossed a red line. When the party’s headquarters came down, Weah urged supporters not to take the law into their own hands. That restraint has held. The fear is that it will not hold forever.

There is also a double standard that many Liberians notice. The government moves quickly against today’s opponents, but justice for the war’s victims keeps slipping. The TRC recommended a war crimes court in 2009. Boakai has backed one, but lawmakers will not take up the bill until January 2027, and the proposed US$1.2 billion national budget sets aside no money for it. Many of the men accused of atrocities in the TRC report have died without facing a judge.

For families who lost a father at a checkpoint or a daughter in a massacre, that contrast is hard to accept. Accountability that reaches the current opposition but not the warlords can look less like justice and more like politics.

What is at stake

Liberia heads toward the 2029 elections with its peace intact but its politics raw. How the courts handle Koffa’s retrial and Howard-Taylor’s case will shape whether Liberians see a government cleaning house or settling scores.

The test implied by Sirleaf’s warning is simple to state and hard to meet. Prosecutions must be swift, transparent and visibly evenhanded. They must reach allies as readily as rivals, and they must sit alongside a real reckoning with the war, not in place of one.

Gbowee’s generation of women prayed outside the negotiating rooms in Accra until the men inside signed. The peace they won has now outlasted the war that came before it. Whether it outlasts this moment depends on whether every Liberian, in power or out of it, still believes there is a place for them inside the system.

World.title: Liberia: Justice Ministry Defies Court Order to Release IB Atlantic IV, Seven Crew Members
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Ministry of Justice has failed to comply with a court order directing the release of the mysterious vessel IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members by 4:00 p.m. Wednesday, November 18, raising fresh questions about the government’s continued detention of the vessel and its crew despite judicial intervention.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Assigned Circuit Judge D. Onesimus Banwon of Criminal Court ‘A’ for Montserrado County had ordered the Ministry of Justice to release the vessel and its crew by the stipulated deadline following a habeas corpus petition challenging their continued detention.



However, as of approximately 5:00 p.m. Wednesday, FrontPage Africa observed that the court’s order had not been carried out.

The seven crew members remained detained aboard the vessel, while lawyers representing them confirmed that their clients had not been released.

Judge Banwon was also observed leaving the court premises at approximately 4:00 p.m., around the time the deadline expired, with the vessel and its crew still under state custody.

The apparent failure to comply with the order has raised questions about the Ministry’s handling of the case and the legal basis for the continued detention of the vessel and its crew.



When contacted late Wednesday evening to confirm whether the vessel and its crew had been released and, if not, to explain the delay, Solicitor General Cllr. Abrahim Sillah declined to provide an explanation.

“I will refer you to find out from the court, my brother,” Sillah told FrontPage Africa.

Ministry Struggles To Explain Continued Detention

Sources within the Ministry of Justice, who spoke to FrontPage Africa on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly, disclosed that the Ministry was still struggling to formulate an explanation for the continued detention of the vessel and its crew.

According to the sources, the difficulty stems from the fact that the public had previously been informed that an investigation was underway into the vessel’s movements and the circumstances surrounding its interception.

The sources said authorities were facing pressure to explain why the vessel and its crew remained detained despite the court’s directive and the absence of publicly disclosed investigative findings establishing grounds for their continued custody.

They further indicated that the Ministry was contemplating releasing the crew members and vessel early Thursday morning, November 19, in an apparent effort to comply with the court’s order, although the Wednesday deadline had already passed.

Such a move, if carried out, would come after the government had missed the deadline established by the court.

As of Wednesday evening, however, no official confirmation had been issued that the release had taken place.

Nearly Three Months In Custody

The detention of the IB Atlantic IV and its seven crew members has become one of Liberia’s most unusual maritime security cases, beginning with the vessel’s unexplained presence off York Island in Grand Cape Mount County in August.

The Comoros-flagged vessel initially attracted attention after lingering in Liberian coastal waters, prompting concerns among residents and security authorities about its presence, movements and possible activities.

The situation escalated when Liberian security forces, including the Armed Forces of Liberia Coast Guard, reportedly attempted to intercept the vessel as it moved farther offshore toward Rivercess County.

On August 4, then Armed Forces of Liberia Chief of Staff Major General Davidson Forleh confirmed that security forces were pursuing the vessel.

The ship reportedly evaded the initial Liberian pursuit before being intercepted by Ivorian authorities on August 9, transforming the incident into a cross-border maritime security matter.

Its interception in Côte d’Ivoire raised additional questions about how the vessel had moved from Liberia’s coastal waters into the custody of a neighboring country and what authorities had discovered during the operation.

Liberia’s Investigation And The Vessel’s Return

On August 14, Information Minister Jerolinmek M. Piah publicly confirmed that the vessel had been arrested by Ivorian authorities and disclosed that the Liberian Government was engaging its Ivorian counterpart to facilitate its return.

The government also disclosed that a Liberian fishing vessel had reportedly gone out to sea to meet the IB Atlantic IV, prompting the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority to investigate the circumstances surrounding the encounter.

The development widened the scope of the investigation, placing additional focus on the relationship between the foreign vessel and the Liberian fishing boat.

Questions also emerged over the vessel’s cargo, movements, initial presence off York Island and whether any prohibited materials or other suspicious items had been discovered.

Although allegations and speculation about possible contraband circulated during the incident, no publicly established findings have confirmed those allegations.

Following diplomatic and security engagements between Monrovia and Abidjan, the vessel was eventually returned to Liberia in late August, reportedly arriving on August 27 under the command of the Liberian Coast Guard.

Its return was expected to provide Liberian authorities an opportunity to conduct further investigations into its activities and the circumstances surrounding its interception.

Instead, the vessel and its seven crew members remained under security control, with no comprehensive public account of the investigation’s findings.

Court Intervention

The continued detention eventually prompted the vessel’s management and the seven crew members to seek judicial intervention through a habeas corpus petition challenging the legality of their confinement.

Judge Banwon’s order directing their release by 4:00 p.m. Wednesday represented a significant judicial intervention, placing the Ministry of Justice under a clear deadline to act.

The failure to release them by the stipulated time has brought renewed attention to compliance with judicial orders and the constitutional protections afforded to persons held by state authorities.

For the crew members, the ordeal has meant weeks of detention aboard a vessel whose movements have attracted national and regional attention.

For the government, the case presents an increasingly difficult challenge: explaining the circumstances that led to the vessel’s pursuit, its interception in Côte d’Ivoire, its return to Liberia, the prolonged detention of its crew and the apparent failure to comply with a court order directing their release.

As Wednesday night approached, the IB Atlantic IV remained in custody, its seven crew members were still detained, and the public continued to await answers to a maritime mystery that began off Liberia’s coastline and has now become a test of compliance with judicial authority.

World.title: Liberia’s First Foreign Policy:A Feminist Bet in a Retreating World
World.content:
Monrovia – For 179 years, Liberia conducted its foreign relations without a written foreign policy. On Tuesday, November 17, that changed. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs launched what it calls the first foreign policy document in the nation’s history, and with it a Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy that the government bills as Africa’s first.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The launch drew foreign ministers, Nobel Laureate Leymah Gbowee and leading figures of Africa’s women’s movement to Monrovia. It gives Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti a signature achievement weeks before Liberia takes the presidency of the United Nations Security Council.



But a close reading of the government’s own announcement raises questions the ceremony did not answer. Who pays for it? How will success be measured? Can it survive a change of government? And how does a policy built around protecting rights square with some of the deals Monrovia has already struck abroad?

From presidential statements to a written policy

Since independence in 1847, Liberia’s foreign policy has lived in the speeches of its presidents rather than in a document. According to the Foreign Ministry, the last update came in 1971, when William R. Tolbert, Jr. restated the country’s foreign policy after succeeding William V. S. Tubman.

Much has changed since Tolbert. The Organization of African Unity became the African Union. ECOWAS and the Mano River Union took on larger roles.



Liberia went through civil war, peacebuilding and democratic consolidation, and is now an elected member of the UN Security Council for 2026–2027.

A written policy is a genuine step. It gives diplomats, investors and partners something to hold the government to. The ministry says the drafting was led by seasoned diplomats, including former ministry officials, with input from ambassadors and missions abroad.

One detail stands out. Cabinet endorsed the policy on May 28, 2026, almost six months before Tuesday’s launch. The ministry has not explained the delay, and the press release does not say where the public can read the full document.

Is it really Africa’s first?

The government’s headline claim needs a qualifier. In 2021, Libya’s then Foreign Minister Najla Mangoush announced at the Generation Equality Forum in Paris that Libya was committing to a feminist foreign policy. At the time, gender-policy trackers recorded Libya as the first African nation to do so.

Libya’s commitment, however, never became a working policy. Analysts noted that its transitional Government of National Unity could not implement it alone, and Mangoush was dismissed in 2023.

Liberian officials have themselves used more careful language in the past. When it validated its feminist foreign policy roadmap, the ministry described Liberia as the first country in Africa to formally commit to a feminist foreign policy, following a government decision in February 2024. The defensible claim is narrower than the headline: Liberia is the first African country to formally adopt and launch a written gender-responsive foreign policy.

Joining a club that is shrinking

Liberia is adopting a feminist foreign policy just as several of its pioneers walk away from it. Sweden coined the concept in 2014 and dropped it in 2022 after a change of government. The Netherlands, Argentina and Germany have since followed, making Germany the fourth country to introduce such a policy and then abandon it.

The pattern is consistent: the policies were tied to a party or a minister, and they did not outlive them. A November 2025 report on the field asked openly whether feminist foreign policy was facing its obituary. Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Spain remain among the active adopters.

The lesson for Liberia is direct. The policy carries the stamp of President Joseph Boakai and Minister Nyanti. Unless it is written into law, funded in the national budget and built into the Foreign Service, it could be shelved by whoever wins the 2029 election.

What the policy promises

The broader foreign policy rests on six priorities: economic diplomacy, national sovereignty, regional integration, peace and security, citizen protection and international cooperation.

The gender-responsive component, which dominates the government’s announcement, has five pillars:

* Women’s rights

* Women’s economic empowerment and inclusive trade

* Women, peace and security

* Climate justice and natural resource governance

* Women’s political representation and leadership

The ministry says the policy grew out of a review that found gaps between Liberia’s gender-equality commitments and the actual presence of women in foreign policy and diplomatic leadership. The Ministry of Gender validated it, and UN Women supported the process, which has run through stakeholder dialogues since at least 2025.

Earlier ministry events produced concrete promises that can now be tested. These include quarterly gender audits at the Foreign Ministry, a Women in Diplomacy Fund, and plans to revise the Foreign Service Manual to require gender parity in training and promotions.

What the announcement leaves out

No price tag. The press release names no budget, no timeline and no targets. A policy without a budget line is a statement of intent, and the government’s reliance on UN Women raises the question of how much of it Liberia owns.

No role for the Legislature. The policy was endorsed by Cabinet, not passed into law. That makes it easy to launch and just as easy to reverse.

Little on hard diplomacy. Six broad priorities get a single sentence. There is nothing on how Liberia will manage relations with the United States and China, its place in a divided ECOWAS, or how economic diplomacy will bring in investment.

The citizen-protection test. “Citizen protection” is listed as a core priority. Yet the government has agreed to accept third-country deportees from the United States, a deal now under scrutiny in the US Senate through Resolution 886. The ministry has not said how that arrangement fits the new framework.

Women at home. A foreign policy that puts women’s political representation at its center will be judged by Liberia’s own numbers. Women remain a small minority in the Legislature, and the ministry has not published how many of Liberia’s ambassadors and senior diplomats are women.

The first test: December at the Security Council

The policy’s first real test comes quickly. Liberia holds the Security Council presidency in December, giving it control of the Council’s agenda for a month. Ministry officials have already pledged to prioritize women’s issues during Liberia’s Council term, and in September President Boakai launched the country’s third National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security in New York.

If the December agenda carries the policy’s pillars into the Council chamber, the launch will look like the start of something. If not, critics will call it a ceremony.

The questions for the government are plain:

1. How much will the policy cost, and where is it in the budget?

2. Where can the public read the full document?

3. What will change in Liberia’s embassies by the end of 2027?

4. Will the government ask the Legislature to write the policy into law so it outlasts this administration?

5. Why did the launch come almost six months after Cabinet’s endorsement?

World.title: Liberia: ArcelorMittal Certifies 40 Liberian Railway Workers, Deepens Local Skills Development
World.content:
A cross-section of the newly certified Train Assistants and Dispatchers alongside Training and Rail Management of ArcelorMittal Liberia.

ArcelorMittal Liberia has certified 40 Liberian railway professionals as 38 Train Assistants and 2 Dispatchers, marking another significant milestone in the company’s commitment to developing local talent and building a highly skilled workforce to support its expanding mining, railway and port operations.

The newly certified personnel completed more than a year of intensive theoretical and practical training, demonstrating the technical competence, operational discipline, and safety awareness required to work in one of Liberia’s most critical industrial sectors. The certification ceremony, held on November 18, 2026, at AML Railway Headquarters in Buchanan, celebrated not only individual achievement but also the growing success of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s long-term workforce localization and human capital development strategy.

As the company advances its multi-billion-dollar expansion program and increases production capacity, developing Liberian talent to take on technical and leadership roles remains a key priority.



The latest graduates join a growing number of switch tenders, train assistants, dispatchers, shunt drivers, train drivers, maintenance personnel, and other railway professionals who have been trained and employed through ArcelorMittal Liberia’s structured Operations technical development programs.

Building skills for Liberia’s industrial future

Railway operations are among the most safety-critical and technically demanding aspects of ArcelorMittal Liberia’s business. Every train movement, operational decision, and communication has a direct impact on the safety of employees, equipment, and infrastructure. For that reason, the company has invested heavily in establishing a structured competency-based training career pathway aligned with international railway operating standards.

The newly certified employees underwent extensive classroom training and practical field exposure covering subjects such as train handling, hazardous commodities, safe train movement, shunting operations, rail safety procedures, wagon operations, dispatching systems, speed and acceleration management, gradients, and yard operations.



The program also included rigorous theoretical and practical assessments to ensure participants met competency requirements before certification.

Speaking during the ceremony, the AML Manager for Operations Training and Compliance, Ruth Negash, praised the graduates for their hard work, safe learning, dedication to excel and perseverance.

She noted that certification was earned through commitment and demonstrated competence, stressing that ArcelorMittal Liberia’s training standards are intentionally rigorous because “we want excellence.”

Negash emphasized that safety remains at the center of every railway role, reminding graduates that their responsibility is to protect themselves, their colleagues, and the equipment that enables operations.

“The railway is Liberian. It’s not going anywhere. It belongs to you and you must take your job very seriously to excel in your careers with high standards for safety, competency and productivity.” she said.

She further highlighted the company’s continued investment in developing future train drivers and railway leaders, noting that certification represents only the beginning of a lifelong learning and career development journey.

Competence before Certification

Manager, AML Operations Training and Compliance, Ruth Negash

The certification exercise formed part of a broader Rail Operations Technical Training and Compliance initiative aimed at strengthening technical competency, operational efficiency, and drive towards best and sustainable safety performance across the railway system.

According to Rail Operations Technical Trainer Madalitso Chabwera, the certification process was designed to verify that participants had successfully met all prescribed competency requirements.

“Our goal is to develop personnel who are technically competent, operationally disciplined, and committed to continuous improvement,” he said.

He noted that the certification was not simply recognition for attending training, but confirmation that each participant had demonstrated the knowledge, practical skills, and professional judgment required to perform safely and effectively in railway operations.

Chabwera described the certification exercise as an important foundation for structured career progression and continued workforce development within ArcelorMittal Liberia’s railway operations.

“Competence is built when theory is understood and practice is respected,” he told participants.

Supporting workforce localization

Rail Operations Technical Training Specialist, Madalitso Chabwera

The certification reflects ArcelorMittal Liberia’s broader vision of empowering Liberians to take increasing ownership of the country’s industrial infrastructure.

Over the past few months, the company has strengthened its rail training systems through technical gap assessments, competency evaluations, development of structured career pathways, added switch-tender training programs, and upgraded the design of new operating procedures aimed at improving safety, performance and productivity.

General Manager for Railway Operations, Felix Lage, said the achievement demonstrates the immense potential of Liberian talent when given access to training and development opportunities.

“Liberians have talent. We just need to find them, develop them, train them, and put them to work,” he said.

He encouraged the graduates to view the certification not merely as securing employment, but as the beginning of a professional career with long-term growth opportunities.

“You do not have a job. You have a career,” he told the graduates.

Career Pathways and future opportunities

For many of the graduates, becoming a certified Train Assistant or Dispatcher is only the first step on a structured career pathway that can lead to higher technical and supervisory positions.

Deputy General Manager for Railway Operations, Mulbah Gbozee, challenged the graduates to continue building their skills and preparing for greater responsibilities within the operation.

He noted that graduates could progress through several levels of railway operations, including Shunt Driver, Train Driver, Dispatcher, Superintendent, Rail Operations Manager, and other leadership positions.

“This is just the start,” Gbozee told participants. “The opportunity is in your hands.”

The company recently completed gap assessments, theory refreshers, technical assessments, and competency verification exercises, ensuring that employees meet the international railway standards required for advancement within the newly developed AML Railway Operations training pathway framework.

Deputy General Manager for Railway Operations, Mulbah Gbozee

Training Liberians to drive expansion

The certification comes at a critical time as ArcelorMittal Liberia continues implementing its expansion plans, which will significantly increase mining and railway activity.

The focus on workforce development aligns with ArcelorMittal Liberia’s longstanding commitment to skills transfer, localization, and sustainable economic development. Through structured training programs, apprenticeships, learnerships, scholarships, and technical development initiatives, the company continues to create opportunities for Liberians to acquire world-class industrial skills while building long-term careers.

A proud achievement

On behalf of the graduates, newly certified Train Assistant Victor James thanked the company, trainers, supervisors, and mentors who supported their development throughout the program.

He described the certification as an important milestone that has opened new opportunities for career growth and professional advancement.

For the graduates, the certificates represent the successful completion of hundreds of hours of training and practical experience. For ArcelorMittal Liberia, they represent something much larger: another step in building a highly skilled Liberian workforce capable of supporting one of Africa’s most significant mining, railway, and logistics operations.

As the company continues its expansion, the investment in people remains as important as the investment in infrastructure. By equipping Liberians with internationally aligned technical skills and creating clear pathways for advancement, ArcelorMittal Liberia is helping to build the next generation of Railway professionals while contributing to Liberia’s broader human capital development and economic transformation.

World.title: Liberia’s Embassy Hails Washington’s Report, but Leaves Out ‘Corruption’
World.content:
MONROVIA — The U.S. State Department’s 2026 Investment Climate Statement on Liberia makes two arguments. First, the economy is improving. Second, the state is still failing the investors it wants to attract.

On Tuesday, the Embassy of the Republic of Liberia in Washington answered with a press release. It praised the first argument in detail and wrapped the second in diplomatic language.

What the Embassy praised



The Embassy said it was “particularly heartened” by six findings:

• Growth of 5.1 percent in 2025

• A 31.5 percent rise in export volumes

• Inflation down to 8.5 percent by December 2025



• Investment opportunities in mining, agriculture, energy and other sectors

• Laws allowing up to 100 percent foreign ownership in many sectors

• Membership in international arbitration systems, a $40 million World Bank trade project, and modernization of the Freeport of Monrovia

It also listed President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s governance initiatives: asset declarations, reviews of public contracts and work toward a specialized anti-corruption court.

None of that is false. The report does acknowledge it. As FrontPageAfrica reported earlier this month, the statement acknowledges what the government likes to say: growth reached 5.1 percent in 2025, exports surged, and inflation cooled.

What the Embassy left out

The word “corruption” appears nowhere in the Embassy’s release. Neither do “bribery,” “cronyism,” “extortion,” or “procurement.” The report’s criticism is reduced to one sentence about “areas requiring continued attention.” It lists those areas as “institutional effectiveness, regulatory administration, infrastructure, access to finance.”

The report itself is much blunter. It says:

• Stakeholders widely regard corruption as the main brake on Liberia’s democratic consolidation and economic growth.

• Some officials put short-term personal gain ahead of the investment climate.

• Political cronyism often influences decisions that should be based on merit.

• Businesses can easily operate illegally if they pay the right political interests. Companies that follow the rules get little help and may be targeted for bribes.

• Corruption is worst in government procurement, contract and concession awards, customs and taxation, regulatory approvals and government payment systems.

• Multinational firms often report being charged fees that are not in their investment agreements. Accounts of extortion “at multiple levels of government are common.”

• Civil society groups investigating corruption report being targeted with bribe requests, visa threats and unfounded legal allegations.

Calling all of this “regulatory administration” is not a summary of the report. It is a rewrite.

Same reforms, different weight

The two documents also disagree on how far reforms have gone. The Embassy presents Boakai’s anti-corruption measures as accomplishments. The report calls them “nascent reform efforts.”

The details matter. According to the report, the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission is still advocating for a specialized criminal court, and the Legislature is still considering removing the statute of limitations on corruption prosecutions. The Embassy does not mention the statute-of-limitations amendment, arguably the most concrete reform in the pipeline.

The report also says Liberia’s membership in the ECOWAS, African Union and UN anti-corruption conventions “has not produced measurable reductions in corruption.” It says the laws are on the books but enforced inconsistently, and that even-handed enforcement is “the exception rather than the rule.”

The quiet pushback

The most telling paragraph in the release is its most diplomatic. The Embassy notes that “such assessments draw upon multiple institutional, public, and private-sector sources.” It offers to “enrich the analysis with updated official statistics” toward a “more balanced understanding.”

In diplomatic language, this politely questions Washington’s sources. The report’s corruption findings rest on business surveys and U.S. Embassy reporting, meaning what investors say happens to them. Official statistics can update a GDP figure. They cannot rebut a company’s account of being charged an unofficial fee at the port.

Ownership: the full picture

The Embassy highlights that Liberian law allows up to 100 percent foreign ownership in many sectors. The report adds a qualifier the release omits: the 2010 Investment Act restricts market access for foreign investors, including Americans, in certain sectors. Both statements are true. Investors need both.

Year after year, the same findings

The strongest indictment may be repetition. Two years ago, the 2024 statement already said that government decisions affecting the business sector are driven more by political cronyism than investment climate considerations. It also said Liberia’s association with these conventions has done little to reduce rampant government corruption and that no laws explicitly protect NGOs that investigate corruption. The 2026 statement repeats these findings almost word for word.

When Washington’s language on cronyism and corruption barely changes over three reports, the problem is not missing context or outdated statistics. The underlying conditions have not changed enough to justify new wording.

The real test

The Embassy is right that dialogue with Washington is useful, and its tone is constructive. But investors read the same report the Embassy read, and they will notice which half it chose to quote.

A more convincing response would answer the corruption findings directly. It would publish procurement and concession complaints and how they were resolved, report LACC prosecutions and convictions, push the statute-of-limitations amendment through the Legislature, fund the specialized court, and give investors a protected way to report unofficial fees.

Until then, the growth figures will keep getting the press releases and the fine print will keep getting repeated.

World.title: Liberia’s Jodie Marian Reid Joins Continental Stakeholders at CAF Women’s Football Forum in Cairo
World.content:
MONROVIA — Liberian football administrator Jodie Marian Reid has participated in the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Women’s Football Club Development Forum, held November 13–14 at the Renaissance Cairo Mirage City Hotel in Cairo, Egypt.

By Christopher C. Walker, [email protected]

Reid, who serves on both the CAF Women’s Committee and the continental body’s BK Task Force, joined club representatives, member association officials, and football executives from across Africa to chart strategies for strengthening women’s club football.



The two-day summit focused on evaluating the state of the women’s game on the continent, with deliberations centered on professionalization, financial sustainability, and raising the competitiveness of domestic leagues.

Delegates exchanged best practices and examined structural bottlenecks hindering club growth, including governance models, talent development pathways, and private-sector investment.

Pushing for Action Over Rhetoric

Speaking on the sidelines of the forum, Reid stressed that advancing the women’s game requires moving past policy discussions toward tangible institutional backing.



“The development of women’s football requires more than passion for the game; it requires deliberate investment, strong institutions, effective leadership, sustainable club structures, and collective commitment,” Reid said. “We must move from conversations to concrete actions that create lasting opportunities for women and girls in football.”

Reid’s presence in Cairo underscores Liberia’s active representation in CAF’s decision-making circles as the confederation seeks to overhaul the women’s football ecosystem.

Outcomes from the gathering are expected to guide upcoming CAF initiatives aimed at making domestic women’s competitions more commercially viable, professionally managed, and visible across the continent.

World.title: Zambia Railways calls for removal of illegal structures
World.content:
Zambia Railways has called on local authorities across the country to emulate Lusaka City Council by removing illegal structures and trading activities constructed within railway reserves to safeguard railway infrastructure and public safety.

Zambia Railways Manager Public Relations, Sombe Longwani, says the company welcomes the recent operation by Lusaka City Council to remove illegal structures and trading activities in Kamwala.

Ms Longwani said similar interventions should be extended to other towns where people have encroached on railway reserves.

Ms Longwani added that the presence of structures and trading activities within these areas compromise the integrity of railway infrastructure and affect the company’s ability to effectively manage and maintain its railway corridor.

She highlighted that railway reserves are critical operational areas that must remain free from encroachment to protect infrastructure, ensure public safety and facilitate the smooth movement of trains.

Ms Longwani has warned that people conducting activities close to railway tracks are exposed to the risk of serious injury or death in the event of a train accident or derailment.

“Rail safety is a shared responsibility, and this is why we continue to appeal, as well as sensitise the public on the dangers of encroachment, especially an event that we have a derailment,” she stated.

Ms Longwani also expressed concern over the dumping of waste within railway reserves, saying the practice poses risks to train operations and the environment.

She has since appealed to members of the public to respect railway boundaries and refrain from constructing structures or conducting activities within the reserved areas.

“Our appeal to the Public remains simple, we need to safeguard railway infrastructure by keeping railway reserves free from illegal settlements and activities”, she further added.

Ms Longwani noted that Zambia Railways remains committed to working with relevant government institutions, local authorities and other stakeholders to protect railway infrastructure and promote public safety.

World.title: Katotobwe reaffirms private sector-led economic growth
World.content:
Government has reaffirmed its commitment to promoting private sector-led growth, economic diversification, value addition, investment and job creation as key drivers of Zambia’s economic transformation.

The commitment was made by Minister of Trade and Export Caroline Katotobwe during a stakeholder’s engagement cocktail hosted by ABSA Bank Zambia in Lusaka.

“Whilst Government has an important responsibility to provide policy direction, maintain a stable and predictable regulatory environment for businesses to thrive, the private sector remains critical to Zambia’s economic transformation,” Ms Katotobwe said.

She said the private sector remains critical to driving production, innovation and employment creation.

Ms Katotobwe said the establishment of the Ministry of Trade and Export in October 2026 reflects the Government’s commitment to strengthening the country’s trade and export development agenda.

She said the Ministry is promoting domestic and international trade by focusing on increasing Zambia’s participation in regional and global markets while collaboration with financial institutions such as ABSA remains absolutely critical in advancing the trade and export agenda.

The Minister encouraged ABSA to continue supporting small and medium enterprises, women-owned and youth-led enterprises, agribusiness and value addition initiatives and export-oriented businesses by ensuring financing is accessible to both established and emerging enterprises with export potential.

Ms Katotobwe said the Ministry remains committed to engaging with the private sector to better understand the challenges businesses face in accessing markets and participating in trade and to work with relevant institutions to address those constraints.

She commended ABSA Bank Zambia for hosting the engagement and encouraged the bank to continue leveraging its regional presence, financial expertise and partnerships to support Zambian businesses, facilitate investment and expand access to trade finance.

Meanwhile, ABSA Bank Zambia Managing Director, Mizinga Melu said the bank organised the meeting to allow the Minister to meet its clients and share the Government’s trade and export agenda.

“As a Bank, we have been reflecting on the role we can play to push the Grow Zambia agenda,” Ms Melu said.

She said ABSA is also looking forward to growing the tourism sector and has reduced its interest rate by two percentage points following the recent reduction in the monetary policy rate by the Bank of Zambia.

World.title: Chieftainess Shimukunami commends President Hichilema
World.content:
Chieftainess Shimukunami VIII of the Lamba people in Lufwanyama District has commended President Hakainde Hichilema’s visionary leadership on infrastructure development especially in rural parts of the country.

The traditional leader whose Chiefdom is benefiting from the World Bank financed Improved Rural Connectivity Project (IRCP) and managed by the Road Development Agency (RDA) says the area is not only getting improved road network but also other support community infrastructure such as a school, water infrastructure, market shelter and other amenities.

Chieftainess Shimukunami was speaking when Minister of Infrastructure and Urban Development Collins Nzovu, accompanied by RDA Chief Executive Officer Nelson Chuma and other government officials paid a courtesy call at her palace.

She noted that the completion of two roads in her chiefdom is extremely important to the people.

She revealed that due to the first ever proper road, travelling from the chiefdom to Chingola-Solwezi road now takes few minutes as compared to the past when movements were hard.

“We presented these projects some time ago, and I am very pleased that the UPND Government has finally delivered on them for the people of Chitunda. We can now travel directly from the palace to Chingola, connect to the Solwezi Road and proceed towards Chingola. This has made movement much easier,” she said.

She added that the area through which the road passes is also very busy, particularly in terms of trading and other economic activities.

And She hailed Mr Nzovu with his entourage for inspecting the road projects stating that leaders who are delivering development to the people of Zambia are expected to come on the ground and monitor the progress of works.

“My people believe in the President’s vision and are happy with the development agenda. They are confident that Zambia can move from its current position to a higher level of development through this vision.

The traditional leader added that the situation has changed with more health infrastructure and personnel serving the community, alongside the improved road network,” she said.

Meanwhile, Mr Nzovu highlighted that support community infrastructure including a permanent classroom, teachers houses and water reticulation at Kasungu primary school are being constructed.

The Minister explained that this is to ensure that the growing community within road U053 are receiving social services.

“the decision to do the road network and support infrastructure around the community is what President Hakainde Hichilema has directed us to do,” he said.

Mr Nzovu assured Chieftainess Shimukunami that the road will be handed over to the chiefdom by December this year.

The Minister expressed satisfaction with the contractor on the road works being done.

Addressing the contractor, Zhongmei Engineering Group Limited, Mr Nzovu stressed the need to ensure that a proper drainage is done on the U053 road in Lufwanyama.

Confirming with the RDA Director on some of the dangers that quickly damage roads, Mr Nzovu observed poor drainage and overloading.

Mr Chuma explained that a good drainage system especially on gravel helps the road to remain in good condition for a longer period.

RDA Copperbelt Province Roads Engineer Bernard Zulu said the World Bank funded project deals with rehabilitation of primary feeder roads of 112.2 kilometres in Chingola and Lufwanyama districts of Copperbelt province.

He noted that the 243-million-kwacha project runs for seven months and by the end of December, works are supposed to finish.

He added that the scope of works have other components of drilling boreholes of which five have been drilled, constructing bus and market shelters, and a storage facility in Lufwanyama.

World.title: Govt. reaffirms commitment to recruiting more health workers
World.content:
Muchinga Province Minister, Jairo Simbeye, has reaffirmed government’s commitment to recruiting more health workers as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s healthcare system and address human resource gaps in the sector.

‎Mr Simbeye says the recruitment drive demonstrates the government’s commitment to improving access to quality healthcare services through the availability of competent and motivated health personnel.

‎The Provincial Minister was speaking during a combined graduation ceremony for 219 nursing and midwifery graduates from Chilonga, and Micheal Chilufya Sata Colleges of Nursing and Midwifery Schools held under the theme “shaping the future of healthcare in nursing, midwifery and public health nursing”.

‎Mr Simbeye indicated that the government recognises human resources for health as a strategic priority in achieving an effective healthcare system.

‎He pointed out that healthcare infrastructure alone cannot guarantee quality service delivery without competent, ethical and committed health professionals to manage facilities and attend to patients.

‎Mr Simbeye stressed that the qualifications obtained by the graduates come with the responsibility of safeguarding lives, particularly during childbirth, newborn care and the prevention of diseases.

‎He urged the graduates to uphold professionalism, accountability and integrity, warning them against negligence, discrimination, breach of patient confidentiality, misuse of medicines and public resources, as well as other unethical practices.

‎Mr Simbeye further encouraged the newly qualified nurses and midwives to embrace rural postings, stating that healthcare workers serving remote communities play an equally important role in saving lives and preventing disease outbreaks.

He added that government was working to bridge the rural-urban development gap through increased investment in infrastructure and service delivery.

‎And, Mr Simbeye disclosed that the government had constructed 14 maternity annexes in Muchinga, contributing to a reduction in the maternal mortality ratio from 132 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2025 to 86 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2026.

‎Mr Simbeye further highlighted government’s collaboration with the Swiss government through Solidarmed in supporting 10 nursing and midwifery training institutions, as well as selected health facilities, through infrastructure development and the provision of medical and surgical supplies.

He said Mpika, Isoka, Nakonde and Chinsali District Hospitals had also benefited from mini skills laboratories, while Nakonde received a student boarding hostel.

‎He also encouraged the graduates to consider volunteering in their communities while awaiting further employment opportunities.

‎‎Mpika Diocese Bishop, Edwin Mulandu, advised nurses and midwives to recognise the human needs behind every medical diagnosis by providing compassionate care, exercising sound professional judgement and continuously improving their knowledge and skills.

‎Bishop Mpundu also called for improved support for health professionals deployed to rural areas, particularly young women, through adequate accommodation, staff safety, supportive supervision and opportunities for further training.

World.title: Respect Fashion Sakala’s decision to retire
World.content:
International striker Fashion Sakala’s announcement that he has retired from international football will no doubt divide opinion among Zambian football fans.

Some will feel he still had much to offer the Chipolopolo. Others will question the timing. Others still will be disappointed that a player who wore the captain’s armband has chosen to step away.

All those feelings are understandable. But they must not overshadow one fundamental truth: this was a personal choice, and it deserves respect.

Sakala did not stumble into the national team. He earned it, from playing barefoot in Eastern Province, to being taken to trials on his father’s bicycle, to leading Zambia and singing the national anthem with his teammates.

He has given his country his energy, his talent and his pride. He has felt the joy of the proud moments and the pain of the disappointing days, just as the supporters have.

No player owes the nation an endless career. International football demands sacrifice, physical and mental, away from family and club commitments. When a player, after much reflection, decides the time has come to step aside, that decision should be honoured, not attacked.

Respect does not mean we must all agree with the decision. Fans are entitled to wish he had stayed longer. What respect means is that we do not turn disappointment into insults, speculation or bitterness.

Sakala has thanked God, his family, his teammates, coaches, staff, FAZ and the supporters. He has left with gratitude, and with a message of hope to the young boy playing barefoot today that there is a place for him in the Chipolopolo too.

That is a dignified exit.

Zambia will move on. New players will come, new leaders will emerge, and the Chipolopolo will continue. But as we turn that page, let us remember what Sakala gave, and let us wish him well.

He wore the jersey with pride. Now let him cheer for Zambia with that same pride, as a supporter, like the rest of us.

(Written by Mulenga Chapoloko)

World.title: SUPER LEAGUE: Eagles open five-point lead
World.content:
Green Eagles have opened a five-point lead at the top of Stream B of the Super Division after coming from behind to beat Green Buffaloes 2-1 in a midweek fixture at Independence Stadium in Choma.

The Eagles needed a stoppage-time goal to edge the Buffaloes in an entertaining encounter.

Buffaloes made a bright start to the game and took a 13th-minute lead through Golden Mashata, much to the dissatisfaction of the home crowd.

Eagles replied after 35 minutes with an equaliser netted by experienced striker Moses Phiri, the former Zanaco and Nkana striker.

The home side had to wait until four minutes into second-half stoppage time to net the winner through winger Joy Yolamu.

Goals from Phiri and Yolamu propelled Coach Perry Mutapa’s side to victory.

“It was an exciting game, though certainly not an easy one. Most importantly, we must learn to finish games off in the first half,” Mutapa said after the match.

“The most cardinal thing today was having impact players who came in and did their part. When you look at last season, things were very difficult for the team around this exact stage of the campaign. I am very happy that our impact players stepped up and delivered today,” he added.

Eagles now have 17 points, five ahead of second-placed Buffaloes, after seven matches played.

In Stream A, Kansanshi Dynamos and Trident forced a goalless draw in the Northwestern derby in Solwezi.

Kansanshi are seventh on the table with six points, just a point above eighth-placed Trident, from seven matches played.

Nkana top Stream A with 16 points, followed by Konkola Blades on 15 points.

World.title: Live by your word on term limits, Katolo tells Hichilema
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema must practise what he preaches on presidential term limits, lawyer and Zambia Must Prosper (ZMP) vice president Milner Katolo has said. Mr Katolo said the President had on several occasions gone on record saying he would not want a third term. However, he said, the President had stayed completely quiet as some people called for the term limit to be removed from the Constitution. Mr Katolo said he found the silence shocking, given the President’s past position. He suspected that the silence was a strategy, because it made no sense for someone so vocal on the issue to say nothing now.

“Hichilema has been on record that people should just do two terms. So, it is quite shocking that he has remained quiet over this matter brewing over the removal of term limits.”

Mr Katolo said term limits were introduced to keep leaders in check. He said the country was coming out of the difficult era of the United National Independence Party (UNIP), when then President Dr Kenneth Kaunda wielded too much power. Presidential terms, he said, ensure that leaders do not hold too much power for too long. He said he did not understand where the excitement for removing the limit was coming from. The country’s forefathers, he said, had made it clear that an individual could only serve two terms.

“People should know that presidential terms allow people not to have too much power and are kept in check.”

Mr Katolo said Zambians would not allow a few people to mutilate the Constitution, which was put in place to protect fundamental human rights. He said people should respect what the forefathers put in place, which was done for the good of the Zambian people and not for selfish gain. He accused some individuals of sponsoring surrogates to push a narrative of limitless rule. The aim, he said, was to ensure that they clung to power. Lawyer Linda Kasonde and activist Brebner Changala have also criticised the police this week for blocking protests against the removal of the term limit.

Under the current Constitution, Article 106(3) provides that a person who has twice held office as President is not eligible for election as President. That provision bars President Hichilema from standing in the 2031 election, as he will have served the maximum two terms. Article 106(1) sets the presidential term at five years, running alongside the term of Parliament. Any amendment requires the procedure set out in Article 79, including a two-thirds majority in the National Assembly. The ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) holds around 180 seats and would need 187 votes to pass such a Bill, according to Ms Kasonde.

The President’s past statements are now at the centre of the debate. In 2022, speaking at the United States Institute of Peace, President Hichilema said Zambians should not entertain moves towards a presidential third term. He said no President is special and that such moves breed autocratic behaviour. He also opposed former President Edgar Lungu’s third-term bid, which was challenged in the Constitutional Court. Mr Katolo said the President should now live by those statements.

Ms Kasonde has also pointed to the numbers in Parliament. The leading opposition party, NRPUP, declared after the 13 August general election that it would collaborate with the ruling party, which could bring a two-thirds majority within reach. Some civil society groups are calling for a referendum instead. Ms Kasonde has warned that a referendum carries its own risks, noting that the 2016 referendum failed to meet the required threshold. She has pointed instead to the third-term attempt under former President Frederick Chiluba, which ended after resistance from civil society and within the ruling party.

Ms Kasonde has noted that Minister of Justice Jack Mwiimbu announced on 13 November that the Executive would not interfere with parliamentary debate on whether to remove the term limit. Mr Mwiimbu has since said Government will not stop citizens from petitioning Parliament or MPs from moving motions to amend the Constitution. Government has also distanced the President from the proposals to abolish term limits. Mr Katolo, however, said the President himself had remained silent on the matter.

World.title: Citizens free to petition Parliament on Constitution, says Mwiimbu
World.content:
Minister of Justice Jack Mwiimbu says Government will not stop citizens from petitioning Parliament or Members of Parliament from moving motions seeking amendments to the Constitution or any other law. Mr Mwiimbu said the right to petition Parliament is a constitutional entitlement that should be respected rather than condemned. He cautioned against threatening or intimidating individuals who exercise their democratic rights.

Those opposed to particular petitions or motions, he said, are equally free to express their views through lawful means. He was speaking during the ministerial handover ceremony at the Ministry of Justice, where he took over from Princess Kasune, now Minister of Tourism.

Mr Mwiimbu said citizens have the freedom to raise matters of national importance through Parliament. He said elected representatives are equally entitled to introduce motions on issues they consider necessary for the country’s governance. Government, he said, will not interfere with these rights, regardless of the differing political opinions surrounding the issues being raised. He expressed concern over the tendency by some members of the public to condemn individuals who exercise their constitutional rights. Disagreements, he said, should instead be addressed through established democratic and legal processes.

The Minister said it would be wrong for Government to stop a petition before the parliamentary process has been concluded. Doing so, he said, would undermine the constitutional freedoms enjoyed by citizens. His remarks come as the national debate over the presidential term limit gathers pace. Article 106(3) of the Constitution bars a person who has twice held office as President from standing again. Calls to remove the provision have drawn strong opposition from civil society, the Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) and opposition figures.

Mr Mwiimbu also said Government is working towards enacting the Political Parties Bill within the constitutional framework. The Constitutional Court has directed that the law must be enacted by 12 April next year. He said the process will involve consultations with relevant stakeholders to ensure the legislation addresses concerns from different sections of society. Disability Rights Watch executive director Wamundila Waliuya has separately called for the Bill to be enacted. He wants it to encourage political parties to promote the participation of persons with disabilities.

The Minister pledged to build on the work done by his predecessor. He said the Ministry of Justice remains central to the Grow Zambia Agenda through legal and institutional reforms. It will facilitate the legislation, contracts and agreements needed to support the country’s economic ambitions. He said effective laws and institutions are essential in assuring investors that their investments, safety and rights are protected. Investors and tourists, he added, want to know that their businesses and personal interests sit within a secure and stable legal framework.

Mr Mwiimbu called for closer collaboration between the Ministry of Justice and other ministries to speed up the enactment of laws needed to advance the rule of law agenda. He urged ministries and public institutions to work closely with his Ministry when preparing legislation. He also asked them to involve the Ministry in the drafting, review and execution of contracts and agreements. He said legal certainty and a strong justice system were critical in attracting both local and foreign investment. The Ministry, he said, occupies a strategic position in maintaining law and order and strengthening the administration of justice.

Ms Kasune said significant progress was made in legislative reform during her time at the Ministry. She cited the constitutional amendment process that resulted in legislation providing for mixed-member proportional representation. She said 67 bills were enacted, 78 bills were submitted in 2025 and 197 statutory instruments were processed during her tenure. Ms Kasune also credited the Attorney General’s and Solicitor General’s offices with recovering K75.6 million and securing K3.6 million in default judgements against Cyber Caliber Energy Limited.

Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha congratulated Mr Mwiimbu on his appointment and commended Ms Kasune for her service. Solicitor General Marshal Muchende urged both ministers to serve Zambians with dedication and integrity in their new portfolios. Mr Mwiimbu has also met the LAZ Council, which is pressing for a review of the Legal Practitioners Act and the Law Association of Zambia Act. He expressed in-principle support for those proposals, subject to their consistency with Government policy.

Addressing the meeting under the theme “𝐃𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐮𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐚𝐧 𝐄𝐫𝐚 𝐨𝐟 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐲: 𝐔𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐅𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞,” Murwira called for a renewed Africa-Nordic partnership anchored on dialogue, mutual respect, peaceful coexistence and shared prosperity.
