World.title: Africa: The Political Choices Behind Better Gynaecological Care
World.content:
guest column

Effective interventions exist for many neglected gynaecological conditions. The challenge is ensuring that national health systems are organised, equipped, and financed to deliver them.

Picture a 15-year-old girl who misses school every month because of heavy menstrual bleeding. She feels dizzy and exhausted, but is told that what she is experiencing is simply part of becoming a woman. Even when she seeks help, a healthcare provider may dismiss her symptoms as normal. She does not know that her condition can be assessed and treated.

Her experience reflects a much wider problem. Across Africa, women and girls continue to live with conditions that cause pain, disability, stigma and lost opportunities, not necessarily because effective interventions do not exist, but because health systems too often fail to recognise their needs and provide appropriate care.



Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB), obstetric fistula and female genital schistosomiasis (FGS) often go undiagnosed and untreated. HMB affects 10–30% of women of reproductive age in Africa, and up to 56 million women and girls in sub-Saharan Africa may have FGS. Approximately 500,000 women and girls worldwide live with obstetric fistula, with the greatest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and Asia.

Although clinically different, these conditions reveal how women's health needs can fall between the cracks. Established programmes, financing priorities, and pathways to care fail to prioritize these conditions across health systems.

For women experiencing heavy menstrual bleeding, symptoms are often normalised, delaying diagnosis and treatment. Obstetric fistula exposes failures in timely access to emergency obstetric care, while women already living with the condition face further barriers to surgical repair and rehabilitation. FGS—a gynecological condition caused by waterborne parasites—frequently goes unrecognised because neglected tropical disease programmes and sexual and reproductive health services operate separately, even though women need care from both.

These are different failures, but they raise a common political question: if effective interventions exist, why do so many women still struggle to access them?

Part of the answer lies in how health priorities are set. National health strategies, essential service packages, and government budgets determine which conditions receive attention, which services are available, and what health systems are expected to deliver. When women's needs are inadequately reflected in these decisions, even proven interventions can remain out of reach.

This is not simply a question of resources, although financing constraints are real. It is also about how existing resources are allocated, how services are organised, and whether health systems are accountable for meeting women's needs beyond pregnancy and childbirth.

Consider FGS. In Kenya, efforts to integrate its recognition and treatment into existing sexual and reproductive health services have demonstrated how programmes can work across traditional boundaries. But translating such approaches into routine care requires sustained investment, trained providers, appropriate diagnostics, and clear responsibilities across programmes.

The lesson is broader than any single condition. Integration cannot mean adding new responsibilities to already stretched health services without providing the resources and capacity to deliver them.

So what needs to change?

First, governments must make these conditions explicit priorities within relevant national health policies, essential service packages, and Universal Health Coverage plans. Recognition in policy is not sufficient on its own, but it provides a foundation for allocating resources, defining responsibilities, and monitoring progress.

Second, those priorities must be reflected in financing and service delivery. This does not necessarily mean creating new vertical programmes. It means strengthening existing primary healthcare, reproductive health and maternal health services, while ensuring access to specialist care where needed. Depending on the condition, that may require investments in provider training, diagnostics, medicines, emergency obstetric services, surgical care or referral systems.

Third, accountability must extend beyond whether a policy exists or a programme has been launched. The more meaningful questions are whether women receive timely diagnoses, can afford appropriate treatment, complete referrals, and experience improvements in their health and quality of life. Existing national and regional monitoring systems should help answer these questions.

This agenda is becoming more urgent as health financing comes under pressure. Official development assistance declined sharply in 2025, adding to the challenges facing countries already working with constrained health budgets. Stronger domestic leadership and resource mobilisation are essential, but international partners must also continue supporting country-led priorities, particularly where additional investment is needed to expand access to care.

There is a compelling economic case for doing so. Research by the McKinsey Health Institute and the World Economic Forum suggests that closing the broader women's health gap could add up to US$1 trillion annually to global GDP by 2040. Yet women's health should not have to be justified solely by its economic returns. Freedom from preventable suffering, access to appropriate treatment, and the ability to live with dignity are important outcomes in their own right.

On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Pathfinder International, the Global Leaders Network, and PMNCH brought these overlooked conditions into a shared policy conversation among health leaders, funders, researchers, and women’s health advocates. The 5th International Conference on Public Health in Africa (CPHIA) from 23rd - 27th November in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the inaugural Women's Health Africa Summit in Abuja, Nigeria on 1 December provide a further opportunity to advance that discussion with governments and partners, connecting it to existing national and continental health priorities.

Close 

The task now is to turn that momentum into decisions about what health systems will recognise, what governments and partners will finance, and how progress will be measured.

For the girl missing school because of heavy bleeding, these decisions are not abstract. They determine whether she will continue to suffer in silence or find a healthcare provider who recognises her symptoms and can offer effective treatment.

That is the real test of political commitment to gynaecological health: not whether these conditions receive greater attention, but whether women and girls experience better care when they need it.

Dr Amina Dorayi - Regional Portfolio Director, West and Central Africa, Pathfinder International

Dr Lwazi Manzi, Head of Secretariat of the Global Leaders Network for Women, Children and Adolescent Health, Private Office of the President of South Africa

Rajat Khosla, Executive Director, Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health

World.title: Ethiopia: Red Cross Warns of Worsening Humanitarian Crisis in Oromia
World.content:
Internally displaced people from the Oromo community in western Oromia shelter in Adama, Ganda Saqaqalloo area, receive community support at a mosque (file photo)

Addis Abeba — The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has warned that the humanitarian situation in Ethiopia's Oromia region is deteriorating amid persistent armed conflict, deadly civilian attacks and growing displacement, saying it is struggling to reach all communities affected by the escalating insecurity.

The organization said on Thursday that communities across several zones of Oromia were enduring severe hardship as fighting and insecurity continued to disrupt their lives. The ICRC, working alongside the Ethiopian Red Cross Society (ERCS), said it had intensified humanitarian assistance in conflict-affected areas, particularly in western and southern Oromia, over recent weeks.

Oromia has been grappling with a protracted armed conflict involving federal forces and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) since 2019, alongside increasingly fragmented security crises, intercommunal violence and clashes along regional boundaries. The deteriorating security situation has also been accompanied by growing public grievances over local governance, alleged coercive practices and economic disruption.

Lat October and early November saw a spike in civilian causalities after armed men killed at least 48 people were killed and more than 31 others seriously injured in a six-hour assault on in Shirka Woreda in Southeast Oromia zone. A subsequent attack in the area reportedly claimed dozens more lives.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The latest security crisis has also intensified along the Oromia-Somali regional border. Fighting erupted in Moyale on October 18 following a dispute over the display of a regional flag and the fatal shooting of a 13-year-old girl, subsequently spreading across several districts along the border between the two regions. The clashes have triggered significant displacement, disrupted local services and deepened food insecurity. The fighting has also paralyzed livestock markets and cross-border trade, further undermining pastoralist livelihoods in Borana.

Meanwhile, insecurity persists in parts of Wollega, in western Oromia zone, where conflict involving overlapping armed factions continues to expose civilians to risks of displacement and restricted access to essential services.

Igor Moroz, deputy head of the Red Cross Oromia Regional Office, said the organization was conducting relief operations in conflict-affected areas, including the former East Wollega, Horo Guduru Wollega, Guji and Borana zones.

"Our team is doing everything they can to reach those suffering amidst the conflict and war with aid," Moroz said.

The organization said it had assisted tens of thousands of households in recent weeks through its local branches. Its interventions included providing medical assistance to 125,000 patients, rehabilitating and handing over two health centers to local communities, and undertaking work on two additional facilities.

In response to water shortages, the Red Cross said it had constructed 300 hand-pump water points, benefiting more than 90,000 people. It also distributed agricultural tools to over 7,000 households to help communities affected by the crisis restore their livelihoods.

Additionally, the organization said it had provided financial assistance to 2,900 households that lost property due to conflict in the former East Wollega, West Wollega and East Borana zones.

The statement also highlighted the plight of 2,300 displaced households in Sasiga and Angar, which faced severe hardship at the beginning of the year. A Red Cross official said an assessment visit found displaced residents in distress and without basic possessions, prompting the organization to provide water and other essential services.

As insecurity persists, the Red Cross said it had engaged armed actors, government authorities and religious leaders to stress the importance of respecting international humanitarian law. It had also trained first responders in the proper handling of human remains during emergency situations. It is also closely monitoring humanitarian emergencies linked to insecurity across Ethiopia.

Close 

Regarding the recent deadly security incident in the border town of Moyale, it said that while investigations were ongoing, it stood ready to provide necessary assistance in coordination with humanitarian partners.

Moroz underscored the growing scale of the crisis and the limitations facing humanitarian responders.

"We are seeing the humanitarian crisis in Oromia grow increasingly worse; we help the people we can, but we cannot be everywhere," he said.

Late last week, Addis Standard reported that the Red Cross had provided food grains and other assistance to households displaced by drought and insecurity in the Oromia region's Central Zone. In a statement at the time, the organization said it had reached more than 500 households, including residents of Fentale district facing food shortages due to drought and households displaced by insecurity in Amaya district. World.title: South Africa: Could Donated AI Wealth Plug SA's HIV Spending Gap?
World.content:
A new generation of wealthy tech founders are gearing up to give — but there are fears their contributions could hamper, rather than improve, the fight against HIV.

Nearly two years after the US cut its health funding dramatically, South Africa's HIV programmes are still playing catch-up.

A windfall could come from AI company founders who are promising to donate much of the astronomical sums they stand to gain when they list their companies on the stock market to charity.

Anthropic (maker of Claude), listed its shares on the stock exchange on 18 November — an Initial Public Offering (IPO) valued at nearly $1.4-trillion (about R23.8-trillion). OpenAI (maker of ChatGPT) valued at $1.1-trillion (about R18.8-trillion) is expected to do the same next year .

But although such support could greatly help in the HIV space, it needs to be carefully implemented to make sure it responds to and respects the real needs of vulnerable communities, HIV activists say.

Other funding sources, such as scaled-up government support, grassroots giving and private sector partnerships are needed to chart a balanced future.

"We're in what may be the most precarious moment in 45 years."

That's how Mitchell Warren, executive director of the United States (US)-based HIV advocacy organisation Avac, describes the global HIV response, nearly two years after President Donald Trump's administration slashed US health funding.



In South Africa, programmes for the people hardest to reach and most at risk of HIV infection are still scrambling to recover.

But a rescue may be coming from an unlikely place: the multi-trillion-dollar fortunes of AI founders who have promised to give much of their wealth away when their companies are listed on the stock market.

However, whether that money arrives, and whether it will help the people who need it the most, is far from certain.

What was lost

South Africa pays for most of its government HIV programmes. Before the US cuts in early 2025, South Africa funded 76% of its response , including 90% of the antiretroviral (ARV) drugs given to people living with HIV in the world's largest treatment programme. The US President's Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) supplied 17% and the Global Fund to Fight Aids, TB and Malaria 7% .

So the country didn't run short of ARVs. But US money filled the gaps the state didn't reach : testing, prevention and treatment for groups with a higher chance to get HIV, such as men who have sex with men, transgender women, sex workers, people who inject drugs, and adolescent girls and young women.

Keeping those services going, which involved tailor-made clinics for such groups including mobile clinics, is "significantly harder" now, Warren says. The US cuts were "so deep, so real, so hurtful, so retaliatory" that many programmes are "still reeling", he says. And the Global Fund, which is putting $345-million (about R5.84-billion) into South Africa's response in the current three-year cycle , is tapering its support to the country and will stop it entirely from 2034 .

The AI windfall

Anthropic (maker of Claude), listed its shares on the stock exchange on 18 November — an initial public offering (IPO) valued at nearly $1.4-trillion (about R23.8-trillion). OpenAI (maker of ChatGPT) valued at $1.1-trillion (about R18.8-trillion) is expected to do the same next year . OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman pledged in May 2024 to give most of his proceeds to charity. Anthropic's Dario Amodei and his co-founders have pledged 80% of theirs .

If those promises are honoured, the resulting sums could dwarf anything global health giving has seen to date. The two companies' pledges alone could add up to $100-billion (about R1.69-trillion) a year . Compare this with the Gates Foundation, one of the biggest donors in global health currently, which gave away around $8.5-billion (about R144-billion) in 2025.

An early sign of what this AI-fuelled giving boom could look like came on 29 October , when the Global Fund approved a mechanism to unlock new philanthropic money for malaria programmes. The so-called Malaria Impact Accelerator could add billions of dollars to the fund's grants by 2031, by allowing philanthropic donors to supplement the Global Fund's existing malaria funding.

The Global Fund doesn't name the philanthropic donors who have pledged towards the fund, or the sums involved beyond a $1-billion (about R16.9-billion) donation target that needs to be raised by the end of March. But GiveWell, a US-based nonprofit that coordinates and directs philanthropic donations , says it's aiming to spend at least $2.5-billion (about R42.3-billion) in new malaria funding from 2027 to 2032, and "potentially several times that amount".

Warren says there are conversations about doing the same for HIV. Such funders are unlikely to write small cheques, he says, and a great use of the grants would be to further scale up lenacapavir , the six-monthly HIV prevention injection which was launched in June in South Africa.

If between one and two million HIV-negative people take the jab each year , the country could end Aids as a public health problem by 2043.

"There's a huge opportunity to go bigger and faster," Warren says, but it can't be "just a procurement exercise", he adds. Health workers must be trained, demand created and key populations (groups with a higher chance of getting HIV) involved.

A question of strategy

But not everyone is cheering. Many of the new donors have previously expressed support for " effective altruism ", a heavily metrics-driven philosophy that prioritises saving the most lives per dollar.

Brett Davidson, a New York-based South African veteran journalist and former director of the media and narratives division of the Open Society Foundations public health programme , says a drawback of this ideology is that it can overlook the need to tackle the injustices that drive disease. "It's just about saving the largest number of lives in the most cost-effective way. It's not interested in systemic transformation," he says.

Margaret McCluskey, a Washington, DC-based senior strategic advisor to The Aurum Institute, a leading South African healthcare research body, fears a shift to technology-focused solutions might lead to interventions lacking in technical, on-the-ground expertise. "Will they understand that they need epidemiologists to tell them what the problems are?"

She also worries about a bias towards novelty. "Everybody wants something new. But there are things that work that have been abandoned, and should be funded."

Other options: grassroots and government

There are more ways to raise the required funds to right South Africa's HIV funding, HIV activists and programme consultants say. One source of support, which many nongovernmental organisations (NGOs) have increasingly turned to, is small-scale, or grassroots philanthropy, which draws on the generosity of ordinary people rather than just the super-wealthy.

An example of this is giving circles, a growing form of community philanthropy, which can be harnessed to steer support towards NGOs and civil society groups that have been struggling since the US cuts. Davidson, in New York, says he is a member of such a circle formed at the start of this year consisting of South Africans living abroad. The circle supports Shout-It-Now, an organisation that delivers free sexual and reproductive health services to South African youth, including HIV prevention and gender-based violence support. As of mid-November, it had raised $7 500 (about R127 000).

Shout-It-Now, which was almost 90% funded by Pepfar before the US cuts , is looking to crowdfunding as one way to future-proof its finances. The point isn't just to raise cash, says Pontsho Pilane, the organisation's external affairs director, but to connect South Africans living abroad around a common cause to "give back to their country".

Close 

Corporate South Africa is another potential fundraising target, says Shout-It-Now chief executive Ntombifikile Mtshali. But unlocking funding from the private sector and wealthy individuals in the country means first you need to change minds, she says: "A lot of people in corporate South Africa, in the rest of society, think HIV is no longer a problem, because they know what it used to look like, and it no longer looks like that."

She welcomes that the South African government is increasingly coming to the table when NGOs ask them to partner on grant applications, says Mtshali. This is a prerequisite for many donors nowadays, she says, as donors want local buy-in to ensure that projects will last beyond the duration of the initial grant.

Rebuilding, not replacing

For all the pain they brought, the upheavals of the last two years offer opportunities to rebuild South Africa's HIV programmes better than they were before, says Warren.

"After an earthquake, architects don't build back the exact same buildings that fell," he says. "By definition, they were not resilient buildings." The task now is to build ones that last, he says.

Heather Sherwin, a Cape Town-based expert in global health financing, agrees. South Africa's challenge is now to ensure that it moves to an integrated HIV service model that maintains funding for at-risk groups, while also retaining the many skilled staff who were trained and paid through aid-funded HIV schemes. "There's all these very skilled people who can really add to the system," she says.

Sherwin favours locally-grounded interventions, and does not believe in waiting for OpenAI and the other AI giants to step into the breach and save South Africa's HIV programmes. "We don't yet know how AI philanthropy will use their money in Africa, and specifically for HIV," she says. "I think it's short-sighted to think that they will come in and replace what was lost."

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 19, 2026
World.content:
Ghana Defends $61m Presidential Jet Purchase

Ghana's government has defended its purchase of a $61 million French-made Falcon 6X presidential jet amid criticism of the cost and timing of the purchase. Opposition politicians have accused President John Mahama's administration of misplaced priorities, arguing that the money could have addressed pressing needs such as unemployment and public services while many citizens struggle with the cost of living. However, the government said that the purchase was approved by Parliament last year, financed without borrowing and justified by improved economic conditions. Officials also said that the new aircraft will replace an ageing presidential jet that has experienced recurring maintenance problems. The Defence Ministry says the Falcon 6X has a longer flying range, reducing the need for refuelling stops during international trips. An economist at the University of Ghana has nevertheless questioned whether buying the aircraft was the best option, calling for a cost-benefit analysis comparing the purchase with leasing.

Nigeria Moves Closer to State Police After Unanimous Approval by 36 Legislatures

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigeria has moved closer to introducing state police after all 36 state legislatures approved a proposed constitutional amendment allowing states to establish their own police forces alongside the federal police. The resolution exceeds the required approval from at least 24 states but still needs President Bola Tinubu's assent and further legislation before implementation. Supporters said that decentralised policing would improve responses to local security threats, including kidnappings, banditry and communal violence. However, critics warned that governors could abuse the system to target political opponents, while concerns remain about police capacity, training and accountability. Under the proposed arrangement, federal police would retain responsibility for national security threats, terrorism, cybercrime and border protection, while state forces would enforce state laws and investigate local offences. The proposed legislation also includes safeguards, including independent state police commissions to oversee recruitment, discipline and accountability.

Survey Finds Nearly Three-Quarters of Malawi's Population Drink Contaminated Water

Nearly three-quarters of Malawi's population are drinking water contaminated with faecal matter, despite most households using improved water sources, according to a National Statistical Office survey. The study found contamination in 74.6% of household drinking water samples, compared with 35% at the source, highlighting risks during water collection, transportation and storage. 91.2% of households use improved sources such as boreholes and piped taps. But just 8.9% have safe drinking water services. Organizations in the water sector have called for more investment in rural water infrastructure and tougher action to prevent contamination. The survey also showed large inequities in access to basic water services, with 93.2% of urban residents having access to them, compared to 68.9% in rural communities. The findings, drawn from national household surveys conducted in 2025 and 2024, were released to mark African Statistics Day.

Zimbabwe Court Reserves Judgment on Mnangagwa Term Extension

Zimbabwe's Constitutional Court has reserved judgment in two legal challenges against constitutional amendments extending President Emmerson Mnangagwa's term in office to 2030 and extending the tenure of sitting MPs. The applicants argued that several provisions were added to the legislation without following constitutional procedures and that the changes should not benefit leaders already in office when they were enacted. One challenge also questions Mnangagwa's decision to sign the legislation, alleging a conflict of interest. The amendments, signed into law in July, have sparked a wider legal and political dispute over presidential succession and the country's electoral timeline. Constitutional lawyer Lovemore Madhuku, representing the applicants, said the court was asked to invalidate the entire amendment act if it found that the additional provisions had been unlawfully introduced. The hearings took place under heightened security in Harare, with police preventing groups of war veterans and journalists from entering the courtroom.

U.S. Praises Nigerian Military After 125 Kidnap Victims Rescued

The United States has praised Nigerian military operations that rescued 125 kidnapped people and dismantled terrorist camps during operations conducted between 6 and 12 November. Nigeria's Defence Headquarters said troops also killed eight suspected terrorists, arrested 10 alleged collaborators and logistics suppliers, recovered weapons and cleared explosive devices. The largest rescue involved 119 travellers abducted along a road in Borno State. Washington said it supports Nigeria's efforts to combat kidnappings and hold perpetrators accountable, as security cooperation between the two countries expands amid ongoing insurgency, banditry and mass abductions. Other operations across several states led to the destruction of suspected criminal hideouts, the recovery of ammunition and the surrender of 12 terrorist fighters and their family members. Nigerian Defence Minister Christopher Musa said US support, including intelligence-sharing, satellite imagery and military training, was helping the country's forces target insurgents and armed groups.

Close 

COP31 Launches Second Global Stocktake Amid Deadlock Over Climate Finance

Countries at COP31 in Antalya have launched the second Global Stocktake, a five-yearly assessment of progress under the Paris Agreement, as negotiations remain deadlocked on climate finance, fossil fuels and a just transition. The review is expected to conclude in 2028, two years before the 2030 climate targets deadline. The COP31 Presidency says 21 issues remain unresolved, with new draft texts expected as ministers work towards an agreement before the summit closes. Civil society groups have urged developed countries to deliver promised climate finance, while discussions on just transition and gender highlighted the need to protect workers, communities and women as economies shift towards greener systems. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said governments had two years to turn commitments from the first Global Stocktake into measurable progress, despite difficult geopolitical conditions. The discussions also highlighted concerns that climate action must address the needs of vulnerable communities, including women whose work and experiences are often overlooked in climate planning.

World.title: South Africa: MSF Warns of Healthcare Crisis as Anti-Migrant Hostility Grows
World.content:
MSF is responding to the humanitarian needs of thousands of displaced migrants passing through the Musina repatriation centre

Anti-migration sentiment and violence continue to be a growing concern in countries such as the United Kingdom and South Africa, where hostility towards migrants, refugees and asylum seekers has resulted in fear, discrimination and insecurity. The two countries have very different political and social contexts, but the consequences are strikingly similar. Migrants face dangers to their safety, interruptions to their livelihoods and growing obstacles to essential services.

In South Africa, anti-migrant protests have erupted countrywide, resulting in deaths, property destruction and displacement. Tens of thousands of people have been left in fear for their lives and livelihoods. However, hostility towards foreign nationals is not new. Since 2008, hostility towards African migrants has erupted in repeated waves of violence, which the government has treated as isolated incidents rather than a systemic social problem.

Hostility is most often directed at African and Asian foreign nationals, including people from Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Malawi, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Somalia and Ghana.

In the United Kingdom, public debate frequently centers on asylum seekers. Asylum seekers, particularly those who arrive by boat across the English Channel, have become a target of public outrage and political debate, often given the context of claims that they are placing an unfair burden on public services and the economy. Online narratives have portrayed them as "invading" the country, abusing welfare, or representing a criminal threat.



In both countries, migrants and asylum seekers are blamed for unemployment, crime and pressure on public services. These claims often outrun the evidence.

These parallel experiences formed the focus of a webinar hosted by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). These parallel experiences formed the focus of a Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) webinar. The discussion brought together insights from MSF teams working in both contexts to examine how anti-migration sentiment translates into violence, exclusion and barriers to healthcare, and what these experiences reveal about the treatment and protection of people on the move.

Growing hostility towards migrants and asylum seekers reflects a wider shift towards nationalism and increasingly restrictive views about who belongs in a country, said Candice Sehoma, Senior Advocacy Manager, MSF Southern Africa and the moderator of the MSF briefing.

"We are witnessing countries increasingly turning inward, drawing harder boundaries around who belongs and who does not," she said. She described the situation as part of a global climate marked by growing nationalism, hostility and aggression towards people perceived as outsiders.

Sehoma said that South Africa recently experienced a wave of anti-migrant violence and intimidation in the lead-up to a deadline set by anti-migrant groups, which demanded that all undocumented migrants leave by 30 June, 2026. The deadline sparked nationwide protests targeting foreign-owned businesses, as well as door-to-door harassment of people in their homes. In the UK, she said, migration is becoming an issue of national interest. Since 2025, anti-migrant demonstrations have been taking place around the country, with them reportedly increasing in 2026.

Migration has been an increasingly contentious national issue.

However, the consequences extend beyond protests, discrimination and physical attacks.

She said that exclusion and hostility do not end with violence, discrimination or social marginalisation. They have very real consequences for people's health and access to care. "When people are targeted, criminalised or made to feel unwelcome, they may face additional barriers to accessing essential health services, including delaying or avoiding healthcare altogether for fear of discrimination," she said.

Sehoma said that these experiences compound the existing health challenges faced by people on the move.

The human cost of increasingly dangerous migration routes

Fouzia Bara, MSF's Head of Migration Task Force, said migration should not be viewed solely through the lens of border security and political debate, arguing that greater attention must be paid to the human cost of migration policies and the dangers people face along their journeys.

Bara is a senior humanitarian strategist and health advisor with over 20 years of field experience leading complex medical and emergency operations across conflict zones and migration corridors. She oversees MSF's response along the Atlantic migration route and the France-UK corridor, two of the most volatile and politically sensitive migration contexts in Europe and Africa.

"Migration is not something new. It's a natural phenomenon," said Bara.

She said that people move for various reasons, including conflict, persecution, climate change, and economic insecurity, as well as the search for better opportunities. She cited global displacement figures of approximately 117.8 million people, pointing out that most displaced people remain within or close to their countries of origin. Contrary to common perceptions in Europe, she said, only about four to five percent of displaced people reach the continent, while many others remain in transit countries or neighbouring states.

Conflict and persecution remain among the main drivers, but Bara said people are also moving because of climate change, economic insecurity, and the hope of a better life abroad.

"I've met many, many migrants in different countries, and they never ever have been happy to leave their country, their family, their habits, their culture, but it was a necessity for different reasons," she said.

However, the journeys undertaken by those seeking safety and better opportunities are becoming increasingly dangerous. Bara said MSF teams were witnessing growing levels of violence, exploitation, and physical and psychological harm along migration routes.

She attributed some of these dangers to increasingly restrictive migration and border policies, particularly in Europe, which have forced people to take longer and more perilous routes rather than preventing them from migrating. "Those policies, securitisation of European countries for different migration policies, do not prevent people from leaving. People are still leaving their countries when they have to leave," she said.

In addition, the longer routes are exposing migrants to shipwrecks, human trafficking, smuggling, abuse and exploitation.

She also described the harm caused by pushbacks and detention, where people are held in facilities with no accountability for how they are treated physically and mentally. Detention, she said, is increasingly a trend.

Bara highlighted the dangers along the Atlantic migration route, where people travelling from West Africa towards Spain's Canary Islands can cover approximately 2,400 kilometres by sea. She described cases of survivors suffering burns and hypothermia, including one group whose boat remained at sea for 23 days. "When we supported the people who survived these 23 days, it was terrible. Even our staff got really emotionally disturbed by the situation of migrants, physically and mentally," she said.

Violence, she added, does not end when migrants reach their destinations. People also face institutional violence, rejection and xenophobia in countries of arrival, including in Europe, where they may encounter additional barriers to healthcare and other support.

She highlighted the importance of providing mental healthcare to migrants who have reached safer destinations but continue to experience the psychological effects of violence and trauma.

MSF is supposed to treat people who are sick, she said, but in this context it is treating people who left their country in good health, in good condition, and have been damaged on the way. Migrants, she said, are becoming more vulnerable and more sick, which makes supporting them essential.

UK asylum policies and anti-migrant hostility deepen mental health crisis

Ghita Benjelloun, MSF UK's Migration Programme Manager, described an increasingly hostile environment for migrants and asylum seekers, pointing to restrictive immigration policies, far-right demonstrations and growing anti-migrant sentiment.

Benjelloun has worked in the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, Syria, Haiti, Yemen and India, as well as on MSF's search and rescue project in the Mediterranean Sea. Her experience spans internally displaced people, people on the move, and refugees and asylum seekers in host countries. She presented the UK context, covering policy, the rise in hostility, and MSF's work with asylum seekers and refugees.

"Migration is a journey of violence"

"Unfortunately, migration is a journey of violence," she said, and that violence takes many forms, including institutional ones. The UK, she said, remains a major destination for asylum seekers and refugees. In the year ending June 2026, just under 90,000 people arrived. About 60% were men, and the rest included women and unaccompanied minors. Roughly 28,000 arrived by irregular routes, most of them crossing the Channel from northern France in small boats. The main nationalities among those arriving included Somalis, Sudanese, Eritreans, Iranians and Afghans.

Benjelloun said the past two decades have seen increasingly restrictive migration policies. This has made it increasingly difficult for people to seek protection through safe and legal routes. Asylum seekers must be physically present in the UK to claim asylum. As a result, many have little choice but to undertake dangerous journeys, during which they risk trafficking and exploitation.

She also pointed to changes to family reunification arrangements and growing uncertainty around refugee status.

Family reunification, which was available until recently, is no longer possible. The refugee status was given for a longer period, for 10 years, then they reduced it to five, and now it's two and a half years. The latest measure, known as earned settlement, ties the duration of a person's status to how much they earn. Together, she argued, these policies have a heavy toll on mental health. "There is no more feeling of settlement, and there is no more family network, which is very important for people's recovery," she said.

Benjelloun described a "huge rise" in anti-migrant sentiment and far-right protest.

Since February 2025, there have been 69 recorded protests across the country, ranging from a few hundred people to thousands. Last year, a protest in London drew more than 10,000. The riots, she said, have recurred every summer for the past three years, and they point to a significant spread of racism and misinformation about migration.

A study by Asylum Matters and Praxis, covering more than 200 charities and organisations that support migrants, found that 47% of staff had experienced threats and harassment. Benjelloun said protests take place outside asylum accommodation, including a weekly Friday demonstration in front of a hotel where MSF works. Rescue crews have also been targeted. The Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), the British search and rescue charity that picks up people crossing the Channel, has been threatened and at times attacked.

MSF began its migration work in the UK in 2023, initially partnering with Médecins du Monde (Doctors of the World) to provide mobile healthcare services at Wethersfield, a former military site used to accommodate asylum seekers. The organisation's teams found a serious mental health crisis among residents, with 62% of patients experiencing severe psychological distress and 30% reporting suicidal thoughts. The site itself, she said, was a source of distress for the men held there.

MSF has since shifted its model.

Since July 2025, it has run a mental health service in Birmingham focused on post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) among asylum seekers and refugees. Benjelloun said that the focus reflects the violence people endure in their home countries, on the journey and after arrival. She said PTSD prevalence in this population is about 31%, five times that of the local population. The service has delivered more than 1,000 consultations. 88% of service users have been victims of violence, and 13% experienced violence in the UK itself. 63% have been suicidal at some point, and 23% are survivors of torture.

"This just gives you the level of violence that migrants have been through," she said.

"We are advocating for safe routes, for opening of safe routes, and a compassionate and fair asylum system," said Benjelloun. She added that the organisation is also advocating for improved access to appropriate mental healthcare and greater protection for young people whose ages are disputed. She warned against placing them in adult accommodation where they could face exploitation.

Xenophobic violence threatens access to healthcare in South Africa

In South Africa, anti-migrant hostility has increasingly extended beyond protests and intimidation, with organised groups targeting foreign nationals and attempting to prevent them from accessing public services, including healthcare, according to Khanyisa Mapipa, Head of Health at public interest law centre SECTION27.

Mapipa, a human rights lawyer who has litigated several cases involving access to healthcare, traced the country's recurring waves of xenophobic violence back to 2008, when South Africa experienced its first nationwide attacks against foreign nationals.

The violence claimed 62 lives, including South Africans and foreign nationals. It left approximately 1,700 people injured and displaced around 100,000 others. The government deployed the South African Defence Force to restore calm, while civil society organisations ran relief efforts for displaced people, many of whom fled to neighbouring countries.

A second wave followed in 2015. Eight deaths were documented, hundreds of people were injured, and thousands were displaced. The government condemned the violence and set up an inter-ministerial committee and launched social cohesion efforts. A further wave of anti-migrant mobilisation emerged in 2021, involving organised groups such as Operation Dudula, which expanded into vigilante raids and harassment of foreign nationals and into blocking them from jobs, healthcare and public services. Mapipa said 354 deaths were recorded in this period.

However, she cautioned that it "coincided with unrest over our former president Jacob Zuma's imprisonment, so it was difficult to attach a motive behind the killings."

More recently, anti-migrant mobilisation intensified during 2025 and 2026, with groups including March on March and Put South Africa First issuing demands for undocumented migrants to leave the country. The groups entered workplaces without police authorisation or any legal mandate, blocked services, and demanded people's documents, "all in the name of trying to rid the country of illegal migration." On the deadline day, there were about 120 anti-migrant protests around the country.

Mapipa said that these groups often failed to distinguish between documented and undocumented migrants, with both groups facing intimidation and exclusion from basic services.

"There's seemingly no distinction between documented and undocumented migrants, as we've seen instances of both documented and undocumented people being denied access to basic healthcare services, education, and other public services," she said.

Mapipa said the violence had also contributed to the departure of thousands of people who fled the country. Some African governments began repatriating their citizens. At least 100,000 people were repatriated between July and November 2026. This included 90,000 voluntary returns and 10,000 deportations. She identified high unemployment, economic pressures and disputes surrounding immigration and asylum policies as factors contributing to xenophobic hostility. Such attacks, she said, often intensify when communities are experiencing economic hardship and looking for someone to blame.

What the law says

Mapipa said that South Africa's Constitution guarantees access to healthcare for everyone within the country's borders, regardless of nationality or immigration status.

Section 27(1) provides that everyone has the right of access to healthcare services, including reproductive healthcare. Section 4 of the National Health Act, which flows from that provision, entitles pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers and children under six to free services at public health establishments, "irrespective of documentation status or nationality." Primary healthcare is free for all, and the only exclusion for non-citizens in the Act is organ transplants, which section 61(3) denies to non-residents.

She highlighted a legal victory secured by SECTION27 against the Gauteng Department of Health in 2023, after migrant pregnant women and mothers were being charged for services that should have been provided free of charge. The organisation challenged a patient classification policy that required some foreign nationals to pay substantial fees, effectively preventing vulnerable women and children from accessing essential care.

As a result of the case, Gauteng changed its policy manual. Documented asylum seekers and refugees are now means-tested in the same way as South Africans, meaning hospital administrators assess whether they can contribute to the cost of their care. Services for pregnant and breastfeeding women and for children under six have been confirmed as free.

Despite these legal protections, Mapipa said anti-migrant groups continued to interfere with access to healthcare facilities, prompting further legal action.

In October 2025, with anti-migrant protests escalating, SECTION27 initiated legal proceedings on behalf of MSF and the Treatment Action Campaign (TAC) against the Gauteng Department of Health, the City of Johannesburg and others. The case was against the government for not restoring calm at health facilities where anti-migrant groups were standing outside and preventing people from entering. In December 2025, the court ordered the Department of Health and the City of Johannesburg to come up with a plan to ensure that patients could access facilities and receive care.

The case has moved into its second phase, which seeks to extend the plan across the province.

Mapipa warned that preventing migrants from accessing healthcare has serious consequences, particularly for people requiring continuous treatment for chronic and communicable diseases.

SECTION27's observations included patients missing medication for HIV and tuberculosis, as well as disruptions to sexual and reproductive health services, antenatal care and screening for sexually transmitted infections.

She warned that the consequences would go beyond those targeted, and could endanger the public health of whole communities. Mapipa said that interruptions to HIV and TB treatment, routine screening and childhood vaccinations could have wider implications for disease prevention and control. "When these services are disrupted, they don't only impact the individual who is facing intimidation at the facility, the migrant person or the undocumented person, which includes South Africans... They don't only impact those people, but they also threaten the health of the country," she said.

To prevent patients from going without essential medication during the June 2026 disruptions, MSF, TAC and Wits RHI worked with government district health offices to establish an emergency system that enabled people to continue receiving HIV, TB and other chronic medication. The aim was to prevent an outbreak or epidemic caused by people going without treatment.

"These kinds of efforts, while commendable, do place a significant strain on public health facilities and public health provision, because now the government has to then cater for people in a parallel fashion, as opposed to them going through the system," she said.

Not a new problem, but a new level of organisation

While legal action helped reduce the physical blockades of healthcare facilities in South Africa, anti-migrant intimidation and fear continued to prevent many foreign nationals from seeking medical attention, said Claire Waterhouse, MSF Southern Africa's Director of Advocacy and Analysis.

Waterhouse said MSF had witnessed several outbreaks of anti-migrant hostility during its more than 25 years of working in South Africa. What changed in June 2025, she said, was that anti-migrant groups began blocking access to public clinics in a far more organised way than before. Earlier incidents were sporadic and isolated, such as a blockade of Kalafong Hospital in 2022, but previous incidents had never been on this scale or so organised.

MSF conducted an assessment in August 2025, visiting 15 healthcare facilities in Gauteng, after reports of patients being turned away from treatment. Its teams directly witnessed patients being turned away at more than half of the facilities visited. The organisation also visited or called more than 50 patients who confirmed they had been turned away from over 24 primary healthcare facilities across Gauteng.

Among those most affected were women in the late stages of pregnancy and people living with HIV and other chronic conditions. She said that it was "worrying and disturbing" that healthcare workers and facility security guards were sometimes part of the turning away.

Waterhouse said MSF teams were forced on several occasions to help women already in labour find safe facilities where they could deliver their babies.

Midwives, nurses and doctors set up a WhatsApp group for pregnant women, she said. MSF referred every pregnant woman who contacted it to the group for advice on where to deliver safely or how to deal with antenatal problems. It was, she said, "a huge support to pregnant women who were really afraid." She described it as one of many examples of communities, medical professionals and small organisations working together.

MSF became an applicant in the court case on clinic blockades, and the December 2025 judgment ordered immediate action to end the obstruction of health facilities. Part B of the case is still under way. Physical blockages decreased after the judgment, Waterhouse said, but many patients remained too frightened and traumatised to try again.

Close 

She said some patients remained traumatised by their previous experiences and were too frightened to return to clinics. Others encountered incorrect healthcare charges that further discouraged them from accessing services. The situation deteriorated further in the lead-up to June 30, 2026, when anti-migrant groups imposed a deadline demanding that migrants leave the country. Waterhouse said MSF witnessed threats, intimidation, and violence across several provinces, including the Western Cape, KwaZulu-Natal, Gauteng and Musina.

Many left without their belongings, and some travelled injured or in precarious medical condition.

"We saw more times than I can count mothers with babies that were under one or two weeks old. I think three times we saw mothers who had had caesarean sections to deliver their babies within the last three or four days and were then also having to travel with their things, with other children, with this newborn and in incredible pain as a result of that surgery," she said.

The displacement created an urgent humanitarian crisis.

People gathered at several large sites across the country as they tried to reach embassies and consulates for documentation or to catch buses. Waterhouse said conditions were harsh, particularly during the winter months, with inadequate shelter, insufficient food and cooking facilities, limited access to clean water and too few toilets, washing facilities and blankets. Overcrowding and minimal protection measures were also major concerns, especially at sites where many children were staying alongside unrelated adults.

Many had gone months without healthcare or mental health support despite experiencing violence, intimidation and significant emotional distress. MSF teams provided medical assistance at several locations. The organization saw between 400 and 500 patients a week at the peak of the response in July and August.

The most common problems were respiratory infections, gastrointestinal illness, hypertension, diabetes, HIV and TB, along with injuries from violence, sometimes at the hands of anti-migrant groups, communities or, in some cases, authorities. Others had injuries from the journey itself. "I cannot overstate how high the levels of emotional distress and trauma were," she said.

Many patients had avoided healthcare facilities for months, and some had stopped taking medication for chronic conditions because they feared being turned away or attacked.

Patients with HIV or TB had defaulted on treatment or were close to doing so. That caused them great distress, and it carries a high risk of drug resistance, worsening illness and in some cases death. Waterhouse said the mental health effects will have long-term consequences, particularly for children, who showed "a lot of fear, a lot of paranoia, a lot of uncertainty about who they could trust."

Many families were separated on the journey, and children spoke to MSF psychologists about their worry of finding each other again.

Lack of water and sanitation can turn minor ailments serious quickly, she said. A small cut without clean water to wash it can become infected, and a child with mild diarrhoea who lacks clean water can quickly become dehydrated. These problems, she said, affect public health as well as individual health, "which is why we all need to be concerned about them."

In response, MSF launched an emergency intervention in South Africa and Zimbabwe following the June 30 deadline, focusing on primary healthcare, continuity of treatment for chronic conditions, mental health support and assistance to vulnerable groups.

In South Africa, teams gave brief support in Cape Town at the start, ran mobile clinics at several displacement sites in Johannesburg, and worked at the large Musina repatriation site until it scaled down and closed in mid-August. In Zimbabwe, MSF has worked at the Beitbridge reception centre and expanded to the Nyamapanda border post with Mozambique after realising how long and severe people's journeys were. Many arrived at Nyamapanda hungry and sick, having gone weeks without shelter, meals or healthcare.

Across these sites, MSF has provided primary healthcare, individual and group counselling, play therapy for children, referrals with MSF or community escorts where needed, treatment for chronic disease, dignity packs with items such as sanitary pads and soap where possible, and water and sanitation support or advice in specific situations.

What MSF is calling for

The problem has not stopped, Waterhouse said. Things are "a little bit quieter" in South Africa now, but MSF continues to receive concerning reports about access to care and about anti-migrant intimidation, violence and threats.

"MSF condemns anti-migrant violence in South Africa and across the world, and the South African government and other relevant actors need to work urgently to actively protect the right to access healthcare for all people who are in South Africa," she said.

She also called on authorities to ensure that migrants leaving South Africa could do so with dignity, adequate humanitarian assistance and access to healthcare. Countries receiving returning migrants, she added, must make arrangements to integrate them into their healthcare systems, particularly pregnant women, children and people living with chronic conditions. People leaving South Africa with chronic conditions should be given an adequate supply of medication such as antiretroviral therapy, she said, to maintain continuity of care and reduce the risk of defaulting or drug resistance, which is "a public health risk as well as an individual risk."

World.title: South Africa: Six Family Members Killed in Botshabelo Shooting - South African News Briefs - November 19, 2026
World.content:
press review

Six Family Members Killed in Botshabelo Shooting

Six members of the same family, including a two-year-old boy, have been shot and killed in a house in K-Section, Botshabelo, in the Free State, reports EWN. Police said three armed men forced their way into the home after failing to enter a hut where women initiates were staying. They opened fire on those inside before fleeing on foot. The homeowner's wife was wounded in the attack. Police have launched a manhunt and opened cases of six counts of murder and one of attempted murder.

Search Resumes for Soweto Girl Swept Away by Floods



Search and recovery efforts are expected to resume for 11-year-old Anqobile Njiyela, who was swept away by floodwaters in Snake Park, Dobsonville, Soweto, reports SABC News. She was among a group of learners dropped off by scholar transport after school when they encountered severe flooding. City of Johannesburg divers, police K9 units and community members, assisted by a police helicopter, have been involved in the search. Johannesburg EMS has urged residents, particularly those in low-lying areas, to avoid crossing flooded rivers and streams.

Western Cape Better Prepared for Water Restrictions, Says DA

The Democratic Alliance in the Western Cape says the province is better prepared to manage water restrictions amid declining dam levels and concerns over El Niño conditions, reports EWN. The Department of Water and Sanitation has announced precautionary cuts of 7% for domestic and industrial use and 15% for irrigation. At the same time, Level One restrictions are set to take effect in Cape Town on 1 December. Dam levels have dropped to 70.4%, down 13.4 percentage points from the same period last year. DA spokesperson Dave Bryant said investments in water infrastructure, early-warning measures and clearing invasive vegetation have strengthened the province's resilience. He cautioned against applying uniform restrictions across areas with different water needs.

World.title: Malawi: Three in Four Malawians Drinking Contaminated Water, Shock Survey Finds
World.content:
Nearly three in four Malawians are drinking water contaminated with faecal matter, even though most households say they use improved water sources, according to a National Statistical Office (NSO) survey.

The NSO found faecal contamination in the drinking water of 74.6 per cent of the population when it was tested in the household, compared with 35 per cent when it was tested at the source.

Its report says contamination rises sharply between the water source and the home, pointing to transport, handling and storage as the weak points.

The findings are alarming because 91.2 per cent of households use improved sources such as boreholes, protected wells and piped taps.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

But only 8.9 per cent enjoy safely managed drinking water services, the report found.

"Faecal contamination, which shows that water may have come into contact with human or animal waste, was found in drinking water of 74.6 percent of the population when it was tested in the household, compared with 35.0 percent when it was tested at the source," the report says.

The report also found that rural communities are especially vulnerable, with women and girls often bearing the burden of collecting water from distant sources.

The gap between urban and rural areas is wide. Basic service reaches 93.2 per cent of urban residents but only 68.9 per cent in rural areas.

Water Services Association of Malawi (Wasama) executive director Vitumbiko Mkandawire said the findings should be a reminder that an improved source is not the same as safe water.

He called for more investment in piped and reticulated systems, especially in rural areas, and stronger water safety plans nationwide.

Horizon Action executive director Mwandira said the figures were alarming and called for strict measures to stop contamination between collection points and the consumer.

The study drew on the Integrated Household Survey 2025 and the Malawi Demographic and Health Survey 2024. It was released to mark African Statistics Day.

World.title: Gambia: NPP's Adama Barrow Leads Presidential Race With 28 Percent in Gambia Participates Opinion Polls
World.content:
President Adama Barrow leads a close three-way presidential race, with 28 per cent support in the latest opinion poll by Gambia Participates.

The Round 3 survey, published on November 18, found United Democratic Party leader Ousainou Darboe at 25 per cent and Coalition 2026 candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda at 24 per cent. Nineteen per cent of respondents were undecided, while 4 per cent supported other candidates.

The poll found no clear leader in Brikama. Regionally, Barrow recorded his strongest support in Basse and Janjanbureh. Bensouda led in Kuntaur, Kanifing and Banjul, while Darboe's highest share was in Mansakonko.

More respondents expected Barrow to win than said they would vote for him. Thirty-seven per cent named him as the likely winner, compared with 28 per cent who selected him as their preferred candidate. The survey report treats these as separate measures.



The poll found different levels of support across age groups. Bensouda had his highest support among people aged 18 to 24, at 41 per cent. His support fell across older groups, from 30 per cent among those aged 25 to 34 to 7 per cent among people aged 55 and above.

Barrow's support generally increased with age, rising from 25 per cent among respondents aged 18 to 24 to 41 per cent among those aged 55 and above.

Darboe's support was 19 per cent among the youngest respondents. It rose to 30 per cent among those aged 45 to 54 before falling to 28 per cent among people aged 55 and above.

The share of undecided voters was highest among respondents aged 25 to 34, at 21 per cent. It was 20 per cent among those aged 35 to 44 and 18 per cent among those aged 45 to 54. Among the youngest and oldest age groups, 14 per cent were undecided.

Support was similar among men and women. Barrow received 29 per cent support among women and 27 per cent among men. Darboe received 24 per cent among women and 26 per cent among men. Bensouda's support was 25 per cent among women and 24 per cent among men.

Women were slightly more likely to be undecided than men, at 19 per cent compared with 18 per cent.

The survey also asked respondents about the issues they considered most important. The cost of living was the leading concern, with 72 per cent selecting it. The report said concern about corruption increased from 29 per cent in Round 2 to 43 per cent in Round 3. Security and healthcare also remained among the issues raised by respondents, although their shares declined.

Close 

Compared with Round 2, Barrow's stated support fell from 32 per cent to 28 per cent. Bensouda's rose from 19 per cent to 24 per cent, while Darboe remained at 25 per cent.

The share of undecided respondents increased from 17 per cent in Round 2 to 19 per cent in Round 3. Support for other candidates rose from 2 per cent to 4 per cent.

Gambia Participates said the earlier survey rounds involved different respondents, so the changes do not track the views of the same people over time. Essa Mbaye Faal and Mama Kandeh, who had received 3 per cent and 2 per cent respectively in Round 2, withdrew before Round 3 and were not included in the latest questionnaire. The report said the results do not show whether their former supporters moved to another candidate or remained undecided.

The survey measures respondents' stated preferences for individual candidates, not their parties or coalitions. Gambia Participates described the results as a snapshot of opinion and said preferences could change before election day.

World.title: Deion Sanders receives 'about five' death threats every day as Colorado football coach
World.content:
Just a few years ago, Colorado’s football program had largely been forgotten. Then Pro Football Hall of Famer Deion Sanders arrived in Boulder, bringing his larger-than-life personality and celebrity to the program.

Colorado’s on-field results under Sanders have been uneven, but his tenure has also been marked by significant off-field challenges. Sanders has continued coaching while managing serious health issues. More recently, police records obtained by The Athletic detailed how his personal safety has been at risk at times.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

According to a September report, Sanders regularly received death threats. At one point, he said he was receiving "about five" threats per day. Public records from Boulder shed light on how authorities handled many of those situations.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

In May 2023, a pair of university police officers waited for Sanders outside his office. Once the two-time Super Bowl winner met the officers, they told Sanders about a series of threatening voicemails on a Colorado football ticket office phone line that mentioned him.

At the time, Sanders was just six months into the job and had yet to coach a game. "I guess this confirms what you are working on," Sanders told Evis McGee, a member of his personal security team, after learning about the voicemails, per the police report.

DEION SANDERS SAYS ALLEGED $50,000 OFFER TO SILENCE CRITICS WAS 'A JOKE' AMID COLORADO'S STRUGGLES

The voicemails proved not to be an isolated incident. The Athletic ultimately discovered 15 closed University of Colorado police cases involving harassment or suspicious activity directed at Sanders since he left Jackson State and was named the Buffaloes head coach. Two additional cases remain open, with records unavailable, and most stem from 2023.

In a YouTube video posted in January by Sanders’ son, Deion Jr., Michael Rhodes warned players to "be mindful of who comes in [the facility] with you, especially on the elevator." Rhodes delivered those comments during an introductory meeting ahead of the 2026 season.

"Don’t let somebody coerce you into scanning them up on the floor, because everybody’s trying to get to Coach Prime," he continued. Rhodes is the head of Sanders' university-paid security team.

"Some people say, ‘Coach, what do you need a head of security for?’ We get death threats all the time," said Sanders. "Why? I’m a Black man making it happen. … That stuff is real.

"How many death threats we get?" Sanders was shown in the video asking Rhodes.

He responded: "About five every day."

MATT RHULE DRAWS THE LINE AFTER FAN VERBALLY ATTACKS HIS 13-YEAR-OLD DAUGHTER FOLLOWING LATEST NEBRASKA LOSS

Colorado athletics said its security efforts involve Sanders’ personal security team as well as the CU Boulder Division of Public Safety.

"The safety of Coach Prime is our top priority, and we take every threat seriously," the athletics department said in a statement. "CU Athletics works closely with the CU Boulder Division of Public Safety to coordinate security efforts with Coach Prime’s entire team, including his security detail, and respond appropriately to reported threats."

Nearly half of the 15 closed cases The Athletic reviewed were found to have ties to one individual who repeatedly mailed threatening letters. The letters contained incoherent passages and biblical references, along with racist remarks directed at Sanders.

World.content:
Retired NBA icon Russell Westbrook spent Thursday afternoon in steady rain at Jesse Owens Park in South Los Angeles, handing out 1,500 Thanksgiving meals, groceries and winter coats to local families.

Three months after retiring from the NBA, the former league MVP worked the distribution line himself through his Why Not? Foundation.

Video shared (via NBA reporter Joey Linn) showed Westbrook loading food packages alongside volunteers in the rain. Westbrook grew up playing at Jesse Owens Park, and three years ago he partnered with the Los Angeles Clippers to refurbish and reopen its main basketball court in his honor.

Thursday marked the foundation's 14th annual Thanksgiving giveaway and its largest yet. Volunteers packed the supplies Tuesday at It's Bigger Than Us in Baldwin Hills Crenshaw Plaza, backed by LA County Parks and Recreation, Los Angeles County, and Cal Dental USA.

The expanded budget came from Westbrook's sixth annual Why Not? Poker Night in Las Vegas in September, which raised over $900,500 and pushed the event's six-year total near $3 million.

"We started this at Jesse Owens Park 14 years ago, and we show up every November," Westbrook said.

"This is home. We've been blessed with more this year, so why not give more back to the community?"

FORMER CLIPPERS STAR WARNS OF TEAM'S UPHILL BATTLE AFTER BRUTAL KAWHI LEONARD SALARY CAP PUNISHMENT

He retired as the NBA's all-time triple-doubles leader, the 2017 MVP, a nine-time All-Star, a two-time scoring champion, a three-time assists leader, and an Olympic gold medalist.

World.title: LSU poked the SEC bear, then folded: RJ Luis benched after conference leaders discussed expulsion or boycott
World.content:
One day after Will Wade sent RJ Luis onto the court, LSU has backed down from its latest fight with the SEC.

LSU President Wade Rousse announced late Thursday afternoon that the Tigers would no longer play Luis, abruptly reversing course after the former professional basketball player scored 11 points in Wednesday night’s win over Louisiana-Monroe.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"In my role as president of the LSU System, after further review, I have instructed LSU men's basketball coach Will Wade not to play RJ Luis," Rousse said.

LANE KIFFIN’S ROSTER FIGHT SET THE STAGE, WILL WADE JUST THREW A GRENADE IN LSU-SEC WAR WITH RJ LUIS

That’s quite the turnaround from the message Wade delivered after Wednesday’s game.

"He was eligible, and he played," Wade said.

For a school locked in a federal lawsuit with the SEC over the roster battle involving Lane Kiffin’s football program in September, playing Luis was another escalation.

Less than 24 hours later, LSU put down its sword related to the basketball player.

LSU puts down sword in RJ Luis fight after warning from SEC

Not even 24 hours after RJ Luis scored 11 points in the LSU win, the Tigers waived the white flag regarding this fight that involved their basketball team.

Why the sudden change of heart?

SEC presidents were already scheduled to hold a call Thursday afternoon to discuss several topics. But after Luis played Wednesday night, the conversation was set to take on a different tone.

ATTORNEY COMPARES SEC COMMISSIONER GREG SANKEY TO ‘KIM JONG’ IN LSU-RJ LUIS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUIT

Multiple sources told OutKick that options including SEC schools boycotting games against LSU and renewed discussions about potentially expelling the Tigers from the conference were back on the table.

"That was the final straw for SEC leaders, they were ready to penalize them (LSU) in some form or fashion," one source familiar with the discussions told OutKick. "You can only poke the bear so many times before they decide to pounce, and they (SEC Presidents and Chancellors) had seen enough nonsense from LSU.

"Who knows if they would have actually boycotted games, or even tried. But, lawyers from schools within the conference were going through their options. This whole thing is just annoying. Like, get your sh-t together, and I mean everyone involved."

SEC FILES BOMBSHELL LAWSUIT AGAINST LSU, LANE KIFFIN WHILE PRO PLAYERS FIGHT FOR COLLEGE ELIGIBILITY IN COURT

Sources also told OutKick that SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey spoke with Rousse on Thursday afternoon before the scheduled presidents’ meeting, delivering a blunt and honest assessment of the thinking of conference leaders of what could happen if LSU continued playing Luis.

The message apparently landed.

Less than two hours after the conversation with Sankey and consultations with its own general counsel, LSU announced that Luis would no longer play. Rousse did not participate in the full call with the other SEC presidents.

Where do we go from here? Well, there's a federal lawsuit, and maybe more

LSU’s decision does not necessarily mean Luis is finished fighting.

The former professional football players involved in the separate LSU eligibility case are still considering a civil lawsuit against the SEC over what they contend was interference with their court-ordered ability to play.

Could Luis pursue some type of damages of his own? A statement from one of his attorneys suggests this dispute could be far from over.

"The SEC's decision to threaten a member with expulsion if it plays an eligible student-athlete is reprehensible and seriously harms a young person who was caught in the middle of a power struggle having nothing to do with him," one of RJ Luis's attorneys, Elliot Abrams, said in a statement.

COLLEGE ATHLETICS' LATEST MESS: COURT ORDERS SAY PRO ATHLETES CAN PLAY, BUT SEC AND BIG TEN READY TO FIGHT

The latest showdown began last Friday, when a Baton Rouge judge granted Luis a preliminary injunction. The scope of that order — and whether its protections extended to LSU playing him — became a central point of contention.

In a statement Monday, the SEC said it would abide by the order and would not punish LSU for rostering Luis.

Playing him was another matter.

On Tuesday, the conference made clear that it disagreed with LSU’s interpretation of the court order.

"LSU’s decision today to rely on its own interpretation of the Court’s order to justify its actions is inconsistent with the expectations and responsibilities of [SEC membership]. This is a deeply concerning and disappointing development."

The SEC wants to enforce its membership rules. LSU relied on its interpretation of a Baton Rouge judge’s order to put a former professional player on the court.

On Wednesday night, the Tigers tested how far they could push that argument.

By Thursday afternoon, they had their answer.

Peace talks on the way between LSU and its own conference? Ehh..

This basketball dispute is another chapter in a fight that had already spilled into federal court.

Three months ago, the SEC filed a federal lawsuit against LSU as Sankey testified in a Baton Rouge courtroom in the case brought by Dae’Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who were seeking to play football for Kiffin’s Tigers.

The federal case has since produced its own stream of legal jabs.

On Wednesday, the SEC asked a judge to strike language from LSU’s motion to dismiss in which the school’s attorneys accused the conference of making "hallucinated" claims against a defendant.

A judge ordered LSU’s lawyers to issue a public apology through a press release. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill pushed back in a filing, telling the court that would not happen.

LSU LEAVES FORMER PRO-ATHLETES OFF FINAL ROSTER, ONE NIGHT BEFORE SEC TAKES LANE KIFFIN AND TIGERS TO COURT

That same day, attorney Tony Clayton, representing Luis, filed a motion seeking to hold the SEC in contempt over the conference’s Tuesday statement.

So, yes, there were already plenty of reasons for tension between LSU and its conference before Wade sent Luis into Wednesday’s game.

Playing him amounted to throwing another grenade into an ongoing legal battle.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Now, LSU has retreated on the basketball front, leaving Luis sidelined while the broader fight continues.

Will that open the door for peace talks between LSU and the SEC?

Given the lawsuits, threats and courtroom clashes hanging over this relationship, I wouldn’t count on a ceasefire just yet.
