National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is out after President Donald Trump backed his firing over concerns he lacked the cybersecurity credentials for the job, Fox News has confirmed.

Kirsten A. Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, will step into the position in an acting capacity.

Davies, who was Senate-confirmed, will join Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, White House technology advisor Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the administration's national security and cyber leadership team.

An administration official separately told Fox News that Cairncross did not want to serve another two years in the role. Cairncross took office Aug. 4, 2025, after Senate confirmation, and the exact date of his departure remains unclear.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

Senior administration officials welcomed Davies' appointment on X.

"Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity," Rubio wrote.

Clayton praised her background, writing, "With nearly two decades of leadership experience in the technology space, Kirsten Davies will be a strong asset for the Trump administration in her new position with the Office of the National Cyber Director. It has been my pleasure to work closely with Kirsten on national security matters, and I look forward to now working with her to navigate an increasingly dynamic and fast-moving cyber landscape."

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth wrote, "The Department congratulates Kirsten Davies on her new role as the National Cyber Director. Throughout her tenure at DOW, she has proven herself to be a dedicated patriot and professional, and we are confident she will advance President Trump’s America First agenda across the cybersecurity landscape."

US INFRASTRUCTURE CRUMBLES AS ADVERSARIES POWER UP – LEAVING AMERICANS DANGEROUSLY EXPOSED: CYBER EXPERT

Davies thanked Trump, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Hegseth in her own post on X, calling the moment a critical juncture for U.S. technology.

"Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come …but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on, as well as build cyber talent for our future. Under President Trump’s leadership we will have a more secure, resilient; and supercharged technological future," Davies wrote. "I am honored to continue to serve."

The leadership shakeup follows a nearly weeklong stretch of technical disruptions that hit air travel, major banks, Microsoft services, Apple, Marriott, the National Weather Service and internal systems at the National Security Agency.

A Nov. 13 Federal Aviation Administration outage triggered a nearly five-hour nationwide ground stop and thousands of flight cancellations after contractor work on air traffic control wiring overloaded the system.

Administration officials have pushed back against speculation that hackers or foreign adversaries were behind the disruptions. Rubio said Tuesday that officials found "zero evidence" tying the incidents together or to malicious actors, while Clayton said the outages appeared linked to routine software patches and system upgrades rather than a coordinated cyberattack.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Retired police sergeant issues warning over Mamdani's NYPD shake-up ahead of Thanksgiving parade
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

EXCLUSIVE: A retired police sergeant with nearly three decades of law enforcement experience warned that she would not bring her own family to New York City amid Mayor Zohran Mamdani's plans to dismantle a specialized NYPD unit responsible for counterterrorism support and crowd control.

"I wouldn't take my family there right now," retired Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a spokesperson for the National Police Association, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview.

Smith's warning follows Mamdani's announcement that the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG), a roughly 500-officer specialized unit involved in counterterrorism, major event security and protest response, will be disbanded as part of a broader overhaul of how the nation's largest police department handles demonstrations.

MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS

The democratic socialist mayor has defended the decision as fulfilling a campaign promise to separate counterterrorism operations from the policing of constitutionally protected protests.

Critics, however, argue that dismantling the established unit could undermine the coordination and specialized training needed to respond to emergencies.

Smith, who spent 29 years in Chicago-area law enforcement and has experience supervising crowd control operations, said the consequences could extend beyond protests.

"One of the beauties of this strategic response group is that these are a group of officers who are used to working together," Smith said. "They train together. They have specialized knowledge of how to deal quickly and safely with these types of situations, including an active shooter."

MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE

Her concerns come as New York City prepares for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade Nov. 26, an event expected to draw enormous crowds of visitors to Manhattan.

Smith warned that breaking up the specialized unit could create vulnerabilities if its responsibilities were redistributed without preserving existing operational relationships.

"First and foremost, I'm concerned that any intelligence may be lost or may be ignored for a large scale event like this," she said.

NYPD Assistant Commissioner Brad Weeks told Fox News Digital the restructuring will not affect security arrangements for this year's Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, explaining that the new First Amendment Support Team and Patrol Support Division will not begin operating until February 2027.

FLORIDA EYES POACHING NYPD OFFICERS AFTER MAMDANI DISMANTLES ELITE UNIT

The department also said counterterrorism personnel currently assigned to the Strategic Response Group will be transferred to the NYPD's Counterterrorism Bureau, consolidating those capabilities within the specialized bureau.

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, Mamdani's office directed the outlet to remarks the mayor delivered during a news conference earlier this week.

"I've long said that counterterrorism and protest response are fundamentally different responsibilities and that New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani said.

The overhaul also imposes new restrictions on police tactics during protests, including prohibitions on long guns and tear gas, according to the mayor's office.

Pepper spray will no longer be permitted as a general crowd management tool, while officers assigned to the new Patrol Support Division will receive specialized training and retain arrest powers when necessary.

MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES

Mamdani said the initial changes would take effect in approximately 90 days, with a First Amendment Support Team (FAST) operating within the NYPD's Community Affairs Bureau during the transition.

A separate civilian-led Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, housed within the Office of Community Safety, is scheduled to launch in 2028.

The mayor said the division would focus on engaging with protest organizers, mediation and preventing tensions from escalating.

Mamdani rejected suggestions that civilians would be expected to confront violent demonstrators without police support.

"Now, police will always be present in the case of any kind of violence," he said. "So this idea that New Yorkers' safety will be compromised is not true."

FAR-LEFT GROUPS CHEER MAMDANI FOR DISBANDING ELITE NYPD PROTEST TEAM

Smith, however, questioned whether the new approach could preserve the capabilities of officers accustomed to responding together during major incidents.

"It is a political decision on his part. And it's an incredibly dangerous one," she said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch defended the restructuring, saying the department would maintain the resources necessary to respond to serious threats.

"I would never support changes that diminish the NYPD's ability to protect New Yorkers or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat," Tisch said in the city's announcement.

Mamdani's announcement also drew praise from far-left activist organizations that have long criticized the NYPD's handling of demonstrations.

NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE

World.title: Democrat lawmaker hit with federal indictment over alleged $240K COVID fraud scheme

An Alabama state representative has been indicted for allegedly orchestrating an extensive fraud scheme to obtain private and taxpayer-backed loans and grants to fund his personal expenses, the Justice Department announced Thursday.

Officials identified the lawmaker as Patrick Lorn Sellers, 53, who has represented a district near Birmingham since November 2022 and was recently re-elected to a second term.

Sellers was also a church pastor and former chief of staff to the president of the Alabama State Missionary Baptist Convention (ASMBC).

Between July 2020 and May 2021, Sellers allegedly siphoned more than $240,000 in grants and loans intended to provide relief during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Alabama.

MINNESOTA FRAUD MASTERMIND GETS NEARLY 42 YEARS IN PRISON IN MASSIVE $250M 'FEEDING OUR FUTURE' SCHEME

The alleged scheme specifically targeted the federal and state governments and a private nonprofit.

Those benefits were used to cover personal expenses, including credit card bills, mortgage payments, auto loan payments, water bills and even his daughters' college tuition, officials said.

In one notable instance, Sellers allegedly took control of an affiliate nonprofit belonging to ASMBC and applied for pandemic relief funds without notifying the convention’s president or board.

After Sellers obtained the money, the charity's actual leaders were denied funding when they legitimately attempted to apply for assistance, officials said.

DOJ’S ‘OPERATION GHOSTBUSTERS’ TARGETS MASSIVE STUDENT-AID FRAUD SCHEME BUILT ON FAKE ENROLLEES

He also repeatedly lied on federal and state relief applications, claiming he operated multiple nonprofits that employed as many as 10 people when, in reality, he had no employees, according to prosecutors.

In addition, Sellers reportedly claimed to operate a landscaping business and fabricated tax forms for returns he had never filed with the IRS.

GOP LAWMAKER’S FRAUD CRUSADE TAKES DRAMATIC TURN AS SCANDAL ENGULFS HIS OWN CAREER

"Under U.S. Attorney Williams, we have a mandate to aggressively pursue corrupt public officials, no matter what position they hold or what power they wield," Assistant U.S. Attorney Brett A. Janich said in a statement.

Because the payouts were handled electronically across state lines, Sellers now faces four felony counts of wire fraud alongside strict demands to forfeit the illegally obtained funds.

The maximum penalty for wire fraud is up to 20 years in prison.

World.title: Justice Department seeks dismissal of its lawsuit in Alaska Senate race
World.content:
The Trump administration on Thursday asked an appeals court to toss a civil suit it filed last month in Alaska that sought to take the extraordinary step of blocking certification of a state-run election unless the incumbent Senate Republican emerged victorious.

Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ended up winning the race this week.

The lawsuit, filed by the Justice Department in October, followed President Donald Trump’s repeated claims that the inclusion of candidate Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot, alongside Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, was a stunt to “defraud” voters.

Dan J. Sullivan and Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, R-Alaska. AP; Getty

In its filing Thursday, the Justice Department asked the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to declare the lawsuit moot, citing Peltola’s victory.

“The United States brought this lawsuit to ensure that the State and its officers fulfill Alaska’s obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward wrote in the filing.

He added that the government “therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means” of examining whether votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan were intended to be cast for the incumbent.

The ability to prove voters miscast their ballots was seen by many as an insurmountable hurdle when the lawsuit was initially filed.

Before the Trump administration filed its lawsuit, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that Dan J. Sullivan was eligible to remain on the ballot.

On Nov. 1, a federal judge in Alaska rejected the administration’s plea to separate and preserve certain ballots in the Senate election, following a request from the Republican-led state government that the judge permanently dismiss the “meritless lawsuit.”

Trump insisted in the weeks leading up to the election that the two Sullivan candidates would confuse voters and said that he was the one who encouraged the lawsuit.

“I’m the one that said do it,” he told reporters during his midterm blitz in October.

Days after the administration filed its lawsuit, The New York Times reported that Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to jump into the race. Peltola has denied any wrongdoing.

Trump argued that Peltola should be prosecuted over the allegations, saying on Oct. 28, “This is voter fraud at the highest level,” and that Peltola “should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted, and so should the fake Dan Sullivan.”

Peltola won Alaska’s Senate race with an outright majority, meaning the state did not have to use its ranked choice tabulation process to determine a winner. As a result, the votes cast for either Sullivan did not affect the outcome.

Alaska is not the only place where the Trump administration tried to intervene in the election process, which is conducted by state officials under U.S. law.

In California, the DOJ demanded state officials set aside roughly 20,000 ballots that it alleged were sent to noncitizens. California officials argued that the list of alleged noncitizens provided by the DOJ was outdated and included legitimate voters.

The Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s efforts a day before the election, and the Justice Department moved to dismiss its lawsuit later that week.

World.title: Trump’s pick for agency providing election security says Jan. 6 was not an attack
World.content:
The nominee selected by President Donald Trump to lead the agency tasked with protecting elections in the U.S. refused Thursday to answer who won the 2020 presidential election or call the riot on Jan. 6, 2021, “an attack.”

Michael LoSapio, who is nominated to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, was pressed by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., on the issues during a confirmation hearing before the Senate Homeland Security Committee.

Asked specifically who won the presidential race in 2020, LoSapio said, “I’m not going to answer the question about an election six years ago.”

“My only involvement in the 2020 election was voting for the president of the United States,” he added, referencing Trump.

Blumenthal accused LoSapio of “ducking the question in a way that betrays your lack of independence and objectivity.”

CISA has not had a director confirmed by the Senate since Trump returned to office in January 2025, when Jen Easterly vacated the role.

The agency, which was established during the first Trump administration, was meant to protect the country’s critical infrastructure, including its elections, from hackers or cybercriminals.

LoSapio, who serves as the chief information security officer at data and software company Palantir, was also asked whether there was an attack on the Capitol on Jan. 6.

Blumenthal pressed him on the issue, saying, “You don’t know?”

“No, I don’t believe it was an attack,” LoSapio said. “I wasn’t involved in politics. I know what I saw on the news.”

Blumenthal asked LoSapio about the nature of the riot once again, to which he maintained that “it was not an attack.”

Trump’s own account of Jan. 6 has changed over the years, as he initially sought to distance himself from the riot, calling what happened “acts of violence and destruction” on Jan. 7, 2021.

Though, as he hit the campaign trail in 2024, Trump shifted gears to call it a “day of love,” and later, when he returned to office, he pardoned roughly 1,500 people and commuted the sentences of another 14 in connection with the attack. Trump’s Justice Department also tried to launch a controversial “anti-weaponization” fund, which critics have called a “slush fund” to compensate the president’s allies.

LoSapio is one of 13 nominees who appeared before the committee Thursday seeking to take over federal oversight, inspector general, Postal Service and District of Columbia Superior Court positions.

To be confirmed as CISA director, LoSapio requires the committee to vote to advance his nomination to the full Senate, whose vote by a simple majority will determine whether he is confirmed. The clock is ticking for Trump nominees, as Democrats will take over control of Congress in January.

The result of the 2020 presidential election has shaped CISA’s leadership. Trump fired its first director, Chris Krebs, just weeks after the election over his assertion that it was a secure race.

LoSapio isn’t the first Trump nominee to skirt around questions regarding 2020’s presidential race.

On Wednesday, Cody Hiland, Trump’s pick for a federal appeals court seat, told Blumenthal, “I’m not going to answer that,” when asked who won the election.

Asked why he would not answer, Hiland said, “Because it’s going down a political track on an issue that happened six years ago, and I don’t want to come close to an ethical violation.”

“We know the White House told you, ‘Don’t answer that question,’” Blumenthal responded.

World.title: Classified NSA network is still down, leaving some staff working from home
World.content:
An internal classified computer network used by the National Security Agency remained down on Thursday, resulting in some employees being ordered to work from home for a third day in a row, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

The network first went down on Tuesday due to a technical problem that occurred when maintenance on the network was underway. Both sources told NBC News the issue has created an inconvenience but has not affected the NSA’s work collecting electronic intelligence around the world and overseeing cybersecurity.

There is no sign that the outage was caused by a cyberattack, the sources said.

Even though the NSA’s network issue came amid an unusual series of mass outages that have wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails over the past few days, U.S. officials have said say there is no indication that the technical problems were caused by a coordinated cyberattack.

Nonessential staff at the NSA are being told to check in with their supervisors and find out if they need to come into the agency’s headquarters in Fort Meade, Maryland. Otherwise, they are advised to work from home, according to a telephone information line for the workforce and the two sources familiar with the matter.

While the NSA does not release the precise number of agency employees, former officials have said it employs tens of thousands of people. In 2024, a Maryland state government document put the number of NSA employees at 39,000. The agency has since made some workforce reductions as part of broader cutbacks across the federal government.

The outage also affected a worksite in Georgia that handles the NSA’s electronic intelligence work in the Middle East, the sources said.

In a statement Tuesday, the NSA acknowledged experiencing a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”

“While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the statement said. “NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”

The NSA, which oversees the nation’s vast electronic surveillance efforts, is considered one of the world’s most sophisticated cybersecurity and electronic spy agencies.

With powerful eavesdropping and code-breaking tools as well as a well-educated workforce, the NSA prides itself as a center of digital expertise.

While it is not uncommon for government networks to suffer brief disruptions or outages, such a high-profile technical problem threatens to tarnish the reputation the agency has built, according to former officials and experts.

World.title: White House national cyber director is leaving the administration
World.content:
White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving the Trump administration, a White House official confirmed Thursday.

Cairncross will be replaced by Kirsten A. Davies, who currently serves as the chief information officer at the Defense Department, a source close to the White House told NBC News.

Davies will serve in an acting capacity, the source said. The position requires Senate confirmation.

Axios was first to report the personnel changes.

Cairncross has served as head of the Office of the National Cyber Director since August 2025. The office oversees all government cybersecurity policy and strategy.

National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross speaks at Semafor's "Silicon Valley and The World" conference in Menlo Park, California, on Monday. Godofredo A. Vasquez / AFP via Getty

He has been directly involved with the White House’s deliberations over AI policy, including after Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick directed Anthropic to take down its two most powerful AI systems over the summer due to national security concerns.

Cairncross is leaving his post after a series of tech outages affected both private companies and government agencies over the past week. Administration officials as well as Democratic members of Congress have said the outages do not appear to be the result of cyberattacks, though some have suggested AI may have played a role.

The White House, when reached for comment Thursday night, did not provide details about the staffing changes.

Cairncross’ previous White House roles include senior adviser to the White House chief of staff during Trump’s first term.

During the 2016 election cycle, Cairncross was the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer. He worked for the RNC again during the 2024 cycle, serving as then-chief operating officer Chris LaCivita’s deputy.

The source close to the White House said Davies will strengthen the president’s cybersecurity team, which includes Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also serves as national security adviser.

Rubio welcomed Davies to her new position in a social media post.

“Congratulations to the new National Cyber Director Kirsten Davies — look forward to working together to strengthen America’s cybersecurity,” Rubio wrote on X.

World.title: Walmart stocks up on inflation-weary shoppers ahead of the holidays
World.content:
Walmart isn’t just adding inventory for the holiday shopping season; it’s also racking up more customers looking for discounts as inflation maintains its grip on the U.S. economy.

The retail giant on Thursday said it gained market share and raised its sales outlook for the third time this year as bargain hunters across income levels hit stores and fill their online shopping carts.

“Looking ahead, we expect a strong holiday season,” CEO John Furner said on an earnings call with analysts Thursday.

Walmart, which is generally considered a barometer for the U.S. economy, has long been a go-to store for consumers seeking discounts. Rising prices have pushed many consumers to rethink where they shop, and Walmart has benefited from more higher-income shoppers. As it draws more affluent customers, the company has launched a fashion-forward women’s apparel brand and expanded its e-commerce and advertising businesses.

Walmart isn’t alone in gaining momentum with thrifty shoppers ahead of the holidays. Rivals Target and Costco are also seeing customers respond to their value offerings, both posting sales increases and Target raising its outlook.

The results illustrate the resilience of American consumers, who keep spending even while grocery and gas prices rise and paycheck growth lags the pace of inflation.

“In spite of that, consumers are finding ways to get what they need for their families,” Matthew Shay, president of the National Retail Federation, told NBC News on Wednesday.

Still, it’s shaping up to be a strong holiday season, and not just for Walmart. The National Retail Federation forecasts that sales in November and December will top $1 trillion in the U.S. for the first time. But that doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying more items; rather, they’re paying a higher price at checkout.

This season, Walmart said it lowered the price of 7,700 items by the end of the third quarter while expanding deals on groceries. The company said it will also offer a Thanksgiving meal basket for 10 at $3.50 per person, including turkey, Stove Top stuffing, mashed potatoes and other staples.

Walmart also raked in more revenue from its membership fees, which surged 17% in the quarter. The company announced a bundled deal that includes memberships to Walmart+ and its warehouse-club subsidiary Sam’s Club, as well as perks including free access to streaming platforms and gas savings.

While shoppers seem to be sold on Walmart heading into the holidays, Wall Street was a bit more cautious. The company’s stock slipped about 1% to $126 a share amid a broader market sell-off Thursday, even as quarterly revenue and profit surpassed investors’ expectations.

Goldman Sachs analysts said they still rated Walmart’s stock a “buy,” projecting it’ll hit $132 a share.

Nonetheless, they also flagged risks to the company’s outlook, including the potential for an economic slowdown and more intense price competition from its big-box and online rivals.

World.title: White House national cyber director leaving his post
World.content:
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will be leaving his position, a White House official told CBS News.

Cairncross was fired, multiple sources told CBS News.

White House chief of staff Stephen Miller — who took over for Susie Wiles earlier this month — had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, sources said, telling people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.

Miller immediately teed up a search process for a replacement. Cairncross will be replaced by Kirsten Davies, who serves as the Pentagon's chief information officer, the sources said.

Axios was first to report that Cairncross will leave.

Cairncross' departure comes as the U.S. reels from a series of technological outages over the last week that have hit Microsoft services, air traffic control systems, banks and the National Security Agency's internal network.

Authorities investigating the outages have "seen nothing that would indicate that they are related," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told lawmakers this week. He said he is "98% confident" the outages are not the result of malicious foreign activity, though he acknowledged that he had "absolutely not" seen so many outages in a short period of time.

The national cyber director, a Senate-confirmed post, advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates cyber strategy across the federal government. An attorney, Cairncross has served in the role since August 2025.

The job was created in 2021. In recent years, the U.S. has faced a series of cyberattacks linked to actors in Iran, Russia, China and other U.S. adversaries.

The Trump administration released its cyber strategy in March, which Cairncross' office oversaw. The seven-page document vowed to "detect, confront, and defeat cyber adversaries before they breach our networks and systems," harden critical infrastructure, maintain a U.S. edge in artificial intelligence and modernize federal tech systems.

In a November 2025 appearance at the Aspen Cyber Summit, Cairncross said one of the administration's primary goals is "introducing costs and consequences" on adversaries.

"I think, as a country, we have not done a terrific job of sending a signal to our adversaries that this behavior is not consequence-free," he said. "And we need to do that because it is scaling and it is becoming more aggressive every passing day."

If the Trump administration intends to nominate another permanent national cyber director, it only has a narrow window before the Senate changes to Democratic control in January.

In a statement, Cairncross called the role "the honor of a lifetime."

"I leave my role as Director of Cyber incredibly proud of our work to strengthen America's cybersecurity, protect our critical infrastructure, confront foreign threats, and position America to lead the world in Super Intelligence. None of it would have been possible without President Trump's extraordinary leadership," he said.

World.title: Army delays detonation in Iowa that could send toxic dust into Illinois
World.content:
The U.S. Army has delayed plans to detonate unstable explosives at a munition plant in Iowa, after elected leaders and environmental groups raised concerns about the risks of a plume of dust containing toxic lead particles that could spread across parts of Iowa and Illinois.

The dust plume is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces.

The detonation originally was scheduled for noon CT Friday, Nov. 20, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, a small community of 360 people four hours west of Chicago near the Mississippi River. However, on Thursday evening, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced the explosion would be delayed until Monday.

"Public safety is the Army's top priority, and I have directed Army Materiel Command to postpone tomorrow's controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa until Monday, November 23. This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Telle wrote in a post on X.

The Army plans two controlled detonations involving 68 barrels of lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive used in military ammunition since World War I. The Associated Press reported the material totals about 5 tons. According to the Environmental Protection Agency, the material has deteriorated during storage, allowing lead azide to recrystallize and become increasingly sensitive to friction and shock.

"In March of this year, the Army uncovered degrading Lead Azide housed in bunkers at the installation and immediately began communicating with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the modeled impact area about the danger it posed," Telle wrote in a post on X. "In coordination with the Environmental Protection Agency, experts, and the local community, it was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area. Public communication is essential to public trust. Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."

In a statement after the Army postponed the detonation, U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) wrote on X, "The American people deserved better than this."

"This whole operation was poorly planned and poorly communicated. Families were abruptly told to avoid the area, unsure if they would return to broken homes and whether their air and water could be at risk due to toxic lead exposure. This was unacceptable and a failure of leadership of epic proportions," Duckworth wrote. "Moving forward, I will continue to demand answers about how we even got to this point and accountability to make sure the Army never allows unsafe conditions to get this dire again."

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) called on the Army to hold a community town hall meeting on Saturday to answer questions from the public before proceeding with the demonstration on Monday.

Thursday afternoon, two environmental groups filed a lawsuit in the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to block the detonation. Earthjustice, a nonprofit public interest environmental law organization, filed the suit on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter. They are challenging the validity of the emergency permit granted by the EPA.

"The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt, general counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a news release. "When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal."

The barrels had been stored at the plant for more than 20 years in earthen-covered containers, sitting in a bath of ethanol and water to keep the material stable, said Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command. A routine check earlier this year found that some of the water had evaporated, Barati told the AP.

The Army says moving or transporting the material now poses an unacceptable risk of accidentally detonating it, potentially even killing the explosives technicians handling it. After evaluating alternative disposal methods, military officials determined that detonating the explosives in place was the safest available option. Barati said the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather. "We're really concerned that it will detonate on its own," she told the AP. The Army describes such operations near populated communities as highly uncommon, it told CBS News Chicago.

The Army says it is taking several steps to limit the amount of lead-containing dust released during the explosions, including earthworks, soil wetting and air monitoring. According to the AP, the barrels are surrounded by concrete and buried under soil, with sand barriers stacked two stories high around them. Barati said the soil will be sprayed with water and the air misted to try to keep the majority of the lead on Army property. EPA's permit also requires environmental monitoring at the installation and off-site locations, along with post-detonation sampling and cleanup measures.

Residents urged to evacuate as explosions could shatter windows

The planned detonations are powerful enough that the Army is warning of possible damage to nearby buildings, including shattered windows. Residents in Middletown's City Park neighborhood are being asked to temporarily evacuate their homes from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. Friday. Residents who can't leave should stay inside with windows and doors closed, officials said.

In its Nov. 15 public advisory, the Army says residents should expect loud explosions, ground vibrations and a visible dust plume. Temporary accommodations will be available at the Armed Forces Reserve Center in Middletown.

Elected officials urged Army and EPA to delay planned detonation

A group of Democratic and Republican elected officials from Illinois and Iowa had urged the Pentagon and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to delay the planned detonation and seek safer alternatives.

"While we understand the urgent need to address these volatile materials, their detonation has the potential to spread lead contamination in and around the region. We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives," they wrote to Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle and U.S. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin. "Iowa and Illinois residents understandably are concerned about the potential health impacts of the scheduled detonation."

The elected officials who signed the letter include:

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois)

U.S. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois)

U.S. Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Illinois)

U.S. Rep. Mary Miller (R-Illinois)

U.S. Rep. Eric Sorensen (R-Illinois)

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker

U.S. Sen.-elect Juliana Stratton (D-Illinois)

U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek (D-Iowa)

They also raised concerns about communication with the public before the detonation.

"Our offices have received reports of poor communication from the Army and EPA about the detonation plans and anticipated monitoring after the detonation. In addition, there are significant concerns about appropriate Army and EPA oversight of this contractor-operated facility, the site of which remains on a Superfund list. We urge you to examine the contractor's handling of this and other hazardous material to prevent any future issues," they wrote.

Toxic lead dust could travel miles downwind

Following the initial blast, airborne toxic dust becomes the main concern. According to the Army's published plume forecasts and public safety advisory, the explosions are expected to release particles containing lead into the atmosphere.

The preliminary maps show a potential airborne plume stretching northward across eastern Iowa, the Mississippi River, and potentially into far northwest Illinois. The Army notified communities as far as 100 miles away Sunday, the AP reported, and thousands of people live along the plume's projected track.

In addition to airborne dust, toxic dust particles are expected to settle on surfaces. That raises concerns about possible lead contamination on agricultural land, residential properties, playground equipment and other outdoor surfaces.

A plume of dust containing toxic lead particles is expected to spread across portions of eastern Iowa and northwest Illinois Friday, potentially settling on farmland, playgrounds and other surfaces. National Weather Service

Actual exposure levels and the extent of any contamination will depend on the amount of lead released, atmospheric conditions and how much material settles out of the plume.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that does not degrade naturally over time. Once deposited, it can persist in soil for decades and may be transported through erosion or runoff into waterways.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warns that no safe blood lead level has been identified in children. Even relatively low levels of lead in the blood have been linked to learning difficulties, developmental delays and behavioral problems. Lead exposure is also especially dangerous to pregnant women.

Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a professor at the University of Iowa's Department of Occupational and Environmental Health, told the AP it is encouraging that the Army and EPA are working to minimize the dust, but it's still unknown how much will end up in the air and on surfaces. He said he is particularly concerned about toddlers who put everything in their mouths. Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University who has helped communities recover from chemical disasters, told the AP that high doses over a short period can cause lead poisoning and make people feel sick.

The Army's forecasts do not establish that harmful exposure will occur at every location within the projected plume. The Army says extensive modeling predicted that lead particle levels in the air may be elevated but still well below the level at which the EPA would require protective action, according to the AP. Environmental sampling will be needed to determine where lead was deposited and at what concentrations.

Weather conditions will determine where the plume travels

Wind direction, speed and vertical motion in the atmosphere will play critical roles in determining the plume's eventual path. Officials expect the dust to linger for no more than an hour, depending on wind speed, according to the AP.

Current forecast guidance suggests gusty southerly winds of 20 to 30 miles per hour Friday will carry the plume northward through eastern Iowa, keeping it well west of the Chicago metropolitan area. Communities closer to the Mississippi River and the Illinois border could be more relevant to potential downwind exposure. The exact path remains subject to change as the detonation approaches.

Under the EPA's emergency permit, the operation cannot proceed if certain unfavorable weather conditions are forecast, including surface winds below 1 mph or above 15 mph, strong winds aloft, thunderstorms, precipitation or temperature inversions. There is no word yet on whether Friday's gusty winds could cancel the detonation.

The Army is required to update its plume forecasts six hours before the operation, and hourly thereafter until the detonations are completed.

Army promises environmental monitoring and cleanup

The permit requires soil and surface-wipe sampling to begin within 24 hours in accessible public and consenting private areas where modeled lead-dust deposition meets a specified threshold. The Army must also submit environmental findings and proposed remediation plans to EPA.

For residents potentially affected by dust deposition, the Army recommends wet-cleaning surfaces that people frequently touch, including outdoor toys, playground equipment, patio furniture and windowsills. However, questions remain about the extent of contamination that could occur beyond the ammunition plant, the effectiveness of cleanup efforts and how residents will know whether their properties are safe.

This photo provided by the U.S. Army shows the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on May 14, 2024. (Shawn Eldridge/U.S. Army via AP) Shawn Eldridge

EPA issues emergency permit for detonation

On Nov. 13, the EPA issued an emergency permit allowing the Army to detonate the lead azide at a location not authorized for the activity under the facility's existing hazardous-waste permit. In its Nov. 16 public notice, EPA said the emergency authorization was necessary to address an imminent threat to public safety posed by the unstable explosives.

The detonation is being regulated under the federal Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, or RCRA, which governs the treatment, storage and disposal of hazardous waste. However, federal emergency-permitting provisions allow greater flexibility than ordinary permitting procedures. Under 40 CFR § 270.61, applicable environmental requirements must be incorporated into emergency permits to the extent possible and consistent with the emergency situation.

The emergency permit issued for Middletown includes specific environmental safeguards and incorporates applicable federal hazardous-waste regulations. It remains unclear whether EPA modified or omitted any requirements that would ordinarily apply to this operation because of its emergency designation.

The EPA's authorization does not mean the detonation will produce no environmental contamination.

CBS News Chicago has sought additional information about the EPA's environmental risk assessment and the standards that would trigger cleanup of affected properties.

The Illinois Department of Public Health referred CBS News Chicago's questions about potential health impacts back to the EPA. Environmental and public health officials in Illinois have urged the military to conduct comprehensive sampling in that state after the detonations, the AP reported.

Iowa Health and Human Services told CBS News Chicago it was made aware of the planned detonation only very recently and is coordinating with other state agencies as they assess and respond to the public health concerns. The agency said the Army released two maps showing possible exposure but did not say what conditions the modeling included.

Community concerns grow ahead of detonation

Some residents and environmental advocates are questioning whether the planned detonation has received sufficient independent scrutiny. Protest organizers have called for greater transparency, independent environmental review and assurances that any contamination resulting from the explosions will be properly addressed.

U.S. Sen.-elect Josh Turek was among those calling for the detonation to be delayed, arguing the public needs a better understanding of the potential health impacts, the AP reported.

Middletown residents learned in March that the Army needed to dispose of the degraded lead azide, after the plant paused operations for a review and the material was discovered, the AP reported. The Army previously held a public open house on Oct. 15, where military officials discussed the safety operation and answered residents' questions.

Some schools in the region canceled classes Friday before the detonation was delayed, including in Danville, a few miles from the plant. Superintendent Pat Wallace said his initial intention was to keep schools open, but the uncertainties made closing "the most responsible decision." He wrote that he is not suggesting the detonation will create unsafe conditions: "The reality is that we simply do not know exactly what conditions will look like Friday afternoon," the AP reported.

In Mediapolis, less than 20 miles northeast of the plant, city officials learned of their potential exposure Sunday, when the Army's map put the town in the center of the dust exposure area, the AP reported. The school district announced Tuesday it will close Friday with no events or sports practices, and the public library will also close. The local fire department plans to hose down playgrounds that could be covered in lead particles. City officials said the EPA will have a command center in Mediapolis to sample air, soil and water during and after the detonation, and the city plans to do its own testing.

"The biggest issue we're having is the lack of information," Deputy City Clerk Amy Stucker told the AP. Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds' office said it was first briefed on the public advisory Monday.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture advised bringing animals, bales of hay and water indoors. Staff at the Iowa State University Extension office in Des Moines County fielded calls Thursday from residents "deathly afraid" for their animals and vegetable gardens, staff member Morgan Hoenig told the AP. "We ran out of soil test kits yesterday," she said.

The Army recommends that those within the projected exposure area consider avoiding outdoor activities, remaining indoors with windows closed and setting ventilation systems to recirculate air until officials announce that the exposure period has ended.

The latest official plume forecasts, public advisories and safety instructions are available on the U.S. Army's Iowa Army Ammunition Plant information page.

World.title: Marine Corps hero under federal investigation
World.content:
Henderson, Nevada — One of the most celebrated Marine Corps veterans, whose heroism during the Iraq War earned him the nation's second-highest award for combat valor and a place in military history, is the subject of a criminal investigation over allegations stemming from his tenure as a high school instructor for a Junior Reserve Officers' Training Corps, CBS News has learned.

Retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal, who served in the Marine Corps for 34 years, is under investigation by the Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the primary federal law enforcement agency for matters involving the Navy and Marine Corps.

The allegations against the highly decorated Marine veteran have not been disclosed by the law enforcement agency. However, federal agencies told CBS News that the investigation concerns the period of time when he worked as a JROTC instructor at the Basic Academy of International Studies. The academy is a public high school in Henderson, Nevada, operated by the Clark County School District.

The federal investigation marks a dramatic turn for a Marine whose actions on the battlefield made him a symbol of military courage. Kasal's heroism was captured in a 2004 photograph showing him in the Second Battle of Fallujah. His uniform was soaked in blood, and he was being helped out of a building by two Marines. His right leg was shattered, and his body riddled with gunshot wounds and grenade fragments, but he still gripped a pistol and combat knife. The scene was later immortalized in statues installed at two Marine bases. He retired after 34 years of service and was the recipient of two Purple Hearts and the Navy Cross, the second-highest decoration for combat valor, behind the Medal of Honor.

The commemorative statue of 1st Sgt. Bradley Kasal being carried by Lance Cpl. Chris Marquez and Lance Cpl. Dan Shaffer, after taking heavy fire during the Second Battle of Fallujah in 2004. U.S. Marine Corps Cpl. Juan C. Bustos/DVIDS

On Wednesday, the Marine Corps told CBS News that the service is "aware of the allegations against a retired Marine Sergeant Major which occurred while he was employed as a civilian JROTC instructor by the Basic Academy of International Studies."

The Marine Corps also said that the Naval Criminal Investigative Service "is actively investigating the allegations, as the Department of the Navy's lead for felony-level criminal investigations."

Separately, Denise Caskey of NCIS confirmed that its field office at Camp Pendleton in California is conducting the investigation.

NCIS does not typically confirm active investigations, making this an unusual case. The agency commonly investigates matters of homicide, sexual assault, fraud and even terrorism and espionage cases. The agency also conducts counterintelligence investigations, working with other federal agencies to identify threats to national security.

Kasal did not reply to CBS News' multiple attempts to contact him.

CBS News traveled to Henderson, Nevada, and over the course of the last two weeks spoke to nearly 40 people, including former students, school district employees, city officials, parents, U.S. military service members and Marine veterans who served with Kasal. Some asked for anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly or feared reprisal.

The cadets CBS News spoke to alleged Kasal often gave rides home to a select group of female cadets. He would take them to Starbucks and spend time with certain students outside of school-sponsored functions. Some also described instances when he was alone with a cadet in a room.

A former school district employee told CBS News that Kasal was advised on several occasions about the perceptions surrounding his relationships with students and was warned against putting himself in potentially compromising situations, including being alone in a room with a cadet.

One former female cadet described developing an unusually close relationship with Kasal after meeting him in 2020, when she was 14. She said she confided in him about difficulties at home and personal matters, including her relationships with boys. After knowing her for barely a year, Kasal offered to adopt her, saying in a text message, "I'm not asking as charity. I'm asking because your [sic] wanted."

When her family members learned of Kasal's offer, she said, they made it clear that adoption was not an option. She said that her relationship with Kasal continued, and she remained comfortable confiding in him about deeply personal matters. The cadet alleged some of their conversations involved sexual rumors that had been spread about her and why Kasal believed some of the problems she was experiencing stemmed from her relationship with her father. In retrospect, she said she realizes that those conversations were inappropriate for an instructor to have with a teenage student.

She now says she thinks Kasal crossed other boundaries, alleging that Kasal invited certain cadets to spend time at his home and at his cabin, she said, including for at least one birthday celebration. He did not extend invitations to everyone in the program. She also claimed that Kasal drove one student home nearly every day.

The Clark County School District told CBS News Kasal was hired by the school district three months after he retired from the Marine Corps, in August 2018. He resigned in August 2025, the school district said.

Enrollment in Basic Academy's JROTC program fluctuates from year to year, averaging roughly 135 students. The program is overseen by a senior Marine instructor and a senior enlisted leader.

When Kasal transitioned from the Marine Corps to the high school JROTC program, he sought to restructure it to more closely resemble the military service.

Some former cadets described him as professional and organized, crediting him with establishing strict standards and bringing a sense of discipline to the program. They also praised the time, energy and personal resources he devoted to his students.

Samantha Francisco, 22, who was in the program from 2018 to 2022, said, "I can't say enough about how amazing he was," and that "he genuinely cared about everybody and taught us incredible lessons." She added that she and her husband, who was also in the JROTC program, still talk weekly about Kasal or something he taught them.

Ashley Vazquez Romo, 22, another cadet from that period, said Kasal "poured his heart and soul into the program." She recalled that he sometimes helped pay for program outings and purchased equipment, including a CPR training mannequin, so students could practice.

Damien Greenwell, 22, who participated in the JROTC program from 2018 to 2022, told CBS News that he deeply respects Kasal for his military service and mentorship, especially to cadets with a troubled home life. But Greenwell also said that over the years he questioned Kasal's conduct on several occasions, adding that even if the decorated Marine's intentions were innocent, his actions could appear inappropriate to an outside observer.

"He would mentor us on how to be a proper leader — which is his job — but he would go a bit beyond this. Sergeant Major [Kasal] helps people in a time of need and that's very honorable," Greenwell said.

"If someone couldn't eat, he would pay for their food. If someone didn't have a ride home, he would help them out. It's awesome, it's great and very commendable," Greenwell said. "But if you're regularly getting Starbucks for a girl … it looks kind of weird … and with driving people home on a consistent basis, it looks bad. You need to have a certain kind of boundary between you and students."

Greenwell told CBS News he remembers a night that still "shocks him a little." It happened in 2024, two years after Greenwell graduated.

Greenwell claimed he went to Lowe's home improvement store around 9 p.m. and saw Kasal's truck in the parking lot. In the store, he observed Kasal walking with a student who he believes was a senior at the high school or a newly minted graduate.

"It was just really weird to me," Greenwell said, recalling that he briefly exchanged greetings with Kasal and the student before the two continued down the aisle. CBS News is withholding the student's name for privacy reasons.

Greenwell said over the years of observing Kasal, he developed doubts about him. He believed the optics could be interpreted as inappropriate, but at the same time wonders if Kasal could just be trying to help students navigate the difficulties of life. But even if he found a relationship between Kasal and a student odd, he was "not gonna say anything. Like, who am I to tell [a] sergeant major?"

Daniel Gillian, who participated in the program from 2018 to 2022 and later enlisted in the Marine Corps, said JROTC was good for him and that Kasal was part of the reason he ended up joining.

The program "gave me a lot of structure and discipline," Gillian said, adding that Kasal helped him "become a better person overall, and once you become a better person, things will fall into place for you."

Gillian said he never witnessed Kasal engage in inappropriate behavior. He sees Kasal as having made an effort to create memorable experiences for students by organizing group hikes, camping trips and other activities outside the classroom. He said Kasal recognized that some students did not have a good home life, and he wanted to make the JROTC program enjoyable and inclusive, emphasizing that all cadets were invited to participate.

Still, he acknowledged that Kasal appeared to favor certain cadets, sometimes buying them coffee, for instance. Gillian said Kasal had also bought coffee for him, but he didn't think it was inappropriate, describing him as a "nice guy."

Gillian also alleged Kasal would take cadets on hikes without seeking permission from the school, but he said this was more a matter of convenience. The hiking trail was only a few minutes away from Basic Academy.

"It was about a 10-minute drive from Basic, and [about] 20 cadets would go. Whoever wanted to go, they would go. We would all carpool," Gillian said, and the hikes were just about an hour.

"Legally, you gotta get [trips] ran through the school, and they gotta approve of it, … but [Kasal is] not gonna wait for [the school] to take two weeks to [approve] an event that takes one day to get back."

One former male cadet, who joined the program in 2019 and now serves in the U.S. military, alleged that Kasal invited him to visit his cabin in Iowa over the summer.

The trip was not school-sponsored, he said, and "it was just going to be the two of us." He says he declined the invitation because he was playing a sport that summer. At the time, he said, he did not consider the invitation to be inappropriate, believing Kasal had extended it because they shared an interest in the sport.

Greenwell said that at one point, he heard a rumor that Kasal was trying to adopt a fellow cadet but that he didn't believe it was true. When CBS News told him that Kasal had offered to adopt a former female cadet, Greenwell said he was "very surprised, shocked and disappointed."

"Even if you have the best intentions in the world, it still looks bad, no matter how you put it, because she's a minor," said Greenwell.

The Defense Department and local school districts share responsibility for overseeing JROTC programs because they are federally sponsored and operate in high schools nationwide. Although instructors are employed by school districts, they must also be certified by their respective military branches, which are responsible for monitoring their professional conduct and ensuring compliance with military standards.

The military services certify and oversee instructors, while school districts handle employment decisions, classroom supervision and compliance with local education policies.

JROTC instructors must acknowledge in writing that they will not engage in prohibited activities between JROTC instructors and students. The rules ban instructors from developing personal, intimate or sexual relationships with cadets, engaging in inappropriate communications and attending social gatherings with students on a personal basis. The restrictions apply from an instructor's first contact with a cadet until six months after the student leaves the JROTC program.

Under the rules, instructors are generally not allowed to give students rides in their personal vehicles, including rides home from school. Exceptions may be made when a student's safety or welfare is at risk or for official school functions involving multiple students. The rules specifically prohibit an instructor from transporting a single student in their personal vehicles.

Instructors are also not allowed to have cadets or other students in their homes. Other interactions, such as purchasing coffee or refreshments for students, are not explicitly prohibited. But such interactions could raise questions about compliance with the rules.

Instructors must sign the acknowledgment before beginning their duties as JROTC instructors and recertify it annually.

When CBS News received the initial news tip regarding Kasal, the Marine Corps said it was aware of allegations and of an investigation, but made no mention of NCIS' involvement.

The Henderson Police Department initially said it had no record of a complaint about Kasal. The Clark County Detention Center and the Clark County District Attorney's Office also did not have any complaints about Kasal on file when contacted some two weeks ago.

Later, during that same period, a spokesperson for the Henderson Police Department said the Clark County School District Police Department was handling the matter. Multiple calls and emails to the Clark County School District and the school district's police department went unanswered. Lt. Bryan Zink of the Clark County School District police department referred inquiries to the school district.

Last week, when CBS News emailed to check in on its inquiry, an email sent in error to CBS News asked a human resources manager to "disregard the request."

When CBS News asked why the request for information was being disregarded, Bryan Callahan, the district's public information officer, emailed for the first time: "We are looking into your request."

When questioned by a CBS News reporter in Henderson earlier this week, Callahan said he was not aware of an investigation of Kasal by the Clark County School District or the school district's police department.

Before he retired from active duty, Kasal reflected on his time in Iraq. The Second Battle of Fallujah in November 2004 was the bloodiest battle involving U.S. Marines since the Vietnam War, marked by brutal house-to-house fighting against Iraqi insurgents.

In 2018, Kasal told CBS News' David Martin that he had entered the building to rescue fellow Marines trapped by insurgent gunfire during one of the war's bloodiest battles. By the time he emerged, Kasal had been shot seven times, shielded a wounded Marine from an exploding grenade and refused medical treatment until others received care.

His actions earned him his second Purple Heart and the Navy Cross.

The photograph of Kasal became an iconic symbol of Marine resilience and sacrifice. The Marine Corps Heritage Foundation named a photojournalism award for Kasal.

The photograph inspired a bronze statue called the "No Man Left Behind" monument, which is installed at both Camp Pendleton in California and Camp Lejeune in North Carolina, according to the Marine Times. The sculpture was the work of John Phelps, a Navy Vietnam veteran whose son Chance was killed in Iraq in 2004, the newspaper reported.

When CBS News first learned about the criminal investigation into Kasal earlier this month, the retired sergeant major was in New York as the guest of honor at an event hosted by the NYPD Marine Corps Association to commemorate 251 years since the founding of the U.S. Marine Corps and honor Marines who also serve as New York City police officers. The New York Post reported that Kasal was presented a framed retirement shadowbox by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch at police headquarters in Manhattan.

James LaPorta reported from Henderson, Nevada. Julia Kimani Burnham and Eleanor Watson reported from Washington, D.C.

Editor's note: For the past three years, James LaPorta has served as a judge for the Marine Corps Heritage Foundation annual awards program. He has never judged the award category named for retired Sgt. Maj. Bradley Kasal.
