03 Why it moved

First and heaviest is the market’s fear of a glut. Lithium shares have fallen for six sessions, and the pattern fits investors pricing a surplus, though we have no fresh data on Chinese carbonate prices for Thursday.

Second is the sell-off around it. The S&P 500 fell 2.02% and the VIX fear gauge rose 15.80%, so funds cut risk across the board. The usual lithium drivers did not rescue the miners: the dollar index barely moved at 103.92 (up 0.06%) and the 10-year US Treasury yield edged down to about 5.0%.

Third is positioning. On 3 November our own wrap recorded six-month lows for Albemarle and SQM as investors trimmed profit forecasts ahead of earnings and worried about 2027 oversupply. Thursday looks like the same trade continuing. Confidence in oversupply fears as the main cause is medium; in the Wall Street panic as the accelerator, medium.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation with a sharper edge. LIT is down 10.46% over 20 sessions and 28.4% over 60, and it has fallen 40.7% from its high of 91.62 on 11 May.

Albemarle and SQM peaked together on 16 April and have since lost 61.5% and 49.8% respectively. That is not a correction; the market has repriced the whole industry.

Our own price history since 2010 offers one cool-headed fact. After 41 earlier falls in LIT of this size or larger, the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 23 cases, or 56%, with a median gain of 0.9% and a worst case of a further 14.9% loss. History is not a forecast, and a coin-flip with a small median is hardly a reason to buy.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile is the most exposed. SQM is its flagship lithium company, and its share price is now 49.8% below its April high, which squeezes the profits that feed royalties and investor confidence in the Atacama salt flat.

Argentina and Bolivia sit in the same Lithium Triangle, the cluster of salt flats holding much of the world’s known reserves. Lower prices make new projects there harder to finance, though we found no specific Argentine or Bolivian news for Thursday.

For savers in São Paulo, Mexico City or Santiago holding lithium funds through global platforms, the lesson is that a theme can be right in the long run and still lose half its value in seven months.

06 The names to watch

Albemarle is the bellwether. It has fallen six sessions in a row and sits exactly at its 12-month low of 82.93, so any bounce or break there will be read as a verdict on the whole sector.

SQM has fallen two sessions in a row but is 15.11% lower over 20 sessions. Its 12-month low of 47.85 is the line to watch.

In China, the Guangzhou Futures Exchange starts trading lithium hydroxide futures on 26 November, as reported. They are not carbonate futures, but a new way to bet on prices usually brings more volatility, and more price discovery.

07 What would end it

The nearest support is the 12-month lows, set on Thursday itself: 54.33 for LIT, 82.93 for Albemarle and 47.85 for SQM. Resistance is far above, at the 12-month highs of 91.62, 215.62 and 95.31.

What would change the picture is Chinese carbonate prices stabilising, or evidence that producers are cutting output. Calmer Wall Street would also help, since the VIX at 28.44 is a stress reading.

The honest answer to whether it stops: not until the surplus shrinks. The sell-off may pause sooner, as 56% of past cases suggest, but a durable recovery needs the glut to ease.

08 What to watch

Chinese carbonate: Whether the price stabilises or falls further, since it drives producers’ earnings.

Whether the price stabilises or falls further, since it drives producers’ earnings. 26 November: Launch of lithium hydroxide futures on the Guangzhou Futures Exchange, a new gauge of price expectations.

It prices a 0.25-point rise at 92.5%, a 0.5-point or larger rise at 5.1%, no change at 2.9%, a 0.25-point cut at 0.2% and a 0.5-point or larger cut at 0.1%.

These prices are bets, not polls. They show traders expect the Fed, the US central bank, to raise rates again in December, which would lift the dollar and US yields and weigh on lithium miners.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are lithium stocks falling?

Mainly because investors fear a lithium oversupply, and because a broad Wall Street sell-off hit risky shares on Thursday, November 19, 2026.

Is LIT the price of lithium?

No. LIT is an exchange-traded fund that holds shares of lithium miners, so it reflects company profits and investor mood, not the metal’s spot price.

How does this affect Chile?

SQM, Chile’s lithium champion, closed at US$47.85, which is 49.8% below its April high, reducing the profits that support Chilean royalties and investment.

Will lithium stocks rebound?

After 41 earlier falls of similar size, LIT was higher 20 sessions later 56% of the time, with a median gain of 0.9%. That is history, not a forecast.

The Merval, the index of Buenos Aires’ biggest listed companies, closed at 81,146, down 0.96%, after ending the day within 34 points of its low. The peso slipped too, to 1,565 per US dollar, down 0.36% on the day. That is the weakest peso close in at least 12 months. The trigger sat far from Buenos Aires. The Merval, an index of the leading companies on the Buenos Aires exchange, priced in pesos, closed at 81,146, down 0.96% from Wednesday’s 81,933. It traded between 81,112 and 83,082 and finished at the bottom of that range.

03 Why it moved — a Wall Street sell-off hit Argentine shares

First, and heaviest, global fear (HIGH confidence). The S&P 500 fell 2.02%, the Dow Jones fell 2.19%, the Nasdaq fell 2.25%, and the VIX rose 15.80% to 28.44. When investors get scared, they sell emerging markets first, and Argentina is among the most volatile.

The same day, other Latin American currencies fell harder than the peso. The dollar rose more than 1.5% against the Colombian peso, 1.24% against the Mexican peso, about 1% against the Brazilian real and 0.68% against the Chilean peso.

Second, worry about the US Federal Reserve (MEDIUM confidence). Minutes of the Fed’s 27–28 October meeting, published on 18 November, showed officials seeing risks that inflation could persist, and prediction markets now price a 0.25-point rise in December at 92.5%. The US 10-year yield actually edged down to about 5.0% and the dollar index rose only 0.06%, so this was more a flight from risk than a rates shock.

World.title: Wheat Fund Rises 1.4% as Soybeans Slip | Grains Wrap, Nov 19
World.content:
Wheat and corn funds rose while soybeans slipped on 19 November, a day Wall Street fell 2%, as Brazil's planting pace weighs on soy prices.

Key Facts Soybeans: The SOYB soybean fund fell 0.55% to US$25.44, its second straight loss.

The SOYB soybean fund fell 0.55% to US$25.44, its second straight loss. Corn: The CORN fund gained 1.13% to US$17.07 but is 15.9% below its 1 September peak.

The CORN fund gained 1.13% to US$17.07 but is 15.9% below its 1 September peak. Wheat: The WEAT wheat fund rose 1.37% to US$21.47, yet is 23.3% under its 28 August high.

The WEAT wheat fund rose 1.37% to US$21.47, yet is 23.3% under its 28 August high. Brazil: Conab, Brazil’s crop agency, put soybean planting at 66.8% of the area on 6 November.

Conab, Brazil’s crop agency, put soybean planting at 66.8% of the area on 6 November. Mood: The S&P 500 fell 2.02% and the VIX jumped 15.80%, yet two of three grain funds rose.

Today’s Focus Wheat and corn rose on Thursday, 19 November 2026, while soybeans slipped for a second session. The split came on a nervous day, with US shares down 2.02% and the VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, up 15.80%. Soybeans are the weakest link because Brazil, the world’s biggest supplier, is planting a large crop quickly. Conab says planting reached 66.8% of the area by 6 November, ahead of the previous week’s pace. Corn and wheat are bouncing from deep lows rather than starting a recovery. Wheat is down 20.5% over 60 sessions and corn 14.8%, so some of Thursday’s gain looks like bargain-hunting after a long slide. Grain prices are sliding because the Southern Hemisphere harvest looks big, and only stronger export demand, or a weather scare in Brazil, can reverse that.

Think of the grain market as a three-lane road where the traffic has slowed for weeks. On Thursday, 19 November 2026, wheat and corn nudged forward while soybeans edged back.

The odd part is the backdrop. Shares fell sharply and fear jumped, yet farm-crop funds mostly rose, which suggests traders were covering earlier bets on falling prices rather than chasing a new theme.

Assessment — Rebound in wheat, pressure on soybeans MEDIUM Thursday looks like a pause in a downtrend for corn and wheat, and a continuation of it for soybeans. The fund moves are modest against the weeks of losses that came before them. The variable to watch is Brazil’s planting and weather over the coming weeks, because that decides how large the harvest, and the supply hitting world markets, will be.

The soybean-tracking fund, SOYB, closed at US$25.44, the corn fund CORN at US$17.07 and the wheat fund WEAT at US$21.47. These are exchange-traded funds that follow futures prices, not the price of a tonne of grain itself.

03 Why it moved

The first and heaviest cause is supply, mainly in soybeans. Conab’s latest survey projects Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean crop at 181.6 million tonnes on about 49.3 million hectares, a 0.7% increase on the previous season. Mato Grosso, the biggest producing state, had planted 95.6% by 6 November.

The second cause is demand, which is mixed. The US Department of Agriculture’s weekly export sales, carried by the RT economic calendar (USDA units, mostly thousand tonnes), showed net sales of wheat at 344.8 (previous 182.8), corn at 1,588.1 (previous 2,881.4), soybeans at 1,501 (previous 1,154.8), soybean meal at 198.1 (previous 360.9), soybean oil at 0.9 (previous 1.7), pork at 32.1, beef at 7.1 and upland cotton at 118.7. Gross sales were wheat 408.7, corn 1,627, soybeans 1,622.1, pork 36.2, beef 8.8 and upland cotton 128.4. Marketing-year totals were corn 1,630, soybeans 1,501, soybean meal 199.1, wheat 344.8 and soybean oil 0.9, while next-year corn sales were 41.9, soybean meal 1 and soybeans 0.

The third cause is market mechanics. With US shares falling and fear rising, investors often close grain positions to raise cash, and then buy back when the panic eases. The dollar index barely moved at 103.92, up 0.06%, and the 10-year Treasury yield edged down to about 5.0%, so neither explains the split.

Our best reading, with medium confidence, is that corn and wheat benefited from short-covering after steep falls. Soybeans lacked that support because the big Brazilian crop outweighs it.

04 The trend behind it

Over the past year the picture is one of retreat from late-summer highs. Soybeans are 4.9% lower over 60 sessions and sit 17.2% above their 13 January low, so they are the most resilient.

Corn is only 3.6% above its 29 June low of 16.47 after falling 3.99% over 20 sessions. Wheat has fallen 6.00% over 20 sessions, making this a continuation of the downtrend, not a new phase.

Our own price history since 2011 offers a cautionary note. After soybean falls of this size, in 62 earlier independent cases the fund was higher 20 sessions later in 38 of them, or 61%, with a median gain of 0.7% and a worst loss of 10.1%.

Wheat’s record is weaker: in 76 comparable cases it was higher 20 sessions later only 31 times, or 41%, with a median of minus 0.6% and a worst loss of 23.9%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is both the winner and the pressure point. A large crop brings volume, but lower world prices cut the dollar value of each tonne that farmers, traders and the government earn from exports.

Argentina, the other great exporter of soy products and corn, faces the same price pressure from the Brazilian harvest. Both countries earn their export dollars in these crops, so soft prices tighten the supply of foreign currency that supports the real and the peso.

For importers such as Mexico, which buys large volumes of US corn and wheat, cheaper grain is a relief for food and animal-feed costs.

06 The names to watch

The three funds, SOYB, CORN and WEAT, are the quickest way to follow the market from an ordinary brokerage account. Corn and wheat sit nearer their lows, so they react more sharply to any change in mood.

In Brazil, listed grain handlers and farm-input companies move with crop prices and the real. Investors should watch weekly planting data from Conab, especially Rio Grande do Sul, where only 3% had been planted by 6 November.

07 What would end it

The downtrend would ease if planting slows or weather damages Brazilian fields. The nearest support is the corn fund’s 12-month low of 16.47 and the soybean fund’s 21.71 low; resistance sits at the 28.14 soybean high.

There is no single date that settles it. The weekly Conab planting updates and the next monthly crop survey are the checkpoints, and a calmer stock market would also remove the forced selling that has crept into commodities.

08 What to watch

Brazil planting: Weekly Conab progress, especially Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná, shows whether the crop stays on schedule.

Weekly Conab progress, especially Rio Grande do Sul and Paraná, shows whether the crop stays on schedule. USDA export sales: The weekly report shows whether foreign buyers keep taking US wheat, corn and soybeans.

The weekly report shows whether foreign buyers keep taking US wheat, corn and soybeans. Risk appetite: A calmer VIX would reduce forced selling in grain funds.

A calmer VIX would reduce forced selling in grain funds. Support levels: Corn at 16.47 and soybeans at 21.71 are the 12-month lows that traders will defend.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did soybeans fall while wheat and corn rose?

Soybeans face a large Brazilian crop, whereas corn and wheat, after long declines, attracted buyers closing earlier bets on lower prices.

Why does Brazil matter for grain prices?

It is the world’s largest soybean exporter, and Conab projects 181.6 million tonnes for 2026/27, so its harvest sets the global supply.

What role does China play?

China is the main buyer of Brazilian soybeans, which is why Chinese demand matters for prices; we could not confirm October shipment figures.

Are SOYB, CORN and WEAT the grain prices themselves?

No. They are funds that track futures, so their prices differ from the cost of a tonne of grain.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest, a global risk-off wave, which we rate as high confidence. The S&P 500 fell 2.02%, the VIX surged, and the dollar index edged up 0.06% to 103.92, a combination that usually hurts emerging markets. Gold’s fund also fell 1.76%, a sign that investors were raising cash rather than hiding in safe havens.

Second, US stockpiles grew, with medium confidence. The US Energy Information Administration (eia.gov) reported that commercial crude stocks rose 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million in the week to 13 November.

The signals conflict in one place. The 10-year US Treasury yield edged down to about 5.0%, which normally helps risk assets, yet shares still fell. The best-supported reading is that fear about equities outweighed lower borrowing costs, and the oil bounce was a short-term rebound after a weak week.

04 The trend behind it

The WTI-tracking fund is 5.46% lower over five sessions and 15.03% lower over 20, and sits 18.5% below its 23 October peak of 169.53. It is still 108.7% above its December 2025 low of 66.17, so the war premium has been trimmed rather than erased.

Petrobras tells the harsher story: 36.42% down over 20 sessions and 37.7% below its 12-month high. Ecopetrol is 26.8% below its September high, so this is a continuation of a slide that began in late October, not a fresh phase.

Here is what earlier episodes suggest, with the caveat that history is not a forecast. After 33 earlier falls of this size in the WTI fund, it was higher 20 sessions later in 16 cases (48%), with a median move of -1.3% and a worst case of -32.4%. For Petrobras, after 7 comparable falls, it was higher in 5 (71%), with a median of +6.7% and a worst case of -23.3%.

05 What it means for Latin America

Brazil is the clearest case of a volume story meeting a weak share price: Petrobras, the state-controlled producer, is at a three-month low.

Colombia is most exposed: Ecopetrol, a state-run company, is at a six-month low, and oil income feeds the national budget. Mexico’s state producer Pemex benefits from higher crude but is hurt when investors turn cautious on state producers.

Argentina’s YPF fell hardest, though its Vaca Muerta shale field remains the country’s main oil growth story.

06 The names to watch

Petrobras is the bellwether: its 12-month low is 11.54 from 7 January 2026, and 26.16 is the ceiling set on 23 October. Ecopetrol’s range runs from a low of 9.21 to a high of 18.26, and it is now closer to the middle than the top.

YPF is the most volatile, since it trades on Argentine politics as much as on crude.

07 What would end it

The first sign would be the VIX falling back from 28.44; a calmer market would lift the producers even if crude stayed flat. The second is US crude stocks: another build would keep the pressure on prices.

For the WTI fund, 169.53 is resistance and 66.17 is the 12-month floor; nothing in between is a strong anchor. For Petrobras, 11.54 is the line that matters. The honest answer is that the slide stops when fear fades, not when oil rises.

World.title: Copper Fund Falls an Eighth Day to a 6-Month Low | Copper Wrap, Nov 19
World.content:
The CPER copper fund fell for an eighth session to a six-month low, while Freeport-McMoRan lost 4.53% and Southern Copper 3.25%.

Key Facts Copper: The CPER copper fund fell 1.00% to US$33.76, its eighth straight loss and a six-month low.

The CPER copper fund fell 1.00% to US$33.76, its eighth straight loss and a six-month low. Miners: Freeport-McMoRan fell 4.53% and Southern Copper 3.25%, both at six-month lows.

Freeport-McMoRan fell 4.53% and Southern Copper 3.25%, both at six-month lows. Cause: A risk-off day: the S&P 500 fell 2.02% and the VIX fear gauge jumped 15.80% to 28.44.

A risk-off day: the S&P 500 fell 2.02% and the VIX fear gauge jumped 15.80% to 28.44. Chile and Peru: Chile is the largest copper producer and Peru is among the top three.

Chile is the largest copper producer and Peru is among the top three. Prediction markets: Polymarket, a real-money prediction market, prices a 0.25-point US Federal Reserve rate rise in December at 92.5% (US$43.5 million traded, 7:39 p.m. ET, 19 November).

Today’s Focus Copper is being sold hard. The fund that tracks copper futures closed at US$33.76 on Thursday, November 19, 2026, its eighth straight daily fall and its lowest close in at least six months. The trigger was a broad retreat from risk. The S&P 500 fell 2.02% and the VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, rose 15.80% to 28.44, with the Nasdaq down 2.25%. Copper is also being hurt by worries about global growth, since the metal goes into factories, grids and cars. Miners are suffering most, because their profits swing more than the metal’s price. For Chile and Peru, which lean heavily on copper, the question is whether this is panic or the start of a lasting downturn. What matters today. A metal tied to factories, grids and electric cars is falling alongside shares, which suggests investors are pricing a weaker world economy, not just a bad day.

01 The session in one read

Think of copper as the economy’s pulse: it goes into wiring, pipes, motors and cars. On Thursday, November 19, 2026, that pulse weakened for an eighth straight session.

The tracking fund closed down 1.00% at US$33.76, a smaller fall than the miners’ but the longest losing run in this wrap. The importance lies in the company it kept: equities and gold fell too.

Assessment — Risk panic, not yet a collapse MEDIUM Copper is falling mainly because investors are cutting risk everywhere. The dollar and bond yields barely moved, so this is not a classic currency or interest-rate story. The variable to watch is whether the VIX settles back below 28.44 and equities stabilise, since copper has been trading as a risk asset.

02 The board

The metal’s fund fell modestly, while the producers fell sharply. Freeport-McMoRan dropped 4.53% to US$49.12 and Southern Copper dropped 3.25% to US$141.46.

That gap is typical in a rout. A miner has fixed costs, so a small move in the copper price becomes a large move in profit, and shareholders sell first.

03 Why it moved

First and heaviest was risk aversion. The S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,176 and the VIX hit 28.44, with the Nasdaq down 2.25% and the Dow Jones down 2.19%. Copper, with its tie to factories and power grids, was caught in it.

Second was China, the buyer of roughly half the world’s copper. When global growth worries rise, traders question Chinese demand first; this is our reading, not a reported data point.

Third, and weaker, were worries that the Federal Reserve may raise rates in December: minutes of its October meeting, published on 18 November, showed officials seeing risks that inflation could persist, and prediction markets price a 0.25-point rise at 92.5%. Gold’s tracking fund fell 1.76%, but the US 10-year yield edged down to about 5.0% and the dollar index barely moved at 103.92, so rates cannot be the main explanation. Our confidence is medium: the equity link is well supported, while the China and Fed links are circumstantial.

04 The trend behind it

This is a continuation, not a fresh shock. The fund is 12.24% lower than 20 sessions ago and 15.7% lower than 60 sessions ago, and sits 18.5% below its 22 September high of 41.43.

Miners have fallen further. Southern Copper is 34.9% below its 25 August peak of 217.40, and Freeport-McMoRan is 38.5% below its peak of 79.91 from the same day.

Our own price history gives a calming but incomplete message. After 12 earlier 20-session falls of this size, copper was higher 20 sessions later in 7 cases, a median gain of 3.1%, but the worst case lost a further 11.6%. History is not a forecast.

05 What it means for Latin America

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, and Peru ranks among the top three behind it and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Both economies earn a large share of export income and tax revenue from the metal, so a lasting slide squeezes budgets and weighs on the Chilean peso and Peruvian sol.

State-owned Codelco in Chile and private producers in Peru feel it through lower revenue. Southern Copper operates in Peru and Mexico, and Freeport holds a stake in Peru’s Cerro Verde mine, so both falls land directly on Latin American output.

For travellers and importers, a weaker peso makes Chile cheaper for dollar holders but raises the cost of imported goods for locals.

06 The names to watch

Southern Copper closed at its lowest in at least six months, at 22.8% above its November 2025 low of 115.21. Its own history is kinder than Freeport’s: in 15 earlier falls this size it was higher 20 sessions later in 11 cases, with a median gain of 14.9%.

Freeport-McMoRan, at 23.9% above its 12-month low of 39.63, shows a coin toss: higher 20 sessions later in 10 of 21 earlier cases, median change of -0.1%, worst case a further 50.1% fall.

07 What would end it

Support is the 12-month low of 30.77 on the copper fund, 8.9% below today’s level, with the round 30 mark beyond it. Resistance sits at 35 and then the September high of 41.43.

A calmer VIX or a Chinese stimulus signal would end the slide. The Federal Reserve’s December meeting is the dated test, and a loss of 30.77 would mean a new phase.

08 What to watch

VIX fear gauge: A fall back from 28.44 would show equity fear easing and would probably relieve copper.

A fall back from 28.44 would show equity fear easing and would probably relieve copper. China demand: Monthly Chinese output and property data will show whether demand is holding up.

Monthly Chinese output and property data will show whether demand is holding up. Support at 30.77: A close below the 12-month low would open a new leg lower for the copper fund.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, where users bet real money, lists a market on the US Federal Reserve’s December decision, with US$43.5 million traded as of 7:39 p.m. ET, 19 November 2026. It prices a 0.25-point rise at 92.5%, a 0.5-point or larger rise at 5.1%, no change at 2.9%, a 0.25-point cut at 0.2% and a 0.5-point or larger cut at 0.1%.

These prices are bets, not polls. They show traders expect the Fed, the US central bank, to raise rates again in December, which would lift the dollar and US yields and weigh on copper and the currencies of Chile and Peru.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did copper fall on Thursday, November 19, 2026?

Mainly a broad retreat from risk, with the S&P 500 down 2.02% and the VIX up 15.80%, with worries about Chinese demand a likely secondary factor.

Does the CPER fund show the spot price of copper?

No. It tracks copper futures, which are contracts for later delivery, so it can differ from the price of physical metal.

How does it affect Chile and Peru?

Chile is the top producer and Peru is among the top three, so lower prices cut export income and tax revenue and can weaken their currencies.

Will copper recover?

Our records show that after 12 earlier falls this large, copper was higher 20 sessions later in 7 cases, but the worst case fell a further 11.6%. That is history, not a forecast.

World.title: Costa Rica Ranks Among the 10 Safest Countries to Visit in 2027
World.content:
Costa Rica is the only Central American country named among the 10 safest destinations for travelers in 2027, according to the Risk Map 2027 released by Swedish risk-management firm Safeture and travel intelligence company Riskline. The annual map rates every country on Riskline’s five-level scale of Low, Moderate, Medium, High and Extreme. It weighs security, crime, health and environmental risks, and access to medical care.

Costa Rica appears on the list of standout safe countries alongside Bhutan, Canada, Chile, Denmark, Iceland, New Zealand, Singapore, Slovenia and Switzerland. Riskline’s analysts chose those countries from every region of the world. The list is not ranked. Within Central America, Costa Rica, Belize and El Salvador share the region’s lowest risk rating. Panama and Nicaragua are rated Medium. Guatemala and Honduras are in the High category.

El Salvador’s rating is one of the biggest changes on the 2027 map. The country moved from Medium to Moderate, making it one of only six countries worldwide whose risk level improved over the past 12 months. The others were the Maldives, Bangladesh, Cameroon, Mozambique and Nepal.

That puts El Salvador in the same tier as Germany, Finland and Cyprus, which all slipped from Low to Moderate this year. Honduras is the region’s most prominent concern on the map. San Pedro Sula, its second-largest city, is one of the 10 least safe cities in the world, alongside Kabul, Port-au-Prince, Bamako, Goma, Guayaquil, Port Moresby, Quetta, Sana’a and Tehran.

Fifteen countries moved to a higher risk level this year. Most of them are in the Middle East, where Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates jumped from Moderate to High. Saudi Arabia and Jordan rose from Medium to High, and Iran moved up to Extreme. Closer to home, Cuba rose from Moderate to Medium.

The 10 least safe countries on the 2027 map are Colombia, Haiti, Iran, Myanmar, Niger, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Yemen, and the West Bank and Gaza. “This year’s map shows how quickly the risk picture can change,” said Jonas Brorson, chief marketing officer at Safeture.

The two companies say the map gives a broad picture and does not replace a full risk assessment. Ratings can also vary a lot within a single country. A separate 2027 assessment by security firm Global Guardian also placed Costa Rica and Panama among Central America’s most stable destinations. That report identified Guatemala and Nicaragua as the region’s most serious concerns.

Costa Rica’s place on the safest list comes as the country continues to deal with drug-related violence, which has kept homicides near record levels in recent years. Most of that violence is concentrated in specific urban and coastal areas and involves criminal groups, not visitors.

The full Risk Map 2027 can be downloaded free at safeture.com/riskmaps.

World.title: Costa Rica Hit by 3.6 Million Malware Attempts as Hackers Shift to Targeted Attacks
World.content:
Costa Rica had about 3.6 million attempted malware infections between September 2025 and September 2026, according to the latest Latin America threat landscape report from cybersecurity company Kaspersky. That is the second-highest figure among the five Central American and Caribbean countries in the report. The Dominican Republic led with 4.2 million, followed by Costa Rica, Guatemala with 3.4 million, Panama with 3.3 million and El Salvador with 1.2 million.

Kaspersky’s previous annual report, which covered a slightly different period, put Costa Rica at 3.9 million attempts. Across Latin America, Kaspersky said it blocked 592 million malware infection attempts over the 12 months, an 18% drop from the year before. Brazil and Mexico accounted for the largest totals, with 330 million and 102 million respectively.

The company cautioned that the decline does not mean the region is safer. Rather than relying mainly on mass campaigns built to infect as many devices as possible, attackers are increasingly concentrating on specific targets, particularly government agencies and large industries.

Government institutions accounted for 27.3% of blocked malware attempts across Latin America, followed by process manufacturing at 12.5%, retail and wholesale trade at 11.5% and healthcare at 8.3%. The report does not break those shares down by country. Costa Rica knows what a targeted attack on the state can cost. In 2022, the Conti ransomware group crippled Finance Ministry systems and other public institutions, prompting the government to declare a national emergency.

The figures reflect detections among users of Kaspersky’s own products, so they point to trends rather than the total number of attacks in each country. Among the most common threats the report identified are pirated programs and unauthorized license activation tools. These downloads often ask users to switch off their antivirus first, which gives malicious software an easy way in.

Once installed, spyware bundled with pirated software can harvest passwords and other confidential data, exposing individuals and organizations to fraud or extortion. Adware is another frequent problem. Although it is mostly associated with unwanted ads and browser redirects, some programs can also steer users toward fraudulent websites and more serious threats.

Fabio Assolini, Kaspersky’s lead security researcher, said many people in the region still put their digital security at risk to get paid software for free, and that criminals exploit that demand by hiding highly malicious files inside copies of expensive programs. Assolini said the overall drop in detections reflects a change in strategy, as attackers move away from simple mass-distributed malware toward professional operations capable of causing greater financial and operational damage to governments and major industries.

Kaspersky recommends a zero-tolerance approach to pirated software, downloading programs only from developers’ websites or official app stores, installing security updates promptly, and using reliable security software at home and at work. The regional decline may look encouraging, but the report suggests the more important question is no longer how many attacks are occurring, but how much damage a single successful one can cause.

World.title: Costa Rica Is Latin America’s Priciest Place to Retire as the Dollar Hits a Record Low
World.content:
Costa Rica is regularly ranked among the best places in the world to retire, but one analysis of cost-of-living data found it is also the most expensive country in Latin America in which to retire comfortably. A record-low dollar is widening that gap for retirees whose income arrives in U.S. currency.

The analysis, published in September by Bloomberg Línea using NetCredit and Numbeo data compiled by Visual Capitalist, estimated that $556,000 in savings is needed to retire comfortably in Costa Rica. That placed the country 16th worldwide and first in Latin America, ahead of Uruguay at $451,000 and Mexico at $356,000.

The same analysis put the U.S. figure at about $738,000, meaning Costa Rica still costs roughly a quarter less than retiring at home. Its estimates assume nearly 15 years of retirement and exclude taxes and health care costs, and the authors noted that results can vary significantly by city, housing and lifestyle.

Costa Rica’s standing in lifestyle rankings remains high. International Living’s 2026 Global Retirement Index placed it third with a score of 87.6, behind Greece and Panama, and ranked it first in the index’s climate category. A separate index by Global Citizen Solutions ranked Costa Rica’s Pensionado visa fourth in the world.

The exchange rate is now eroding the cost advantage those rankings rely on. The dollar closed at 444.85 colones on Nov. 18 in the central bank’s Monex market, the lowest level since the platform began operating in November 2006. It started 2026 at 497.07 colones, a decline of 10.5%, and analysts expect further declines before year-end.

For a retiree living on a $1,000 monthly pension, the minimum income required for Pensionado residency, the difference shows up every month. At January’s rate, $1,000 converted to about 497,000 colones; at Wednesday’s rate, it brings about 445,000, roughly 52,000 colones less each month, or about $117 at current rates. Banks also pay less than the Monex average when they buy dollars from customers.

International Living’s index estimated monthly living expenses in Costa Rica at about $1,500 for a single person to roughly $4,000 for a couple seeking a comfortable lifestyle. The Bloomberg Línea analysis cited high housing costs, prices for some foods, transport, electricity, imported goods and exchange-rate risk as factors behind Costa Rica’s higher requirement.

The pressure on the dollar is seasonal and expected to continue, as the high tourist season, year-end aguinaldo bonuses and tax payments increase the supply of dollars in the country. International Living’s next index is expected in the coming weeks; the 2026 edition was released in December 2025.

World.title: Court File Alleges Diablo-Linked Group Tortured US Surfer Kurt Van Dyke for His PINs
World.content:
The men who killed American surfer Kurt Van Dyke in February allegedly belonged to a group linked to Alejandro Arias Monge, the alleged drug trafficker known as “Diablo,” according to the court file in the case. The file also alleges that Van Dyke was bound and tortured to force him to reveal the PINs for his bank cards.

Van Dyke, 66, was found dead on Feb. 14 in Hone Creek, near Cahuita on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast. A Santa Cruz, California, native known in surfing circles as “King,” he had run Hotel Puerto Viejo for decades. His killing was first reported as a robbery.

Two suspects are in custody. A 31-year-old woman surnamed Arroyo Ramírez, who had a long relationship with Van Dyke, and a man surnamed Gutiérrez Víctor were detained on Nov. 12. On Nov. 15, the Talamanca Criminal Court ordered both held for six months of pretrial detention while prosecutors investigate them for aggravated homicide.

Neither has been charged or convicted, and both are presumed innocent. The allegations described below come from the prosecution’s case file and have not been tested in court.

According to the file, the plan took shape on the morning of Feb. 14. Arroyo Ramírez allegedly persuaded Van Dyke to come to her home in Hone Creek under false pretenses. Prosecutors allege that once he was there, she sent WhatsApp messages telling the others he was unprotected and how to get in.

The file states that the attackers entered, immobilized Van Dyke and tied his hands and feet. They then allegedly tortured him and inflicted stab wounds as they tried to obtain his bank PINs. Prosecutors attribute the killing to a structured group acting together to seize his assets and take his life.

A neighbor called 911 at 10:35 a.m. to report that armed men had broken in, restrained both people inside and stolen the woman’s car and phone, according to the file. Security cameras recorded Van Dyke calling for help at about 10 a.m. Investigators found no sign of forced entry.

The medical-legal report concluded that Van Dyke died of asphyxia caused by compression of the neck, with a fractured hyoid bone, and that he had been tortured. He was found under a bed with his hands and feet bound, a sheet around his head and multiple stab wounds. Investigators allege that the woman staged the robbery and reported her own vehicle stolen to conceal her role.

The car was later recovered in good condition, and investigators determined that her account did not match the evidence. The file also describes alleged threats in the months before the killing. On Jan. 4, Arroyo Ramírez allegedly demanded $1,500 from Van Dyke and threatened to send people from Diablo’s group to harm another former partner of his and their son.

Arias Monge was captured on July 24 in San Bernardino de Sarapiquí at the end of an operation authorities named Némesis, and he is being held at La Reforma prison. Reports on the file have not said whether he is a suspect in the Van Dyke case. Investigations into his network have already reached a police officer and two Pococí judges.

The case is being handled under file 26-000171-0829-PE by the organized crime unit of the Limón Prosecutor’s Office, under the supervision of the deputy prosecutor’s office for money laundering. The OIJ is still looking for two more men believed to have taken part in the attack.

Anyone with information can contact the OIJ’s confidential line at 800-8000-645.

World.title: El Niño Could Thin Out Costa Rica’s Winter Humpback Whale Season
World.content:
Humpback whales from the North Pacific are about to begin arriving off Costa Rica’s Pacific coast, but this season opens under one of the strongest El Niño events in decades. Researchers and tour operators across the region are warning that warmer water could mean fewer whales or a later arrival.

Costa Rica is one of the few places visited by two separate humpback populations. According to the International Whaling Commission, whales that feed off the northwestern coast of the United States travel to Costa Rica’s tropical Pacific waters from December to March to mate, give birth and nurse their calves. A southern population that feeds near the Antarctic Peninsula and southern Chile visits from July to mid-November.

The southern season that just ended had already raised concerns. In August, guides with Priscilla Tours in the Golfo Dulce reported fewer humpbacks than in past years. One guide described a morning when only one of roughly 30 to 40 boats saw a whale and said it had happened twice this season.

A captain with more than 12 years of experience said the whales now spend longer periods farther out rather than staying inside the gulf, and linked the change to warmer water. The guides also reported partial or total bleaching on some corals.

Their observations are anecdotal, and no figures quantifying a decline have been published. A McGill University-led study, which used satellite tracking data from 2009 to 2016 on 42 humpbacks tagged off Costa Rica, Panama and Ecuador, found that the whales combine local conditions such as sea temperature and food availability with long-term memory of their Antarctic feeding grounds to time their migration.

According to one account of the findings, the whales began leaving earlier in years when sea surface temperatures peaked early, particularly El Niño years, and in Costa Rica warmer water coincided with lower chlorophyll and earlier departures. That account noted the study does not prove warming caused this year’s reported drop in sightings.

The northern whales face their own pressures. The U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a better than 79% chance that El Niño will remain strong to very strong through the January to March 2027 period. A recent University of Hawaii study of North Pacific humpbacks during the 2014 to 2016 marine heat wave found that whales facing food shortages cut their activity to save energy. That helped them survive but did not sustain early-stage pregnancies.

Similar concerns are coming from Mexico. Astrid Frisch Jordán, head of the whale conservation group ECOBAC in Bahía de Banderas, said early this month that the high sea temperatures would probably reduce the number of whales or delay their arrival, adding that warm water usually means fewer whales. The season there is expected to begin in the first half of December.

The main viewing areas remain the southern Pacific coast, including Dominical, Uvita, Bahía Drake, Isla del Caño and the Golfo Dulce, along with Manuel Antonio, Quepos, Jacó and parts of the Gulf of Nicoya in the central Pacific, and the Golfo de Papagayo, Tamarindo, El Coco and Sámara in the north.

Under rules from SINAC and the Environment Ministry, boats must keep at least 200 meters (656 feet) from the whales and carry a whale-watching permit. Whether this season follows the pattern seen in warm years should become clear in the coming weeks, as the first northern whales reach Costa Rican waters.

World.title: Don’t Drink This Bottled Water, Costa Rica’s Health Ministry Warns
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Health is warning the public not to buy or drink NIMBU purified water from lot 27/08/26. Laboratory tests found coliform bacteria at levels far above what is allowed in drinking water. Check the label before you open a bottle. The affected lot is printed as 27/08/26 and carries sanitary registration number AS-CR-21-08146. The water is made by Eliviana S.A. for Alpemusa S.A.

Tests by the Laboratory of Pharmaceutical Analysis and Advisory found total coliforms above 1,600 MPN per 100 milliliters (3.4 fluid ounces). The permitted maximum is less than 1.1, which puts the sample more than a thousand times over the limit. Coliforms are the bacteria labs use to judge whether water is safe to drink. When they show up, the water may also carry other germs that can make you sick. The lab also identified Rhizobium radiobacter, a bacterium normally found in soil.

The problem came to light after a consumer reported dark particles floating in a bottle from a different lot of the same product, dated 28/05/2025. The ministry says its findings show contamination in at least two lots. If you have bottles from either lot, don’t drink them. The ministry’s warning centers on lot 27/08/26, but some reports describe it as covering the brand as a whole, so the safest choice until the investigation ends is to avoid NIMBU water entirely.

If you already drank it and feel unwell, see a doctor rather than treating yourself at home. The ministry lists gastrointestinal symptoms, fever and general malaise as the signs to watch for. No formal recall has been announced, which means bottles from the affected lot may still be on store shelves. You can report any bottles you find, or any illness you suspect is linked to the product, through the Ministry of Health’s official channels.

The warning comes as Costa Rica heads into an El Niño dry season in which the national water utility has already asked households to cut water use. The ministry said it will keep investigating to determine how far the contamination reaches.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Top Prosecutor May Face Lawmakers Over Slain Journalist’s Threat Complaints
World.content:
Costa Rica’s ruling party wants the top prosecutor and its acting chief of judicial police to explain to lawmakers how they handled the threat complaints filed by journalist Camilo Rodríguez before he was shot dead on Monday. Nogui Acosta Jaén, head of the Pueblo Soberano caucus, announced in the Legislative Assembly that his party will file a motion in the Special Permanent Commission on Security and Drug Trafficking.

The motion seeks to summon Attorney General Carlo Díaz Sánchez, Deputy Prosecutor Mauricio Boraschi Hernández and acting Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) Director Michael Soto Rojas. The summons is not yet approved. The motion must be filed and voted in the commission, where it was expected to be taken up on Thursday. The ruling caucus holds five of the commission’s nine seats.

Acosta said the inquiry should examine how the justice system processed Rodríguez’s complaints and how people who speak out on social media can be protected. He also pointed to one of the journalist’s videos in which, according to Acosta, Rodríguez suggested that the person threatening him had links to the attorney general. Acosta did not present evidence to support that claim, and the Public Ministry has not responded to it publicly.

Opposition lawmaker Claudia Dobles of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana said she supported calling the judicial officials but questioned why the motion leaves out Public Security Minister Gerald Campos Valverde. The motion comes two days after the ruling caucus approved, by 29 votes to 21, a separate motion demanding the resignations of Díaz and Ombudswoman Angie Cruickshank over their inspection of the new maximum-security prison. Opposition lawmakers criticized the timing of that vote.

On Wednesday, the Public Ministry announced that Díaz will personally lead a specialized team of organized crime prosecutors and prosecutors from Heredia to direct the murder investigation alongside the OIJ. Díaz said the decision reflected the seriousness of the case and that the team would act with rigor and technical precision.

Rodríguez, 50, was killed on the afternoon of Nov. 16 on Route 32 in San Miguel de Santo Domingo, Heredia, as he was returning to San José from Guápiles. According to preliminary reports from authorities, two men on a motorcycle pulled up beside his vehicle, fired repeatedly and fled.

Vladimir Muñoz, acting deputy director of the OIJ, said the attackers had information about the journalist’s vehicle and took advantage of it being stopped in traffic. Investigators are trying to establish whether other people followed Rodríguez and alerted the gunmen, a line the OIJ first raised earlier this week.

Agents searched Rodríguez’s apartment overnight Monday into Tuesday and seized four cellphones, a hard drive, other electronic devices and documents for forensic analysis, according to the Public Ministry and OIJ. No arrests had been announced as of Thursday morning, and authorities have not confirmed a motive.

Prosecutors have said that one of the main lines of investigation concerns Rodríguez’s public allegations about links between organized crime, drug trafficking and political parties. Investigators have not ruled out other motives, including business disputes. Rodríguez had reported multiple threats against him before his death. Díaz has said the journalist was referred to the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection office but declined the protection measures offered, which are voluntary.

Hundreds of people attended his funeral Mass on Wednesday afternoon at the Cathedral of Nuestra Señora del Carmen in Cartago, where mourners greeted the casket with applause and calls for justice. Bishop Mario Quirós of Cartago asked for comfort for the family and for a more just society.

His mother, Sara Chaverri, called for justice and for the country to act against crime. His brother Andrés Rodríguez thanked the public and said the institutional response must go beyond catching the gunmen and lead to changes that address the violence. Burial followed at the General Cemetery of Cartago.

The killing has drawn condemnation from the government, judicial authorities, the United Nations, Reporters Without Borders, the U.S. Embassy and a joint statement from the European Union, Canada, the United Kingdom and Switzerland, which called it an attack on freedom of expression and of the press.

Rodríguez is the third journalist shot dead in Costa Rica in a quarter century, after radio host Parmenio Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. How quickly investigators identify both the gunmen and whoever ordered the killing is likely to shape public confidence in the country’s justice system for years to come.

World.title: Why Costa Ricans Head for Puriscal When the Rains Stop
World.content:
Ask a Costa Rican where to go on a Sunday in late November and there is a good chance the answer will be Puriscal. The city sits in the hills about an hour west of San José, close enough for a day trip and far enough to feel like the countryside most Ticos remember from childhood. For a few weeks between the end of the rains and Christmas, everything that makes the place worth the drive arrives at once.

Puriscal has never needed a beach or a volcano to draw visitors. What it offers is simpler: winding ridge roads, long views across the Central Valley, small farms, butcher shops with wood fires going and a pace of life that the capital lost long ago. This is the season when all of that is at its best.

The first reason is the weather. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) forecast the dry season to settle over the Central Valley during the second week of November, and in Puriscal the change is easy to feel. Afternoon downpours give way to blue skies, and the trade winds that Costa Ricans call the Christmas winds begin to blow across the ridges.

Those winds matter here more than in most places. They clear the haze, cool the air and open up views that stay hidden behind cloud for much of the rainy season. On a clear December morning a visitor can stand on a ridge above Santiago de Puriscal and see the valley on one side and the hills falling away toward the Pacific on the other.

The timing also flatters the land. The rainy season has left the hills green, though in a drier-than-normal El Niño year the pastures may start turning gold sooner than usual. Back roads that turn to mud in the wet months are dry and passable again, which opens routes through villages that many visitors never reach.

The second reason is pork. Puriscal is known across the country as the home of the chicharrón, and families here have been raising pigs and curing meat for generations. People drive out from San José every weekend of the year for a plate of fried pork with yuca, tortillas and a squeeze of lime, but in the weeks before Christmas the habit becomes a pilgrimage.

The reason is the Feria del Chicharrón, the fair that has filled the center of Santiago de Puriscal in the early weeks of December for more than two decades. Vendors start frying before the morning mist has lifted, and by midday the smell of pork and woodsmoke has spread across the town. Past editions have added live music, craft stalls, carnival rides and a horse parade to the food.

The crowds are real and the fair has drawn more than 6,000 visitors to the canton in a single week, a large number for a town of this size. Last year it opened on the last weekend of November and ran through Dec. 8, and anyone planning a trip this year should check the dates with the organizers before setting out.

The calendar does the rest since the aguinaldo, the extra month of salary that Costa Rican workers receive at the end of the year, lands in December, and the school year ends around the same time. Families have a little more money and a lot more free time, and a drive to Puriscal costs far less than a weekend at the coast.

Pork is also the meat of the Costa Rican Christmas. It goes into the tamales that families make together in December and onto the table as roast leg on Christmas Eve. Plenty of visitors leave Puriscal with a cooler in the trunk, stocked by the same butchers their parents bought from.

There is more to do than eat. The canton lies where the dry forest of the Pacific slope meets the wetter forest of the highlands, and that mix draws birdwatchers, who find the trails easier going once the rains stop. Others come for the old tobacco country, the roadside stands selling fruit and local produce or simply the drive itself.

What Puriscal offers in these weeks is a version of Costa Rica that many people assume has disappeared. It has clean air, green hills, good food cooked over a fire and neighbors who still greet strangers in the street. Costa Ricans have always known where to find it, and this is the time of year they go.

World.title: International News: Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as security forces launch major operation against gangs
World.content:
International News: Heavy fighting erupts in Haiti as security forces launch major operation against gangs

By Zoila Palma: Heavy fighting erupted in Haiti today as the country’s armed forces and police launched an aggressive security operation to regain control of Martissant, a strategic corridor connecting the capital, Port-au-Prince, to the country’s western and southern regions.

The operation marks the first major attempt in five years to remove powerful gangs that have maintained control of the area, AP reports.

Haiti’s National Police reported that at least 34 suspected gang members were killed during clashes involving police officers and a task force that includes personnel from Vectus Global, a private security firm founded by former U.S. Navy SEAL Erik Prince.

Local media reported heavy gunfire and explosions from explosive drones as armored vehicles moved through Martissant. The area is located along Route 2, a major transportation link that previously carried thousands of commuters and shipments daily. Since gangs seized control in 2021, movement through the corridor has been severely restricted, with armed groups reportedly charging motorists tolls and opening fire on vehicles attempting to pass. The disruption has also affected the delivery of goods and humanitarian assistance, forcing residents and aid workers to rely on dangerous alternative routes.

The violence in Martissant dates back to June 2021, when rival gangs attacked each other, setting homes on fire, killing residents and destroying businesses before taking control of the local police station.

A United Nations report estimated that the clashes displaced at least 19,000 people and affected approximately 800,000 others. Subsequent reports documented the displacement of more than one million people and the relocation of hundreds of public and private institutions. Meanwhile, a UN-backed gang suppression force has intensified operations in several areas, including Tabarre and the Artibonite region, targeting gang strongholds and clearing roads, schools and other facilities previously controlled by armed groups.

El Salvador has also deployed approximately 2,500 troops to Haiti following an October 18 attack in which four Salvadoran personnel went missing.

Acting on orders from President Nayib Bukele, Salvadoran forces have targeted the residences of two powerful Haitian gang leaders, Jeff and Lanmò San Jou, although neither leader was killed.

Thousands of Haitians reportedly took to the streets this week in support of Bukele’s intervention, while security experts have raised concerns about unilateral military operations and civilian casualties linked to explosive drone attacks.

World.title: Cabinet extends Garifuna Settlement Day wishes, urges caution on the roads
World.content:
Cabinet extends Garifuna Settlement Day wishes, urges caution on the roads

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Cabinet has extended warm wishes to all Belizeans as the country celebrates Garifuna Settlement Day today, November 19.

In a release issued from Belmopan, Cabinet said the day honours the rich history, resilience and cultural contributions of the Garifuna people to Belize.

It said the national observance recognises the traditions, music, language and heritage that continue to enrich Belize’s cultural identity.

With activities taking place across the country, Cabinet also issued a reminder to motorists.

Drivers are urged to exercise caution, remain attentive, observe speed limits and make responsible choices on the road.

Cabinet wished everyone a joyful and safe Garifuna Settlement Day.

World.title: International News: APEC Summit overshadowed by big-power politics
World.content:
International News: APEC Summit overshadowed by big-power politics

By Zoila Palma: Chinese President Xi Jinping has called on Asia-Pacific economies to strengthen cooperation in trade and technology development as leaders gathered in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Thursday.

However, discussions on economic cooperation and open trade were overshadowed by growing geopolitical tensions and a rare trilateral meeting involving Xi, U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, AP reports.

Addressing leaders from the 21 APEC economies, Xi urged countries to prioritize shared interests and maintain openness in trade and technological development.

“APEC members are like passengers riding the same boat,” Xi said, calling on members to work together, support one another and strengthen economic ties amid global challenges.

The summit featured traditional diplomatic engagements, including bilateral meetings, a gala dinner and a group photograph, while showcasing China’s technological advancements through artificial intelligence and robotics.

Trump, meanwhile, highlighted the strength of the U.S. economy, claimed his administration had attracted trillions of dollars in investments and said he expected to secure additional trade agreements. He also pledged to oppose what he described as “globalist” efforts to regulate artificial intelligence.

Technology competition between the United States and China remained a major concern, particularly Washington’s restrictions on China’s access to advanced computer chips used in artificial intelligence.

The United States recently tightened controls on remote access to advanced AI technology, a move experts say closed a significant loophole that had allowed China access to billions of dollars’ worth of advanced Nvidia chips.

Chinese leaders have emphasized the need for fair access to AI technology and cooperation on cybersecurity, financial stability and economic growth.

World.title: Xunantunich open but ferry limited to pedestrians; ATM and Nohoch Che’en under review
World.content:
Xunantunich open but ferry limited to pedestrians; ATM and Nohoch Che’en under review

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Institute of Archaeology says the Xunantunich Archaeological Reserve is open today, Thursday, November 19, but the ferry is operating as a pedestrian crossing only.

Visitors will not be able to take vehicles across the Mopan River and should be prepared to walk up to the site from the crossing.

In a notice issued at 6:00am, the Institute also advised that the Actun Tunichil Muknal (ATM) Cave and the Nohoch Che’en Archaeological Reserve are experiencing elevated river levels.

Its team is monitoring both sites and was expected to issue a further update within about an hour to confirm whether they will open to visitors today.

All other archaeological reserves across the country are open for visitation.

The Institute of Archaeology, a branch of the National Institute of Culture and History (NICH), says it will continue to monitor conditions and provide updates as needed.

Tour operators and visitors with bookings for ATM or Nohoch Che’en are advised to confirm the status of the sites before travelling.

World.title: 2027 could bring record heat, higher fuel costs and tougher economic pressure for Belize
World.content:
2027 could bring record heat, higher fuel costs and tougher economic pressure for Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Economist has released a preview of its annual forecast, The World Ahead 2027, and several of its themes have direct implications for Belize.

The publication expects 2027 to be the hottest year on record, driven by a “super El Niño,” with more droughts, heatwaves and extreme weather.

For Belize, that points to pressure on farmers, water supplies and hydro power generation, at a time when the country is already leaning more on expensive diesel to keep the lights on.

The outlook also anticipates continued fallout from the Iran conflict, including disrupted energy flows and tight fertiliser supplies. Belize imports its fuel and much of its farm inputs, so higher global prices feed quickly into electricity bills, transport and the cost of food.

The Economist warns as well that government borrowing costs are rising across wealthy countries. Higher global interest rates matter for Belize, which carries a public debt of about BZ$4.65 billion.

Taiwan is another theme. The publication describes the next two years as dangerous for the island, given China’s military ambitions and Taiwan’s 2028 elections. Belize is one of the few countries that maintains diplomatic relations with Taiwan, a partnership of 37 years that brings significant development support.

On energy, the outlook argues that renewables offer countries a way out of volatile global fuel markets. That is relevant to Belize’s ongoing debate over electricity costs and energy security.

The full edition of The World Ahead 2027 is being published today by The Economist.

World.title: Belize gets sunshine for Garifuna Settlement Day with just a few showers
World.content:
Belize gets sunshine for Garifuna Settlement Day with just a few showers

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The weather is cooperating for the 19th.

According to the Met Service, today will be sunny with cloudy spells, and tonight will be partly cloudy. Showers or thunderstorms will be isolated for most of the country.

There is a medium chance of a few more showers offshore this morning, inland this afternoon and over the south tonight. Those celebrating in Dangriga, Hopkins, Seine Bight, Punta Gorda and other southern communities may want to keep an umbrella close this evening.

Daytime highs will reach 87°F on the coast, 90°F inland and 76°F in the hills.

At sea, winds are from the northwest at 5 to 10 knots, becoming northeast. Seas are slight, with waves of 1 to 3 feet.

The outlook for Friday and Friday night is for generally fair weather with isolated showers or thunderstorms. A few are possible inland on Friday afternoon.

Today’s tides include a low at 11:56am and a high at 5:55pm, followed by a low at 12:37am and a high at 6:33am on Friday.

The sun rose at 5:59am and sets at 5:16pm. The moon rises at 1:33pm and sets at 1:58am Friday.

World.title: Dickie Bradley blasts idea of bringing El Salvador’s hardline crime model to Belize
World.content:
Dickie Bradley blasts idea of bringing El Salvador’s hardline crime model to Belize

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Attorney Richard “Dickie” Bradley is warning the government not to model Belize’s crime response on El Salvador.

Bradley’s comments come as the government looks at President Nayib Bukele’s hardline strategy, with Home Affairs Minister Michel Chebat expected to visit El Salvador to study it.

The veteran attorney says Belize’s violence is the product of deeper failures at home.

“This is a crisis of leadership and a failure to tackle social and economic problems,” Bradley said.

He argued that the number of people driving the violence is small. In his words, it is not a thousand or 2,000 young men shooting up the place, but “a handful of people.”

Bradley pointed to the recent deadly shooting on the Coastal Road, which left four men dead and preceded the declaration of a State of Emergency. He said the response exposed “the lack of any kind of solution, any attempt at solution.”

He was sharply critical of the Salvadoran approach, describing it as a “Nazi Gestapo approach” in which people are picked up and treated “like animals.” He alleged that detainees in that country face inhumane conditions that do not make the news.

Bradley said that instead of developing its own plan, the government has decided to “check on Bukele and see if we could bring something back here.”

The government has said it is exploring a range of measures to address crime, including legislative reforms and a second chance programme for at risk young men.
