World.title: BOJ rate hikes raise mortgage payment fears
World.content:
At a time when Jamaicans are already struggling with punishing cost of living, homeowners carrying hefty mortgages are expressing fresh concerns following two consecutive policy interest rate hikes by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ).

It has raised fears among them that monthly mortgage payments could climb further and place additional financial pressure on their already stretched pockets.

The BOJ raised its benchmark policy rate on September 29 by 50 basis points from 5.5 per cent to 6.0 per cent – the bank’s first rate increase since November 2022 – and again on Thursday to 6.5 per cent, a decision the central bank said was taken in the context of “an upside risk that inflation could remain above the target range until late 2027”.

READ: BOJ increases policy rate to 6.5% as inflation pressures persist

Jamaica’s annual inflation rate eased to 8.2 per cent in October from 8.6 per cent in September, but remained above the Bank of Jamaica’s target.

The policy rate is what the BOJ pays deposit-taking institutions on balances held at the central bank, and serves as a benchmark for borrowing costs.

One woman, who is in her eighth year of mortgage payments, said she is apprehensive, maintaining that her budget cannot handle any more pressure.

“You budget for a certain amount that your mortgage rate will be, and you don’t know what percentage it’s going to be increased by and when they do it, they’re not going to give you a grace period or anything,” she said.

The mortgager reflected on the 2022 rate hike, and the subsequent cycle of five cuts that brought it down from seven per cent.

“A [few] years ago, when the interest rate went up, our mortgage went up and so did the home insurance, and then when the BOJ reduced the rates, the mortgage went down,” she explained.

With the interest rates up again, she said she is “of course” worried.

“Because right now, I am maxed out; I don’t have any extras. Nothing working with…I’m maxed out. If it increases, I don’t know what I would do. I [would] just hope that eventually it’s going to decrease again.”

There are some Jamaicans, however, who say their mortgages have not decreased since that 2022 spike, as some commercial banks were slow to reduce their lending rates, prompting calls for a reduction from lobby groups including the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica (PSOJ), Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association (JMEA) and Jamaica Chamber of Commerce.

One male mortgager said the 2022 increase added a huge chunk to his payment that he is still grappling with.

“By itself, it added $28,000 to my monthly payments. What’s worse is that mere days after being informed about the interest rate increase, I was informed that the peril insurance rate has been increased as well, resulting in another increase in my monthly payment,” he explained.

That was four years ago, and unlike some, he says, he has not gotten any relief. Now with the BOJ increasing rates again, the possibility of additional hikes is distressing.

“I am very apprehensive about the possibility of another increase, because I simply cannot afford it. I am paying approximately $40,000 more in monthly mortgage payments in just four years, when my salary hasn’t budged. Considering all the other increases in cost of living, the struggle is real,” he lamented.

One female mortgager who borrowed directly from the National Housing Trust and is about halfway through paying off a 25-year mortgage said her relief at not necessarily being subject to an increase because of the interest rate hike is immense.

“I am terribly relieved because since that time there have been adjustments based on policy changes so the mortgage I started out with is not the mortgage I now pay,” she explained, adding, “I am very relieved, and I am still thinking and trying to find a way to exit the agreement before the 25 years because…I really look at it now, and I don’t want to be trapped that long.”

Another male mortgager, who is nearing retirement age and has around $8 million left to pay on his own mortgage, was less concerned about any potential increases.

“I think, yeah, there are people who legitimately would want to worry about these things. I really don’t. I have the mortgage already, I have to pay it. The only thing I could maybe try to do is shop around for another entity, financial company that might offer me a better rate. But that’s a lot of hassle,” he said.

Realtor and CEO & Qualifying Director for Easton Douglas Consultants Ltd, Kari Douglas explained that it was unlikely that the increase would drastically affect the housing market locally, maintaining that there are factors in purchasing a home that carry more weight than the current interest rate.

However, she did have advice for potential homeowners.

“A rate increase raises the cost of borrowing, so buyers should test their budget, confirm whether their rate is fixed or variable, and buy only what they can comfortably carry if rates move again. Take the time to get a proper valuation so you’re paying a price that the market supports and borrowing against real value,” she urged.

Douglas said prospective purchasers should also shop around and compare the rates, fees and terms of different banks, building societies, and credit unions to ensure the lowest possible rates.

World.title: ‘I will not be baited into a one-sided apology’, says Burchell
World.content:
Nekeisha Burchell

KINGSTON, Jamaica—Member of Parliament (MP) for St James Southern, Nekeisha Burchell, has stated that she will not be baited into a one-sided apology over statements she directed at the MP for St Andrew West Rural, Juliet Cuthbert-Flynn, during a tense sitting of the House of Representatives on November 17.

Burchell, while responding to an off-mic quip from Cuthbert-Flynn about her ability to adequately prepare for parliamentary debates, said “mi go a gud, gud school enuh. Mi neva run fi a living”.

Cuthbert-Flynn, a four-time Olympian and minister of state in the ministry of national security and peace, and other Government MPs were incensed by the remark. The member for St Catherine East Central, Alando Terrelonge, rose on a point of order to demand that Burchell withdraw the statement. He accused Burchell of disrespecting athletes. She eventually withdrew the remark after she was ordered to do so by deputy speaker of the House, Heroy Clarke.

The next morning, the dispute erupted into a below-the-belt war of words when Cuthbert-Flynn posted on social media that she was “proud to have earned my living on my feet”.

Burchell has come under pressure to apologise to both Cuthbert-Flynn and Jamaican athletes in general.

But, in a video posted to social media on Thursday, she indicated that there will be no such apology even while stating that, “I have tremendous respect for Jamaica’s athletes, and the discipline and sacrifice behind their achievements”.

Burchell said she has since spoken with athletes, adding that, “I’ve taken the time to speak with managers and leaders in the sporting fraternity and generally they understood this was a personal retort directed at Juliet, not an attack on athletes as a group”. She said if there’s any athlete who took offence, “no disrespect was intended”.

Describing Cuthbert-Flynn as chief heckler, Burchell said she has observed since entering the Parliament, that Government members “throw stones and hide their hands. When somebody responds, they present themselves as the victims and demand one-sided apologies”.

She accused the Government of using its parliamentary majority to condemn the response “while ignoring the attacks that provoked it – kind of how they deal with Beenie Man”, she said. “I was baited into a retort, but I will not be baited into a one-sided apology that pretends the provocation never happened”.

Burchell insisted that there cannot be one standard of respect for the majority and another for the minority. She has declared that she will not be bullied into silence.

The first-term MP who represents the opposition People’s National Party has often locked horns with Government members. She began her video by expressing regret for “allowing myself to be drawn out in Parliament this week, and I shouldn’t have”. She outlined her educational and professional achievements before entering representational politics, moving from Mt Alvernia High School to the University of the West Indies, to the London School of Economics.

“I built a career running campaigns across the Caribbean and working in different countries, just making a name for myself.

“So imagine standing in Parliament trying to make a contribution, and somebody across the floor is repeatedly questioning your education, your ability, and tell you that you didn’t even write your own speech? Me, who has been writing speeches for presidents, prime ministers and business leaders for nearly two decades,” Burchell said.

“And she just wouldn’t stop, the remarks kept coming, getting more personal and insulting, while I’m on my feet trying to concentrate,” she added.

Responding to Cuthbert-Flynn’s comment that she made her accomplishments on her feet, Burchell said, “I understood exactly what she’s saying; she was suggesting that while she worked for her achievements, I somehow slept my way to mine. Burchell said it’s the same sexual insinuations she has had to endure since entering representational politics, from both males and females.

World.title: How Dis Mek? Fern Gully crafts
World.content:
At Fern Gully in St Ann, Jamaican craftsman Vernant ‘Oneil’ Campbell proudly states that the iconic sculptures at the popular landmark are “not made in China”, a declaration that is more than a catchy marketing pitch, but a testament to the local craftsmanship and creativity behind the souvenirs they sell.

From Marlins to stingrays and the famous ‘Ready Freddie’, the area is renowned for its homegrown art that catches the eye of hundreds of thousands of visitors annually.

Campbell and his colleague Craftsman Audley Ricketts spoke to the Observer about the production process behind their creations, describing the time it takes to learn, execute, and deliver the carvings.

Check it out on the latest episode of How Dis Mek!

— Dana Malcolm

World.title: ODPEM employee was not PNP actor, says Opposition
World.content:
Dayton Campbell

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The People’s National Party (PNP) has strongly rejected claims that a senior Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) employee, who resigned amid an investigation into the handling of hurricane relief supplies, was affiliated with the Opposition party.

In a statement on Thursday, the PNP said a thorough review of its membership records found no evidence that the former employee had ever been a member of the party or acted on its behalf.

PNP General Secretary Dr Dayton Campbell described attempts to portray the former employee as a political saboteur as predictable but deeply concerning.

“That the Government and its surrogates would once again try to create a distraction and pass the blame for their failed relief effort is not surprising. What is shocking is the claim that one employee in logistics could have caused all of this on his own,” Campbell said.

Campbell argued that attributing the reported failures to a single employee raised serious questions about the Government’s oversight and management of the relief operation.

“If one employee could direct donor funds, keep containers sealed for a year, stop homes from reaching homeless families and allow food to spoil while mould ran rampant, then that speaks to the gross incompetence of a Government that failed not only to manage the relief effort but to manage its own staff,” he said.

He further questioned who authorised the transactions, who was responsible for supervising the employee, and when the minister with responsibility for ODPEM would be held accountable.

“Jamaicans who gave generously, and families still without a roof, deserve the truth. Who authorised these payments? Who supervised this employee? And when will the minister responsible accept accountability?” Campbell asked.

The Opposition has also called on Prime Minister Andrew Holness to provide a full account of ODPEM’s management of relief supplies following Hurricane Melissa, in light of the findings outlined in a report by the Auditor General’s Department. The October 2026 compliance audit identified several deficiencies, including 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables, 15 unopened containers not recorded in ODPEM’s inventory and approximately $780 million in shipments omitted from the agency’s donation schedules. READ: ODPEM audit finds expired food, insect-infested supplies and millions in unaccounted donations ODPEM has since responded to the findings, disputing claims of missing funds and housing units. READ: No missing houses, no missing money

The PNP maintained that the prime minister must answer for the agency’s operations, particularly given his decision to bring ODPEM under the Office of the Prime Minister immediately following Hurricane Melissa.

According to the Opposition, the findings point to serious failures in the management and distribution of disaster relief supplies.

“This can only be described as an abject failure of leadership and accountability by the prime minister,” Campbell said.

World.title: BOJ increases policy rate to 6.5% as inflation pressures persist
World.content:
The Bank of Jamaica in Kingston.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) has increased its policy rate for the second consecutive month, raising it by 50 basis points to 6.5 per cent, effective Thursday, as the central bank moves to contain persistent inflationary pressures.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the BOJ said its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) unanimously agreed to the increase amid concerns that inflation could remain above the bank’s target range until late 2027, signalling a more prolonged period of elevated prices than previously anticipated.

The policy rate represents the interest paid by the central bank to deposit-taking institutions on balances held in their current accounts at the BOJ.

The decision comes despite a slight easing in headline inflation, which declined to 8.2 per cent in October 2026 from 8.6 per cent in September, according to the Statistical Institute of Jamaica (STATIN). However, it said inflation remains significantly higher than the 2.9 per cent recorded in October 2025.

The BOJ attributed the continued inflationary pressures primarily to rising food prices, transportation costs and electricity rates compared with the previous year.

Meanwhile, core inflation, which excludes agricultural food products and fuel, increased to 5.4 per cent in October, up from 5.3 per cent in September and 3.7 per cent in October 2025.

According to the central bank, the increase in core inflation suggests that higher agricultural and fuel prices are beginning to affect the cost of processed foods and certain services. However, relative stability in the foreign exchange rate has helped to moderate some of these pressures.

The MPC also highlighted continued uncertainty surrounding the inflation outlook, particularly due to ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

It warned that prolonged conflicts, coupled with worsening agricultural production conditions resulting from an intensifying El Niño phenomenon, could further drive inflation expectations and place additional pressure on consumer prices.

Despite these risks, the BOJ indicated that the policy rate increases implemented so far should be sufficient to support a timely return of inflation to its target range.

READ: BOJ increases policy rate to 6% to contain inflation

World.title: No missing houses, no missing money
World.content:
Director general, Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), Commander Alvin Gayle addressing a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House in St Andrew on November 18. (Photo: JIS)

THE Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) has challenged findings in the Auditor General’s report suggesting discrepancies in accounting for 200 prefabricated houses donated by the People’s Republic of China, insisting that all units were received, handled, and stored appropriately.

Speaking at a post-Cabinet media briefing at Jamaica House on Wednesday, ODPEM Director General Commander Alvin Gayle sought to clarify the report’s findings, maintaining that all prefab houses received in the aftermath of last year October’s Hurricane Melissa were accounted for.

“I need to address something that has come to me in the media space, regarding the fact that only some 31 prefabricated houses that were donated to the GOJ [Government of Jamaica] by the Republic of China [have] been accounted for. This is not the case. What is the case is this — 200 houses were donated to the GOJ, they were received by the ODPEM, 169 of those units have been distributed and 31 remain in our custody,” said Gayle, using the moment to also declare that all monies channelled through the agency were accounted for.

His comments came in response to an Auditor General’s Report tabled in Parliament on Tuesday, investigating the agency’s management of resources received under the Hurricane Melissa relief initiative. It charged that ODPEM had several instances of inefficient receipt, storage and distribution of donated fixed assets.

The report said 200 prefabricated houses were received by the agency, valued at more than $139 million. That donation is represented among a revised ODPEM schedule in July 2026, reporting that 1,332 fixed assets valued at $443 million were donated to the Government of Jamaica by various countries and entities in support of Hurricane Melissa relief efforts.

However, the report claimed that ODPEM had provided warehouse receipt forms to support only 1,084 assets donated, while the remaining 248 were unseen.

“We have so far verified the existence of the 11 motor vehicles, 31 prefabricated houses, and the 353 chainsaws. We found no evidence that the internationally donated fixed assets were recorded in ODPEM’s inventory records or fixed asset register. Further, receipt forms were not provided for the remaining 248 assets noted on ODPEMs schedule,” the report said.

It also highlighted that ODPEM’s records bore no evidence of receipt forms for the prefab homes.

The audit report outlined that omitting donated assets from the fixed asset register risked creating inaccurate financial and asset records, and infringed on ODPEM’s ability to track, monitor, and maintain the assets entrusted to its care.

Acknowledging that risk, Gayle told the media briefing on Wednesday that ODPEM had initiated corrective action before the latest attorney general report was made public, including changes to leadership, logistics operations, and measures to improve warehouse management.

The director general said the agency has committed to strengthening its inventory management and operational capacity, pointing to a new standard of operating procedures introduced to fortify the receipt, recording, storage and distribution of relief supplies across its warehouses.

“To support these measures, ODPEM is upgrading its integrated management accounting system to improve the tracking of donated goods, strengthen audit trails and reduce reliance on manual processes. Existing warehouse and inventory policies are also being reviewed to ensure compliance with government financial and asset management requirements, while donated fixed assets are being reconciled with ODPEM’s asset register,” added Gayle.

Among its corrective measures, Gayle also pointed to ODPEM’s enlistment of the Major Organised Crime and Anti-Corruption Agency to investigate internal discrepancies involving relief supplies and assets, including weaknesses in inventory management and warehouse controls. Gayle noted that ODPEM was fully cooperative with the ongoing investigation, and clarified that anyone found culpable of wrongdoing will be held accountable in accordance with the law and disciplinary procedures.

He further acknowledged the auditor general’s findings concerning the use of approximately $45 million from donated funds to facilitate the customs clearance of relief supplies consigned to third parties.

Gayle told the media briefing that such payments were used as an exceptional measure to facilitate the urgent clearance of humanitarian shipments and prevent delays in the delivery of relief supplies to affected communities, but admitted that they were unapproved for use in such circumstances.

“While the expenditure was undertaken in the context of the emergency response, ODPEM acknowledges that the payments fell outside the approved purpose of the donated funds and that the necessary financial controls and supporting documentation should have been maintained.

“Steps have since been taken to restore the funds to their designated account. Approval has been granted for an additional allocation, and the donation account will be reimbursed in full upon receipt of those funds,” he said.

The director general maintained, however, that all prefab homes were accounted for, with only 31 left for distribution.

“Two hundred were donated, 169 were distributed and 31 remain in our custody. And those 31 were seen by the attorney general as reported in the report,” he continued.

World.title: Tufton outlines measures to tackle shortcomings in the public health sector following worrying review
World.content:
Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton addressing the House of Representatives on Tuesday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

MINISTER of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton has pointed to a raft of measures that is being implemented to address the “systemic problems” besetting the country’s ailing health-care sector.

Tufton outlined the measures in Parliament on Tuesday after he tabled a report which detailed shocking shortcomings faced by patients including delayed admission and treatment, late diagnosis, lack of treatment, long waiting lists and discourteous staff. These were among more than 1,000 client (patient) complaints recorded at hospitals across Jamaica’s four Regional Health Authorities (RHAs) during the first quarter of the year.

The Jamaica Observer reported on the review findings on Wednesday, highlighting that just over 10 per cent of the complaints have been cleared up. The findings are contained in a 50-page Ministry of Health and Wellness Report titled, ‘Institutional Performance Review’ that was ordered by Tufton.

Tufton had vowed to be open and transparent when he ordered the review, and on Tuesday he said it was “self-imposed”.

“This is a new effort that we’re embarking on. I know it lends fodder for those who like to criticise because there’s a lot to criticise here,” Tufton said at the conclusion of his presentation, a seeming acknowledgement of the numerous deficiencies in the public health-care system.

Tufton pointed to the health ministry’s implementation of the accountability framework scorecard, which rates 13 public health entities against 18 governance and accountability indicators, and the client care connect, which managed 1,045 client feedback cases across the four RHAs. He suggested the review also offered a blueprint for the way forward.

By way of action, he said all regional health authorities have been mandated to implement plans to clear their backlog of open cases, and expand the QR Code feedback system launched by the South East Regional Health Authority so every patient can be heard and every concern tracked to solution.

The minister said that by January 2027, the portfolio score should reach at least 60 per cent and one in four client cases should be resolved within the quarter.

“By April 2027, no entity should remain in the critical category and at least half of all cases should be resolved,” he stated.

Beginning in the 2027/28 fiscal year, the service level agreements with each regional health authority will incorporate the framework indicators and targets for resolving patient concerns.

“We will follow the resources to ensure that primary healthcare and prevention gets adequate support at the level of the regional authorities,” Tufton assured.

He also committed to meet personally with board chairs and each will be asked to submit a 90-day recovery plan by November 30 and report monthly to the health ministry. “Where there is no measureable improvement by January, the performance of the board will be reviewed,” Tufton said.

For hospitals with the highest number of patient complaints, beginning with Cornwall Regional, St Ann’s Bay and Kingston Public, the ministry will meet with the board chairs, regional directors and chief executive officers and require reviews of the level of the individual departments. “This is to identify which units are struggling and why, and learn from those that are doing well,” said Tufton.

He highlighted that Cornwall Regional Hospital was doing well in a few areas. “Their physiotherapy department is excellent, their dialysis department is world class. They don’t keep patients in A&E, they triage them to wards. These are examples that we could teach many other institutions,” said the minister.

Regarding Cornwall Regional, he was careful to point out that the review was not a condemnation of an entire institution, but rather “it is recognising the weaknesses and correcting them”.

He told the Parliament that the review represents the first integrated assessment of two principal mechanisms through which the ministry measures organisational performance and accountability. Pointing out that government mechanisms were already in place to do that, Tufton explained that “we have come up with a format because we believe it agitates more aggressively for the value for money preposition”.

The accountability framework scorecard evaluated 13 public health entities against 18 governance, leadership and accountability indicators, while the client care connect tracked and monitored over 1,000 patient feedback cases across the four regional health authorities.

“Taken together, these instruments provide a comprehensive review of how well our institutions are governed, how effectively they respond to the public they serve, and where improvements are required, to strengthen performance and public trust,” said Tufton.

Significantly, the review found that no regional health authority was performing at the highest level on both governance and client (patient) experience.

“While some institutions demonstrate strong compliance on governance requirements, that strength is not always reflected in the patient experience,” Tufton acknowledged. He pointed to the North East Regional Health Authority as an example, noting that it achieved the highest governance score in the portfolio, yet it resolved less than one per cent of the client cases reported during the review period.

“That finding should give us pause because accountability is not measured by the number of reports that we produce, the meetings we hold, or the policies we approve. Accountability is measured by outcomes, it is measured by whether concerns are addressed, whether service is improved and whether citizens feel heard”.

Meanwhile, Tufton acknowledged that nearly 90 per cent of patient complaints remain unresolved and identified several recurring challenges across the public health portfolio. These relate primarily to management and client services. Monthly performance reporting was flagged as a weakness, so too the absence of timely audited financial statements; digital transformation initiatives were progressing too slowly, and inconsistent measurement of governance breaches was also present. Of particular concern is that complaint resolution mechanisms lacked the responsiveness that citizens expect and deserve.

Tufton argued that these are not merely administrative concerns. He argued that “unresolved complaints represent a missed opportunity to learn, delayed reports constrained decision-making, while weaknesses in governance increase risks, and inefficiency consumes resources that could be directed to patient care”.

World.title: Jahshii counts blessings on début EP N.U.M.B
World.content:
Dancehall artiste JahshiiContributed

For an artiste whose musical identity has long been rooted in resilience, learning to acknowledge his blessings is proving just as important for Jahshii as overcoming the obstacles.

The entertainer is therefore making room for gratitude, reflection, and personal growth with his forthcoming début EP, N.U.M.B (Never Underestimate Mi Blessings).

A seven-track collection, Jahshii says he hopes the project will encourage listeners to appreciate their own journeys while remaining determined to overcome life’s challenges.

Set for release on November 27, N.U.M.B represents a personal milestone for the Born Fighter deejay, who says the music draws heavily from his thoughts, lived experiences, and the lessons gathered along the way.

“The project means a lot to me. It’s seven songs with wah deh pan mi mind, me life experiences and dem thing deh. Das why me call it N.U.M.B (Never Underestimate Mi Blessings) because it’s all about acknowledging my blessings and not taking dem for granted,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

Produced by Sweet Music Production and distributed worldwide through ONErpm, the EP finds Jahshii exploring themes of gratitude, faith, resilience, and self-awareness, while maintaining the motivational messaging that has become a recurring feature of his music.

For the artiste, the intention is not simply to entertain but to leave listeners with something they can carry beyond the music.

“Mi fans can expect motivation from it, self-awareness and ultimately determination. My music always have dat, messages fi get people fi stay determined. Memba a we say born fighter ennu, so this is a project weh means a lot and I hope the people take a lot of lessons from it when dem listen,” he added.

That fighting spirit runs through the project’s track list, which includes Glory, Manifest, Survivor, Learn Enough, Prove Dem Wrong, Pretend Teeth, and Powers.

The upcoming release comes amid a period of continued musical activity for Jahshii. In October, he released 4th Charge alongside UPSTATE, followed by Fighter, a collaboration with Carlostha1st and ikeed. His recent appearance at Appleton Estate Livewire in Clarendon has also kept him connected to Jamaica’s live entertainment circuit.

Beyond the music, Jahshii has increasingly spoken about the importance of using his platform to encourage young people and promote positive messages, sentiments that align with the project’s emphasis on personal development and determination. His reflections on fatherhood have also formed part of this broader outlook.

With N.U.M.B, however, the artiste is offering listeners something particularly personal: A collection of music inspired by what occupies his mind, the experiences that have shaped him and, perhaps most importantly, the blessings he refuses to take for granted.

As he prepares to deliver his first official EP, Jahshii is reminding listeners that being a fighter does not mean focusing solely on the struggles. Sometimes, it also means recognising how far you’ve come, appreciating what you have, and finding the determination to keep going.

World.title: Delay Another Day: How James Bond can save the EU
World.content:
Pattinson will star as Bond, although as the EU is funding the project, we have been forced to cast Ursula von der Leyen as his boss, M.

Budgetary constraints mean that instead of swanky cocktail bars and high-rolling casinos, late-night scenes will be filmed inside the Hairy Canary pub and at Maison Antoine friterie.

There are nine films planned. Here are the synopses:

Dr. Non — In which Bond tries to scrap the need for unanimity in the Council and replace it with permanent use of qualified majority voting.

Omnibussy — Bond tries to make life easier for Europeans by slashing red tape but runs into opposition from frustrated industry groups and concerned NGOs.

The Man With The Golden Envelope — A faithful, true-to-life recreation of Qatargate.

World.title: UK ‘playing catch up’ with Nordic countries on crisis preparations, says minister
World.content:
Jarvis pointed out a national risk register that highlights widespread power outages, the loss of drinking water and terrorist and state threats as among the most significant risks to the U.K. He added: “If you look at the things that I’ve said in Parliament on the record [and] the conversations that we’re having nationally about the nature of the world that we are living in, I think there is a lot of conversation about the different threats that we face.”

He added: “There is a bit of balance to be struck because we absolutely don’t want to alarm the public — but we do want the public to be alert, we want the public to be prepared.”

Jarvis downplayed concerns that some in the U.K. government felt after Cabinet ministers joked about their personal stockpiles — including Housing Secretary Angela Rayner, who said hers would include “mascara, concealer, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, some baked beans and a tin of custard.”

“As the security minister, there are lots of things that I worry about at any one time. That isn’t one of them,” he said. “I think it’s quite helpful in terms of promoting the conversation. I think it’s quite helpful in terms of focusing people’s minds about what they would do in their own households.

“That’s the essence of this campaign. It’s about making sure that there is that resilience in households … so I’m entirely relaxed that people are having a conversation about Sauvignon Blanc or whatever it might be.”

Jarvis said he had “obviously followed my own guidance” when building his own home stockpile, including a radio and torch, and had not added any special treats beyond the checklist. He does, however, have a ready supply of eggs at home. “I’ve always found it incredibly relaxing to keep chickens, not least when you have a reasonably busy and demanding job,” he said. “There’s something very peaceful about them.”

Find the full episode of Westminster Insider “Stockpiling Britain: Does Westminster know something we don’t?” here.

World.title: 5 takeaways from the Spanish election debate
World.content:
The latest POLITICO poll puts Feijóo’s PP at 29.5%, narrowly ahead of Sánchez’s Socialists on 27.2%, with just 10 days to go before Spaniards head to the ballot box. While the two parties are effectively neck and neck, the prime minister faces an uphill battle to remain in power.

Vox is polling at 19.6%, putting the right-wing bloc close to half the vote — and Feijóo in a strong position to form the next government. Meanwhile, the two main parties to the left of the Socialists, Frente Amplio and Podemos, are polling at a combined 8.1%, leaving Sánchez’s camp with little room to build a governing majority.

With that polling picture, both Sánchez and Feijóo approached Thursday’s debate as an opportunity to sway undecided voters and the 55% of the electorate who are not yet certain they will cast a ballot. POLITICO breaks down the showdown …

Sánchez and Feijóo shake hands for the cameras before a debate where the personal animosity was evident. | Oscar Del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images

A record under fire

Feijóo sought to present himself as a steady hand while portraying Sánchez’s record in office as one of mismanagement, invoking this year’s two deadly train disasters as evidence.

The PP leader tied the deterioration of Spain’s high-speed rail network, which was once a source of national pride, to government corruption and neglect, asking Sánchez whether he really believed passengers could still travel by train without fear. “I myself have taken high-speed trains 130 times over the past few years,” he said. “And I thank God that I am nonetheless able to attend this debate tonight.”

Feijóo also seized on Spain’s deepening housing crisis, which Sánchez cited as the main reason for calling the snap election, to question what the government had achieved since taking office in 2018. The prime minister struggled to rebut Feijóo’s charge that he had failed to deliver promised homes, repeating his vow to enact progressive housing measures if reelected.

World.title: Stockpiling Britain: Does Westminster know something we don’t?
World.content:
A ‘Black Sky event’ — a major blackout that could knock out communications, disrupt food supplies and bring everyday life to a standstill — is among the scenarios emergency planners worry about.

Now the government’s new ‘Be Ready’ campaign is urging Britons to stockpile food, water and other essentials.

But why are politicians suddenly so keen for us to prepare for the worst?

This week, host Patrick Baker meets the MPs who think the government isn’t going far enough.

He hits the supermarket with Conservative Shadow Minister for Defence, Security and Resilience David Reed to put together a 72-hour emergency kit — and find out what threats have him worried.

Liberal Democrat MP and Shetland islander Alistair Carmichael, Chair of the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee, explains what the rest of Britain can learn from life on a remote island, where power cuts and disrupted supplies are familiar hazards.

Baroness Tracey Paul discusses a new House of Lords report warning of ‘potentially catastrophic risks’ and accusing the Government of complacency.

And, in a podcast first, Patrick gets rare access to the Government’s National Situation Centre inside the Cabinet Office. There, alongside POLITICO’s Dan Bloom, the minister responsible for resilience Dan Jarvis explains why Britain needs to learn from its Nordic neighbours — and why he’s not bothered by Cabinet ministers joking about stockpiling sauvignon blanc.

World.title: What does Europe want from Andy Burnham’s reconciliation bid?
World.content:
This week’s EU-UK reset has been long in the making. After the final squeeze by negotiators, will the summit pave the way for a closer relationship and maybe even lead to Britain rejoining the bloc – or are the strains of the Brexit divorce still too raw to overcome?

As British Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives in Brussels to sign off on a deal covering agri-food, energy and youth mobility, Anne McElvoy asks how Europe sees Britain’s desire to move closer to the fold and what might come next. She’s joined by Sandro Gozi MEP, who chairs the EU delegation to the EU-UK Parliamentary Partnership Assembly and is a member of the centrist Renew Europe Group. Gozi previously sat in Italy’s parliament and was Secretary of State for European Affairs in the Renzi and Gentiloni governments from 2014 to 2018.

Later in the podcast, she’ll talk to Nick Thomas-Symonds, who until a few months ago led the UK’s negotiations on the reset deal. He made way for the current EU Relations Minister Hamish Falconer when Andy Burnham moved into 10 Downing Street, but still keeps a close eye on the London-Brussels relationship from the government backbenches in the House of Commons. Does he think the deal will pave the way for a much bigger debate about Britain and Europe and what the costs might look like?

World.title: EU-UK summit — live updates
World.content:
The British PM is in Brussels to ink a host of post-Brexit agreements — and start talking about what comes next.

Andy Burnham heads to Brussels Friday for his first formal summit with the European Union as British prime minister.

More than a decade after the U.K. voted for Brexit, the two sides are hoping to move a little closer, eying deals on food and drink rules, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. London and Brussels are also seeking agreement on the thornier question of reduced tuition fees for European students in the U.K.

The long-in-the-works summit comes as Burnham eyes a wider reset in Britain’s relationship with the bloc in the coming years. POLITICO’s team on the ground will be poring over Friday’s deals, parsing leaders’ words, and asking what comes next in the post-Brexit rapprochement.

World.title: How to watch the UK-EU summit like a pro
World.content:
On tech, British firms are concerned that they could be shut out of parts of the EU public administration market because of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA) and its new sovereignty requirements. They’ve lobbied hard for reassuring language in talks, both with the negotiators working on the law and with those drafting the joint statement.

On health, the U.K. and EU are looking to strike a deal to tackle medicine shortages by sharing intelligence on supply disruptions and stockpiles. As Brussels steps up efforts to manage medicine shortages across the bloc, Britain risks being left out of the increasingly joined up system. Closer cooperation could help both sides “avoid procurement battles” for limited stocks and “tit-for-tat export bans, as happened during the pandemic,” said Mark Dayan, Brexit lead at the Nuffield Trust.

One area the statement will definitely cover is the question of tuition fees. EU countries want European students studying at British universities to qualify for lower domestic fees, as they did before Brexit.

The U.K. is open to the idea but wants, in turn, assurances its businesses won’t be hit by new EU Made in Europe rules. Brussels says it can’t give those assurances yet, so the statement is likely to include a compromise to delay talks by up to six months. Only then will we find out how much lower tuition fees might get.

Another key question is whether the implementation of the agri-food, emissions trading and youth mobility deals will be contingent on a successful outcome for tuition fee talks — which some member countries have been pushing for. This will be determined by the wording of the final statement, but the latest version does not make this link explicit.

What does Burnham want to talk about?

Since Labour Party conference in September, Burnham has talked up building a closer relationship with the EU — ditching some of the caution that characterized his predecessor’s approach to European relations.

World.title: The web is held together by volunteers. AI could tear it apart.
World.content:
The PHP Foundation, which was only established in 2021 despite the coding language itself existing since the early 1990s, has two members of staff and 13 contractors. “Having very few individuals responsible for some key piece of infrastructure is just problematic,” said Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member.

Out of office

Many tools like PHP have their origins in the 1990s, when foundational software and programming languages were developed in the messy, community-minded early days of the web. Those that worked well or were useful were gifted as a common good, picked up by other software developers and became building blocks for a vast number of digital technologies on which governments, critical infrastructure and citizens now rely.

Many open-source software libraries form the basis for widely used software like Android. Facebook was originally built using PHP, and household names like Spotify, Etsy and Wikipedia are just some top destinations that still use it as the basis for their services and websites.

The homepage of the PHP website is seen in Singapore on Oct. 22, 2026. | Yong Teck Lim/Getty Images

When cybersecurity agencies and companies issued an urgent warning in October that there were major flaws in PHP identified with the help of AI, and that they should either update their systems or shut them down, it was a public revelation that the architecture upon which our digital world relies is almost comically fragile.

Adermann explained that it is common for people who have worked on a PHP project for years in their spare time — developing a level of specific expertise that’s very hard to replicate — to duck out when they start families or can no longer find spare time.

That became especially apparent during the process of fixing the recent PHP flaws: One person involved in pushing out technical updates had a scheduled medical procedure and “was simply not available,” he said. “It was like, ‘okay, how do we figure it out, who can even do this now?’”

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strikes damage Austrian and Dutch embassies in Kyiv
World.content:
Shattered windows, wrecked cars and a blast crater marked the aftermath of a Russian bombardment in Kyiv, on Thursday 19 November 2026. The strikes damaged both the Austrian and Dutch embassies, though staff at both missions escaped without injury. Ukrainian authorities said Russia fired anti-ship missiles and 98 drones across the country, logging strikes in 18 locations and damaging several diplomatic premises and historic sites in the capital.

 

Around 10 people were working inside the Austrian embassy when an explosion rocked the area during office hours, deputy head of mission Daniel Ruethlin said, as footage showed workers covering damaged vehicles with plastic sheeting amid the debris. Nearby, the Dutch embassy was hit by a projectile, according to Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen, with no casualties reported there either.

Notably, the Dutch mission was struck two days after Dutch weapons manufacturer Destinus revealed that Ukraine had used its arms in recent attacks on the Crimean Bridge, prompting Russia’s embassy in the Netherlands to accuse The Hague of openly participating in the war. No evidence has been provided linking the embassy strikes to that announcement, which nonetheless laid bare the relentless danger facing civilians and diplomatic staff in Kyiv.

World.title: 10,000 identical inflatable rings raise questions over Ceuta migrant crossing
World.content:
A police report points to possible logistical preparations ahead of the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta at the end of July, after detecting the use of thousands of inflatable rings of the same model, black with a printed design, during the crossing at Tarajal beach.

 

The officers believe that "it does not seem possible" for the migrants themselves to have bought the rings directly from shops or online, as there would not have been enough stock to meet a sudden purchase of thousands of units on the same day without prior planning or orders.

The analysis, based on aerial images and photographs from different points along the Tarajal border, suggests that a single large batch had been purchased in advance, then distributed at specific locations and widely used during the crossing.

Images on social media and in the press do not make it possible to clearly identify points of sale. However, some migrants interviewed said they had bought the rings in the Moroccan town of Fnideq, while others said they had acquired them on Tarajal beach itself, before entering the breakwater.

The judge requests information on the rescues

Judge María Tardón, who is handling the case at the National Court, has asked the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Tarifa for information about the rescues carried out on 30 and 31 July, when the mass crossing took place, including the times, locations, identities of the people rescued and the units involved.

The magistrate has also asked the organisation Hazte Oír, which has joined the proceedings as a popular prosecution, for photographs and videos of a Ford Focus with a Spanish number plate in order to identify its two occupants.

According to the complaint, the vehicle was parked on the Tarajal breakwater in the early hours of 30 July and its occupants provided assistance to only some of the people who were crossing.

World.title: Nobel economist Joseph Stiglitz deems youth protests across Europe 'legitimate'
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands have taken to the streets in France, Denmark, Italy and Spain in recent weeks to speak out against rising living costs, housing crisis and poor pay.

 

Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz said he understands the youth's worries and that their concerns were "legitimate".

"Part of the problem [...] is inequality across generations," said Stiglitz.

"They can't afford housing. They're not given the education that would make them productive. AI is giving rise to new sets of anxieties," he said.

The former World Bank chief economist said that the world the next generation is inheriting is filled with uncertainties linked to rising inequality, climate change and other issues.

Protests have filled European countries' streets in recent months, fuelled by widening wealth gaps. "I think those are legitimate complaints," said Stiglitz. These pressures drive fear within younger generations that they may never match the living standards their parents enjoyed.

'I pay €460 for 5 square metres'

Last week, hundreds of thousands of protesters took to the streets in Spain for the first nationwide 24-hour strike since 2012.

Marching through pouring rain, protesters in Madrid carried signs chanting "we have no home", speaking out against rising living costs.

"People work a lot, and it isn't enough to pay the rent, to pay for a house," said Paula Diaz, a 25-year-old theatre technician who lives with her parents.

Protestors block Madrid's Gran Via main avenue during a nationwide general strike in Spain, Wednesday, 11 November 2026. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Arturo Leon, 24, is a student in Barcelona and pays €460 a month for a 5-square-metre bedroom in a shared apartment with four others. "We do not have a contract, and there are lots of things in the flat which are broken, but the landlord refuses to fix," he told Al Jazeera.

Sanchez called this month's election, initially scheduled for 2027, after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the demonstrations.

'We don't want mice in our schools'

In Italy, thousands of students called for more school funding as they marched, set up tent camps and occupied schools to make their demands heard.

"We don't want windows falling on our heads, and we don't want mice in our schools. We want clean buildings, and I want to live in a better world than this one," said Sofia Cataldi, a 16-year-old Roman student.

This call for a better life sounds like an echo of student protests that have been rumbling in France since the beginning of September.

Students chant during a demonstration demanding increased education funding in Paris, Tuesday, 10 November 2026. AP Photo/Teresa Suarez

"The state of schools, the state of hospitals, staffing levels in schools and hospitals, the way things are getting worse and worse across all public services — these are issues that really resonate with us," said Aurelane Thos, a 38-year-old nurse.

"We're stressed about our studies, but when you have a bunch of cops in front of the high school every morning, you only want to keep protesting," said Mathilde, a 17-year-old pupil in Paris.

Stiglitz backs taxing the rich

The 83-year-old American economist has been a long-time advocate of taxing the ultra-wealthy. He argues that governments would have room to respond to social demands if they were willing to raise more revenue.

"There is so much money at the top that even a small tax rate on the top generates a huge amount of money," he said.

Stiglitz backs proposals such as the suggestion by French economist Gabriel Zucman for a minimum levy of around two per cent of fortunes above €100 million.

There is so much money at the top that even a small tax rate on the top generates a huge amount of money Joseph Stiglitz Nobel Prize-winning economist

Such tax revenues would allow more money to be spent on public services and should be levied at the European Union level. He argues the bloc's free movement of people and capital made tax avoidance easier.

But the Columbia University professor warned that tax alone won't solve Europe's challenges. European countries should rethink parts of their public spending and implement more flexible pension systems that reflect longer life expectancy, while taking into account physically demanding jobs.

"Students may not fully understand," Stiglitz said, that beyond the usual budget pressures, "this is a particularly difficult time."

World.title: Four men found guilty of raping woman drugged by husband in UK
World.content:
Four British men were found guilty on Thursday of multiple sexual offences, including rape, against a woman whose then-husband drugged her and advertised her for sex online.

 

Her then-husband, Philip Young, also filmed her without her knowledge at their home in Swindon, in a case bearing striking similarities to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France.

Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity, expressed her "relief" at the verdict and urged other women who have experienced similar abuse to come forward, saying they "can be believed and understood."

“Knowing what has happened to me without my knowledge or consent has been incredibly difficult to process, and this abuse has cost me my life as I knew it,” she said outside Winchester Crown Court in southern England.

“The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."

The 49-year-old mother of three spoke after a jury found the four men, aged between 32 and 62, guilty of sexually abusing her at her home in Swindon after being recruited online.

The verdicts and guilty pleas

Philip Young, had previously pleaded guilty to dozens of offences, including 11 counts of rape and 11 counts of administering a substance with intent.

Norman Macksoni, 48, was convicted of rape, while Richard Wilkins, 62, was found guilty of rape and assault by penetration.

Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was convicted of assault by penetration and sexual touching, while Mohammed Hassan was found guilty of sexual touching.

A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, admitted one count of assault by penetration, two counts of sexual assault and one count of rape.

Justice Pushpinder Saini said the four men faced “significant” prison sentences and praised Joanne Young for her "amazing bravery throughout these proceedings.”

World.title: Europe Tonight discusses; Will Sánchez's bid to unite the left work?
World.content:
As Spain readies to head to the polls in snap general elections on 29 November, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is going head-to-head with his conservative rival, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, in a televised debate on Thursday.

 

Both men will be looking to consolidate a lead, with most opinion polls suggesting the government majority could swing to the right.

Joining Euronews' weekly evening show Europe Tonight, Antonio Roldán, a former member of parliament and professor at IE School of Politics, Economics and Global Affairs, discussed the upcoming elections with our presenter Mared Gwyn Jones.

Among the topics discussed were whether Sánchez's major risk in triggering this election, hoping to unite the left, will pay off, as well as what a coalition government between PP and Vox could mean for Spain.

Discover the full conversation in the video above.

Watch on Europe Tonight Antonio Roldán, former member of parliament and professor at IE School of Politics, Economics and Global Affairs, discuss the upcoming elections with our presenter Mared Gwyn Jones.

World.title: Europe Tonight: Theresa Fallon on whether world leaders could redraw global spheres of influence
World.content:
Historic talks between the leaders of China, the US and Russia concluded earlier today without a major breakthrough. China has published what it describes as a “trilateral peace declaration”, in which the three countries commit to reforming the UN and increasing the production and supply of oil and gas.

 

US President Donald Trump also praised his “great relationship” with Russian President Vladimir Putin after both leaders held their first face-to-face talks since they met in Alaska last year.

On his way back from China, Trump called into a separate meeting of Ukraine’s European allies in Berlin, where he questioned Europe’s decision to continue funding Ukraine. However, the US President has assured that he will not make decisions without consulting Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Euronews' evening show Europe Tonight welcomed Theresa Fallon, founder and director of the Centre for Russia Europe Asia Studies, to discuss the topic in depth alongside our presenter Mared Gwyn-Jones. Among the questions raised were whether the Yalta Conference – where the Soviets did walk away with a good deal – is a fair comparison to the recent talks, and whether these leaders could redraw spheres of influence.

Discover the full conversation in the video above.

World.title: COP 31: Is the rich world doing enough to support climate-vulnerable countries?
World.content:
COP31 negotiators from more than 200 countries are racing in Turkey to reach a contentious deal ahead of Friday's deadline, but tensions have emerged over climate financing and the phase-out of fossil fuels.

 

Earlier this week, the EU's climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, told Euronews that Europeans do not want to focus on money, but on implementation.

On Thursday, Euronews' weekly evening show Europe Tonight welcomed Sandrine Dixson-Declève, Honorary President of the Club of Rome, to discuss whether COP31 can be called a success, as well as whether the rich world is handing out crumbs to poorer countries grappling with the impacts of climate change.

To find out what Dixson-Declève has to say, watch our full interview above.

World.title: Podcast: Living on the breadline, France's 35-hour week and a divisive tax
World.content:
The French government's decision to raise the minimum wage has failed to satisfy protesters struggling to make ends meet amid the cost-of-living crisis. Also, did the introduction of the 35-hour working week actually help reduce unemployment? The evidence is mixed. And a look at the history of France's second-largest tax, the CSG, and why it's dividing politicians.

Advertising

French unions and workers have been protesting over the rising cost of living and wages that are failing to keep up with inflation. In response, the government has agreed to increase the minimum wage, known as the Smic, by 1.6 percent – putting an extra €24 a month into the pockets of the lowest earners. But the measure has failed to satisfy unions and public sector workers, who took to the streets again this week for a day of strike action. We hear what it's like to live on the breadline and the arguments for raising public sector wages. (Listen @0')

France introduced the 35-hour working week in 2000, aiming to reduce high unemployment by spreading work among more people. After five years of research, labour economist Elio Nimier-David has found that the reform failed to achieve its intended goals, while the question of how much people should work continues to divide politicians today. (Listen @19'20'')

The CSG, or general social contribution, was introduced in 1990 and is now France's second-largest tax after VAT, raising billions of euros to fund the country's social security system. But its broad reach and proportional rate have made it a political target, as presidential candidates debate how to ease the cost-of-living crisis and put more money back into people's pockets. (Listen @15'10'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.
