Air Astana expects to receive three Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft in 2026-2027, which are planned for flights to the U.S. The ministry also noted that it signed agreements with Boeing in 2025 to supply 33 aircraft valued at $15 billion.

Lastayev said direct flights would strengthen business and tourism ties, create new opportunities for companies and improve transport connectivity between Central Asia and the U.S.

World.title: ‘Economic Outcast’: US Pressure on Iran Tests Central Asia’s Trade and Transit Ambitions
World.content:
ASTANA — Washington’s new campaign to isolate Iran is putting Central Asia’s growing trade and transport links with Tehran under pressure. The dilemma was underscored in September, when the first 55-container train carrying Chinese goods was dispatched toward Iran through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, highlighting the commercial potential of a route increasingly exposed to sanctions risks.

On Aug. 24, the United States (U.S.) Department of the Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast at President Donald Trump’s direction, targeting Iran’s financial networks and economic partners. As the campaign expands, Central Asian governments and businesses face a difficult question: how to preserve access to strategically important trade routes without jeopardizing their financial and commercial ties with the United States.

The campaign soon acquired a broader diplomatic dimension. On Sept. 2, Axios reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had instructed U.S. embassies to deliver diplomatic démarches to host governments, demanding that they “immediately and systematically” sever trade relations with Iran. According to U.S. officials cited by Axios, special instructions were sent to several Central Asian capitals, including demands to close branches of Iranian Bank Melli and Bank Saderat, which Washington links to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The U.S. Treasury also warned that entities facilitating financial transactions or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran could lose access to the U.S. financial system. On Oct. 1, Washington expanded the campaign to Iran’s automotive and railway sectors, authorizing sanctions against individuals and entities operating in those industries. The move is particularly significant for regional connectivity, as rail transport has become an increasingly important part of Iran’s efforts to maintain economic links with neighboring countries.

Although these measures do not automatically prohibit every shipment transiting Iranian territory, they increase the potential exposure of foreign banks, insurers, logistics companies and other businesses dealing with Iranian entities.

Why Iran matters to Central Asia

For Central Asian countries, Iran is more than a neighboring trading partner. It provides landlocked economies with access to the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman through ports such as Bandar Abbas and Chabahar, opening alternative routes to international markets. Iran’s interest in Central Asia is equally strategic. Tehran views the region as a gateway to the markets of China and Russia and an opportunity to ease its long-standing economic and diplomatic isolation. Developing transport links, including the North-South corridor and the Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway, has become an important part of this strategy.

Kazakhstan has been particularly active in developing this southern direction. On June 28, Kazakhstan and Iran signed a 27-year Build-Operate-Transfer agreement for a Kazakh transport and logistics terminal at Shahid Rajaee Port in Bandar Abbas. The agreement includes a two-year construction period followed by 25 years of operation, with commercial operations expected to begin in the third year. The project is part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to strengthen the International North-South Transport Corridor and diversify export routes beyond traditional connections through Russia and China.

Trade figures also illustrate the economic importance of the Iranian market. According to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of National Economy, freight transportation along the North-South corridor increased 12% in 2025, reaching 3.5 million tons. Trade turnover between Kazakhstan and Iran grew 26.4% to $430.2 million over the same period.

Tehran sees Central Asia as a long-term strategic partner

For Tehran, strengthening these connections is part of a longer-term strategic orientation toward Eurasia, not simply a response to Western sanctions. Mohammad Hossein Masoumzadeh, senior researcher at the Governance & Policy Think Tank (GPTT) in Tehran, described Iran’s engagement with Central Asia as a strategic priority rather than a temporary adjustment to geopolitical pressure.

“Iran’s approach toward Central Asia is not merely a tactical or temporary reaction to the intensification of Western sanctions; rather, it is part of a fundamental, strategic, and long-term pivot toward Eurasia and a neighborhood-first policy,” he said.

Masoumzadeh highlighted railway connections through the Sarakhs and Incheh Borun border crossings, which link Iran with Central Asian railway networks. Although the countries use different railway gauges, specialized bogie-exchange facilities at border terminals help facilitate cargo movement between networks.

He also pointed to the potential of maritime connections across the Caspian Sea. Iran’s northern ports, including Amirabad and Anzali, and Kazakhstan’s ports of Aktau and Kuryk could form part of a multimodal transport network connecting Central Asian economies with Iran’s southern ports and international shipping routes. The new China-Iran railway connection is another example of this growing connectivity. Masoumzadeh described the September shipment as a significant step toward developing alternative Eurasian trade routes.

“The launch of the container train from China to Iran passing through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan is a tangible manifestation of the revival of the New Silk Road,” he said.

He added that the route “certainly has the potential to become a regular and commercially viable trade corridor.”

Its main advantages, according to Masoumzadeh, include shorter transit times compared with traditional maritime routes, as well as an alternative to international waterways facing geopolitical tensions and rising insurance and shipping costs. However, he acknowledged that the threat of U.S. secondary sanctions poses a serious challenge for private businesses and logistics companies in transit countries.

“The experience of recent years has shown that when tangible economic interests and the political will of governments are aligned, innovative solutions emerge to manage these risks,” he said.

To maintain regional participation, Masoumzadeh proposed independent financial and banking mechanisms, including settlements in national currencies, barter systems and regional clearinghouses. He also highlighted the potential of joint regional transport companies and logistics consortiums to distribute commercial risks among participating countries.

Harmonizing customs tariffs, digitalizing border processes and removing infrastructure bottlenecks would also be essential to making the corridor commercially competitive. However, alternative payment arrangements cannot automatically shield companies from U.S. sanctions. Transactions involving designated entities or targeted sectors may still carry risks regardless of the currency used.

Secondary sanctions could reshape regional calculations

Pressure on Iran could have consequences well beyond its borders, particularly for countries that have invested in transport routes through Iranian territory. Dr. Dania Arayssi, assistant director of the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, said Operation Economic Outcast was making commercial engagement with Iran considerably riskier for Central Asian countries.

The pressure comes as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have been expanding their economic and transport links with Tehran. Banks and major companies are likely to reduce their exposure to Iran to protect access to the dollar-based financial system, while governments may seek to avoid an open rupture in relations with Tehran.

Arayssi said the campaign could fundamentally reshape Central Asia’s long-standing multi-vector foreign policy, forcing regional governments to make more difficult geopolitical choices. She also identified Uzbekistan as particularly exposed because it relies on Iranian transit routes. According to her estimate, around 60% of Uzbekistan’s transit to European and Turkish markets passes through Iran.

“Washington’s pressure does undermine the region’s connectivity plans, because an alternative corridor can itself become a source of geopolitical risk,” she said.

At the same time, Arayssi noted that Central Asian countries cannot simply abandon Iranian routes because they offer access to ports on the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. She expects Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to pursue a cautious balancing strategy rather than immediately terminate their economic projects with Iran.

“They’ll keep Iran projects alive on paper and show the U.S. they are complying through tighter banking checks,” she said, adding that governments could also seek exemptions from Washington while investing more heavily in alternative routes, including the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea and the Trans-Afghan railway.

Alternative routes offer options, but not immediate replacements

The Middle Corridor, officially known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, connects China and Central Asia with the South Caucasus and Europe through the Caspian Sea. Its growing importance reflects the region’s efforts to diversify trade routes and reduce dependence on traditional transport networks. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), cargo volumes along the corridor increased 62% in 2024 to reach 4.5 million tons. However, infrastructure constraints, port capacity, vessel availability and coordination between countries continue to affect its competitiveness.

Another potential alternative is the Central Asia-South Asia (CASA) railway project, which would connect Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan with Afghanistan and Pakistan, providing access to Pakistani seaports. On Oct. 1, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates signed a memorandum of understanding to explore the project. The parties plan to conduct technical and economic studies and assess the feasibility of the required railway infrastructure. The initiative remains at the planning stage. Both routes could expand Central Asia’s access to international markets, but they cannot immediately replace the commercial and geographical advantages offered by Iranian ports.

For Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, the challenge is therefore not simply whether to maintain trade with Iran, but how to preserve access to strategically important markets and ports while limiting their companies’ and financial institutions’ exposure to measures that could affect their broader international economic relationships. How successfully regional governments navigate the expanding reach of economic sanctions will be an important factor in determining the future of these connectivity plans.

World.title: Tokayev Sets Goal of Turning Kazakhstan Into Central Asia’s Academic Hub
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan aims to attract 100,000 international students by 2029 and strengthen its position as Central Asia’s academic hub through international research partnerships, artificial intelligence development and university modernization, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the third Strategic Partners Forum on Nov. 19.

Addressing international university leaders, scientists and education experts, Tokayev said the country must move beyond hosting foreign university branches and focus on research, technological innovation and retaining world-class expertise, Akorda reported.

“Our strategic goal is to transform Kazakhstan into an academic hub of Central Asia and become part of the global market for knowledge, particularly relevant and high-quality knowledge,” he said.

From international campuses to joint research

Tokayev described international academic partnerships as the first stage of Kazakhstan’s ambitions. Universities from 11 countries have established branches in the country, enrolling more than 12,000 students and employing nearly 1,500 lecturers, including more than 600 foreign professors.

Kazakhstan currently has 132 universities with more than 800,000 students. The number of international students has increased from 31,000 last year to 41,000, with more than 8,000 receiving financial support from Kazakhstan. The country plans to raise this figure to 100,000 by 2029 through the national Study in Kazakhstan initiative.

Kazakhstan has also become the first country in the region to join the Lisbon Recognition Convention, covering Europe, and the Tokyo Convention, covering the Asia-Pacific region. The move strengthens international recognition of Kazakh university qualifications.

The next stage, Tokayev said, will focus on scientific cooperation, joint research laboratories and breakthrough technological projects.

“Now I have set the task of retaining world-class knowledge in Kazakhstan in the form of qualified personnel, scientific achievements and innovations,” he said.

The forum also featured an exchange ceremony for a signed agreement between Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Science and Higher Education and the United Nations University on establishing a regional research hub in Almaty.

AI and research partnerships

Tokayev highlighted the role of artificial intelligence in transforming higher education and research, noting that Kazakhstan’s universities should focus on developing practical solutions and technological innovations. He cited the development of the national language models KazLLM and AlemLLM, as well as the launch of Qazaq AI Research University, as examples of progress.

“Strong universities are the foundation of the future,” he said.

Shymkent to become a regional education hub

Astana and Almaty have traditionally served as Kazakhstan’s main centers of science, culture and intellectual development, hosting the country’s leading national universities. Tokayev said Shymkent should now become a major scientific and educational hub for southern Kazakhstan.

The city has launched an educational program with Arizona State University and opened a branch of Türkiye’s Gazi University.

Tokayev also announced his decision to grant national university status to South Kazakhstan University named after Mukhtar Auezov, saying it should become a center of high-quality education, advanced research and intellectual development for the region.

Education to support economic transformation

Tokayev linked higher education development to the nationwide People’s Construction program, which will include social, transport and energy infrastructure projects across Kazakhstan.

He stressed that universities must prepare specialists capable of supporting infrastructure development, digital transformation and the expansion of AI across industries.

“Building a knowledge-based economy has become a long-term constitutional commitment that both the current government and all subsequent governments will have to fulfil,” he said.

Tokayev also emphasized that the rule of law and anti-corruption efforts are essential to creating a stable and predictable environment for international academic partnerships.

Concluding his address, he called for deeper cooperation with international universities and researchers.

“Science is an invaluable asset intended to serve the progress of all humanity, which means that knowledge has no borders and should have none,” he said.

World.title: ‘What special status does the Russian language have?’: Russian-language education debated again in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

A lawmaker from the ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), Hikmat Babaoglu (Mammadov), has proposed reviewing state funding for Russian-language school education. He made the proposal on 16 November during a plenary session of the Milli Majlis, Azerbaijan’s parliament, as lawmakers discussed the 2027 state budget.

According to Babaoglu, 157,000 pupils study in Russian-language classes, compared with 1.57 million in Azerbaijani-language classes. The state spends 2,000 manats (around $1,177) a year on each pupil.

The MP stressed that “national identity and national ideology are shaped through education”. He also questioned whether Azerbaijan had any state-funded schools that taught in English or Chinese:

“Why is that? It is something worth thinking about.”

He said a similar situation existed in higher education.

Over the past two years, the future of Russian-language education in Azerbaijan has repeatedly come under discussion. This time, however, a lawmaker from the ruling party raised the issue from the parliamentary podium and backed his argument with budget figures. This raises a question:

Is this a debate about education spending, or does it reflect relations between Baku and Moscow?

What do the figures tell us?

According to the figures cited by the MP, around 9% of all schoolchildren in Azerbaijan study in Russian-language classes. Based on his estimate of annual spending per pupil, the state spends approximately 314 million manats a year on Russian-language education.

Elshan Azim, head of School No. 35 in the Kalbajar district, cited the same figure. He said that the government allocates 314 million manats a year to Russian-language education, while schools for internally displaced people receive 188 million manats (around $184.7 million). Comparing the two amounts, he stressed:

“For 30 years, these schools have played an important role in preserving the folklore, music, national values and spiritual heritage of their regions.”

Azim argues that if the authorities close schools to save public money, they should assess Russian-language schools by the same criteria.

In recent years, authorities have closed hundreds of small schools in rural areas or merged them with other educational institutions because they had too few pupils. Judging by the headteacher’s remarks, the future of schools for internally displaced people is also under discussion.

The Ministry of Education has not yet commented on the MP’s remarks.

What has the ministry said previously?

In July 2025, rumours spread widely that the authorities might close Russian-language classes. Messages in parents’ WhatsApp groups claimed that schools teaching in Russian would switch to Azerbaijani within three years. The Ministry of Education denied these reports. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova also dismissed them as “fake news” and said Moscow remained in constant contact with Baku on the issue.

In June 2026, Education Minister Emin Amrullayev said that closing Russian-language classes had “never been on the agenda”. He said it was “technically impossible” to shut them down “as early as tomorrow”, adding that parents themselves chose the language of instruction. However, he did not rule out restructuring for “objective reasons”, such as a decline in pupil numbers or a shortage of teachers.

Babaoglu’s proposal, however, concerns a different issue. The MP is not calling for Russian-language classes to close. Instead, he is questioning whether the state should continue to fund them.

Against the backdrop of improving relations with Moscow

The MP’s remarks come amid a period of improving relations between Baku and Moscow. In December 2024, an AZAL passenger plane crashed, killing 38 people. In April 2026, the two sides acknowledged in a joint statement that Russian air defence systems had unintentionally shot down the aircraft.

In September, Azerbaijan placed three Russian propagandists – Semyon Uralov, Ivan Knyazev and Alexey Chadayev – on its wanted list over public calls for a violent change of government. Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador over the matter. Moscow dismissed their remarks as “personal opinions”.

Babaoglu did not mention Russia in his speech. He justified his proposal by referring to the need to preserve “national identity” and concerns over public spending. Moscow has not yet responded to his remarks.

The draft 2027 state budget contains no separate proposal to change the funding arrangements for Russian-language education. The government has also not responded to the issue raised by the MP.

Russian-language education in Azerbaijan

World.title: ‘Your own husband could be human trafficker’: tackling human trafficking in Armenia
World.content:
Every life matters: how people and animals save each other in Armenia

Over the past four years, Armenia has recorded 109 cases of human trafficking. Reports by international organisations show that Armenia is making efforts to prevent human trafficking. However, the government has scaled back its anti-trafficking efforts in the legal sphere.

We tell personal stories, present figures and facts about the scale of human trafficking in Armenia, and examine programmes that support victims.

Married to the enemy?

“My husband would drive me to different addresses in his car. He would wait in the car until I finished work and came out. He would take all the money from me right there in the car, then drive me to the next address,” Anna (not her real name, at her request) recalls.

Anna describes providing sexual services as her work. She says her husband had never been particularly keen on working. After they married, he decided to use his wife’s previous experience in the sex trade to support the family. The situation did not change even after they had a child.

Family life became hell not only for Anna but also for their child.

“I worked day and night. I had no right to complain or refuse. And it wasn’t just sexual exploitation. I also faced physical, psychological and economic abuse. I lived in constant fear and anxiety. He could beat me or insult me in front of other people, then show me affection, try to win me over and say that we were a family. But the very next day, he would take me to other men again. Sometimes I wouldn’t see my child for several days. Different women I didn’t know would look after them,” Anna says.

Years of exploitation, extreme physical and mental exhaustion, beatings and emotional suffering – but above all, anxiety about her child – drove Anna to flee her husband and report him to the police.

Anna says she found the decision difficult:

“The police force is made up mostly of men. I found it difficult to tell them all the details of what had happened to me – the abuse and the sexual services I had to provide. It felt as though I was going through it all over again. I was overwhelmed by shame, but I knew I had no other choice.”

The police offered to take her to a shelter for victims of human trafficking. Anna agreed, and she still lives there.

Shelter residents and those who do not “save” them

The NGO Sexual Violence Crisis Centre provides victims of human trafficking with shelter and support in dealing with the problems they face. In 2025, the government fully covered the shelter’s operating costs. It also signed its first three-year contract with the centre, allowing it to continue its work on a full scale.

Over the years, social worker Mané Chobanyan has witnessed many tragic stories while working with victims:

“The hardest part of social work is accepting that you are not a saviour. One of its principles is that you must not make decisions on behalf of the people you support. As a professional, I can only guide them and show them the options available. I can never influence their decisions. Of course, this can be very difficult at times. You can never be sure that months or even a year of work will not go to waste – that someone leaving the shelter will not return to the same path, trust an abuser or trafficker again, and end up in the same situation.”

Even so, she has no regrets about the effort she puts into helping these people change their lives.

Mané says an atmosphere of fear and intimidation sometimes forces people to remain in situations where traffickers exploit them. This happens most often to victims of labour exploitation. Given their vulnerable position, the prospect of losing their jobs frightens them more than anything else.

“When we work with people who have experienced sexual exploitation, we mainly try to show them that they can change their circumstances and find another job. In cases of labour exploitation, our priority is to inform people about their rights,” she explains.

With financial support from the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs, the Sexual Violence Crisis Centre provides more than just shelter. It also offers psychological and medical care, legal advice and other assistance. Mané says many shelter residents have told her that they would have tried to escape their situations sooner if they had known about the support programmes available.

Anyone who finds themselves in a situation that resembles human trafficking or exploitation can contact the NGO Sexual Violence Crisis Centre for help on +374 77 991280.

US State Department and GRETA say government efforts remain insufficient

The US State Department publishes an annual report on human trafficking worldwide. The Council of Europe’s Group of Experts on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings (GRETA) also publishes a report every four years.

Both reports say that the Armenian government does not fully meet the minimum standards for combating human trafficking, although it has made considerable efforts in this area.

The US State Department welcomed the government’s decision to draw up a new national action plan for 2026–2028, although the authorities have yet to adopt it. However, the report considers the country’s efforts in the legal sphere insufficient.

Articles 188 and 189 of Armenia’s Criminal Code criminalise both sexual and labour trafficking. They provide for prison sentences of five to eight years if the victim is an adult, and seven to 10 years if the victim is a child. However, the US State Department cites statistics that point to shortcomings in the enforcement of these penalties:

“In 2025, law enforcement authorities investigated 29 human trafficking cases: 15 involving sex trafficking, 13 involving labour trafficking, and one in which the type of trafficking remained unspecified. The authorities continued investigating 11 cases from previous years. Prosecutors brought charges against eight suspected traffickers: seven for sex trafficking and one for labour trafficking. In 2025, a court convicted two people of sex trafficking. One person convicted of human trafficking received a 16-year prison sentence, while the other died before the court issued its verdict.”

Reviewing the previous four years, GRETA notes that 90 people received official victim status between 2022 and 2025.

Twenty-two of them were children. Women accounted for most identified victims, except in 2025. Armenian citizens made up 84% of all victims. Most experienced trafficking within Armenia, while a smaller proportion faced exploitation in Russia.

“According to official police statistics, the number of criminal cases opened in connection with human trafficking offences increased during the reporting period: eight in 2022, 19 in 2023, 36 in 2024 and 27 in 2025. Most investigations concerned labour exploitation. Several cases involved the sexual exploitation of children, forced begging or domestic servitude. Between 2022 and 2025, courts issued a total of 11 convictions in human trafficking cases: six for labour exploitation and five for sexual exploitation,” the Council of Europe report says.

As in previous years, GRETA again points out that Armenia still fails to ensure victims of human trafficking receive compensation. To date, no victim has received compensation through criminal proceedings. The government provides one-off financial assistance to no more than seven victims a year.

The government’s efforts – sufficient and insufficient

In 2024, Armenia identified 25 victims of human trafficking. In 2025, that figure rose to 59. Of these, 16 experienced sexual exploitation and 43 forced labour. Eighteen were women, 27 were men, seven were boys and seven were girls. For the first time in four years, the government identified 14 foreign nationals among the victims.

In the first nine months of 2026, authorities recognised 19 people as victims of human trafficking. Fifteen were women and four were men. Three victims were children, one of whom had mental health problems. Two children experienced sexual exploitation, while traffickers subjected the third to labour exploitation. Among adult victims, nine cases involved sexual exploitation and the rest involved labour exploitation. The foreign victims came from Russia, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

“Armenia plans and implements strategic programmes and provides services to combat human trafficking, prioritising the safety and protection of victims. In other words, access to these services does not depend on or remain limited by the progress of law enforcement investigations. This means the state supports both victims and potential victims according to their needs,” says Armine Alaverdyan, head of the Gender Policy Department at the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs.

In 2026, as in the previous year, the government allocated around 32 million drams ($88,000) from the state budget to combat human trafficking.

The funding covers the following services for victims and potential victims of human trafficking:

accommodation;

material assistance, including clothing, food and essential items;

issuing or restoring necessary documents;

medical assistance and services;

psychological support;

counselling;

legal assistance;

care, including in specialised institutions;

interpretation services;

access to basic education;

access to secondary or primary vocational education;

employment assistance;

arrangements for safe return;

one-off financial assistance of 250,000 drams ($694).

According to Armine Alaverdyan, as the number of human trafficking cases rises, so does the need for additional shelter places.

People can stay in the shelter for up to a year, but staff can extend their stay if necessary.

“The state provides support with considerable flexibility. We once had a case in which a person repeatedly broke the shelter’s rules, eventually left, but then asked to return a week later. Naturally, we let them back in. Sometimes, after receiving an initial consultation, a person decides not to accept other forms of support. In cases of sexual exploitation, medical services naturally become more important. This year, only one person received the one-off financial assistance.”

He was rescued

S., a foreign national, came to Armenia on the recommendation of friends. He quickly found a job, unaware of what awaited him in the months ahead.

According to Mané Chobanyan, a social worker at the Sexual Violence Crisis Centre, what happened to S. was like something out of a horror film.

“He did not speak a single word of Armenian. He found himself in a foreign country where people took away all his documents, restricted his freedom of movement, forced him to work and then refused to pay him for his labour. When S. arrived at the shelter, it became clear that our priority was to provide him with a safe environment and help him reclaim his labour rights.”

S. spent more than a year at the shelter. During that time, he taught himself to read and write in Armenian and introduced other residents to his country’s cuisine. Mané says that, despite everything he had been through, S. never lost his faith in people or his will to live. Today, with the help of the shelter staff, he has found a job in administration.

The crisis centre’s social worker says his story is not just one of personal triumph, but also “an example of targeted and effective support that can change a person’s life.”

Combating human trafficking in Armenia: personal stories

World.title: Sanctioned Russian online retailer Wildberries expands operations in Georgia
World.content:
Illustration: Centre for Economic Policy Research (EPRC)

На фоне введения санкций против его основательницы крупнейший российский маркетплейс Wildberries расширяет свою деятельность в Грузии: компания приобрела более 19 гектаров земли, арендовала крупный склад и готовится к запуску сервиса такси.

As the Centre for Economic Policy Research (EPRC) found, Russian online marketplace Wildberries, which began operating in Georgia in October 2024, is no longer focusing solely on expanding its network of parcel collection points.

The company’s Georgian operator plans to expand its logistics infrastructure and enter new sectors.

________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

The authors of the EPRC study argue that this expansion should not be viewed solely as business development. They focus on the company’s links to Russia, the possible impact of sanctions, its role in Georgia’s logistics network, and the political and business connections of the local operator’s owners.

________________________________________________________________________________________________________________

From a single collection point to logistics infrastructure

Wildberries’ Georgian operator, Transcom Group LLC, was registered on 26 July 2022. The platform launched sales in Georgia on 22 October 2024 under a franchise model.

Initially, the platform offered consumers around eight million products. Customers could collect their orders from a single collection point in Tbilisi.

The network later expanded, and Georgian entrepreneurs also gained the opportunity to sell their products through the platform.

A parcel collection point and a warehouse serve different purposes. A warehouse receives, stores, sorts and distributes goods, while a collection point hands over parcels that are already ready for customers.

According to the EPRC study, Wildberries’ operations in Georgia also aim to establish warehouses.

19.25 hectares near the highway

According to Georgia’s Public Registry, in January 2026, Transcom Group acquired four plots of land from the state through privatisation. All four are located close to the Tbilisi-Red Bridge international highway.

The plots cover a total area of 192,521 square metres, or 19.25 hectares. The site lies near the road leading to the Azerbaijani border and customs facilities, making it an attractive location for logistics operations.

The EPRC believes that the concentration of the plots in one area, combined with the company’s existing warehouse operations, suggests that the land could be intended for a warehouse or a larger logistics complex.

However, no public documents currently confirm this. It remains unclear what project the company plans to develop on the land, how large the buildings will be or when construction might begin.

Existing warehouse

In addition to acquiring the plots of land mentioned above, Transcom Group already leases warehouse premises in the village of Gamardjveba, seven kilometres from Tbilisi.

According to the study, the company announced a tender on 28 October to improve mobile phone reception at the warehouse. The technical specifications describe a facility covering around 13,000 square metres.

The lease record gives the building’s area as 12,816.8 square metres. The agreement runs until 19 June 2028.

The study also mentions a second lease agreement that Transcom Group signed in another area near Tbilisi in May 2025. It runs for two years.

The EPRC believes that if the company also develops the planned logistics complex near the highway, it will have much greater capacity to receive, store and distribute goods outside Russia.

Taxi service on the way

Another important finding of the EPRC study concerns the possible launch of a WB Taxi service in Tbilisi.

On 16 and 21 October 2026, Transcom Group announced tenders for branding taxi vehicles. One of them covered the production and application of special vehicle wraps for around 150 cars in Tbilisi.

These documents point to preparations for the launch of the service. However, public records do not yet confirm whether the company has signed the relevant contracts, how many cars it has branded or whether it has started carrying passengers.

By early November, WB Taxi was operating in several cities in Belarus, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. In Armenia, the company launched an early-access service in September.

If the company launches the service in Georgia, the Wildberries group will enter the passenger transport market in addition to online retail and logistics.

In this context, the EPRC highlights concerns about personal data protection. Taxi apps process passengers’ addresses, travel routes, journey times and payment information.

Analysis of this data could reveal where people live and work, their regular routes and other personal details.

The study also cites a 2024 case in which Georgia’s Personal Data Protection Service found that the local operator of the Yandex taxi service had illegally transferred users’ personal data to Russia. The company received a fine of 4,000 lari [around $1,480].

The EPRC says that if WB Taxi launches in Georgia, it will be important to establish who operates the service, where it stores users’ data and on what legal basis it may transfer that data to another country.

What links Wildberries to Georgia’s government?

One important part of the study examines the owners of the company’s local operator and their business connections.

According to records from Georgia’s Public Registry examined by the EPRC, Lasha Megrelidze initially owned Transcom Group. In 2023, he became deputy chairman and an independent member of the supervisory board of Cartu Bank. Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of the ruling Georgian Dream party, established the bank. He initially owned it himself, then transferred ownership to his son. The bank eventually passed to the Cartu charitable foundation, which Ivanishvili himself had established.

Since 2024, Sergi Tvalchrelidze has served as Transcom Group’s director and sole owner. A Public Registry extract dated 11 June 2026 also lists him as the company’s only owner and director. According to the study, Tvalchrelidze personally donated 30,000 lari [around $11,100] to Georgian Dream in 2025.

The EPRC also examines Tvalchrelidze’s business ties with Giorgi Barvenashvili, a Georgian Dream MP. According to a registry extract from March 2025, Tvalchrelidze served as director and owned a 33% stake in Nama Consulting, while Barvenashvili held 34%. Nama Consulting and Transcom Group share the same registered address.

Public records confirm that people involved in bringing Wildberries to the Georgian market and managing its operations have links to Cartu Bank and to business and political circles close to Georgian Dream.

The study’s authors say these connections deserve scrutiny, particularly as the Russian company expands its operations in Georgia and its founder faces EU sanctions.

Who owns Wildberries, and why has she been sanctioned?

On 16 November, the European Union added Tatyana Kim, the founder and head of Wildberries, to its sanctions list. The decision forms part of a new package of sanctions against Russia, aimed at restricting the funding of its war against Ukraine.

The sanctions freeze Kim’s assets in the EU, ban her from entering or transiting through EU territory, and prohibit people and entities under EU jurisdiction from providing her with funds or economic resources.

The Council of the European Union considers Wildberries one of Russia’s largest taxpayers. The company’s tax payments therefore go into the Russian state budget and increase the government’s capacity to finance military spending.

The EU also links the company to Russia’s military supply network. According to Brussels, the platform connects sellers and buyers, making it easier to purchase equipment that could serve military purposes, as well as dual-use goods.

The EPRC study cites a journalistic investigation that found Wildberries had listed products that Russian armed forces could use. The Russian outlet Meduza found listings for goods linked to military needs, including body armour, drone components, batteries and night-vision devices.

Wildberries founder Tatyana Kim says other global online marketplaces also sell such products. The Kremlin, meanwhile, has denied that the company’s warehouses serve military purposes.

Wildberries says the group has no assets or operations in the EU, so sanctions against Kim will not affect its business.

What risks does Wildberries’ expansion pose for Georgia?

The EPRC study identifies several potential risks associated with Wildberries’ expanding operations in Georgia.

The first concerns sanctions. The sanctions against Tatyana Kim could affect the company’s international financial transactions, banking services and relationships with business partners.

This risk also concerns Georgian companies that work with the platform or use its infrastructure.

The second concerns logistics infrastructure. The land purchases and warehouse operations indicate that the company is building capacity for larger-scale operations in Georgia.

However, the infrastructure’s ultimate purpose and the routes goods will take remain unclear.

The third issue is users’ personal data.

If the Wildberries group also launches a taxi service in Georgia, it will gain access to a much wider range of personal information – not only users’ purchases and addresses, but also data about their everyday movements.

Finally, the business and political connections of the company’s local owners are significant. This is particularly important when the company acquires state-owned land and develops infrastructure that could have regional implications.

The EPRC study does not claim that Wildberries’ existing infrastructure in Georgia already supports Russian military supplies, or that it will necessarily take over the functions of warehouses damaged in Russia.

However, the study argues that the scale of the company’s expansion, the sanctions against its owner and the connections of its Georgian operator raise questions that require public and transparent answers.

Wildberries expands its operations in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s permanent population grows, new statistics show
World.content:
Growth in Armenia’s permanent population

The permanent population of Armenia has increased. According to the Statistical Committee, it stood at 3,111,200 as of 1 October 2026. This represents an increase of 20,700 compared with the same period last year. The capital accounted for 32.4% of the total growth.

“Yerevan’s permanent population reached 1,151,400, an increase of 6,700 compared with the same period last year,” the Statistical Committee said.

However, population growth has varied across the country. While Yerevan and the provinces surrounding the capital have seen an increase, some other regions have even recorded a decline.

“In 2026, compared with the previous year, the permanent population fell in two of the country’s ten provinces: by 300 people in Vayots Dzor and by 200 in Lori,” the Statistical Committee said.

Significant growth in provinces surrounding the capital

The largest population increases occurred in three provinces close to the capital: Kotayk, Armavir and Ararat.

Kotayk’s population grew by 4,500, Armavir’s by 4,000 and Ararat’s by 3,100.

“The combined population increase in these three provinces was 11,600, accounting for 56% of the total growth across the republic.”

If we add the capital’s population growth to this figure, Yerevan and the three provinces together accounted for 88.4% of Armenia’s overall population increase. This amounts to 18,300 people.

Rural population increased in every province

As of 1 October 2026, Armenia’s urban population had grown by 9,400 compared with the previous year, while its rural population had increased by 11,300.

Rural communities accounted for around 54.6% of the total annual population growth.

Kotayk recorded the largest increase, at 3,100 people.

Rural populations also grew by 2,600 in Ararat, 2,300 in Armavir, 900 in Aragatsotn and 800 in Syunik.

Notably, no province in Armenia recorded a decline in its rural population.

Largest increase in urban population recorded in Armavir province

Urban populations declined in five of Armenia’s provinces. Lori recorded the largest fall, with a decrease of 600 people.

Urban populations in Shirak and Vayots Dzor each fell by 300, while Tavush recorded a decline of 200.

At the same time, several provinces saw their urban populations grow. After Yerevan, Armavir recorded the largest increase, with 1,700 more residents living in its towns and cities.

“Kotayk recorded an increase of 1,400 people, Ararat 500, Syunik 400 and Aragatsotn 100,” the Statistical Committee said.

Population growth peaked in 2024

Between 2022 and 2026, Armenia recorded its largest increase in permanent population in 2024.

As of 1 October 2024, Armenia’s permanent population stood at 3,067,400. This was 73,600 higher than the figure for 2023.

The Statistical Committee attributes the population trends during this period to two major migration events:

an influx of people following the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022;

the forced displacement to Armenia of the entire population of Nagorno-Karabakh in September 2023.

In addition, the authorities calculated the 2023 figures using data from the 2011 census, while the 2024 figures draw on the results of the 2022 census. Therefore, the difference of 73,600 cannot be considered actual population growth over the course of a year.

Growth in Armenia’s permanent population

World.title: ‘Economic development must not come at expense of sovereignty’: Views on mountain resort project in Abkhazia
World.content:
The president of Abkhazia has announced plans to begin construction of a mountain resort in the Aibga mountain range.

Aibga, however, is a 160 sq km territory whose border between Abkhazia and Russia has never been formally delimited.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union, one part of Aibga fell on the Russian side and the other on the Abkhaz side. The Psou River serves as the de facto boundary between them. Russia lays claim to the other part of the mountain range, a claim that Abkhazia firmly rejects.

Abkhazian President Badra Gunba has announced plans to build a joint year-round ski resort on the slopes of Mount Aibga in cooperation with the Russian ski resort of Krasnaya Polyana.

“These territories are located opposite each other, and everyone who visits would have the opportunity to ski down the slopes of Krasnaya Polyana, then head up the slopes of Aibga and enjoy the unique opportunities it offers as well.

“So there should be no competition here. On the contrary, we should work together on joint projects,” Gunba said.

Former Abkhaz parliament member Ilya Gunia discusses the ski resort project in the context of the territorial dispute in his blog.

Ilya Gunia:

“The project is being presented as a strategic economic breakthrough that could attract investment, create jobs and give the republic’s development fresh momentum.

I agree that tourism needs to be developed and investment attracted. However, I believe that behind the economic prospects lie questions of national importance that cannot be ignored.

Aibga is first and foremost a matter of Abkhazia’s state border and territorial integrity.

A joint Russian-Abkhaz commission on the delimitation and demarcation of the border has been operating for many years. I served as a member of this commission during my time as a member of parliament. It was precisely over the Aibga section that the commission’s work reached a deadlock. The two sides failed to reach an understanding on the issue.

As a former member of the commission, I believe it is necessary to highlight three fundamental problems.

First. Any large-scale infrastructure project in territory whose status remains the subject of an interstate dispute could trigger a serious political crisis. A commercial project cannot begin in an area where the state border has yet to be legally established between the two sides.

Second. Attempts to circumvent existing disagreements under the pretext of creating a unified cross-border space raise serious questions. International cooperation must not become a pretext for weakening state control over one’s own territory.

By taking part in such projects, Abkhazia must act exclusively as an equal partner. Investors’ economic interests cannot take precedence over national interests, and the republic’s laws must remain an absolute priority.”

Third. If the interstate commission has been unable to find a solution to this issue for many years, how does the executive intend to resolve it now? On the basis of what agreements? Within what boundaries will the project be implemented? What are the terms of Russia’s participation, and who will exercise state control over the territory? The people of Abkhazia have the right to know what commitments their state is undertaking.

I am not opposed to developing tourism, attracting investment or building modern resorts. But all this must take place within the law and exclusively on territory whose status is clearly defined and legally protected.

We have no right to put the country’s territorial integrity at risk for the sake of economic prospects.

Abkhazia paid too high a price for its independence for us to treat questions of sovereignty today as a mere formality or a technical obstacle to an investment project.

I therefore urge the republic’s leadership to refrain from making any decisions on the Aibga project until the border dispute has been fully resolved.

The first priority must be to ensure transparency in the negotiations, establish the state border and guarantee the protection of Abkhazia’s national interests. Only then can we have a substantive discussion about implementing projects of this kind.

Economic development is necessary, but it must not come at the expense of sovereignty.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: NGOs in Azerbaijan face re-registration as experts warn of tighter rules
World.content:
Re-registration of NGOs in Azerbaijan

All non-governmental organisations (NGOs) operating in Azerbaijan, as well as branches and representative offices of foreign NGOs, will have to undergo state re-registration. The requirement is set out in amendments to the Law on Non-Governmental Organisations (Public Associations and Funds). The draft legislation has been included on the agenda of Milli Majlis sessions scheduled for 17 and 18 November.

Once the law comes into force, organisations will have just 30 days to bring their statutes into line with the new requirements and apply for re-registration. Authorities will suspend the activities of any organisation that fails to apply or whose application they reject. They will then file a lawsuit seeking its dissolution.

Over the past decade, Azerbaijan has repeatedly tightened the legislation governing NGO activities.

What will the re-registration process mean for these organisations, and who will decide their fate?

What does the draft law provide for?

Re-registration. Local NGOs registered before the law comes into force will have to apply to the “relevant executive authority” within 30 days. Branches of foreign NGOs whose agreements have expired or which have no agreement in place will have to sign a new agreement or extend their existing one within the same period.

New requirements for statutes. Organisations will have to include internal financial control procedures in their statutes, establish supervisory bodies and provide for measures to reduce the risk of terrorist financing. The law will also define different types of NGOs, with each organisation allowed to belong to only one category.

Tenfold increase in the minimum capital required for foundations. The current minimum statutory capital for a foundation is 10,000 manats (approximately $5,882). The draft law proposes raising it to 100,000 manats (approximately $58,820).

Suspension of activities without a court order. This is one of the most significant changes proposed by the draft law. Under the current legislation, only a court can order an NGO to suspend its activities. Under the proposed rules, the executive authority would be able to suspend an organisation for up to one year without going to court. Grounds for suspension would include:

failure to ensure transparency in the organisation’s activities;

failure to comply with requirements on combating corruption, money laundering and terrorist financing;

failure to update the state register within three months of the expiry of the head of the organisation’s term of office;

expiry of an agreement with a foreign NGO branch.

New grounds for dissolution. Under the current law, a court can generally order an NGO’s dissolution if it has received more than two written warnings within a year. The draft law expands the list of grounds for dissolution. These would include posing a “threat to the interests of the state and society protected by law”, failing to hold a general meeting for three consecutive years, remaining inactive for more than three years, and carrying out activities that do not correspond to the organisation’s stated objectives.

Who will decide what constitutes “transparency” or a “threat”?

The draft law uses broad terms such as “failure to ensure transparency” and “threat to the interests of the state”. However, it does not specify the criteria for applying these provisions. If adopted, the law would allow the executive authority responsible for registering NGOs and overseeing their activities to make decisions that previously fell to the courts.

Lawyer Narmin Ahmadli told the Musavat newspaper in a comment that 30 days would not be enough for many NGOs. She said that amending their statutes would require them to draw up internal financial control procedures, which takes time. Lawyer Bakhtiyar Hajiyev, meanwhile, pointed out that the requirement would apply to all public associations and foundations registered before the law comes into force.

Raising the minimum statutory capital to 100,000 manats would make it significantly harder to register small initiatives as foundations. By comparison, this amount is around 85 times the country’s average monthly salary.

Previous tightening of NGO legislation

This is not the first time Azerbaijan has tightened its legislation governing NGOs. In February 2014, President Ilham Aliyev signed around 50 amendments into law. They prohibited banks from processing transactions under unregistered grant agreements, required Azerbaijani citizens to head branches of foreign NGOs and increased fines. The then-chairman of the NGO Forum, Gubad Ibadoghlu, said the changes would severely restrict civil society activities. US, EU and UK diplomats also expressed concern.

In July 2025, new requirements were introduced for registering service contracts funded by foreign sources, along with additional fines. In its 2024 report, international human rights organisation Human Rights Watch urged the Azerbaijani government to review its NGO legislation in line with recommendations from the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

Against the backdrop of the “NGO funding case”

The draft law is being considered amid ongoing criminal proceedings against NGO representatives. In February 2025, the Prosecutor General’s Office reopened the so-called “NGO funding case”, which it had launched in 2014 and suspended in 2022. According to human rights organisation Amnesty International, at least 50 civil society representatives have since been questioned as witnesses or suspects.

Asef Ahmedov, head of the Ganja Regional Public Centre, was sentenced to eight years in prison. Zamin Zakiyev, head of the Ubuntu Association for Social Work initiative, received a seven-year-and-three-month sentence. Prosecutors have requested a nine-year prison term for Bashir Suleymanli, head of the Institute for Civil Rights. The next hearing in his case is scheduled for 19 November. The defendants reject the charges and say they acted within the law.

There has been no announcement of who drafted the bill or which executive authority will oversee the re-registration of NGOs. Government agencies have also yet to explain the reasons behind the proposed changes.

Re-registration of NGOs in Azerbaijan

World.title: Deutsche Bank leak: Bank linked payments to Trump companies in Baku to ‘Azerbaijani Laundromat’
World.content:
Trump-linked companies in Azerbaijan

According to documents leaked from Germany’s largest bank, Deutsche Bank, between 2014 and 2020 the bank repeatedly flagged as suspicious payments received by two companies linked to Donald Trump‘s hotel project in Baku. Some of the funds came from companies associated with a money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”.

The findings were reported in an international journalistic investigation, Inside Deutsche Bank, published on 17 November. More than 200 journalists from over 50 media outlets took part in the investigation. The section focusing on Azerbaijan was published by the Russian-language investigative outlet iStories.

The journalists obtained more than 15 million internal bank files, including email correspondence, client documents and risk assessment materials. The files were provided by two whistleblowers to journalists in India and South Africa.

Trump’s unfinished skyscraper in Baku has been the subject of numerous reports in the past. This time, however, the investigation focused on a different question:

Where did the funds that the bank considered suspicious come from, and what do these findings reveal about the money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”?

Unfinished skyscraper in Baku

Trump International Hotel & Tower in Baku / Archive photo, 2015

The project in question is the 33-storey Trump International Hotel & Tower complex in Baku, construction of which began in 2012. However, the building was never put into operation. Trump’s partners in the project were relatives of Azerbaijan’s then Transport Minister Ziya Mammadov. As iStories notes, the family amassed a multimillion-dollar fortune through government contracts.

Trump’s company withdrew from the project in late 2016. According to Trump’s financial disclosure, he received around $2.5m for managing the project in 2015 and just over $300,000 in 2016. In 2017, the Trump Organization told The New Yorker that Trump had played a “passive role” in the project and had merely licensed the use of his name.

The project was managed by two US companies, DT Marks Baku and THC Baku Services. It is their bank accounts that are covered by the documents obtained by journalists through the leak.

Which transactions did the bank consider suspicious?

According to iStories, Deutsche Bank first flagged a payment to DT Marks Baku as suspicious in August 2014. The funds came from an unnamed client of Danske Bank’s Estonian branch. Deutsche Bank was unable to establish the purpose of the payment or the nature of the relationship between the sender and the recipient.

In April 2015, THC Baku Services received just over $141,000 from Faberlex, a UK-registered shell company. Faberlex was one of the key participants in the money-laundering scheme known as the “Azerbaijani Laundromat”.

The bank continued to identify suspicious payments in subsequent years. As reported by the Dutch investigative platform Follow the Money, Deutsche Bank’s internal analysis linked the funds to both the “Azerbaijani Laundromat” and a Russian money-laundering network associated with oligarchs close to the Kremlin.

According to an internal bank document dated May 2020, the total value of suspicious transactions involving the accounts of Trump’s companies in Baku exceeded $3m.

What was the ‘Azerbaijani Laundromat’?

The “Azerbaijani Laundromat” was a money-laundering scheme exposed in an investigation published in September 2017 by the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), an international investigative journalism network.

According to the investigation, around $2.9bn was transferred through UK-registered shell companies between 2012 and 2014, primarily via the Estonian branch of Danske Bank. Journalists found that some of the funds were channelled to European politicians, while others were spent on luxury goods and other expenses of members of the elite.

The Azerbaijani authorities rejected the investigation’s findings at the time. Presidential spokesman Azer Gasimov described the investigation as “absurd and biased”. The OCCRP website was blocked in Azerbaijan.

In subsequent years, European courts handed down several sentences in cases linked to the scheme. In 2021, former member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) and Italian politician Luca Volontè was sentenced to four years in prison for accepting bribes from Azerbaijani officials. According to iStories, the funds were transferred to him through Faberlex.

Former German Bundestag members Eduard Lintner and Axel Fischer also received suspended prison sentences for accepting bribes in connection with lobbying for Azerbaijan’s interests.

According to the documents, Faberlex and two other companies involved in the scheme, Hilux Services and Polux Management, were formally owned by Maharram Ahmadov, a driver from Baku.

What is the situation now?

The document leak comes amid closer ties between Trump and Baku. In August 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev signed a joint declaration at the White House with Donald Trump and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan.

Deutsche Bank said that the law prohibited it from disclosing information about suspicious transaction reports. In response to journalists’ questions, the bank noted that the events in question had taken place “many years ago”, stressing that “we are a different bank today”.

The Trump Organization did not respond to journalists’ questions, while the White House referred them to the company. Danske Bank said that money laundering “should never have happened” and noted that the case had been closed in 2022 following decisions by the Danish and US authorities.

The Azerbaijani authorities have yet to comment on the newly leaked documents.

World.title: ‘Traffic jams are not caused by buildings’: Yerevan mayor responds to prime minister’s wife
World.content:
Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

“Traffic jams are caused by cars, not buildings. Armenia is experiencing economic growth and an inflow of money. People now have more opportunities – and they are buying cars,” Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan said today.

He was effectively responding to Anna Hakobyan, the wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan. A few days ago, she posted a video on social media showing traffic jams in the capital. She said Yerevan was gradually becoming “the most unfriendly city” to live in.

The prime minister’s wife asked what the authorities should do to prevent life in the city and getting around it from becoming “a reason for a heart attack”. She pointed to economic growth, the rapid construction of new buildings, a rising population, more cars on the roads and an influx of tourists.

“Some people have a professional duty to find an answer to this question. But this task is far more difficult than issuing construction permits to companies investing millions of dollars. ‘Approved’ is a magic stamp that requires minimal effort but has an enormous impact [on the situation],” Hakobyan stressed.

According to the mayor, the city authorities issued a record 108 permits for apartment blocks and residential complexes in 2021. Those are the buildings now being completed and handed over to residents. Avinyan noted that the authorities have not issued as many permits in any year since then. For example, they issued just 37 in 2025.

The mayor acknowledged that the current situation is causing a certain degree of “tension” – and said he shares those concerns. However, Avinyan called for an analysis of the problems and appropriate solutions.

Tigran Avinyan’s explanation apparently failed to satisfy Anna Hakobyan. She immediately posted another video, this time about the “catastrophic traffic jams”. In her post, the prime minister’s wife urged women drivers to stop being patient:

“Keep noisy objects in your cars. Every time you find yourself stuck in traffic for hours, make a loud noise. Make it loud enough for those who have a duty to use their brains and solve the problem to hear you.”

Prime minister’s wife: “You need an astronaut’s health to get from point A to point C”

In her first post, Anna Hakobyan said that getting around the capital required “an astronaut’s health” – in other words, a strong cardiovascular and nervous system.

She also expressed confidence that scientific disciplines exist that can help calculate how many cars Yerevan will have in 25 years, based on current development trends. They can also help determine what measures the authorities need to take now to prepare for that future.

Hakobyan suggested that, alongside the buildings springing up across the city “like mushrooms after rain”, the authorities should build flyovers, as well as elevated, underground and bypass roads.

“You have to actively seek out this knowledge yourself. Nobody will serve it up on a silver platter as a ready-made, multi-million-dollar project that only needs a ‘approved’ stamp,” she said, again alluding to the construction permits issued in the capital.

In her view, traffic planning must take into account how much the population could grow in the coming years and how many more cars the city might have.

“What will happen if between 300,000 and 500,000 people return to their homeland to live permanently over the next five years? And what if 250,000 of them bring their own cars? What are we going to do? Will the same number of people have to leave so that we can all fit on the streets?” Anna Hakobyan asked.

Mayor: “Possible solutions will be presented to the public”

According to Yerevan Mayor Tigran Avinyan, traffic congestion in the capital has three main causes: the growing number of private cars, driving culture and the need to give public transport priority.

He said the city authorities would soon present various possible solutions for public discussion. Avinyan outlined some of the measures under consideration:

fully separating bus lanes from other traffic;

introducing measures to reduce traffic violations;

restricting car use on public health grounds.

On the last point, the mayor clarified that the restrictions would not apply to vehicles coming to Yerevan from other regions. He said the aim was to reduce the overall number of cars within the city.

Tigran Avinyan believes the growing number of private cars is the main cause of traffic jams. He argues that public transport should take priority.

He expects new road construction to help improve traffic flow to some extent. However, he warned that new roads alone would not solve the problem. They would soon become congested again unless the authorities introduced measures such as restrictions on car use, dedicated lanes and tougher fines.

The mayor also addressed environmental concerns. Avinyan identified nitrogen dioxide as a specific pollutant whose levels in Yerevan are rising rapidly year after year as the number of cars increases. He said it causes lung and respiratory diseases.

“The most dangerous thing is that children are the first to suffer from these problems,” Avinyan stressed.

First lady’s appeal

In response to the Yerevan mayor’s remarks, Anna Hakobyan published a new video, saying that people had thanked her for raising the issue.

“They tell me: ‘At last, someone has had the courage to speak about this.’ Every day, hundreds of thousands of people suffer in Yerevan’s traffic jams. So does complaining about the situation now require ‘courage’?”

Hakobyan urged women drivers to stop putting up with the situation and called on men to show greater determination. She suggested that women should make a loud noise whenever they get stuck in traffic.

In her view, government institutions never hear complaints that people “do not dare to voice”.

“Otherwise, we might end up blaming the previous authorities for Yerevan’s traffic jams [the current government, led by her husband, often blames its predecessors for various problems]. If Armenia’s economy had developed in a balanced way over the past 30 years, and the number of cars had increased gradually rather than exponentially, the situation in the Armenian capital would be completely different today,” she said.

Yerevan mayor responds to Anna Hakobyan over traffic jams

World.title: Azerbaijan's real estate lending rises 5.5% to $26.1M by late September
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. Lending to legal entities operating in Azerbaijan’s real estate sector rose by 5.5%, totaling 44.4 million manat ($26.1 million) as of the end of September 2026.

According to Trend’s calculations based on the statistical bulletin of the Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA), compared to the end of August this year, this figure grew by 2.3 million manat ($1.35 million). At the end of August, loans to the sector totaled 42.1 million manat ($24.8 million).

Long-term loans accounted for the largest share of the loan portfolio. At the end of September, loans in this category totaled 33.6 million manat ($19.8 million). Compared to 31.6 million manat ($18.6 million) at the end of August, this represented an increase of 2 million manat ($1.2 million), or 6.3%. Long-term loans accounted for approximately 75.7% of total lending.

The bulk of long-term loans were denominated in the national currency. At the end of September, long-term loans issued in manat totaled 33.2 million manat ($19.5 million). At the end of August, this figure stood at 31.2 million manat ($18.4 million). Thus, a monthly increase of 2 million manat ($1.2 million), or 6.4%, was recorded.

Meanwhile, long-term loans issued in foreign currencies declined. At the end of September, they totaled 300,000 manat ($176,500). The loan portfolio stood at 400,000 manat ($235,300) at the end of August, representing a monthly decrease of 100,000 manat ($58,800), or 25%.

Short-term loans also increased. At the end of September, they reached 10.9 million manat ($6.4 million). Compared to 10.6 million manat ($6.2 million) at the end of August, this represented an increase of 300,000 manat ($176,500), or 2.8%.

Manat-denominated loans accounted for the largest share of short-term lending. At the end of the reporting period, short-term loans in the national currency totaled 7.2 million manat ($4.2 million). This was 300,000 manat ($176,500), or 4.3%, higher than the 6.9 million manat ($4.1 million) recorded at the end of August.

Meanwhile, the volume of short-term loans in foreign currencies remained unchanged at 3.7 million manat ($2.2 million). Thus, the monthly increase in the short-term loan portfolio was driven mainly by loans issued in manat.

The breakdown of total lending by ownership type is also noteworthy. At the end of September, all 44.4 million manat ($26.1 million) in loans issued to legal entities operating in the real estate sector were accounted for by private enterprises. The statistical table showed zero loans to state-owned enterprises.

According to statistical data from the CBA, lending to the real estate sector has undergone significant changes in recent years. The figure stood at 281.3 million manat ($165.5 million) in 2022, 268 million manat ($157.6 million) in 2023, 86.7 million manat ($51 million) in 2024, and 28.3 million manat ($16.6 million) in 2025.

The growth in lending from 42.1 million manat ($24.8 million) in August 2026 to 44.4 million manat ($26.1 million) in September indicates that the upward trend has continued during the current period. However, the available figures show that long-term financing, particularly loans issued in the national currency, continues to dominate the loan portfolio.

For the record, the statistics presented were calculated excluding non-bank credit institutions and without taking overdue loans into account.

World.title: US military spending on conflict with Iran exceeds $48 billion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. The U.S. Armed Forces' spending on the military operation against Iran has exceeded $48 billion since the conflict began in late February.

This was announced by Deputy Pentagon Comptroller Arthur Miller during a U.S. congressional hearing on his nomination for the position of Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Financial Management.

According to Miller, the amount includes expenditures on ammunition, the replacement of military equipment and hardware, as well as the costs of conducting military operations.

Miller clarified that the reported figure does not account for damage inflicted on U.S. military bases in the Middle East. Some of these facilities have sustained significant damage from Iranian drone and missile strikes. The figure also excludes losses incurred by the global economy.

World.title: Kazakhstan's aluminum exports to EU reach 110,184 tons in 2025
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. Kazakhstan exported 110,184 tons of aluminum to the European Union in 2025, valued at 274 million euros, according to Kazakhstan's Ministry of Trade and Integration.

The EU's share of Kazakhstan's total aluminum exports increased from approximately 6% to 54%.

The impact of the EU's carbon regulations on Kazakh exporters was discussed at a session held in Antalya, Türkiye, as part of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

According to the ministry, Kazakhstan's exports of iron and steel to the EU amounted to 396,318 tons in 2025, valued at 337 million euros, accounting for around 6% of the country's total exports of these products.

The session, titled "From Awareness to Competitiveness: Preparing Kazakhstan's Exports for the New Carbon Architecture of Global Trade and Strengthening Trade Connectivity in the Context of the Middle Corridor", was organized by QazTrade JSC jointly with Kazakhstan's Ministry of Trade and Integration and the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. It took place at the QAZAQSTAN Pavilion.

The main topic of the discussion was the EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which, from January 1, 2026, applies to imports of iron and steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity.

Under the mechanism, importers are required to pay for embedded carbon emissions, with the cost linked to the carbon price under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS). The ETS carbon price ranged from approximately 73 to 85 euros per ton of CO₂ in 2023-2025. The first annual CBAM declaration for 2026 must be submitted by September 30, 2027.

For Kazakhstan, the new requirements affect the competitiveness of industrial exports, emissions accounting and verification, production modernization and companies' investment decisions.

During the session, representatives of government agencies in Kazakhstan and the EU, international organizations, experts and major industrial companies discussed exporters' readiness to meet requirements for monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) of emissions, emissions trading mechanisms and carbon allowance transactions, as well as the impact of these requirements on exports and investment.

The session concluded with the identification of key challenges and needs facing Kazakh exporters, an exchange of experience in carbon regulation, and the development of proposals to support businesses, modernize production and strengthen international cooperation.

COP31 is being held at the Antalya Expo Center from November 9 to 20.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics of Kazakhstan, trade turnover between Kazakhstan and the EU amounted to $31.629 billion in January-August 2026, accounting for around 30% of the country's total foreign trade turnover. Trend's calculations based on the bureau's data show that the figure increased by 8.2% compared with $29.240 billion recorded in the same period of 2025.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan SMEs record $2.3 billion in industrial output for 2025
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. Industrial output produced by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Kyrgyzstan, including informal bread production, totaled 201.1 billion soms (approximately $2.3 billion) in 2025.

The figure was calculated by Trend based on statistics published by the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic.

The share of SMEs in the country's total industrial output reached 24.5% in 2025, compared with 20.8% in 2021. The share of SMEs in several product categories changed significantly between 2021 and 2025.

Their share of flour made from cereals rose from 46.2% to 65.4%, while their share of vegetable oil increased from 7.7% to 52.6%. For plastic doors, windows, frames, and similar products, it increased from 21.2% to 25.5%, while the share for furniture rose from 32.3% to 61.7%.

At the same time, the SME share declined in some categories. It fell from 49% to 25.5% for macaroni products without filling, and from 31.9% to 8.7% for mineral water. The regional distribution of industrial output produced by SMEs and individual entrepreneurs varied considerably in 2025.

The highest shares were recorded in the city of Osh (62.2% of the region's industrial output), Osh Region (60.5%) and Batken Region (59%). The corresponding figures were 45.8% in Bishkek, 32.5% in Jalal-Abad Region, 25.6% in Naryn Region, 19.6% in Chui Region, 6.7% in Issyk-Kul Region, and 6.2% in Talas Region.

World.title: Iran maintains South Pars gas output despite Phase 14 platform fire
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. Iran's gas production from the South Pars field, which it shares with Qatar and which is known as the North Field on the Qatari side, has remained unchanged despite a fire that broke out last night on a platform at Phase 14, the Iranian Oil Ministry reported, citing Deputy Executive Director of the Pars Oil and Gas Company Sepehdar Abbaszadeh.

"Gas production on the platform of the mentioned phase (SPD14D) was 14 million cubic meters per day. This amount of gas was met by using the production potential of other platforms. At present, rich gas production from Iran's South Pars gas field continues in the previous volume," he noted.

Abbaszadeh noted that on November 10, at 19:30 (GMT +3:30), a fire broke out on the SPD14D platform. In order to extinguish the fire immediately, a meeting of the committee on emergency situations was held at Pars Oil and Gas Company, and the rescue and fire extinguishing operation was started.

He said that the workers of the platform stopped the gas production in time, emptied the existing gas on the platform and left the platform by means of rescue boats.
