Due to the abnormal weather conditions in the Persian Gulf, with wave heights reaching up to 4 meters, firefighting vessels were dispatched despite the significant risks. By around 05:00 (GMT +3:30) on November 11, seventeen platform workers had been safely rescued, and the fire was fully extinguished to protect the platform and its infrastructure.

The South Pars gas field, known as the North Dome in Qatar, is shared by Iran and Qatar. Its reserves are estimated at 51 trillion cubic meters of natural gas, of which 36 trillion cubic meters are considered recoverable. Iran's share is estimated at 14 trillion cubic meters of gas and 18 billion barrels of gas condensate.

The Iranian side of the field comprises 24 development phases. Iran began production there in 2002 and is currently reported to produce around 720 million cubic meters of gas per day across these phases. Total investment by Iran in the field is estimated at $90 billion.

Approximately 33% of the gas recoverable from the field is reported to belong to Iran. The Iranian side has been developed by Iranian companies, while the Qatari side has largely been developed with the involvement of foreign companies.

World.title: Israeli army strikes Hezbollah facility in Lebanon
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. The Israeli military has struck a Hezbollah facility in the Janta area in eastern Lebanon.

This was stated in a press release by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF).

According to the statement, the strike targeted a facility located in the Bekaa Valley, which had previously been used by Hezbollah to manufacture missiles and store weapons.

The IDF noted that the facility had been targeted several times during the current conflict. According to the military, after receiving information about the recent arrival of Hezbollah militants at the site, the Israeli Air Force struck the facility's entrances to prevent its restoration.

World.title: Azerbaijani MFA offers condolences to Georgia over deadly explosion in Tbilisi
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan has expressed condolences to Georgia in connection with an explosion in a residential building in Tbilisi.

The ministry conveyed its condolences in a statement posted on its official X account.

"We are deeply saddened by the tragic explosion in a residential building in Tbilisi. We express heartfelt condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones, and our thoughts are with all those affected by this tragedy. We wish those injured a swift and full recovery," the statement said.

On November 19, a gas explosion in a residential building in the settlement of Zemo Ponichala in Tbilisi caused a portion of the structure to collapse. Five people died as a result of the incident.

World.title: Azerbaijan celebrates Aghdam City Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 20. Today marks the Aghdam City Day in Azerbaijan, Trend reports.

Thus, Aghdam City Day is solemnly celebrated on November 20 every year, following the decree signed by President Ilham Aliyev on July 31, 2023.

As a result of Azerbaijan's brilliant victory in the Patriotic War, Aghdam was liberated from the Armenian occupation. Today marks 5 years since the liberation.

As a result of the historic victory of Azerbaijan in the 44-day Patriotic War on November 20, the Aghdam region was transferred to the Azerbaijani side on the basis of a tripartite statement signed by the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Armenia and the President of the Russian Federation.

Thus, the Agdam district, liberated from occupation on November 20, came under the control of the Azerbaijani army. In the center of the city of Aghdam, the State Flag of Azerbaijan was raised, the National Anthem was played and this was reported to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Ilham Aliyev.

As a result of military aggression that lasted until May 12, 1994, Armenians occupied 846.7 square kilometers of the territory of the Aghdam region, that is, 77.4 percent of its total territory. Over more than five years, 5897 became martyrs in the bloody battles for the defense of Aghdam. In those battles, 3531 people became disabled, 1871 children lost their parents. More than 126 thousand Aghdam residents were forced to leave their homes.

Aghdam has many architectural and artistic monuments with ancient history. The territory of Aghdam district includes the 19th century tomb, the Khanoglu tomb, the Panah Ali Khan tomb, the Panah Ali Khan palace, two chest-shaped monuments, the Sardaba and Hatem Malik castles dating back to the 15th century, the Juma Mosque and the Shahbulag Mosque.

After the liberation of Agdam from occupation, restoration and reconstruction work began in this city destroyed by Armenians, called the Hiroshima of the Caucasus. In the 4 years since its liberation from occupation, many positive changes have taken place in Agdam, and restoration and reconstruction work continues at a rapid pace. The goal is to make Agdam one of the most beautiful cities in the region. The general plan for the city of Agdam has already been prepared and presented, and work is underway to implement this plan.

World.title: Farmers celebrate downpour in western NSW
World.content:
Pastoralists in the west of the state are celebrating a huge downpour of rain overnight, hailing it a "godsend" ahead of the dry summer forecast.

Garry Mooring, from Rose Isle station on the Darling-Baaka River north of Louth, said he had recorded 204 millimetres since midday yesterday.

"This will see us through the summer now, this rain," he said.

Farmers work in floodwater at Myandetta Station. (Supplied)

Mr Mooring said he had only ever once seen the river level increase so rapidly.

"The river has come up possibly 2 metres. We've been here 57 years, and I can only ever recall once the river rising that quick from local water," he said.

" There should be a lot of people delighted. "

Fears for summer eased

Further downstream, Stuart Le Lievre runs sheep and cattle on a station near Tilpa, where his rain gauges recorded between 85 and 140 millimetres.

"It's bloody wonderful," he said.

"It's been patchy, we got that break back in May and have bugger all since then. The country has held on remarkably well."

A station near Bourke has recorded 173mm of rain overnight. (Supplied)

He said the concerns he had ahead of summer had been put to rest entirely.

"We won't have to worry about summer now, that was our main worry because the Bureau [of Meteorology] were forecasting this really bad El Niño that was going to hit us like hell."

Country across the region had been dying off slowly in the last few months before the rain fell.

"It's been a godsend, to be honest with you.

"It's wonderful for us and those that were lucky enough to get under it," Mr Le Lievre said.

Rapid rise for Darling-Baaka River

At Rose Isle, Mr Mooring said the rainwater tanks were overflowing and the river looked primed for a swim.

"It might be silty, but it's good-quality clean water in there amongst that silt," he said.

Caught off guard by how quickly the rain fell, he said the only casualty was a kayak that was swept away.

"The river rose that quickly; there's a kayak that's escaped. It's heading somewhere down the river, hopefully someone might get an eye on it."

Happily trapped

Despite both being trapped by road closures, Mr Mooring and Mr Le Lievre were happy.

Water lies over the road near Tibooburra. (Supplied)

"I don't think I'd even want to get out, it'll be a week before I could get out of here. But we've got plenty of food," said Mr Le Lievre.

Mr Mooring said he would happily stay trapped if the rain continues.

" I don't mind how long we're isolated for if it keeps raining. "

Water lies across a road in Thomson's Creek, near Tibooburra. (Supplied: Richard Norris )

Most unsealed roads and many sealed roads in the Far West are closed, with the Barrier Highway between Cockburn and Wilcannia, the Silver City Highway between Broken Hill and Wentworth, the Menindee Road between Broken Hill and Menindee and Silverton Roads all open under caution.

World.title: After meeting Putin, Trump tells Europe it could save money ending the war
World.content:
It was a historic meeting held between three of the world's most powerful leaders on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

In the heart of Shenzhen, China's equivalent of America's glittering Silicon Valley, Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down together and engaged in a 90-minute talk.

Afterwards, the three men issued a "joint declaration on peace", declaring that "nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought".

They also said the three countries planned to increase the production and supply of petroleum.

But despite the magnitude of the moment, few concrete decisions were made on the major issues impacting the world and its economy, including trade, the wars in Ukraine and Iran, and AI.

From abandoning a Cold War mentality to nuclear non-proliferation and the war in Ukraine, here are the key takeaways from the summit.

Historic meeting represents a 'galling' break from tradition

Last night's event marked the first formal meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia.

The meeting was unprecedented, undeniably historic and increasingly talked about as the most anticipated summit of the year. (Reuters: Win McNamee/Pool)

While the presidents have previously had separate meetings with each other, and been in the same room at global summits, these were their first combined talks.

"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump said of the meeting, before adding: "We feel the opposite."

Analysts said the significance of the talks was not just in who was meeting, but the message it sent.

La Trobe University professor of international relations Nick Bisley said it symbolised a break with the way international diplomacy had been conducted for decades, under which all nation states should be treated equally.

"To set something up which tries to present the three countries as the 'Big Three' who will work things out themselves and the rest of us just have to deal with it, presents a pretty galling kind of picture," he told the ABC.

Trump calls Putin his 'friend', tells Europe to defund Ukraine

With three major world players seated around the same large, round table, bringing reminders of the long table Putin oversaw during the pandemic, the world anxiously waited to see what the men would discuss.

But before the meeting got underway, Trump had already raised eyebrows by greeting Putin as "my friend".

It triggered a wave of criticism from across Europe and Trump's opponents in the US.

Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin warmly shook hands on the sidelines of the APEC summit. (Reuters: Sputnik/Vyacheslav Prokofyev)

"Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.

Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said he found the meeting of the two "incomprehensible" and warned that Putin "will be even more emboldened" after the meeting.

US senator Chuck Schumer, who leads opposition Democrats in the Senate, called the Shenzhen meeting a "historic embarrassment".

After being asked what he made of the US president's comment, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shrugged and walked on.

In the lead-up to the Shenzhen meeting, Trump had flagged his intention to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.

It did not please Zelenskyy, who had warned against the three leaders using the meeting to discuss the war without Kyiv in the room.

Trump said he and Putin had had a "long discussion" on the conflict already, before adding that the Russian leader "and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war".

Volodymyr Zelenskyy was wary of the meeting between the three leaders. (Reuters: Henry Nicholls)

Putin, in an address to media following the meeting of the three leaders, said Ukraine and Europe were not yet ready to make compromises to resolve the conflict in Ukraine.

But he said Russia had invited EU representatives to Moscow to better understand Europe's position.

Hours after the meeting, Trump told Europe it could save money and lives by ending the war with Russia, according to Politico, which cited five European officials who were briefed on the discussion.

Some of the officials familiar with the call described Trump's tone as strongly critical of Europe's ongoing support for Kyiv, while others said he was just communicating in his usual forthright style.

A US official briefed on the call told the outlet that any suggestion that Trump had told leaders to stop funding Ukraine was "not accurate".

Ukraine also came up in separate talks involving the three leaders.

When the US and Russian leaders met for just under an hour, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted by Russian news agency, TASS, as saying the Ukraine war was the main topic of conversation between the pair.

Few other details were reported, but Ushakov was also quoted as saying that Putin left the meeting "in an excellent mood".

Ukraine was also a topic of discussion between Xi and Trump in their separate meeting.

"We're looking to both help, with respect to the war in Russia and Ukraine, we'd like to see it ended. I think I can speak for both of us, very much," Trump said, sitting across from Xi.

Xi urges Trump and Putin to abandon 'Cold War mentality'

Peace and coexistence also appeared to be key issues of discussion.

Analysts were sceptical ahead of the summit that anything concrete would come from the talks. (Reuters: Sputnik/Vyacheslav Prokofyev)

In his opening statement, Xi told Putin and Trump that major powers should respect each other, and that they "must not touch each other's bottom lines on sensitive issues", according to Xinhua News Agency.

He called on the three countries to abandon a Cold War mentality and not pursue "decoupling and breaking chains".

Xi said the world was "not at peace", so China, Russia and the US — as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council — should set an example. They should work together on global challenges and help keep the peace.

"When major powers get along, the world is at peace. When major powers fight, the world is in chaos," he said, according to China's readout.

In similar translated remarks, Putin said Russia, China and the US could help make the world more stable if they cooperated constructively.

He also said the three leaders should discuss global and regional issues, as well as energy security, before he touched on Russia's war in Ukraine.

"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including, obviously, the conflict in Ukraine," he said.

"We focused on that during our bilateral meeting [with Donald Trump].

"We have shared interests in the fight against the threats and challenges of our times, namely, international terrorism, transnational organised crime, and other such threats."

The US president said the three countries had a responsibility to discuss issues that impacted the "entire planet".

Nuclear a big issue

Ahead of the summit, analysts said one of Trump's goals was to form a new arms agreement with Russia and China after the US-Moscow agreement capping strategic nuclear arsenals lapsed in February.

But no movement appears to have been made on the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START).

On nuclear weapons, Xi did declare a nuclear war "cannot be won and must not be fought", and that "every effort must be made to prevent one".

He also said nuclear weapons should be "completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed", to build a nuclear-free world.

He proposed that the three leaders keep up regular high-level exchanges and set up a crisis communication mechanism.

Despite the talk of peace, Putin's nuclear briefcase, known as Cheget, was reportedly photographed by Russian state media.

The Russian nuclear briefcase always travels with the country's president but is rarely filmed. (RURTR via Reuters)

Trump has suggested that the US, Russia and China could work to reduce the number of nuclear weapons in the world, adding they were uniquely positioned to do so.

He then added it was vital that they co-operate to "combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world". He said this would include ensuring that Iran never had a nuclear weapon.

Spy scandal comes up but no action on AI

With AI now a big talking point around the world, questions had been raised about how the issue would come up during the meeting, particularly in light of the scandal surrounding Nvidia chief Jensen Huang.

AI is transforming US–China relationship The ASEAN summit has become a platform for showing how economies are swept up in the newest and most potent form of US–China rivalry.

Huang resigned after revelations about extramarital affairs, including an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Last night, the US president reportedly referred to it "just briefly" in discussions with Xi ahead of the meeting, adding that he and Xi had spoken about AI "the whole evening" at dinner.

But the joint statement made no mention of AI, nor was it mentioned explicitly in any of the three leaders' speeches before they went behind closed doors.

The Trump administration has moved to restrict the sale of advanced chips needed for AI to China following the Huang scandal, including a ban on their sale to China through third countries.

If countries were hoping for some clarity on the future of AI in a geo-strategic or regulatory sense, the meeting left them wanting.

World.title: British PM tells Google to remove Russell Brand video
World.content:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham says victims have heard enough from Russell Brand, urging Google to remove a YouTube video containing a message from the convicted rapist.

The comedian and actor was sentenced to 10 and a half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four separate women, but protested his innocence in a statement read by his wife Laura Brand and uploaded to YouTube on Sunday.

It drew immediate condemnation from victims' advocates and the UK government, who opened an investigation into whether Brand violated laws prohibiting inmates from broadcasting messages or posting to social media from behind bars.

Andy Burnham wants Google to "show some decency" and remove the content. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Mr Burnham called on social media companies to "take these interviews down", adding that Brand's victims "shouldn't be hearing from him".

"I feel for the victims, they've heard quite enough from this convicted criminal," he said.

UK government minister Matthew Pennycook told the BBC that UK authorities have no power to force a removal of content, but said the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.

"That is up to Google," he said.

"We've made a request in this instance because we feel very strongly that victims shouldn't have to see this content."

Asked if he would change the law on this, Mr Burnham stopped short, saying, "I wouldn't leap to that".

"I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here. Think of the victims, that's the main thing. Show some decency," he said.

A spokesperson for Mr Burnham called it "clearly appalling".

"It is only right that the government asks for content that is distressing for victims to be taken down, and we strongly believe YouTube should remove this content," a ministry spokesman said.

"Removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms."

Video remains online

As of Friday 10am AEST, the video remained accessible on the couple's account, which has more than 6.6 million subscribers, and the video has been viewed more than 950,000 times.

YouTube's owner, US tech giant Google, has refused the UK government's request to remove the video, on the basis that its rules had not been broken, the BBC has reported.

A spokesperson for the company told AFP: "We're aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

Brand's account was suspended from YouTube's monetising program when allegations first came to light in September 2023, so the account has not been able to make money on the platform since then.

UK officials have noted that prisoners are banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

Inmates cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments.

Brand's Facebook and Instagram accounts appear to no longer be available. His X account with 10 million followers remains visible, but there have been no posts since November 11.

The 51-year-old rose to fame in the 2000s as a comedian and actor before rebranding himself as a conservative religious influencer in later years.

British police have confirmed they are investigating additional allegations against him.

AFP

World.title: Extensive police search locates missing hunter near NT national park
World.content:
A 45-year-old hunter who was reported missing yesterday has been found alive and well this morning after an extensive ground and air search near Marrakai.

Multiple agencies, including the NT crocodile management team, were part of the search effort in the Djukbinj National Park area, about 90 kilometres south-east of Darwin.

NT Police said officers searched the area on foot and in all-terrain vehicles, with support from helicopters.

The man was located by a search helicopter around 10:30am.

Police said he had no visible injuries but had been taken to hospital for a medical assessment.

"The NTPF [NT Police Force] would like to thank all teams and individuals involved in the search for their assistance," they said in said in a statement.

Earlier today, NT Police said two men had set off hunting in the area around 5:30am yesterday, with only one of them later returning to the car.

He contacted police around midday, concerned for his friend.

"Humpty Doo police attended the man's last known location and began searching the area yesterday afternoon," the statement said.

"Police Search and Rescue members joined and commenced a ground search, with a helicopter assisting from the air but the man was not located.

"At first light this morning the search recommenced with police members from Humpty Doo, Adelaide River and Batchelor being joined by members from National Parks NT rangers and NT Crocodile Management team members."

World.title: F1 is in Las Vegas, and teams are fighting to hit prize money jackpot
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has won the F1 drivers' championship, his Mercedes team is constructors' champion, and there are just three rounds left in the season.

But the final trio of grand prix, starting this Sunday (AEDT) in Las Vegas, are not just for show.

These three races, for every team other than Mercedes, are the most important three weekends of the 2026 season.

Why? It's all about the money.

While fans mostly focus on the drivers' championship, it is the constructors' championship that carries the most significance for teams.

The prize money handed out at the end of the year is tied to where you finish in the team's championship. The higher you finish, the more money you receive.

While the exact figure each season is not made public, UK outlet The Independent published a rough guide to potential earnings this season, based of figures gathered from 2025.

Potential F1 2026 prize money *as per The Independent, all figures are in USD 1st — $140m 2nd — $131m 3rd — $122m 4th — $113m 5th — $104m 6th — $95m 7th — $87m 8th — $78m 9th — $69m 10th — $60m 11th — $51m

As the champion, Mercedes is expected to be awarded about $US140 million ($208 million).

But the other 10 teams in this year's championship have not solidified their spot in the championship, meaning there is plenty to race for in Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

There is a maximum of 129 points a team can win to finish the season; they would need their drivers to finish first and second in all three grand prix.

Ferrari currently sits in second place with 510 points, 95 ahead of Red Bull. The Scuderia just need 34 more points from the final three races to be certain of second place.

But the battle for third between Red Bull and McLaren should be a belter.

Red Bull sits on 415 points, led by superstar Max Verstappen, who sits second in the drivers' championship with 279 points to his name.

Red Bull sits just 17 points ahead of McLaren, which has been an up-and-down season for drivers Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.

The difference between third and fourth this season appears to be worth roughly $US9 million ($13.3 million), and every point will be crucial.

F1 constructors' standings before Las Vegas 1: 652 — Mercedes CHAMPION 2: 512 — Ferrari 3: 415 — Red Bull 4: 398 — McLaren 5: 112 — Racing Bulls 6: 69 — Alpine 7: 31 — Haas 8: 28 — Audi 9: 12 — Williams 10: 7 — Aston Martin 11: 0 — Cadillac

"We'll do our best to make sure it goes down to the wire and in our favour," McLaren race director Randy Singh told the F1 Nation podcast this week about his team's battle with Red Bull.

"We're treating it like a mini championship on our side, so we're just aiming to do our best at each race."

Racing Bulls appears all but set to place fifth, and Alpine looks to be safe in sixth, with any team below them needing to increase their season tally by more than double just to match them before this weekend's action.

The final five teams in the championship: Haas (31), Audi (28), Williams (12), Aston Martin (7) and Cadillac (0) are separated by just 31 points.

Haas and Audi are separated by just three points with three rounds to go, while Williams and Aston Martin are separated by just five.

If either of these teams can secure a remarkable and unlikely podium placing in the final three races, they will almost certainly leapfrog at least one rival and bag themselves a few extra million dollars.

F1 to have full-time stewards from 2027

Formula 1 will have full-time stewards from next season in a bid to create greater consistency in officiating.

Stewards play a crucial, and at times defining, role in races, as they are in charge of regulating rule breaches and handing out penalties.

Until now, stewards for F1 races have been selected from a pool on a race-by-race basis.

But with the demand for greater consistency in how rules are enforced and penalties handed down, a full-time group will be introduced.

It is expected that a team of 12-15 stewards will make up the team, with a smaller pool starting next season, supported by members of the current stewards pool used.

"The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula 1 World Championship; it is also an investment in the future of our sport," FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem said.

World.title: Wreck of first Australian-built warship found off Far North Queensland coast
World.content:
The wreck of the first Australian-built warship has been discovered off the coast of Far North Queensland 128 years to the day after it sank.

Ex-HMCS Spitfire was built in Sydney's Darling Harbour and launched in 1855, making it the first Australian-built warship and the first to be made with the nation's timber.

Australian National Maritime Museum maritime archaeology manager James Hunter said the New South Wales colonial government at the time was keen to strengthen its naval capability.

Navy divers have examined the wreck of Australia's first Australian-built warship but archaeologists say much more can be learned when they return. (ABC News: Jay Cronan)

"There was this sort of concern because the Crimean War was going on between Great Britain and Imperial Russia, [and there was fear] that the Russians might try to invade Australia and take over the then-colonies here," he said.

The one gun destined for the 19-metre Spitfire, however, was never installed and the ship largely became used for patrolling the coast and taking supplies to lighthouses along the New South Wales Coast.

The wreck of Australia's first Australian-built warship was discovered 128 years to the day after it sank. (ABC News: Jay Cronan)

It was eventually sent up to the newly declared Queensland colony and used as a pilot vessel before being sold to civilians as a fishing boat.

More than 40 years after it was built, the ship foundered during a voyage off the coast near Lockhart River.

"On the 20th of August 1898, it was hit by a gale, and it's a pretty old vessel by this point … It opened up some of the seams between the planks and it started to sink," Dr Hunter said.

The wreck of the Spitfire largely remains under the seabed (ABC News: Jay Cronan)

The crew, made up largely of Aboriginal, Torres Strait Islanders and South Pacific Islander people, was forced to abandon ship. However, they all made it to a nearby island and were picked up by a Japanese steamship, the Omi Maru.

The journey to re-discovery

Dr Hunter said historical records gave different accounts about where the boat went down, making the chance of finding it small.

Earlier this year, Dr Hunter, along with Celeste Jordan from the Queensland Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation (DETSI) began the search, along with the crew of HMAS Diamantina.

"It is … a needle in a haystack. I can't express to you how easy it is to lose a ship and to lose an aircraft," Ms Jordan said.

On August 21, the anniversary of its sinking, the Spitfire was found.

navy divers measured the vessel's stem post and a small boiler. (ABC News: Jay Cronan)

Ms Jordan said while the Great Barrier Reef could protect wrecks from severe weather damage, the rapid marine growth could also disguise them.

"You just look for straight lines and very round things because straight lines and round things don't appear in nature," she said.

Dr Hunter said the wreck largely remained under the seabed, but some distinctive structures such as the stem post and a small boiler were able to be measured by navy divers.

The archaeological team plans to return to the site next year to learn more about the boat's structure and the lives of those onboard.

"These guys [crew members] left in a hurry. They got off that boat really quickly because it was literally sinking underneath them, so they left everything," Dr Hunter said.

World.title: SA woman found guilty of murdering parents with insulin
World.content:
After four-and-a-half hours of deliberations, a Supreme Court jury has delivered guilty verdicts against Raelene Polymiadis.

Polymiadis, a type 1 diabetic, had been standing trial in South Australia’s Supreme Court for five months after pleading not guilty to murdering her parents, Brenda and Lynton Anderson.

The pair died 14 months apart both aged 94 in 2022 and 2023.

The 66-year-old began crying as the verdicts were delivered, and steadied herself on the railing of the dock.

Raelene Polymiadis (centre) walking into court this morning before the jury returned its verdict. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

During the trial, the jury heard Polymiadis injected her parents with fatal doses of insulin.

Prosecutors had told the jury the potential motive was to prevent them from going into residential aged care facilities.

The jury heard that Polymiadis's mother, who was not a diabetic, died on March 16, 2022, at the Flinders Medical Centre from an insulin overdose.

Brenda and Lynton Anderson died about 14 months apart. (Supplied: Nine News)

In his opening address, prosecutor Michael Foundas told the jury Polymiadis had "administered a large dose of insulin to her mum" on March 12 while visiting her at the Noarlunga Hospital.

He said Mrs Anderson was transferred to the Flinders Medical Centre where Polymiadis administered another dose of insulin between March 13 and March 15, 2022.

The court had heard that 14 months later, on May 1, 2023, Mr Anderson, who also did not have diabetes, died and was found to have a "large amount of insulin within his body".

During the trial, Mr Foundas told the court that Polymiadis knew "insulin could be fatal" and had made a series of confessions which were captured on a police listening device in her car.

The jury also heard that a set of notes were found during a search of Polymiadis's house and car. Prosecutors said those notes detailed what she should be saying to police when she spoke to them.

In her final address to the jury, defence barrister Marie Shaw KC, for Polymiadis, said the recordings should not be interpreted as her client confessing to murder, but rather that she was accepting responsibility for her parent's deaths.

"Her sense of responsibility for these deaths, members of the jury, is because her insulin played a part," Ms Shaw said.

However, by its verdict the jury rejected that suggestion.

Polymiadis returns to court in December.

World.title: Melbourne teacher pleads guilty to hidden camera offence
World.content:
A Melbourne primary school teacher has pleaded guilty to spying on hundreds of young students with a hidden camera installed in toilets.

Timothy Blamires, 33, was arrested in April after a cleaner discovered a hidden camera at Kingswood Primary School in the male toilets, pointed towards urinals.

On Friday, Blamires pleaded guilty to 13 charges, including producing and possessing child abuse material and installing an optical surveillance device.

Blamires's offending occurred between October 2025 and April 2026.

Almost 300 children were illegally filmed, according to charge sheets.

Blamires, who faced court via video link from the Hopkins Correctional Centre, was dressed in a green prison jumper as he entered the guilty plea.

More than a dozen parents from the school were in court.

After Friday's hearing, one woman said she was relieved Blamires had entered a guilty plea, allowing the case to proceed to sentencing next year.

"The whole community has really been affected. I don't think there's any member of our local community who hasn't been shaken up in some shape or form," she said.

" Parents have really come together and we're really there to support each other. "

Blamires, a tech enthusiast, was a popular teacher at the school, several parents have told the ABC. However, none suspected the crimes he was committing.

"Obviously, looking back, hindsight is a wonderful thing," the parent said.

Another parent said she felt "frustrated and betrayed".

Blamires, who has been in custody since his arrest, will face the County Court on May 10 for a pre-sentence hearing.

Virgin Australia has announced plans to expand its fleet as part of a longer-term refresh which could see the airline purchase more aircraft from Boeing or Airbus. The Brisbane-based airline, which has 10 Boeing 737 MAX 10 planes on order, may seek to purchase more of that model. Virgin said it will also consider A321s made by Boeing’s rival Airbus. A Boeing 737 at the Renton, Washington plant, in its final position before being rolled off the line. Chris Zappone Virgin, which maintains a fleet of 107 Boeing 737s, has put in a request for proposals to both Boeing and Airbus, the world’s two major plane-makers. The A321 family has variants that can accommodate 200 passengers. The two-class configuration of a 737 MAX 10 can carry between 185 and 210 passengers. “Newer aircraft improve reliability and fuel efficiency as well as the onboard experience,” CEO Dave Emerson said at the company’s annual general meeting on Friday.



“Looking further ahead, we are assessing the role of aircraft in the 200-seat category as part of our longer-term fleet renewal, including the opportunity to add capacity more efficiently on suitable routes,” he said. Virgin Australia is discussing new planes with manufacturers. The Age Emerson has led the airline back to profitability, while pursuing a fleet simplification strategy that helps minimise costly operational complexity. Newer planes underpin bigger profits by lowering operating costs, including fuel. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 currently in the Virgin fleet is around 20 per cent more fuel efficient than the 737-800 that they replace, Emerson said. A Virgin spokesperson separately confirmed: “As part of our future fleet planning, Virgin Australia has issued a request for proposals to Boeing and Airbus for aircraft in the 200-seat category to support future growth and fleet renewal into the next decade.”



Related Article Exclusive

Aviation This Qantas jet was hit by lightning. It’s still grounded two weeks later Airbus refused to comment saying it didn’t provide details of “commercial discussions we may or may not be having with airlines”. Boeing was contacted for comment. One aviation analyst said it was unlikely Virgin would add Airbus planes to its Boeing dominated fleet. Virgin has also refreshed its existing 737 fleet to improve its quality, make the seating more dense and more consistent.



Emerson said that the company “completed the core refurbishment” of its Boeing 737 fleet, with 102 aircraft now featuring refreshed interiors. Currently, 88 per cent of the 737 fleet has Wi-Fi, he said. The company also retired its A320 and Fokker F100 aircraft used on regional routes and introduced the E190-E2, “supporting a simpler and more efficient fleet”, Emerson said. Related Article Aviation Inside the building of a Boeing 737 – from scratch Virgin, like Qantas, has faced sharply higher fuel costs in the past year, stemming from the conflict in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine. While having effectively hedged the initial part of the conflict, the company is exposed to higher fuel costs to come. Underlying revenue and income rose 8.1 per cent to $6.28 billion in the 2026 financial year, with underlying pre-tax earnings lifting 13.4 per cent to $753 million.



Avlaw Aviation consulting director Michael Galvin said Virgin is trying to capitalise “on the golden triangle of Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne ... where there is significant demand”. Virgin has seen Qantas increase the density in their aircraft, moving to the new types when they’ve refreshed their 737s, now getting over 200 seats on the same flight and “that’s using a lot less fuel”. “Fuel is becoming more expensive and it doesn’t look like the price is going to come down in the near term,” said Galvin. “So if you can get more people on an airplane that uses less fuel, it’s a great economic story.” A barrel of Brent crude oil hit US$116.77 on October 23. It’s currently trading around US$92.50. Rising fuel costs have forced the airline to trim capacity by reducing frequency of flights and shedding unprofitable routes. It’s also had to ensure the cost discipline across existing routes.

World.title: This show is a contender for the most must-see musical since Hamilton
World.content:
Sydney Lyric, November 19, until February 14.

“This isn’t going to work,” is an amusingly ironic first line for the best jukebox musical, ever. Finally, the songs have a compelling reason for being woven into the narrative – I was going to say, “like a real musical”, but this is the real thing. Whether you love Neil Diamond’s music or loathe it, the songs are born again as part of a story. His story.

Anthony McCarten’s book is among the finest examinations of an artist’s inner life that I’ve seen on stage or screen. He frames it with therapy sessions that Diamond undertook later in life to try to free himself from the crippling loneliness that underpinned his creativity.

Will Swenson as Neil Diamond in A Beautiful Noise. Jeff Busby

I never took Diamond’s work especially seriously in the ’70s, and less so when I reviewed his 2005 Sydney concert. It wasn’t that the songs were bad (I’ve an abiding love for I’m a Believer, notably Robert Wyatt’s version), but I found many of them fussily arranged and over-produced, disguising the lyrics’ edgy candour.

The sheer weight of their quality becomes undeniable, however, when packed into this show and sung by Will Swenson, who also played Diamond on Broadway. His voice is eerily similar, but stronger, thanks to an odd mix of singing from the back of the throat in a deep baritone that is, by turns, gravelly and plush, while having a nasal edge amplifying vulnerability.

Ashleigh Rubenach as Marcia with Will Swenson. Jeff Busby

He can also act his socks off. When performing Diamond’s first club gig, he exactly catches the jangly mishmash of raw nerves and raw talent, and when he’s depicting Diamond writing a song, he shrewdly balances inspiration and frustration.

Terence Crawford, meanwhile is “old” Neil, in therapy with a doctor played by Monica Sayers. These scenes are just as convincing: skilfully written, with Crawford exhibiting a keen sense of when to keep a lid on the pressure-cooker emotions.

Loading

Another storyline is Diamond’s relationship with his second wife, Marcia, played by Ashleigh Rubenach. She maintains the prevailing high standard in the early flirting scenes, but can’t quite rise to Swenson’s level when the marriage is on the skids, and the stakes are higher. Her rendition of Forever in Blue Jeans makes you realise what a hard act Swenson is to follow, vocally, too. (The show’s very conception means he sings virtually all the songs.)

Michael Mayer’s direction and David Rockwell’s design are masterclasses in fluidity. Steven Hoggett’s choreography is performed with flair by the ensemble, while a nine-piece band under Nigel Ubrihien crisply delivers the songs.

Will Swenson with the cast. Jeff Busby

Ah, yes, the songs. Among the 29 included are Holly Holy, Red, Red Wine, Kentucky Woman, Cherry, Cherry and, of course, Sweet Caroline. But the highlight is I Am… I Said, when Crawford reveals the emotive clout of his own voice, before combining with Swenson in a potent duet. This is a keen contender for the most must-see musical to hit town since Hamilton.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon live updates: Crown prosecutor continues closing address after alleging cold-blooded murder
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial.

The evidence in the trial concluded this week and Justice Natalie Adams has predicted the jury will retire for their deliberations next week.

Court sketch showing Beau Lamarre-Condon in the witness box during his evidence. Rocco Fazzari

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, started his closing address to the jury yesterday and it continues today. Early next week, the jury will hear from defence barrister John Stratton, SC, followed by a summing up from the judge.

Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024.

Hatfield started his closing address by alleging that Baird and Davies were murdered by Lamarre-Condon “in cold blood” after the accused developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with the former TV presenter.

The accused’s testimony was “a story put together afterwards to explain away two deliberate killings”, Hatfield said.

He said there was a “completely overwhelming case” that Lamarre-Condon also broke into Baird’s home on August 17, 2023, six months before the alleged murders, and stole the then TV presenter’s mobile phone and wallet. The accused has pleaded not guilty to this charge.

The alleged break-in formed part of the backdrop against which the men were killed, Hatfield said.

The alleged murders “didn’t just happen out of the blue”, Hatfield said. It was “a case of escalating conduct”, including stalking and break-ins before a murder.

Hatfield pointed to differences in the defence case as outlined by Stratton in his opening address to the court in September and the accused’s own evidence in court. Stratton said the defence case was that Davies had a knife when Lamarre-Condon first encountered him in the hallway of Baird’s home. Hatfield noted that this “was changed to Mr Baird” when Lamarre-Condon gave evidence.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Rainbow Sexual, Domestic and Family Violence Hotline (1800 497 212) and Lifeline (13 11 14).

World.title: Barkly cracks 98% rare earths recovery in Top End breakthrough
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessThe economyBulls N' Bears Barkly cracks 98% rare earths recovery in Top End breakthrough Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS James Pearson November 20, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Barkly Rare Earths has notched up another processing breakthrough at its namesake rare earths project in the Northern Territory, delivering extraction rates of between 97 and 98 per cent in three laboratory tests using a potentially simpler and cheaper processing method. Conducted by independent metallurgical laboratory Nagrom, the testwork involved heating rare earths-bearing material to temperatures of 600 and 700 degrees Celsius without adding any upfront chemicals. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright The heating process is known as dry calcification and effectively prepares the rare earth minerals for extraction, potentially cutting some of the costly and complicated chemical treatment steps traditionally needed to unlock rare earths. The material was subsequently treated with hydrochloric acid, delivering an impressive 98 per cent extraction rate for both magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) and total rare earth oxides (TREO).



‘Having two high-extraction routes now lets us optimise and compare them side by side as we work towards flowsheet finalisation.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Two further tests using sulphuric acid after heating the material achieved 97 per cent MREO extraction, including one conducted at the lower calcination temperature of 600 degrees. The real kicker is that all three tests delivered extraction rates of at least 97 per cent for the four valuable magnet rare earths – neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium. Those critical minerals are essential ingredients in the powerful permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, robotics and advanced defence technologies. Barkly also chalked up a consistent 90 per cent yttrium extraction rate across all three tests. The heavy rare earth is increasingly sought after for aerospace alloys, advanced ceramics, lasers and defence technologies.



Importantly, only eight to 10 per cent of the treated material dissolved during leaching, suggesting the process selectively targeted the valuable minerals rather than unnecessarily dissolving large quantities of unwanted material. The company says these findings could prove invaluable when designing a commercial processing plant, where chemical consumption, energy requirements and waste handling can make or break a project’s economics. Another intriguing result was the extraction of between 97 and 99 per cent of the phosphorus contained in the material. Barkly believes the phosphorus could potentially be recovered as a saleable by-product, opening another avenue to offset processing costs, although further testing is required. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “These tests were undertaken based on our detailed understanding of the mineralogy and they support our working hypothesis that calcination may offer an effective, simpler and lower-cost processing route than a traditional caustic conversion flowsheet.”



The newest tests follow an earlier metallurgical success in August, when 99 per cent magnet rare earths extraction was achieved using a more conventional caustic conversion process followed by acid leaching. Both methods have now demonstrated extraction rates exceeding 97 per cent in preliminary testing, giving management two options to investigate as it searches for the most economical processing route. Next up, the company plans larger-scale tests to confirm the results, refine processing conditions and investigate upgrading the ore before chemical treatment. The metallurgical success adds another dimension to Barkly’s ambitions at its sprawling 5030-square-kilometre project, which already hosts a 40-million-tonne resource grading 2100 parts per million (ppm) TREO, including 710ppm MREO. However, that could be just the tip of the iceberg, with the company outlining a hefty exploration target ranging from 200 million to a whopping one billion tonnes of resource. The junior explorer is also progressing a 10,000-metre aircore program designed to expand the existing resource and test its broader mineralised corridor.



As of mid-October, Barkly had punched 89 holes for 2168m, with further assays still in the pipeline. The company is also tendering for a second rig to accelerate its exploration push. Most recently, the drill bit struck significant rare earths mineralisation in 13 of 16 holes, lifting the overall success rate to more than 93 per cent, with 56 of 60 assayed holes delivering hits. Standout intercepts included 1.5m grading 2171ppm TREO, featuring a richer 0.5m section running at 4550ppm TREO. Another hole delivered the campaign’s widest intercept to date, returning 5.5m at 1035ppm TREO. Barkly says the results have extended mineralisation another eight kilometres into previously untested ground, stretching the mineralised corridor at the company’s flagship project to a sprawling 23km. Management says it’s targeting an updated resource estimate before Christmas, followed by another round of revisions in the first quarter of 2027.



Armed with two promising extraction methods, a substantial rare earths resource and a drill bit continuing to build scale, Barkly now has the task of turning its laboratory success into a commercially competitive operation. If the simpler calcination route stacks up economically, it could prove a valuable piece of the company’s Northern Territory rare earths puzzle. The bloodletting at Wests Tigers has continued, with the NRL side’s deputy chairman Frank Primerano sidelined from the board by troubled owners Holman Barnes Group. Tigers and Holman Barnes Group deputy chairman Frank Primerano has been sidelined from the board. HBG The powerbroker had been a decision maker at the Tigers since HBG reclaimed control of the joint-venture with a high-profile purging of independent directors last December. Amid escalating conflict at the $100 million licensed club operation, the long-time soccer administrator has been shifted off the Tigers board, according to the sources with knowledge of club affairs who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Primerano was deputy to Tigers chairman Barry O’Farrell and the most senior HBG figure in the NRL team’s leadership. It was unclear why he has been taken off the board. HBG declined to comment on Friday.



Primerano remains deputy chairman at HBG, which owns 90 per cent of the Tigers and has the balance of power on its board. The development is the latest in more than two years of dysfunction and unrest at HBG. It comes just two weeks after HBG CEO and Tigers director Daniel Paton was abruptly stood down pending an investigation into allegations brought to the board by chairman Dennis Burgess. Paton has also been removed from the Tigers board. This masthead reported after Paton was stood down that the Australian Rugby League Commission may consider stepping in and taking action over the Tigers’ ownership and possibly even contemplate stripping HBG of its NRL licence. The exit of Primerano from the Tigers board is also sure to attract the ARLC’s attention. According to sources, the HBG board was not told the nature of the allegations made against Paton and two directors when Burgess arrived at a meeting with a lawyer a fortnight ago and two directors abstained from voting to stand him down.



Paton was also not informed what claims had been made about him, sources said. Paton and Primerano had worked closely together on HBG’s diversification from rugby league into soccer, highlighted by its decision to buy the Central Coast Mariners women’s team and purchase of a minority share in the A-League franchise’s men’s side. News Corp also reported that the Tigers and HBG had made an audacious $9 million bid to lure the NRL’s best player, Nathan Cleary, and his partner, Matildas star Mary Fowler, in a package deal in which she would play for the Mariners. The offer was hatched by Paton and Tigers CEO Shaun Mielekamp, himself a former chief of the Mariners, but was turned down by Cleary’s management. HBG’s interest in soccer has caused friction among Wests Magpies loyalists at HGB, which is effectively the Wests side of the merged entity that plays in the NRL. They believe the resources of the poker machine empire should be directed towards rugby league and not another code. The Tigers owners also hold an equity stake in inner-west soccer club APIA Leichhardt FC.





Liquor and Gaming NSW is continuing to investigate complaints about HGB’s decades-old debenture system, which hands significant power over the club to an exclusive group of 20 people. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: The problem with Cameron Bancroft’s 4500-word statement
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion The problem with Cameron Bancroft’s 4500-word statement Michael Gleeson Sports columnist November 20, 2026 — 1:59pm

November 20, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In 4500 words, Cameron Bancroft got very granular. His statement was so detailed, it was compelling. He relayed verbatim conversations with Darren Lehman and David Saker about getting sandpaper onto the ground. Indeed, he recounted multiple Saker conversations. He described numerous conversations with David Warner, who suggested sandpaper be used in the first place. And he described the all care, no responsibility – in fact no care, no responsibility – attitude of Steve Smith rushing away, hands aloft. Cameron Bancroft and Pat Cummins. He recalled the very words of his conversations with media manager Kate Hutchison – one of the few to emerge well from this soap opera – about using sandpaper. Then he got to Pat Cummins and the bowlers, and he suddenly became very vague.



He shifted from Geoffrey Robertson to Dennis Denuto; his account went from granular to “oh, they all knew”. Maybe they did. It stretches credibility to think the people who hold the ball more than others, and consider it like a craftsman a favourite chisel, did not notice differences in the ball. But seeing change and knowing what caused it are two different things. Cummins denied any involvement in the sandpaper plot when he spoke to the media last week. Getty In his lengthy account, Bancroft goes from smoking gun to deductive leap. And those reading it likewise appear to have joined in the same “oh, of course they did” conclusion. It might be thought Bancroft’s sudden mid-rant vagueness was to protect the remnants of a broken relationship with the bowlers and Cummins in particular, but Bancroft had already gone out of his way to individualise Cummins and talk of his anger with him.



The angry man seems unlikely to pull a punch, unless he can’t remember a punch he can throw. Bancroft’s stated aim in his 4500-word recounting was to tell all. That is not consistent with him holding back the single most important bit of knowledge or incriminating specific anecdote indicating what the current Australian captain knew about the team’s use of sandpaper back in 2018. The logical extension of Bancroft suddenly falling back on “they all knew” is that his memory permits no more than assumption. It was a logical assumption, but set against the strident, unequivocal and detailed denials from Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, the assumption must carry less weight. Like Bancroft, Chadd Sayers was prompted to speak out in defence of Usman Khawaja because of their anger at Cummins’ decision to personalise his defence by talking of Khawaja being casual with their friendship. But then neither of them cited a specific moment from Cummins, or any of the other bowlers, that acknowledged the use of sandpaper.



Everyone has acknowledged, even the bowlers, that the team worked on the ball. They all knew Warner was manipulator-in-chief. But not that sandpaper was used. The only way to know that someone knows something, as distinct from assuming they know, is to have been witness to them seeing it, hearing it or of them telling you they know. None of Bancroft, Warner, Khawaja or Sayers have offered such a moment about the bowlers. That is interesting because Bancroft goes out of his way to say in his lengthy statement that there is a difference between knowing the ball was being worked on and sandpaper being used. “I recognise there is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used,” he said. He understands the importance of the distinction but then offers nothing concrete to support it. He does not say how he knows the bowlers knew it was sandpaper. He does not say – as he did of others – I know they knew because we directly spoke about it on this day.



Related Article Australian cricket ‘The biggest traitor’: Khawaja slammed as reporters banned from watching Smith bat Being aware of the important distinction and then failing to attempt to say which category Cummins and each bowler fell into is instructive. Bancroft may well have further incriminating stories to tell about this, but the point is he has not told them in his 4500-word statement. Maybe they will do so at the closed door forum. Incidentally, is there really any reason to close the doors any more on the most public of dirty linen being washed? Short of punishing the whole team (and there was genuine merit in Khawaja’s recommendation at the time that they say ‘we are all in on this’), the real upshot of the latest instalment in the issue is effectively that the three players punished by Cricket Australia remain the three most culpable players.



Bancroft says it was Warner’s idea to use sandpaper, Warner admits it was his idea, but he couldn’t carry the paper because people were looking at him, and Smith knew but didn’t want to know. Related Article Ball tampering ‘Angry, betrayed and alone’: Who knew what in the Sandpapergate saga As all have made clear, that a team was doctoring the ball was no surprise to anyone, least of all the South Africans or the English. It was the sandpaper that was, legitimately, the audacious difference. But can we also take a moment to check on the moral arbiters Nasser Hussain and Michael Vaughan, the former England captains of two Ashes campaigns in which Marcus Trescothick outlined in his book how he had stocked his pockets so full of sticky mints it looked like he had developed a growth in his thighs? Trescothick wondered at how he was never called out by the umpires for having so many of them and using them on the ball.



They were brought onto the field for a very specific purpose, which was not to satisfy a diabetic need for sugar, but to load the ball up to swing. An outside product brought on to change the condition of the ball. Personally, I don’t care if anyone wants to ruin one side of the ball – it doesn’t always work and if it doesn’t you are left with a wrecked ball. But that is not the rule, and sandpaper was still an awful leap. Sticky mints lay somewhere in an ambiguous middle, unless you are a former England captain. This story has, for years, not been about what the team did, but who knew? And assuming people knew remains a stretch from explaining how and why. World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsBondi shooting ‘Light out of darkness’: First responders reclaim Bondi Beach for wedding Clair Weaver Updated November 20, 2026 — 1:53pm ,first published 1:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Their love was born out of the worst day, when two gunmen opened fire on hundreds of people celebrating Chanukah on Bondi Beach. But eleven months later, first responders James McIntosh and Alexandra Edmondson reclaimed Sydney’s iconic beach to celebrate their best day. The couple exchanged vows in a bright and relaxed outdoor wedding that combined beach culture with Jewish tradition on the grass at Archer Park overlooking Bondi Beach on Friday morning. Bondi massacre first responders Alexandra (Lexi) Edmondson and James (Jimmy) McIntosh at their public wedding ceremony at Bondi Beach. Audrey Richardson James and Alexandra celebrate at their Bondi Beach wedding. Audrey Richardson “It was incredible,” said Edmondson, moments afterwards. “It’s been more than what I was expecting. It was beautiful.” Her new husband described himself as “elated”.



Presided over by Rabbi Levi Wolff, of Central Synagogue, the ceremony was attended by about 200 people including survivors and family members of those who died in the December 14 attack, surf life savers, friends, family and a crowd of onlookers. “Just a stone throw away from here on December 14th, they witnessed the worst terrorist attack that our country has ever endured,” Rabbi Wolff said. The ceremony combined beach culture with Jewish tradition. Audrey Richardson Guests gather at North Bondi. Audrey Richardson “In a moment of unimaginable horror when most people would have been overcome by shock, by pain and grief, Alexandra and James ran towards danger. Instinctively thinking of others and not about themselves, helping save lives and demonstrating tremendous courage and humanity.



“Neither of them could possible have imagined that in the midst of that darkness, there flickered a spark, a connection. A love story.” McIntosh, 47, and Edmondson, 36, have become close to Bondi’s Jewish community in the wake of the Bondi shootings, in which 16 people died and more than 40 were injured. Alexandra and James help carry an injured man from the shooting so he could be transported to hospital on December 14, 2025 Flavio Brancaleone They accepted an offer from Rabbi Wolff to perform the wedding in the Noahide tradition, in which people of different faiths can share in key values. Among survivors at the wedding were Liebel Lazaroff, who suffered critical abdominal injuries in the shootings and was treated by Edmondson. He flew in from Texas for the wedding.



“It was really important for me to be here,” he said. “On the day, I remember Lexi coming over to me and telling me to keep my eyes open and focus, and that I would be ok. The doctors told me afterwards staying conscious was critical, as I was five minutes away from not making it. It’s definitely a miracle that I am standing here.” Teacher Andrew Zhukov, who was shot in the leg and whom the couple were pictured carrying from the beach, and Valentyna Poltavchenko, whose 10-year-old daughter Matilda died in the attack, were also in the congregation. Alexandra Edmondson and James McIntosh on their engagement day in Mexico in February this year. McIntosh, a content creator, and Edmondson, a physiotherapist, were acquaintances from a Bondi Surf Club bronze medallion course when gunfire shattered Chanukah celebrations on the beach last year. They were among the first to spring into action, administering first aid, triaging patients and transporting the injured to hospital.



In the weeks following the attack, they attended debriefings and supported each other, forging a bond that soon blossomed into romance. During a holiday to Mexico in February, they got engaged. Rabbi Wolff first met Edmondson and McIntosh on the day after the attack. He offered to marry them after they announced their engagement at a dinner at Central Synagogue in honour of first responders. “Being part of their journey has been an absolute joy and privilege,” he said. “Their love story is a true representation of light winning over darkness. Good over evil. Love over hate.” The couple will attend memorial events in Bondi next month and plan to take their honeymoon early next year.

World.title: Former RAAF pilot ‘led police on wild goose chase’ after killing wife, court hears
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Former RAAF pilot ‘led police on wild goose chase’ after killing wife, court hears Andrew Stafford November 20, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A former RAAF pilot accused of murdering his wife was a liar who had deliberately led police on a wild goose chase in an attempt to cover his tracks, a jury has been told. Robert John Crawford, 49, is accused of killing the mother of his three children and staging her death to appear as a late-night lawnmower accident. Robert Crawford leaving court. AAPIMAGE Frances Crawford’s body was found at the bottom of a retaining wall on the couple’s property west of Brisbane by paramedics in the early hours of 30 July, 2024. Prosecutor Chris Cook said the circumstantial case relied on the jury weighing up the accumulation of evidence and using their common sense.



Quoting Crawford’s barrister, Saul Holt KC, earlier in the trial, Cook asked rhetorically: “What was Frances Crawford doing on a ride-on lawnmower in the wee small hours of a cold night in the Upper Lockyer Valley?” He then said the answer was simple: “She wasn’t.” Frances Crawford’s husband Robert Crawford is on trial for her alleged murder. Cook conceded that while the Crown could not prove exactly where or at what time Frances Crawford had been killed, that was not necessary to satisfy the jury of her husband’s guilt. “You need to be satisfied there was a strangulation event, not that it was Colonel Mustard with the candlestick in the ballroom,” he said.



“Severe force was applied to Frances Crawford’s neck, enough to cause several fractures.” Cook also pointed to scratch marks under Frances’ neck and DNA under a ripped fingernail. “Frances was struggling for her life,” he said. Cook also said Crawford was highly financially motivated to kill his wife, with their marriage on the verge of collapse due to his series of infidelities. “He was about to be kicked out of his beloved home for good,” he said.



Crawford, Cook said, knew he stood to lose half of the estate, including his superannuation, something he detailed in text messages and conversations with other extramarital partners. Related Article Courts ‘Speculation filling holes’ in lawn mower death probe “He knew he stood to lose out. That’s why he was telling his lovers all about it,” Cook said. He also directed the jury to what he said were inconsistencies in Crawford’s claims about how he had found his wife under the mower, including a sketch which showed her pinned with her legs sticking out. He pointed to Frances’ lack of crushing injuries.



“Mr Crawford is a liar,” he said. “He staged the scene, he created a false narrative, he led police on a wild goose chase.” Crawford’s barrister Saul Holt KC on Thursday attacked the crown case as deficient and using speculation to fill evidentiary holes. “(The crash) was unfakeable in the small hours of the morning. A scene like that was unstageable.” A highly experienced officer was not asked to complete a forensic crash investigation despite police having control of the Crawfords’ home and property for multiple days, Holt said.



“It’s a hole in this case that the investigation has never filled and the prosecution cannot fill other than by speculation.” The jury heard nearly four weeks of evidence after Crawford pleaded not guilty at the start of the trial in October. Cook will continue his final address on Friday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

Virgin Australia has announced plans to expand its fleet as part of a longer-term refresh which could see the airline purchase more aircraft from Boeing or Airbus. The Brisbane-based airline, which has 10 Boeing 737 MAX 10 planes on order, may seek to purchase more of that model. Virgin said it will also consider A321s made by Boeing’s rival Airbus. A Boeing 737 at the Renton, Washington plant, in its final position before being rolled off the line. Chris Zappone Virgin, which maintains a fleet of 107 Boeing 737s, has put in a request for proposals to both Boeing and Airbus, the world’s two major plane-makers. The A321 family has variants that can accommodate 200 passengers. The two-class configuration of a 737 MAX 10 can carry between 185 and 210 passengers. “Newer aircraft improve reliability and fuel efficiency as well as the onboard experience,” CEO Dave Emerson said at the company’s annual general meeting on Friday.



“Looking further ahead, we are assessing the role of aircraft in the 200-seat category as part of our longer-term fleet renewal, including the opportunity to add capacity more efficiently on suitable routes,” he said. Virgin Australia is discussing new planes with manufacturers. The Age Emerson has led the airline back to profitability, while pursuing a fleet simplification strategy that helps minimise costly operational complexity. Newer planes underpin bigger profits by lowering operating costs, including fuel. The Boeing 737 MAX 8 currently in the Virgin fleet is around 20 per cent more fuel efficient than the 737-800 that they replace, Emerson said. A Virgin spokesperson separately confirmed: “As part of our future fleet planning, Virgin Australia has issued a request for proposals to Boeing and Airbus for aircraft in the 200-seat category to support future growth and fleet renewal into the next decade.”



Related Article Exclusive

Aviation This Qantas jet was hit by lightning. It’s still grounded two weeks later Airbus refused to comment saying it didn’t provide details of “commercial discussions we may or may not be having with airlines”. Boeing was contacted for comment. One aviation analyst said it was unlikely Virgin would add Airbus planes to its Boeing dominated fleet. Virgin has also refreshed its existing 737 fleet to improve its quality, make the seating more dense and more consistent.



Emerson said that the company “completed the core refurbishment” of its Boeing 737 fleet, with 102 aircraft now featuring refreshed interiors. Currently, 88 per cent of the 737 fleet has Wi-Fi, he said. The company also retired its A320 and Fokker F100 aircraft used on regional routes and introduced the E190-E2, “supporting a simpler and more efficient fleet”, Emerson said. Related Article Aviation Inside the building of a Boeing 737 – from scratch Virgin, like Qantas, has faced sharply higher fuel costs in the past year, stemming from the conflict in the Middle East and the war in Ukraine. While having effectively hedged the initial part of the conflict, the company is exposed to higher fuel costs to come. Underlying revenue and income rose 8.1 per cent to $6.28 billion in the 2026 financial year, with underlying pre-tax earnings lifting 13.4 per cent to $753 million.



Avlaw Aviation consulting director Michael Galvin said Virgin is trying to capitalise “on the golden triangle of Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne ... where there is significant demand”. Virgin has seen Qantas increase the density in their aircraft, moving to the new types when they’ve refreshed their 737s, now getting over 200 seats on the same flight and “that’s using a lot less fuel”. “Fuel is becoming more expensive and it doesn’t look like the price is going to come down in the near term,” said Galvin. “So if you can get more people on an airplane that uses less fuel, it’s a great economic story.” A barrel of Brent crude oil hit US$116.77 on October 23. It’s currently trading around US$92.50. Rising fuel costs have forced the airline to trim capacity by reducing frequency of flights and shedding unprofitable routes. It’s also had to ensure the cost discipline across existing routes.



Virgin recently said it expects domestic capacity to fall by 3 per cent in the first half of 2027. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: This show is a contender for the most must-see musical since Hamilton
World.content:
Sydney Lyric, November 19, until February 14.

“This isn’t going to work,” is an amusingly ironic first line for the best jukebox musical, ever. Finally, the songs have a compelling reason for being woven into the narrative – I was going to say, “like a real musical”, but this is the real thing. Whether you love Neil Diamond’s music or loathe it, the songs are born again as part of a story. His story.

Anthony McCarten’s book is among the finest examinations of an artist’s inner life that I’ve seen on stage or screen. He frames it with therapy sessions that Diamond undertook later in life to try to free himself from the crippling loneliness that underpinned his creativity.

Will Swenson as Neil Diamond in A Beautiful Noise. Jeff Busby

I never took Diamond’s work especially seriously in the ’70s, and less so when I reviewed his 2005 Sydney concert. It wasn’t that the songs were bad (I’ve an abiding love for I’m a Believer, notably Robert Wyatt’s version), but I found many of them fussily arranged and over-produced, disguising the lyrics’ edgy candour.

The sheer weight of their quality becomes undeniable, however, when packed into this show and sung by Will Swenson, who also played Diamond on Broadway. His voice is eerily similar, but stronger, thanks to an odd mix of singing from the back of the throat in a deep baritone that is, by turns, gravelly and plush, while having a nasal edge amplifying vulnerability.

Ashleigh Rubenach as Marcia with Will Swenson. Jeff Busby

He can also act his socks off. When performing Diamond’s first club gig, he exactly catches the jangly mishmash of raw nerves and raw talent, and when he’s depicting Diamond writing a song, he shrewdly balances inspiration and frustration.

Terence Crawford, meanwhile is “old” Neil, in therapy with a doctor played by Monica Sayers. These scenes are just as convincing: skilfully written, with Crawford exhibiting a keen sense of when to keep a lid on the pressure-cooker emotions.

Loading

Another storyline is Diamond’s relationship with his second wife, Marcia, played by Ashleigh Rubenach. She maintains the prevailing high standard in the early flirting scenes, but can’t quite rise to Swenson’s level when the marriage is on the skids, and the stakes are higher. Her rendition of Forever in Blue Jeans makes you realise what a hard act Swenson is to follow, vocally, too. (The show’s very conception means he sings virtually all the songs.)

Michael Mayer’s direction and David Rockwell’s design are masterclasses in fluidity. Steven Hoggett’s choreography is performed with flair by the ensemble, while a nine-piece band under Nigel Ubrihien crisply delivers the songs.

Will Swenson with the cast. Jeff Busby

Ah, yes, the songs. Among the 29 included are Holly Holy, Red, Red Wine, Kentucky Woman, Cherry, Cherry and, of course, Sweet Caroline. But the highlight is I Am… I Said, when Crawford reveals the emotive clout of his own voice, before combining with Swenson in a potent duet. This is a keen contender for the most must-see musical to hit town since Hamilton.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon live updates: Crown prosecutor continues closing address after alleging cold-blooded murder
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial.

The evidence in the trial concluded this week and Justice Natalie Adams has predicted the jury will retire for their deliberations next week.

Court sketch showing Beau Lamarre-Condon in the witness box during his evidence. Rocco Fazzari

Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, started his closing address to the jury yesterday and it continues today. Early next week, the jury will hear from defence barrister John Stratton, SC, followed by a summing up from the judge.

Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024.

Hatfield started his closing address by alleging that Baird and Davies were murdered by Lamarre-Condon “in cold blood” after the accused developed an obsessive and jealous infatuation with the former TV presenter.

The accused’s testimony was “a story put together afterwards to explain away two deliberate killings”, Hatfield said.

He said there was a “completely overwhelming case” that Lamarre-Condon also broke into Baird’s home on August 17, 2023, six months before the alleged murders, and stole the then TV presenter’s mobile phone and wallet. The accused has pleaded not guilty to this charge.

The alleged break-in formed part of the backdrop against which the men were killed, Hatfield said.

The alleged murders “didn’t just happen out of the blue”, Hatfield said. It was “a case of escalating conduct”, including stalking and break-ins before a murder.

Hatfield pointed to differences in the defence case as outlined by Stratton in his opening address to the court in September and the accused’s own evidence in court. Stratton said the defence case was that Davies had a knife when Lamarre-Condon first encountered him in the hallway of Baird’s home. Hatfield noted that this “was changed to Mr Baird” when Lamarre-Condon gave evidence.

World.title: Barkly cracks 98% rare earths recovery in Top End breakthrough
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessThe economyBulls N' Bears Barkly cracks 98% rare earths recovery in Top End breakthrough Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS James Pearson November 20, 2026 — 2:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
