Barkly Rare Earths has notched up another processing breakthrough at its namesake rare earths project in the Northern Territory, delivering extraction rates of between 97 and 98 per cent in three laboratory tests using a potentially simpler and cheaper processing method. Conducted by independent metallurgical laboratory Nagrom, the testwork involved heating rare earths-bearing material to temperatures of 600 and 700 degrees Celsius without adding any upfront chemicals. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright The heating process is known as dry calcification and effectively prepares the rare earth minerals for extraction, potentially cutting some of the costly and complicated chemical treatment steps traditionally needed to unlock rare earths. The material was subsequently treated with hydrochloric acid, delivering an impressive 98 per cent extraction rate for both magnet rare earth oxides (MREO) and total rare earth oxides (TREO).



‘Having two high-extraction routes now lets us optimise and compare them side by side as we work towards flowsheet finalisation.’ Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright Two further tests using sulphuric acid after heating the material achieved 97 per cent MREO extraction, including one conducted at the lower calcination temperature of 600 degrees. The real kicker is that all three tests delivered extraction rates of at least 97 per cent for the four valuable magnet rare earths – neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium. Those critical minerals are essential ingredients in the powerful permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, robotics and advanced defence technologies. Barkly also chalked up a consistent 90 per cent yttrium extraction rate across all three tests. The heavy rare earth is increasingly sought after for aerospace alloys, advanced ceramics, lasers and defence technologies.



Importantly, only eight to 10 per cent of the treated material dissolved during leaching, suggesting the process selectively targeted the valuable minerals rather than unnecessarily dissolving large quantities of unwanted material. The company says these findings could prove invaluable when designing a commercial processing plant, where chemical consumption, energy requirements and waste handling can make or break a project’s economics. Another intriguing result was the extraction of between 97 and 99 per cent of the phosphorus contained in the material. Barkly believes the phosphorus could potentially be recovered as a saleable by-product, opening another avenue to offset processing costs, although further testing is required. Barkly Rare Earths managing director Craig Wright said: “These tests were undertaken based on our detailed understanding of the mineralogy and they support our working hypothesis that calcination may offer an effective, simpler and lower-cost processing route than a traditional caustic conversion flowsheet.”



The newest tests follow an earlier metallurgical success in August, when 99 per cent magnet rare earths extraction was achieved using a more conventional caustic conversion process followed by acid leaching. Both methods have now demonstrated extraction rates exceeding 97 per cent in preliminary testing, giving management two options to investigate as it searches for the most economical processing route. Next up, the company plans larger-scale tests to confirm the results, refine processing conditions and investigate upgrading the ore before chemical treatment. The metallurgical success adds another dimension to Barkly’s ambitions at its sprawling 5030-square-kilometre project, which already hosts a 40-million-tonne resource grading 2100 parts per million (ppm) TREO, including 710ppm MREO. However, that could be just the tip of the iceberg, with the company outlining a hefty exploration target ranging from 200 million to a whopping one billion tonnes of resource. The junior explorer is also progressing a 10,000-metre aircore program designed to expand the existing resource and test its broader mineralised corridor.



As of mid-October, Barkly had punched 89 holes for 2168m, with further assays still in the pipeline. The company is also tendering for a second rig to accelerate its exploration push. Most recently, the drill bit struck significant rare earths mineralisation in 13 of 16 holes, lifting the overall success rate to more than 93 per cent, with 56 of 60 assayed holes delivering hits. Standout intercepts included 1.5m grading 2171ppm TREO, featuring a richer 0.5m section running at 4550ppm TREO. Another hole delivered the campaign’s widest intercept to date, returning 5.5m at 1035ppm TREO. Barkly says the results have extended mineralisation another eight kilometres into previously untested ground, stretching the mineralised corridor at the company’s flagship project to a sprawling 23km. Management says it’s targeting an updated resource estimate before Christmas, followed by another round of revisions in the first quarter of 2027.



Armed with two promising extraction methods, a substantial rare earths resource and a drill bit continuing to build scale, Barkly now has the task of turning its laboratory success into a commercially competitive operation. If the simpler calcination route stacks up economically, it could prove a valuable piece of the company’s Northern Territory rare earths puzzle. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

The bloodletting at Wests Tigers has continued, with the NRL side’s deputy chairman Frank Primerano sidelined from the board by troubled owners Holman Barnes Group. Tigers and Holman Barnes Group deputy chairman Frank Primerano has been sidelined from the board. HBG The powerbroker had been a decision maker at the Tigers since HBG reclaimed control of the joint-venture with a high-profile purging of independent directors last December. Amid escalating conflict at the $100 million licensed club operation, the long-time soccer administrator has been shifted off the Tigers board, according to the sources with knowledge of club affairs who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Primerano was deputy to Tigers chairman Barry O’Farrell and the most senior HBG figure in the NRL team’s leadership. It was unclear why he has been taken off the board. HBG declined to comment on Friday.



Primerano remains deputy chairman at HBG, which owns 90 per cent of the Tigers and has the balance of power on its board. The development is the latest in more than two years of dysfunction and unrest at HBG. It comes just two weeks after HBG CEO and Tigers director Daniel Paton was abruptly stood down pending an investigation into allegations brought to the board by chairman Dennis Burgess. Paton has also been removed from the Tigers board. This masthead reported after Paton was stood down that the Australian Rugby League Commission may consider stepping in and taking action over the Tigers’ ownership and possibly even contemplate stripping HBG of its NRL licence. The exit of Primerano from the Tigers board is also sure to attract the ARLC’s attention. According to sources, the HBG board was not told the nature of the allegations made against Paton and two directors when Burgess arrived at a meeting with a lawyer a fortnight ago and two directors abstained from voting to stand him down.



Paton was also not informed what claims had been made about him, sources said. Paton and Primerano had worked closely together on HBG’s diversification from rugby league into soccer, highlighted by its decision to buy the Central Coast Mariners women’s team and purchase of a minority share in the A-League franchise’s men’s side. News Corp also reported that the Tigers and HBG had made an audacious $9 million bid to lure the NRL’s best player, Nathan Cleary, and his partner, Matildas star Mary Fowler, in a package deal in which she would play for the Mariners. The offer was hatched by Paton and Tigers CEO Shaun Mielekamp, himself a former chief of the Mariners, but was turned down by Cleary’s management. HBG’s interest in soccer has caused friction among Wests Magpies loyalists at HGB, which is effectively the Wests side of the merged entity that plays in the NRL. They believe the resources of the poker machine empire should be directed towards rugby league and not another code. The Tigers owners also hold an equity stake in inner-west soccer club APIA Leichhardt FC.





Liquor and Gaming NSW is continuing to investigate complaints about HGB’s decades-old debenture system, which hands significant power over the club to an exclusive group of 20 people. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: The problem with Cameron Bancroft’s 4500-word statement
World.content:
SportCricketBall tampering Opinion The problem with Cameron Bancroft’s 4500-word statement Michael Gleeson Sports columnist November 20, 2026 — 1:59pm

November 20, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

In 4500 words, Cameron Bancroft got very granular. His statement was so detailed, it was compelling. He relayed verbatim conversations with Darren Lehman and David Saker about getting sandpaper onto the ground. Indeed, he recounted multiple Saker conversations. He described numerous conversations with David Warner, who suggested sandpaper be used in the first place. And he described the all care, no responsibility – in fact no care, no responsibility – attitude of Steve Smith rushing away, hands aloft. Cameron Bancroft and Pat Cummins. He recalled the very words of his conversations with media manager Kate Hutchison – one of the few to emerge well from this soap opera – about using sandpaper. Then he got to Pat Cummins and the bowlers, and he suddenly became very vague.



He shifted from Geoffrey Robertson to Dennis Denuto; his account went from granular to “oh, they all knew”. Maybe they did. It stretches credibility to think the people who hold the ball more than others, and consider it like a craftsman a favourite chisel, did not notice differences in the ball. But seeing change and knowing what caused it are two different things. Cummins denied any involvement in the sandpaper plot when he spoke to the media last week. Getty In his lengthy account, Bancroft goes from smoking gun to deductive leap. And those reading it likewise appear to have joined in the same “oh, of course they did” conclusion. It might be thought Bancroft’s sudden mid-rant vagueness was to protect the remnants of a broken relationship with the bowlers and Cummins in particular, but Bancroft had already gone out of his way to individualise Cummins and talk of his anger with him.



The angry man seems unlikely to pull a punch, unless he can’t remember a punch he can throw. Bancroft’s stated aim in his 4500-word recounting was to tell all. That is not consistent with him holding back the single most important bit of knowledge or incriminating specific anecdote indicating what the current Australian captain knew about the team’s use of sandpaper back in 2018. The logical extension of Bancroft suddenly falling back on “they all knew” is that his memory permits no more than assumption. It was a logical assumption, but set against the strident, unequivocal and detailed denials from Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, the assumption must carry less weight. Like Bancroft, Chadd Sayers was prompted to speak out in defence of Usman Khawaja because of their anger at Cummins’ decision to personalise his defence by talking of Khawaja being casual with their friendship. But then neither of them cited a specific moment from Cummins, or any of the other bowlers, that acknowledged the use of sandpaper.



Everyone has acknowledged, even the bowlers, that the team worked on the ball. They all knew Warner was manipulator-in-chief. But not that sandpaper was used. The only way to know that someone knows something, as distinct from assuming they know, is to have been witness to them seeing it, hearing it or of them telling you they know. None of Bancroft, Warner, Khawaja or Sayers have offered such a moment about the bowlers. That is interesting because Bancroft goes out of his way to say in his lengthy statement that there is a difference between knowing the ball was being worked on and sandpaper being used. “I recognise there is a distinction between knowing a ball is reversing, suspecting it has been altered and knowing specifically that sandpaper has been used,” he said. He understands the importance of the distinction but then offers nothing concrete to support it. He does not say how he knows the bowlers knew it was sandpaper. He does not say – as he did of others – I know they knew because we directly spoke about it on this day.



Related Article Australian cricket ‘The biggest traitor’: Khawaja slammed as reporters banned from watching Smith bat Being aware of the important distinction and then failing to attempt to say which category Cummins and each bowler fell into is instructive. Bancroft may well have further incriminating stories to tell about this, but the point is he has not told them in his 4500-word statement. Maybe they will do so at the closed door forum. Incidentally, is there really any reason to close the doors any more on the most public of dirty linen being washed? Short of punishing the whole team (and there was genuine merit in Khawaja’s recommendation at the time that they say ‘we are all in on this’), the real upshot of the latest instalment in the issue is effectively that the three players punished by Cricket Australia remain the three most culpable players.



Bancroft says it was Warner’s idea to use sandpaper, Warner admits it was his idea, but he couldn’t carry the paper because people were looking at him, and Smith knew but didn’t want to know. Related Article Ball tampering ‘Angry, betrayed and alone’: Who knew what in the Sandpapergate saga As all have made clear, that a team was doctoring the ball was no surprise to anyone, least of all the South Africans or the English. It was the sandpaper that was, legitimately, the audacious difference. But can we also take a moment to check on the moral arbiters Nasser Hussain and Michael Vaughan, the former England captains of two Ashes campaigns in which Marcus Trescothick outlined in his book how he had stocked his pockets so full of sticky mints it looked like he had developed a growth in his thighs? Trescothick wondered at how he was never called out by the umpires for having so many of them and using them on the ball.



They were brought onto the field for a very specific purpose, which was not to satisfy a diabetic need for sugar, but to load the ball up to swing. An outside product brought on to change the condition of the ball. Personally, I don’t care if anyone wants to ruin one side of the ball – it doesn’t always work and if it doesn’t you are left with a wrecked ball. But that is not the rule, and sandpaper was still an awful leap. Sticky mints lay somewhere in an ambiguous middle, unless you are a former England captain. This story has, for years, not been about what the team did, but who knew? And assuming people knew remains a stretch from explaining how and why. World.title: ‘Light out of darkness’: First responders reclaim Bondi Beach for wedding
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsBondi shooting ‘Light out of darkness’: First responders reclaim Bondi Beach for wedding Clair Weaver Updated November 20, 2026 — 1:53pm ,first published 1:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Their love was born out of the worst day, when two gunmen opened fire on hundreds of people celebrating Chanukah on Bondi Beach. But eleven months later, first responders James McIntosh and Alexandra Edmondson reclaimed Sydney’s iconic beach to celebrate their best day. The couple exchanged vows in a bright and relaxed outdoor wedding that combined beach culture with Jewish tradition on the grass at Archer Park overlooking Bondi Beach on Friday morning. Bondi massacre first responders Alexandra (Lexi) Edmondson and James (Jimmy) McIntosh at their public wedding ceremony at Bondi Beach. Audrey Richardson James and Alexandra celebrate at their Bondi Beach wedding. Audrey Richardson “It was incredible,” said Edmondson, moments afterwards. “It’s been more than what I was expecting. It was beautiful.” Her new husband described himself as “elated”.



Presided over by Rabbi Levi Wolff, of Central Synagogue, the ceremony was attended by about 200 people including survivors and family members of those who died in the December 14 attack, surf life savers, friends, family and a crowd of onlookers. “Just a stone throw away from here on December 14th, they witnessed the worst terrorist attack that our country has ever endured,” Rabbi Wolff said. The ceremony combined beach culture with Jewish tradition. Audrey Richardson Guests gather at North Bondi. Audrey Richardson “In a moment of unimaginable horror when most people would have been overcome by shock, by pain and grief, Alexandra and James ran towards danger. Instinctively thinking of others and not about themselves, helping save lives and demonstrating tremendous courage and humanity.



“Neither of them could possible have imagined that in the midst of that darkness, there flickered a spark, a connection. A love story.” McIntosh, 47, and Edmondson, 36, have become close to Bondi’s Jewish community in the wake of the Bondi shootings, in which 16 people died and more than 40 were injured. Alexandra and James help carry an injured man from the shooting so he could be transported to hospital on December 14, 2025 Flavio Brancaleone They accepted an offer from Rabbi Wolff to perform the wedding in the Noahide tradition, in which people of different faiths can share in key values. Among survivors at the wedding were Liebel Lazaroff, who suffered critical abdominal injuries in the shootings and was treated by Edmondson. He flew in from Texas for the wedding.



“It was really important for me to be here,” he said. “On the day, I remember Lexi coming over to me and telling me to keep my eyes open and focus, and that I would be ok. The doctors told me afterwards staying conscious was critical, as I was five minutes away from not making it. It’s definitely a miracle that I am standing here.” Teacher Andrew Zhukov, who was shot in the leg and whom the couple were pictured carrying from the beach, and Valentyna Poltavchenko, whose 10-year-old daughter Matilda died in the attack, were also in the congregation. Alexandra Edmondson and James McIntosh on their engagement day in Mexico in February this year. McIntosh, a content creator, and Edmondson, a physiotherapist, were acquaintances from a Bondi Surf Club bronze medallion course when gunfire shattered Chanukah celebrations on the beach last year. They were among the first to spring into action, administering first aid, triaging patients and transporting the injured to hospital.



In the weeks following the attack, they attended debriefings and supported each other, forging a bond that soon blossomed into romance. During a holiday to Mexico in February, they got engaged. Rabbi Wolff first met Edmondson and McIntosh on the day after the attack. He offered to marry them after they announced their engagement at a dinner at Central Synagogue in honour of first responders. “Being part of their journey has been an absolute joy and privilege,” he said. “Their love story is a true representation of light winning over darkness. Good over evil. Love over hate.” The couple will attend memorial events in Bondi next month and plan to take their honeymoon early next year.

World.title: Former RAAF pilot ‘led police on wild goose chase’ after killing wife, court hears
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Former RAAF pilot ‘led police on wild goose chase’ after killing wife, court hears Andrew Stafford November 20, 2026 — 1:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A former RAAF pilot accused of murdering his wife was a liar who had deliberately led police on a wild goose chase in an attempt to cover his tracks, a jury has been told. Robert John Crawford, 49, is accused of killing the mother of his three children and staging her death to appear as a late-night lawnmower accident. Robert Crawford leaving court. AAPIMAGE Frances Crawford’s body was found at the bottom of a retaining wall on the couple’s property west of Brisbane by paramedics in the early hours of 30 July, 2024. Prosecutor Chris Cook said the circumstantial case relied on the jury weighing up the accumulation of evidence and using their common sense.



Quoting Crawford’s barrister, Saul Holt KC, earlier in the trial, Cook asked rhetorically: “What was Frances Crawford doing on a ride-on lawnmower in the wee small hours of a cold night in the Upper Lockyer Valley?” He then said the answer was simple: “She wasn’t.” Frances Crawford’s husband Robert Crawford is on trial for her alleged murder. Cook conceded that while the Crown could not prove exactly where or at what time Frances Crawford had been killed, that was not necessary to satisfy the jury of her husband’s guilt. “You need to be satisfied there was a strangulation event, not that it was Colonel Mustard with the candlestick in the ballroom,” he said.



“Severe force was applied to Frances Crawford’s neck, enough to cause several fractures.” Cook also pointed to scratch marks under Frances’ neck and DNA under a ripped fingernail. “Frances was struggling for her life,” he said. Cook also said Crawford was highly financially motivated to kill his wife, with their marriage on the verge of collapse due to his series of infidelities. “He was about to be kicked out of his beloved home for good,” he said.



Crawford, Cook said, knew he stood to lose half of the estate, including his superannuation, something he detailed in text messages and conversations with other extramarital partners. Related Article Courts ‘Speculation filling holes’ in lawn mower death probe “He knew he stood to lose out. That’s why he was telling his lovers all about it,” Cook said. He also directed the jury to what he said were inconsistencies in Crawford’s claims about how he had found his wife under the mower, including a sketch which showed her pinned with her legs sticking out. He pointed to Frances’ lack of crushing injuries.



“Mr Crawford is a liar,” he said. “He staged the scene, he created a false narrative, he led police on a wild goose chase.” Crawford’s barrister Saul Holt KC on Thursday attacked the crown case as deficient and using speculation to fill evidentiary holes. “(The crash) was unfakeable in the small hours of the morning. A scene like that was unstageable.” A highly experienced officer was not asked to complete a forensic crash investigation despite police having control of the Crawfords’ home and property for multiple days, Holt said.



“It’s a hole in this case that the investigation has never filled and the prosecution cannot fill other than by speculation.” The jury heard nearly four weeks of evidence after Crawford pleaded not guilty at the start of the trial in October. Cook will continue his final address on Friday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Charges for low-level drug offending reach highest level in a decade
World.content:
Audio player for " Law expert questions approach to low-level drug offences " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2693667%2Fcharges-for-low-level-drug-offending-reach-highest-level-in-a-decade

Law expert questions approach to low-level drug offences Morning Report Download MP3 7m

*This story has been updatd to clarify the charges for low-level drug offending are at their highest level in a decade.

The number of people being charged for low-level drug offending has reached its highest level in a decade, despite a 2019 law change telling police not prosecute unless it's in the public interest.

Authorities had been told to consider a health-centred approach instead, but data collated by the Drug Foundation shows more than 4200 people were charged for unlawful possession or use in 2025 and 2026 period.

Of those cases, 960 had possession or use as the only charge they faced.

In the same year, 15 people were imprisoned for drug possession or use alone.

The report also highlighted that Māori were charged with drug offences nearly five times more than the rate of non-Māori in the last year.

Audio player for " Law expert questions approach to low-level drug offences " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2693667%2Fcharges-for-low-level-drug-offending-reach-highest-level-in-a-decade

Law expert questions approach to low-level drug offences Morning Report Download MP3 7m

The maximum penalty for possession or use is three to six months in prison depending on class, or a fine of $500 to $1000.

AUT dean of law school Khylee Quince Supplied

Auckland University of Technology dean of law school Khylee Quince said the figures needed to be seen as part of a bigger picture which has Māori disproportinately represented in prosecutions and convictions in all offence categories.

"Drug use and possession and drug-related offending is just a smaller picture of that bigger picture."

Quince said there were three main conclusions she could draw:

Police were not applying the 2019 amendment effectively

There was probably still systemic or unconscious bias in the policing of Māori

The Misuse of Drugs Act needed to be overhauled and review the resourcing of helping people who misused drugs.

She said 1000 people were charged solely for possession or use of drugs, 15 were sent to prison and 10 of those people were Māori.

Those people had not been arrested for other offences so had probably been randomly stopped by police when they were in vehicles or on the street.

The 2019 amendment to try and cut down the number of people prosecuted was "clearly not working".

"That tells us that police have either not been properly informed or trained as to how to interpret and apply those legal obligations."

Police were not meant to prosecute unless it was in the public interest and must consider a health-related response instead.

"The police should be policing differently and there's clear evidence that they aren't."

While she welcomed diversity within the police force, she questioned how officers were being trained and equipped to be robust in their interpretation of the law.

"This tells us something about what we should be doing at police college and the way in which these people are supported to do their job in the community."

Worrying trend, Drug Foundation says

Dave Burnside is the lived experience leader at Odyssey Trust, an addiction treatment service based in Auckland.

He said the trend was worrying.

"Particularly when most of the world is turning to a health not handcuffs approach and recognising the futility of criminalising drug use particularly and possession," he said.

Odyssey Trust lived experience leader Dave Burnside. Supplied / Odyssey Trust

Burnside had his own experience with the system, where minor cannabis charges led him on a downward spiral to other offending and prison time.

"It gave me a criminal record, it affected my opportunities in terms of employment, travel, education and other things," he said.

"I ended up spending considerable time in jail over my life, and the offending increased."

It was only when Burnside was able to get treatment later in his life that he was able to break free from that world.

"There are alternatives that exist, and we're just not using them," he said.

He said there needed to be investment and provision for treatment options, as well as a shift in perception.

"One of the key things is that criminalising people, charging more people, imprisoning more people does not make communities safer," Burnside said.

"Those people will come out, they will have lost any sort of employment, any housing, any supports that they've had and be expected to rebuild that with very little support."

NZ Drug Foundation executive director Sarah Helm Supplied/ NZ Drug Foundation

Executive director of the Drug Foundation Sarah Helm said over the period covered by the report, consumption of meth and cocaine had surged, as did the harm it caused.

"It does pose the question whether or not it is in the public interest to continue prosecuting for drug use and possession," she said.

Helm said the figures for Māori were the tip of the iceberg.

"The disparity grows as you move into convictions and imprisonment, with almost 60 percent of people imprisoned for [possession or use] are Māori."

Police's Greg Williams of the National Organised Crime Group investigates the most serious level of drug and gang offending.

Greg Williams, of Police's National Organised Crime Group. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

He said those who were charged with minor drug offences were often also facing more serious crimes.

"What you're seeing in that charging data is a lot of examples of [possession of a drug utensil] but the reality, even the report accepts this, is that it was associated with other more serious offending," he said.

"You can talk about people charged, but actually what this report fails to realise is the other resolutions that occur around the back of this."

Williams said from the start of July 2021 to the end of July 2026 there had been 12,429 people charged with drug offences who went through non-court action, like diversion and warnings.

Police wanted to see more investment in treatment programmes also, but enforcement was still needed against those at the top of the drug trade, he said.

World.title: Bus driver's death confirmed following crash in Wellington
World.content:
The operator of the Wellington bus that crashed in Wadestown on Friday morning is "devastated that one of our drivers has died".

"Our hearts go out to their family, friends and colleagues," Kinetic CEO Tessa Auelua said in a statement with Metlink, which confirmed the driver's death on Friday afternoon.

The businesses were "deeply saddened by the death".

Auelua said supporting the driver's family was their priority.

"We're making sure everyone affected, including our team at the depot, has the care and support they need."

The incident has been referred to WorkSafe.

Firefighters were called to the scene in Wadestown around 8.13am.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

Nearby residents told RNZ they had come onto the street to find a bus had crashed into the bushes.

The rear of the bus had ended up on the pavement at the bus stop on Norwich Street.

Police locked down the street and put up screens around the scene while they investigated.

Earlier, they said there were severe injuries. By noon, a Lychgate Funerals vehicle had arrived and was allowed inside the police cordon.

Police were moving the bus around midday as the scene examination continued. The sound of a broken fence and trees cracking could be heard as the bus was pulled from the bush.

The bus was displaying its route number as 13 while heading towards Brandon Street.

Norwich Street has since reopened after being closed while emergency services attended the scene.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

'Never seen anything like this'

Earlier in the day, local mailman Justin told RNZ it was usually a peaceful neighbourhood.

He'd been doing the route for seven years and had "never seen anything like this".

He said he had deliveries on Norwich Street that wouldn't be done, as he expected police to be at the scene for some time.

Neighbour Karen was sleeping in on her day off when sirens woke her.

She said the intersection was tricky for long buses to manage.

RNZ / Mark Papalii

"That corner is quite difficult to take."

RNZ saw residents milling around, confused and uncertain as to what had happened.

They said nobody would want an incident like this to happen on their street.

RNZ saw two other buses at the scene.

World.title: Pacific countries among minority voting with Israel against Palestinian rights at UN
World.content:
Several Pacific Island countries have joined a small minority of countries voting with Israel against a United Nations (UN) resolution on the right of Palestinian people to self-determination.

The Pacific countries also swam against the tide of the international community on a series of other UN resolutions related to Palestinian people or territory.

In total, 162 countries voted in favour of the United Nations General Assembly Fourth Committee resolution on the right of Palestinian people to self-determination.

Four of the six countries who voted with Israel and the United States against the resolution were from the Pacific: Papua New Guinea, Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and Naoero.

Three Pacific countries abstained: Fiji, Samoa and the Marshall Islands.

Meanwhile, several Pacific Islands nations against the resolution on assistance to Palestinian refugees in the form of operations of the United Nations Relief and Works Agency mandate, was supported by 143 countries.

Fiji, Tonga, Palau and Micronesia were among nine countries who voted against it, alongside the United States and Israel - those abstaining included Samoa, PNG and the Marshall Islands.

A resolution on the rights of Palestinian people over their natural resources was supported by 155 countries.

However, Naoero, Palau, Fiji, Tonga and Micronesia were among the nine countries who voted against the resolution, with Samoa, the Marshall Islands and PNG abstaining.

For the UN resolution to declare Israeli settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as illegal, a core of Israel's staunchest Pacific allies again voted with it.

In total, 143 voted in favour of the resolution which aimed to stop the expansion of illegal Israeli settlements, uphold international law and preserve the possibility of an independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.

The eleven countries voting against the resolution included Palau, Micronesia, Tonga and Fiji - those abstaining included Samoa, the Marshall Islands, Naoero and PNG.

Another resolution addressing Israeli settlement activities in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (including East Jerusalem) and the occupied Syrian Golan, was supported by 149 countries.

But Fiji, Tonga, Micronesia and Palau were among the seven countries who voted against, with Israel.

World.title: Police appeal for information after man accused of sex offending named
World.content:
Police are appealing for information on an investigation into a man accused of sexual offending against four young boys.

On Thursday, RNZ revealed that name suppression had lapsed for Christchurch man Tahu Paki.

Paki faces 18 charges including nine of sexual violation by unlawful sexual connection, two of attempted sexual violation by unlawful sexual violation, two of indecent assault on a young person under 16 and five charges of indecent assault. Paki denies the allegations.

On Friday, Detective Craig Newman issued an appeal for anyone else with information in relation to the investigation to contact Police.

"We have robust processes and highly trained investigators who are dedicated to these cases and ensuring any offenders are held accountable."

On Thursday, the Court of Appeal released a judgement declining his leave to bring a second appeal against name suppression.

In March, Christchurch District Court Judge Michael Crosbie declined Paki's name suppression.

Judge Crosbie said Paki's application was premised on publication of his name causing extreme hardship to himself and his family.

Crosbie's judgement said the Crown opposed interim name suppression, submitting that none of the grounds relied on by Paki reached the level of "extreme hardship".

The Crown also said there were "positive reasons" for not allowing suppression to continue, including that suppression of his name was "impeding the investigation into the alleged offending and is likely impeding additional complainants from coming forward and reporting similar experiences with the defendant".

The Crown said there was "significant public interest" in Paki's name being published.

Judge Crosbie said none of the matters raised by Paki reached the threshold of extreme hardship.

"There is a significant public interest in Mr Paki's name being published and the proceedings being open so that if there are other complainants ... they may feel as though they can safely come forward."

He said he was "not satisfied that publication of his name will result in any hardship beyond that which is an ordinary consequence of alleged offending like this".

"The threshold for "extreme hardship" is very high, and it has not been met in this case."

Paki then appealed to the High Court. Justice Rachel Dunningham declined the appeal in June, and Paki then went to the Court of Appeal.

On Thursday, the Court of Appeal rejected his application for leave to appeal.

Anyone with information can contact Police at 105.police.govt.nz or call 105, quoting file number 250528/2422. Information can also be provided anonymously through Crimestoppers at 0800 555 111.

World.title: Man charged with assault after attack in Avondale liquor store
World.content:
Police have apprehended a man and charged him with assaulting an Avondale shopkeeper on Thursday night.

The incident occurred about 7pm, when the man allegedly attacked a staff member at a liquor store.

"A dispute allegedly occurred after the man was asked to provide ID and this man proceeded to violently assault the worker, before leaving the area in a vehicle," said Auckland City West Area response manager Senior Sergeant Guy Balwin.

Police units were dispatched and tried to divert the vehicle on the motorway soon after.

"The Police Eagle helicopter tracked the vehicle overhead, as it headed west, arriving outside another liquor shop in the Henderson area."

Police arrested the 20-year-old man and charged him with assault with intent to injure, careless driving and failing to stop. The man will appear in the Auckland District Court next week.

World.title: NZ First MP Michael Laws defies calls to quit Parliament, says he will resist 'tyranny'
World.content:
Incoming New Zealand First MP and broadcaster Michael Laws says he will not "kowtow or conform" to those calling for him to stand down, telling listeners of his show he will not quit.

Ranked sixth on New Zealand First's list, Laws has made it back to Parliament after the election, but his future remains up in the air, with his party yet to discuss his fate.

Laws had been heavily criticised for comments he made on his show on The Platform, in which he mocked the Opportunity Party's Kayla Kingdon-Bebb as "severe looking" and questioned "what it's like post-sex".

Laws, who initially defended the remarks as "wry and puckish", later apologised to Kingdon-Bebb over text - an apology she did not accept.

In a video posted to The Platform's YouTube account, Laws has returned to defiance, telling listeners he was "deeply appreciative" of the support he had received from them over the past two weeks.

"It has been a rough ride, it has to be said, but I know that we're fighting the good fight and for those of you who said, 'For God's sake, don't quit', I'm not going to, so I just need you to know that."

He said he was "not here to kowtow or conform", and was instead here to challenge and change.

"The liberal lanyard media managerial orthodoxy has become the new tyranny in New Zealand and that tyranny must be treated as such, and it must be resisted.

"You do not resist by walking away. You resist by advocating, fighting and standing in battle against."

Laws accused that "liberal lanyard media managerial orthodoxy" of trying to get rid of critics who had a different view, perspective and sense of humour.

His comments - which he made on 29 October, but were more widely circulated just three days before the election - were condemned across the political spectrum.

National leader Christopher Luxon quickly ruled out any ministerial position for Laws, while Opportunity called on Laws to stand down entirely.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the comments were "what New Zealand First actually believes", but New Zealand First leader Winston Peters was also quick to reprimand Laws, saying the comments were "simply unacceptable" and the party would meet after the election to discuss the matter.

World.title: Body found in search for missing swimmer off Karioitahi Beach
World.content:
Police have found a body believed to be the swimmer that went missing off Karioitahi Beach last weekend.

Counties Manukau South Area Commander, Inspector Jared Pirret said formal identification procedures were yet to be carried out, but police thought it was Tiaare Honana.

"His whānau have been advised and our thoughts are with them at this incredibly difficult time."

Honana was swimming at Karioitahi Beach with a group of people on Saturday, when he got into trouble in the water and could not be found.

The water-related incident occurred about 6.30pm and four others were rescued safely, one in serious, but stable condition.

The search for Honana continued through the week, with Police Eagle helicopter assisted by Auckland Police Maritime Unit, Surf Lifesaving New Zealand and Coastguard.

World.title: NRL and NRLW 2027 draw released, with lengthy wait for grand final rematch
World.content:
The NRL will introduce a Super Sunday to accommodate Perth's entry in the 2027 season, with an extra game added to the end of each weekend as part of an 18-team competition.

League officials revealed the draw for next year on Friday, with Parramatta and the Gold Coast to kick off the season in Las Vegas alongside Melbourne and Wests Tigers.

The Dolphins, North Queensland and South Sydney have emerged as the biggest winners, while Melbourne and Brisbane have been served two of the most difficult schedules.

NRL round one, 2027 Sunday, February 28 Parramatta Eels vs Gold Coast Titans, Las Vegas

Melbourne Storm vs Wests Tigers, Las Vegas Thursday, March 4 Sydney Roosters vs Brisbane Broncos, Sydney Football Stadium Friday, March 5 New Zealand Warriors vs Canterbury Bulldogs, Mt Smart Stadium

St George Illawarra Dragons vs North Queensland Cowboys, Jubilee Stadium Saturday, March 6 Dolphins vs Cronulla Sharks, Dolphin Stadium

Newcastle Knights vs Penrith Panthers, Hunter Stadium Sunday, March 7 Perth Bears vs Manly Warringah Sea Eagles, Perth Stadium

Canberra Raiders vs South Sydney Rabbitohs, Canberra Stadium

Under the newly constructed draw, no team will have more than one five-day turnaround, with 16 of them shared evenly across the league.

The vast majority of weekends will consist of one game on a Thursday night, two on a Friday and then three on both a Saturday and Sunday.

The NRL had previously steered away from a 2pm Sunday time slot early in the season due to hot weather, but that is no longer possible in the new fixture.

Sunday night games will also be a constant across the majority of the year, with the Bears hosting five of those to ensure more daytime football due to the west coast time difference.

Newcastle will have to wait until round 10 to try to exact revenge on the Sydney Roosters for last year's grand final, with a rematch set for Saturday, May 8.

That is the longest wait for a grand-final rematch since Canberra and the Roosters in the COVID-hit 2020 draw.

The Roosters will have a number of grudge matches locked in before the Knights clash, given they face Brisbane in the opening round and arch-rivals South Sydney in round two.

Payne Haas could feel the wrath of a Lang Park crowd for three straight weeks in 2027, with the ex-Bronco able to set up camp in Brisbane for the month of May.

South Sydney recruit Haas is set to travel to Lang Park to meet Brisbane for the first time in round 10.

After coming up against the Broncos on Thursday, May 6, South Sydney will then face North Queensland at Lang Park the following Sunday for Magic Round.

Assuming Haas is then picked for NSW in State of Origin, he will then feature in the series opener at the same ground on May 26 for the Blues.

Wests Tigers will have to wait only four weeks to take on their former halfback Jarome Luai, after his exit for Parramatta for next season.

Luai's signing with the PNG Chiefs for 2028 derailed the Tigers' season before he was released from his contract a year early to head to the Eels.

The NRLW draw was also released on Friday, with the competition having a trio of prime-time Thursday night matches.

Reigning premiers Sydney will host Wests Tigers to open the season on Thursday, July 1.

St George Illawarra will host Parramatta in round 10, while the Gold Coast hosts Brisbane in round 11 in the other two Thursday night clashes.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Young Aussies stun Argentina at under-17 World Cup
World.content:
Sydney FC prodigy Akol Akon has demonstrated why he's one of the most exciting talents in Australian football as he inspired the Joeys to a shock 2–0 victory over Argentina to launch their U17 World Cup campaign in style in Qatar.

The brilliant young winger had his shot deflected for an own goal on the hour and then produced an audaciously cheeky finish 11 minutes later to seal the opening-day win on Thursday (Friday AEDT) as Carl Veart's side provided a magnificent return to the global boys' competition for the first time in seven years.

Against one of the powerhouse soccer nations, Australia had their backs to the wall, having to make 31 clearances as Argentina enjoyed two-thirds of the possession and 22 shots on goal, but Akon ended up hailing their second-half heist as "amazing".

The 17-year-old livewire provided the real star quality, and it was soon evident why the Sky Blues had wanted to keep him back in Australia for their A-League Men campaign.

He caused havoc from the start down the right flank, his neat through ball in the fifth minute almost resulting in a goal for Central Coast Mariners' Luke Becvinovski.

Akon then struck after the break following another dangerous foray down the right flank that ended with his shot across goal deflecting off the hapless Alvaro Guich and into the net.

In the 71st minute, Mariners' Oli O'Carroll expertly picked off an Argentina attack before Brisbane's Emmett Shaw released Akon with a slide-rule left-foot pass, the winger going on to dummy the goalkeeper before slotting into an empty net.

It only got worse for Argentina when substitute Benjamin Vallejos got sent off for a reckless challenge in stoppage time.

But it wasn't all about Akon, a considerable talent who's already made his national U23 bow.

At the other end, Charlie Wilson-Papps, the young goalie who's on Premier League Brighton's books, made half-a-dozen fine saves and kept a clean sheet.

"I do it for my teammates. I do it for my family at home. So to make them proud is the most important thing," said Akon, as he clutched the player-of-the-match trophy afterwards.

His only worry came with the video checking of his goal. "Ah, that was nerve-racking, man. Because at 1-0, it was a very scary game. So to be able to seal it like that, the coach was telling me it was a goal.

"The first goal? It wasn't really my goal, but I just wanted to do the Tim Cahill, start off the tournament like that. So, yeah, the knee side had to come with it.

"Now, the group, we're really confident, really confident in our ability, and I think that showed today."

Next up on Sunday for the Joeys will be Denmark, who lost 4–0 to Mozambique in their group C opener on Thursday.

AAP

World.title: Football club wishes manager a happy birthday, then sacks him hours later
World.content:
English football club Blackpool has sacked manager Ian Evatt, just hours after the club wished him a happy birthday on its social media accounts.

Blackpool plays in League One, the third tier of English football, and is languishing in 20th position, with just three wins from 13 matches this season.

Evatt was an accomplished player for Blackpool during a successful seven-year stint, where the Tangerines rose from the third tier of English football to the Premier League.

On Thursday, the club posted on social media that morning, wishing Evatt a happy 45th birthday.

Seven hours later, the club posted on social media that he had been sacked.

On the left, Blackpool FC with coach Ian Evatt a happy birthday. On the right, the club announces his sacking on the same day. (X/BBC Sport)

Evatt took over the manager role in October, 2025, helping the struggling club avoid relegation.

But the club finds itself in another relegation battle this season.

"Blackpool Football Club can announce that Ian Evatt has departed his role as Head Coach after 12 months in charge," the club said in a statement.

"During a hugely successful playing career at Bloomfield Road, Ian made over 250 appearances for the Seasiders. In his six years at Blackpool, he played a vital role in the Club's memorable rise from League One to the Premier League, which included two successful play-off campaigns.

"The Club thanks Ian for all of his efforts during his time at Bloomfield Road."

World.title: Paralympian local MP playing her third sport for Australia
World.content:
Politician, Paralympic gold medallist and Australian Para Ice Hockey player.

The unique description belongs to 57-year-old Liesl Tesch MP, who is balancing her role as the Gosford MP with the upcoming 2026 Para Ice Hockey Women's World Championships in Newcastle this month.

After seven Paralympic Games appearances across wheelchair basketball and sailing with a pair of gold medals, most would be more than content with their sporting careers, but Tesch wants more.

While sporting success has tended to follow Tesch wherever she has gone, getting used to it on the ice was not as immediate.

"The first day I felt like a turtle upside down," Tesch told ABC Sport.

"The next day, I was like, 'oh my God, how was I so bad,' [but] I have fallen in love with this sport.

"It just gives me such a rush, and it's [wild] and brutal and crazy."

Loading Instagram content

A second chance

The 2026 Para Ice Hockey Women's World Championships will be the second of its kind, with the inaugural event held in Slovakia last year. Australia competed, finishing sixth, and losing all three of their matches in Dolný Kubín without scoring.

Lynda Holt, 54, is Ice Hockey Australia’s head of para ice hockey and also a Paralympian, and says this time will be different.

"We've all grown in the last year, we've all improved so much, and we have got some new players," Holt told ABC Sport.

"The team is great. I come from a shot put and discus background, a very individual sport on my own, and I'm just loving that we are this team that comes together."

Lynda Holt was part of the team at last year's event. (Supplied: Igor Kupco)

Australia will be joined by Canada, the United States, Great Britain, Norway, and Team World, a combination of players from countries not represented.

The six teams will be split into two groups of three, with Australia in Group A alongside the United States and Great Britain.

The game is played on sleds, and like mainstream ice hockey, it is played six-a-side, with most rules carried over.

For Tesch, it is a much-needed opportunity for women to shine.

"It's a chance for women to get together and play against women because a lot of us, we are training and playing against the blokes," Tesch said.

Australia did not win a game at the last world championships, but they are ready for the challenge this time. (Supplied: Igor Kupco)

Road to the Paralympics

Like several of her teammates, Lynda Holt knows the pressure of competing at a Paralympic Games, and being a part of landmark moments.

A shot put silver medallist at Sydney 2000, she recognises a chance now to be involved in another one, with the sport hoping for Paralympic inclusion as a full women's competition as soon as 2030.

She is not alone. Decorated swimmer Priya Cooper, who won nine gold medals across four Paralympic Games appearances, will also take to the ice, along with Susan Seipel, who won a silver medal as a Para canoeist at the Tokyo Games.

Tesch and fellow Paralympic silver medallist in wheelchair basketball, Lisa Edmonds, have both medalled on the court, and want to be part of a movement for women's para ice hockey players to have the same chance.

The push is on to get a standalone event into the Winter Paralympics. (ABC Sport: Bridget Murphy)

Para Ice Hockey has officially been a mixed gender event since the 2010 Paralympic Games, but Norway's Britt Mjaasund Øyen competed in 1994 as part of the team that won silver.

She was the first of only four women to compete at the level. Fellow Norwegian Lena Schrøder competed in 2018 and will captain Norway at this World Championships.

While the opportunity is there for women to compete alongside men, Holt is part of a wider community wanting a standalone women's tournament, something the event in Newcastle could help provide.

"Our whole goal, our whole movement we have got going on is [that] we have got to get there," Holt said.

"In order to qualify for the Paralympics, we needed to have two World Championships; this will be the second.

"We also need eight teams; we currently have five, and we have got three in development, so come next year, when they decide if we can be part of the Paralympics, we should be ready.

"This is history in the making for us."

Lynda Holt was a shot put silver medallist at Sydney 2000. (Supplied: SE Photography/Shannen Keddie)

The fight for time on ice

Ice hockey's growth in popularity around Australia has meant ice time has been harder to come by, regardless of what discipline you are attempting to play.

The Hunter Ice Skating Stadium, where the team have been training, is also home to several teams belonging to the hometown Newcastle Northstars, including its stand-up men's team, who are the Australian Ice Hockey League's most successful, having won its seventh title earlier this year.

Members of the public are also able to access the space, something Leisl Tesch knows all too well.

"Getting on here with the general public, I remember the first day I did it," she said.

"Everyone's standing up looking beautiful, and I am in this full body armour, but it is really good for speed and turn training with everyone else.

"It is also an inclusion conversation that people with disabilities can get on the ice too."

Holt and Edmonds are both based in Sydney, having to make the trip to Newcastle to train.

Loading Instagram content

"There's not enough ice time for everyone, and it's such an expensive sport, six to seven hundred dollars an hour for the ice," Holt said.

"We're all fighting for it; we've all got goals, ours is the Paralympics."

The tournament starts on November 24, with Canada's clash against Team World. Australia will open its campaign the same day, against the United States.

This content was produced for the ABC’s International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 10, 2026.

The ABC is partnering with International Day of People with Disability to recognise the contributions and achievements of the 5.5 million Australians with disability.

World.title: Aussie has first-round lead in prestigious Tour Championship
World.content:
Emerging Australian golf superstar Karis Davidson has defied the odds to seize the first-round clubhouse at the LPGA's rich and prestigious Tour Championship in Florida.

In a dream debut at the $US11 million ($16.5 million) showpiece, Davidson birdied the first four holes in a flawless seven-under-par 65 at Tiburon Golf Club to nab an early one-stroke lead.

"Just honestly hit some good shots into the green," the 28-year-old said, playing down her hot start after being one of the first to tee off in the elite 60-player field.

"The greens first thing in the morning, especially the Bermuda [grass], is really smooth, so I just had really good visualisation and they just went in.

"So, yeah."

Davidson shares the lead with Korea's A Lim Kim and Thailand's Jeeno Thitikul

American Jenny Bae, Japan's Ayaka Furue, Frenchwoman Pauline Roussin-Bouchard, England's Charley Hull and South Korean Somi Lee all signed for 66s.

Davidson's more celebrated compatriot Grace Kim is also well in contention for the $US4 million winner's cheque — the biggest prize in women's golf history — after opening with a five-under 67.

Fellow major champion Hannah Green is also nicely placed at four-under, while Cassie Porter started with an even-par 72.

AAP

World.title: Who knew what about Sandpapergate? The players break their silence
World.content:
In one chapter of his new autobiography, Sabr, Khawaja provided a detailed account of what he says happened during Australia's 2018 South African tour.

The former batter, who retired this year, alleged sandpaper was used on the ball during the second Test in Port Elizabeth, weeks before Bancroft was caught on camera in Cape Town.

Khawaja described a discussion before the first Test in Durban, alleging a member of the coaching staff told the team they needed to find a way to make the ball move in the air.

"We were all complicit," he wrote.

Khawaja described how Bancroft picked up the ball after a break in play during the Port Elizabeth Test and used sandpaper to roughen one side.

He said the ball was then passed around the fielding team, including to him at gully, and that he noticed how dramatically it was reverse-swinging.

Khawaja recalled one bowler commenting during a huddle:

"Guys, it's going heaps now. Just don't do anything else to it, because it's silly how much it's going."

He alleged a member of the coaching staff later approached Bancroft during the Cape Town Test and encouraged him to do more of what he had been doing to the ball.

Khawaja said that after Bancroft was caught, he argued with team manager Gavin Dovey that everyone should accept responsibility.

"We need to cop this as a team," he wrote.

" We did it as a team, so we cop it as a team. "

Khawaja said most players agreed when he raised the issue at a subsequent team meeting, but then-captain Tim Paine knew not everyone supported the idea.

The chapter ends with him saying, "I can only speak for myself, and it's very clear I knew what was going on."

In a subsequent interview with the ABC's 7.30, Khawaja said he wanted to tell his story and stand by the three players who had been made out to be the only people involved.

"It wasn't just them," he told Sarah Ferguson.

"We were all involved in it as a team, as a squad."

He declined to speculate about whether individual bowlers knew sandpaper was being used.

"Twenty-two pages is what sandpaper is," he said.

"I've tried my best in that to explain my version of events."

World.title: Matildas star Foord named best international player in Asia
World.content:
Caitlin Foord has been named women's international player of the year at the Asian Football Confederation's annual awards in Bangkok, completing a unique treble for the Matildas striker.

The 32-year-old Arsenal forward became the first player to add the international prize to the AFC's women's youth player of the year and women's player of the year gongs, which she also won in 2011 and 2016.

A decade after being named the best player in Asia, thanks largely to her storming performances for the Matildas at the Rio Olympics, Foord was this year a key performer in Australia's home Asian Cup campaign, playing in five of their six matches as they reached the final only to lose out agonisingly to Japan in Sydney.

She set up the winner in Australia's first match, against the Philippines, had another assist in the draw against South Korea and scored in the semifinal against China before laying on the winner for Sam Kerr.

Earlier in the year, Foord had come off the bench to score the extra-time winner for her club side Arsenal against Brazil's Corinthians in the inaugural global club event, the FIFA Women's Champions Cup.

It was another tribute to the Shellharbour star's enduring excellence over a career that stretches back to 2010 when Foord took her professional bow with Sydney FC.

She's gone on to win 152 caps, scoring 42 times, and helped Arsenal win the Champions League in 2024/25, alongside her fellow Matildas Kyra Cooney-Cross and Steph Catley.

Foord is the second Australian winner of the international award, following Ellie Carpenter's triumph in 2024.

AAP

World.title: Cummins's agent criticises 'hysteria' as sandpaper saga continues
World.content:
As the wounds of the sandpaper scandal fester, Pat Cummins's agent has slammed critics of the Australian cricket captain.

In a statement issued late last night, Neil Maxwell rubbished claims the Test captain knew of efforts to use sandpaper in 2018 before the plot was carried out.

"There is no serious case he was an architect of ball tampering or knew sandpaper was going on the field," he said.

Maxwell's comments follow several players, including Cameron Bancroft, declaring the entire team knew of the plot.

Maxwell was critical of the tone of discussion, describing it as "hysteria unfounded in reality".

"When you go through it all calmly and in detail, Pat's eight-year-long position and 68-minute Q&A stands up," he said.

Yesterday, media camped outside Cummins's Sydney home and peppered him with questions about his leadership of the side and Bancroft's explosive claims.

There was an extensive media presence at the practice session held at the Sydney Cricket Ground as well.

Cummins has not thoroughly addressed Bancroft's claims himself. However his agent said he had helped change the culture of Australian cricket in the fallout of the Cape Town incident.

Maxwell said the furore after the third Test match led to then captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and Bancroft being harshly sanctioned.

"It's also true that the players who were suspended paid far too high a price," he said.

"Year-long bans for ball tampering that players in other countries did and were suspended for just a few games. They have always been right to feel aggrieved by that."

Tech.title: Apple is hiring engineers to build its own AI agent
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

Tech.title: A brief history of Nvidia’s recent stock fluctuations
Tech.content:
is an independent reporter focused on business investigations, analysis and news. She previously covered the AI data center boom for Business Insider.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

“We’ve got this,” Colette Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia, said Tuesday night as she closed out the embattled chip company’s third quarter earnings call.

By Thursday, the company’s stock price was hovering at around $150 per share, a nearly 40 percent drop from its all-time high on October 6th, and wiping out a brief post-earnings pop on Tuesday night. Meanwhile, Wall Street was paying up for one of Nvidia’s biggest customers as Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut at $111.50 per share — 34 percent higher than expected.

Looking at the earnings report numbers alone, Nvidia had a blockbuster quarter. Q3 revenue more than doubled from the same period last year up to total $115.8 billion, driven by data center revenue that was up 110 percent and exceeding Wall Street expectations. Nearly $20 billion in revenue came from the highly anticipated Vera Rubin platform, which shipped during the quarter, becoming the “fastest product ramp in company history,” Kress told investors.

“Our momentum is real,” Kress said. “With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade, and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia’s leadership position.”

But investors are stilltrying to reconcile Nvidia’s stellar recent financial performance and position as a central pillar in the AI economy with serious concerns over its future.

The company’s stock has taken a stunning tumble in recent weeks. Fueled first by a broader market sell-off of chip stocks amid concerns about the AI bubble, the stock took another blow following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang amid reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy, according to US intelligence sources cited by The New York Times.

Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s newly appointed chairman of the board, told investors on the call Tuesday that the company “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and has already tapped an executive search firm to help find a replacement. Huang, who cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the company ever since — famously without a succession plan — has become essentially inseparable from it in the eyes of Wall Street and the media. But while Huang may not be ready to let go, posting on X this week that he’d be “honored” to be reinstated as CEO, Nvidia’s executive suite seems ready to move on.

It has been a tumultuous two and a half weeks for Nvidia.

On October 29th, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies believed Jensen Huang to be the target of a Chinese espionage plot. The report centered on his “close relationship” with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company and one of Nvidia’s clients. Nvidia initially contested the report, adding that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang “are not unusual or unexpected.”

Nvidia’s stock seemingly remained unaffected by the reports, at least at first. The share price closed at $213.66 on October 29th, down just 0.8 percent from the previous day. (Julian Barnes, one of the reporters on the story, later commented, “I will confess I was kind of surprised that the world’s initial reaction to our October story was a bit muted.”) The stock closed at a 4 percent drop the next day as the entire Nasdaq fell 2.9 percent, the worst single-day decline since June.

The stock continued to fall through Wednesday, November 4th, the day after the blue wave swept the midterms, stoking fears on Wall Street that the new class of Democratic governors in key states like Texas would slow down data center construction. On Thursday, November 5th, Nvidia’s stock fell 9.2 percent, its largest single-day drop in at least a year. But chip stocks began to recover the next day, and by close on Friday, November 6th, Nvidia was back up 2.8 percent to a share price of $186.64.

Then all hell broke loose. On Sunday, November 8th, Jensen Huang sent a company-wide memo to Nvidia staff in which he apologized for engaging in an extramarital affair. The memo coincided with the opening of an independent investigation by Nvidia’s board into Huang’s alleged misconduct and whether company secrets or national security had been compromised. Huang said he would cooperate fully with the investigation. By the opening bell on Monday, November 9th, Nvidia shares had tumbled 7 percent and trading volume surged past its three-month average as investors reacted to the memo. After a brief rebound, the stock continued to oscillate the next day, as more details of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang’s relationship emerged. By the time the market closed on Tuesday, November 10th, Nvidia shares were down to $168.89, nearly 10 percent below the closing price on the last day of 2025.

The stock rebounded slightly on Wednesday, November 11th, as investors prepared for Nvidia’s third quarter earnings call, scheduled for the following Tuesday, November 17th. By Wednesday night, however, shares had plunged yet again as media reports circulated that Nvidia’s board was considering ousting Huang, and other reports emerged detailing a second alleged affair, this time between Huang and an Nvidia employee.

Nvidia announced Huang’s departure on the morning of Thursday, November 12th, sending the company’s shares falling nearly 14 percent at the open. It closed at just a 4.3 percent dip. The intraday low of $148.80 per share was its lowest price in a year.

On December 1st, Jensen Huang will appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee for transcribed interviews. Nvidia’s general counsel will do the same on December 2nd.

Retail investors have already seized the opportunity to buy the dip. In the first 30 minutes of trading on Thursday, November 12th, retail investors bought $111 million of Nvidia shares in the largest-ever first half-hour of opening for the stock, Bloomberg reported, citing Vanda Research.

They might be onto something.

Nvidia’s average price target is $232.59, with the lowest estimate at $130 and the highest at $350, according to an analysis of analyst projections over the last three months by Google Finance.

Nearly two-thirds of those analysts issued a “Buy” rating for Nvidia in the last three months. Of those, all 30 reiterated that rating post-earnings.

The stock closed at $145.98 on Thursday, a new 52-week low.

Then again, numbers are the core basis for stock market ratings, and numbers may not be Nvidia’s problem right now. It’s everything else — the leadership vacuum, upcoming congressional testimony, regulatory uncertainty, broader questions about neocloud customer financing and sales to China — that will continue to impact the stock in the coming weeks.

Tech.title: Meta now sells 3D movies on Quest VR headsets
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta now offers more than 150 3D movies that you can buy or rent to watch in VR on its Quest 3 and 3S headsets, the company announced today. The movies are available in Meta’s TV app and include titles like Avatar, Spider-Man: Far From Home, Jurassic World Rebirth, Wicked: For Good, and a Billie Eilish concert film co-directed by Eilish and James Cameron.

The company suggests watching movies in a Theater view that’s rolling out with a new Meta Quest update. Theater view “provides a big screen and dims your surroundings to create a cozy, personal cinema experience,” Meta says.

Related 3D movies are finally worth watching

Meta promises that the library will “keep growing, with thousands of titles and international availability coming” when it launches its VR Glasses next spring. If you’re a Disney Plus subscriber, you can also watch 3D movies on Meta Quest hardware in the Disney Plus app thanks to an update rolled out earlier this month.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse Charm might cost $300
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta is planning to price the Muse Charm, a little gadget with a screen that lets you chat with your Muse AI agent, at $300, according to The Information. CEO Mark Zuckerberg revealed the gadget earlier this year and said the company expected to ship the Charm “in time for the holidays in December,” but he didn’t provide a price at the time.

When he announced the Muse Charm, Zuckerberg said that the company had “packed the whole Muse experience,” including real-time voice and avatar technology, into the gadget. It has a fingerprint sensor, and you can tap it to be able to talk to a Muse AI agent without unlocking a phone or opening an app. The Information reports that the Muse Charm will come with a free 12-month 5G data plan from Verizon.

Spokesperson Tyler Yee wrote to The Information that “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.” When reached for comment by The Verge, Yee provided the same statement.

The company is also working on a smartwatch, The Information says, but a launch for that has been pushed to 2027 as Meta tries to get Muse Charm out the door.

Meta also open sourced code to let users make their own Muse gadgets, which my colleague Sean Hollister used to make his own DIY Muse Charm.

Update, November 19th: Noted statement given by Meta spokesperson Tyler Yee.

Tech.title: Google is putting AI chats right on the homepage
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

Based on the GIF shared by Stein, it looks like you can open the sidebar by clicking the gray bar that appears on the left side of your screen. From there, Google will show a list of the searches you’ve made using AI Mode, along with the ability to start a new thread, search your threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

It’s yet another big change for Google’s homepage, which has long presented you with a single bar to kick off your web search. The company brought its AI Mode button to its search bar last year, which opens up a chatbot-like search experience within Google. In May, Google updated its search box to accommodate longer queries and added AI-powered autocomplete.

Stein says Google is rolling out the option because “people are coming to Search with more questions that aren’t just one and done,” adding that “in testing, this sidebar made a big difference for making progress & continuing to explore the web.” The new homepage is rolling out globally on desktop.

Tech.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an “influx of contraband cellphones” used to carry out crimes from prison.

Jammers are generally banned under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, though they’re used at some federal facilities. FCC Chair Brendan Carr claims that giving correctional facilities access to this technology will help prevent prisoners from using phones for illegal activity. “These devices [phones] are being used by inmates to order hits, run drug operations, traffic women and children, and unleash mayhem on our communities from behind bars,” Carr says.

In the months leading up to the vote, trade groups and human rights advocates have raised concerns about the risks of blocking cellphone signals in prisons. The US Chamber of Commerce and the CTIA, a wireless association representing the nation’s biggest carriers, have both warned in letters to the FCC that jamming technology could disrupt lawful communications outside prisons, including 911 calls. Meanwhile, the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) has long argued that cellphones can keep prisoners safe by allowing them to document safety and human rights issues that the outside world may not see.

FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez, the sole Democrat on the Commission, voted for the measure despite the risk of “potential unintended consequences,” according to the Associated Press. “I want to make sure that we don’t harm public safety in the name of helping public safety,” Gomez added.

The FCC says prisons that choose to jam cellphone signals will need to obtain a license, adhere to “technical standards and testing requirements,” and ensure that the jamming technology doesn’t interfere with communications outside the facility. Prisons must also notify nearby communities of testing and when the technology is being deployed.

Tech.title: Sony’s WH-1000XM5 are cheaper than ever for Black Friday
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Back in my day, the only “Doorbuster” sales were at physical retail stores. But now, you can get ultra-low prices before Black Friday whether you want to shop in-store or online. One that stands out is the previous-generation Sony WH-1000XM5 noise-canceling headphones, which are marked down to their lowest price ever, just $169.99 at Best Buy. While their MSRP is $399.99, they’ve been spotted as low as $198 in the last few months.

The WH-1000XM5 launched in 2022, and despite having been succeeded by the WH-1000XM6, they’re still an excellent set of headphones. Their active noise cancellation effect is one of the best out there — competitive with the latest models from Bose and Apple — and the sound profile is tighter and more balanced than the older Sony headphones.
