There are some minor downsides, like a bulky case and all-plastic design, but those seem easier to overlook at this lower price point.

The newer Sony WH-1000XM6 improve the sound and noise cancellation, with quality of life upgrades not present in the XM5, like a folding design and more comfortable headband. However, they’re significantly more expensive, currently discounted to $348 during Black Friday (Amazon, Best Buy), down from their MSRP of $450.

To make shopping a little more confusing, the newer WH-1000XM4C sit between the XM5 and XM6 in terms of price, and are a slightly updated version of the older XM4 model with its foldable design. Our reviewer John Higgins thinks the XM4C’s noise cancellation lags behind, so I’d opt for the XM5 over them, especially at the sale price.

Tech.title: You can now buy a Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Valve announced some updates about Steam Machine availability today, including good news if you want to buy one right now and potential bad news about future supply due to RAMaggedon.

The good news: You can now purchase a 512GB Steam Machine without getting on a waitlist. Initially, interested buyers had to get on Valve’s waitlist if they wanted to purchase one, but the console-like PC is now available in an “add-to-cart” status, according to the company. As I write this, the 512GB versions with and without a bundled controller are showing estimated delivery dates of three to five business days on Valve’s website. If Valve sells through its current inventory, the company says it will indicate that the product is out of stock instead of making another waitlist.

The bad news: If you’re on the waitlist for a 2TB model, you might not get a chance to buy one at all, as Valve says there are more people on the waitlist than there are units available. The company is closing the waitlists for its 2TB models.

Valve says that while it’s still building more Steam machines, “memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels” and that it doesn’t know the number it can make or “at what price we’ll be able to offer them.” The 2TB Steam Machine is “especially constrained.” The company anticipates “having more information” to share about additional supply in January.

After delaying the Steam Machine’s expected early 2026 launch due to the memory and storage crisis, Valve launched the product in June with a price starting at $1,049 for the 512GB model without a bundled controller. A 2TB model without a controller costs $1,349.

Tech.title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
Tech.content:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”

The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

Tech.title: Anthropic’s 7 founders cashed out nearly $2B in record-breaking IPO
Tech.content:
Anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

At the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The company said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”

With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

$104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

More than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

Anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

All told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

Tech.title: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
Tech.content:
On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.

That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. It specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. Co-founder Chenyu Zhao and I spoke onstage toward the end of the day.

Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.

Fireworks, assigned a $17.5 billion valuation by its investors in summer, is reportedly in “early talks” for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.

Here’s some of what Zhao had to say. This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.

How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.

How far behind are open models right now?

A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.

If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.

In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.

Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.

Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.

How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.

Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron, and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

Tech.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX has a plan to eliminate cell phone dead zones
Tech.content:
CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk said, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

“We’ve got a plan that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk said, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”

The company’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he said. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”

Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”

The idea isn’t new, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said during the company’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

Even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk said one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

SpaceX’s plan to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely new class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

“I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he said, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”

Tech.title: Want to see your live AI usage on your Mac’s icons? This clever new app lets you
Tech.content:
There’s a new way to keep an eye on your AI usage and when your limits reset: by using your Mac’s app icons. Yes, really!

Designer Michael Flarup has just launched a new Mac utility called IconSwapper, which lets you replace any app’s official icon with one of your own creation. While you can use this tool to change your icons’ appearance, design, shading, and more, one of the more interesting ways to use it is to swap the icons for AI apps like ChatGPT or Claude with versions that can display your live AI usage.

Doing so is fairly simple, and you don’t have to be technically minded to get this to work. After installing the app on your Mac, you simply choose which application you want to create a “live” icon for — meaning one that responds to a particular app.

Image Credits:IconSwapper

Besides tracking AI usage in ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, you can also create live icons for a number of the built-in Mac apps like Messages, Mail, Safari, Finder, Music, and others like Chrome and Spotify, but these configurations tend to be more fun than they are practical. For instance, you can configure Safari’s compass to follow things like page loads and downloads, or you can make it so that the Finder guy’s eyes follow your cursor around the screen. (That one is hilarious!)

Image Credits:IconSwapper (screenshot)

Of course, there are plenty of other ways to track your AI usage — you don’t need an icon to do that. You can track usage from your account or your harness, even from a fun little gadget. But tracking it from the icon adds a certain whimsy to your Mac desktop setup. (If your dock is crowded, note that you can also see your icon customizations from your tab bar as you switch apps.)

Beyond live icons, you can also change what an icon looks like using IconSwapper’s built-in tools.

There are a surprising number of built-in customizations that are as easy to use as clicking a few buttons or toggling a switch. IconSwapper also comes with a large library of alternative icons for every app that are already ready to use, or you can upload your own.

Image Credits:IconSwapper

Flarup is based in Copenhagen, where he runs a design studio, and he has been drawn to icon design and customization for years. He’s been making his own Mac icons since the early 2000s and even wrote a book about app icons that celebrates the work of designers.

He had been working on a solution that would allow him to customize Mac icons, which had proven tricky because macOS has no official support for theming and protects its system icons. To work around this, he came up with a different technique that involves drawing directly on the icons without replacing them, allowing him to use shaders, motion, and display real data.

Flarup tells TechCrunch that his renderer runs the icon artwork through custom Metal shaders in real time.

Image Credits:IconSwapper

“The breakthrough was figuring out how to send the Dock a bitmap for another running app and have it draw that frame itself,” he explained. “I spent a lot of time getting the artwork to follow the icon through all the little ways macOS moves it, from Dock magnification to the Command-Tab switcher. Once I had that working, I could make the icon react to whatever’s happening,” Flarup said.

That lets users configure icons to do all kinds of fun, new things they never could before, like make light move across a gold icon as you drag your cursor over it, or animate an app’s icon while it’s thinking.

“That opens up a lot of fun ways to make your Mac feel like yours. I’ve always felt the software we use every day could be a little more fun and a lot more personal,” he added.

The app itself is a one-time purchase of $19 as a launch promo but will later sell for $29, its website says.

Tech.title: Meta’s new Muse Charm device may cost $300
Tech.content:
In Brief

Meta plans to charge $300 for Muse Charm, its upcoming Tamagotchi-like AI device that was teased at the company’s Connect event earlier this year, The Information has reported.

When reached for comment by TechCrunch, a Meta spokesperson didn’t deny the claims, merely providing the following statement: “We’re charmed by the interest in our AI devices, and we’ll have more to share soon.”

So far, Meta has made a relatively successful push into consumer AI, launching Muse — its agentic helper — along with a variety of cute avatars that users can use to give the system more of a personality.

Muse Charm, the company’s push into AI hardware, will allow users to carry a physical personification of its software around in their pocket (or potentially wear it around their neck), talking to it, asking it questions, and giving it commands.

It remains to be seen whether customers will bite or not. AI wearables have had a rough go of it so far (here’s looking at you, Humane Ai pin), but companies continue to iterate on the concept in an attempt to break through to a broader audience.

Indeed, $300 is arguably a pretty steep price for a product the size of a keychain, although it’s also a price point that’s in line with what other companies have been charging. The wearable launched by Friend — the AI startup whose device lets you text and talk to an AI persona — is currently retailing for $250. On the other hand, Amazon’s all-new Bee Frontier wearable AI device — which transcribes conversations and tracks tasks — lists for $75 and is currently on a Black Friday, 30% off sale of $52.49. Even with its $99/year subscription to let it tie into a user’s apps (photos, emails, etc.), it’s still far less expensive than Muse Charm.

Tech.title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
Tech.content:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly.

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said.

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X.

AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with.

In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up.

When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.”

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said.

Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.”

Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues.

And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.

“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

Tech.title: Uber tests rides for kids as young as 10, with extra pay for drivers
Tech.content:
Uber has opened its ride-hailing service to children as young as 10 in three U.S. cities as the company tests whether there’s a market for shuttling tweens without an adult by their side. The program, called Uber Kids, launched quietly over the past few weeks in Austin, Texas, Nashville, Tennessee, and Madison, Wisconsin.

The program, which builds on Uber’s existing teen ride-hailing service for passengers ages 13 to 17, is the latest bid by Uber to expand its customer base. Uber is describing this as a limited pilot program, which means it may never expand beyond these cities or even exist by next year. But if successful, it could open up a potentially lucrative market for Uber: busy families with active kids.

The Uber Kids program is stacked with mandatory requirements for parents and drivers. Parents or guardians are the only ones who can order a ride for their child, which they can do by adding the child to their family profile and completing a mandatory onboarding that explains the built-in safety features. A parent or guardian must be present at the pickup locations for the trip to begin and also have to include a note to the driver that explains the drop off.

Meanwhile, only highly rated drivers who have been invited are allowed to participate. Those drivers are required to complete an education module that includes step-by-step instructions and must be opted into live video streaming so parents can watch the trip in real time, according to Uber.

Uber said it also requires PIN verification for every Uber Kids trip, and says all recordings will be encrypted and not available to the driver, and will use sensors and GPS data to detect if the ride goes off course, stops unexpectedly, or ends early.

Drivers who are willing to adhere to those rules to shuttle kids will get a pay bump for the effort, according to Uber. Eligible drivers will earn $7 more on every Uber Kids trip compared to a standard one, the company says on the dedicated Uber Kids web page. Drivers will receive an extra $20 for the first Uber Kids ride they complete.

The extra compensation underscores a key challenge Uber faces as it expands into this younger age group — how to convince drivers to take on that added responsibility. If the program does expand it could eventually compete with existing transportation services such as HopSkipDrive and Zum.

Uber opened its ride-hailing service to minors in 2023 when it launched Uber for Teens, although the company had conducted early pilots several years prior. As the program expanded nationwide, Uber introduced a live video streaming feature.

Tech.title: Fiona the Hippo Died After Eating a Hat. But How Does a Hat Kill a Hippo?
Tech.content:
Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s famous hippo who charmed observers around the world, tragically died on Thursday due to medical complications after ingesting a knit hat that mistakenly entered her enclosure last week, according to zoo officials. Fiona was just nine years old when she died.

According to zoo officials, the hat that caused her death entered her enclosure after a child tossed it into the air. The hat reportedly collided with a ceiling fan, which then launched the hat through a “one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window." A few days after eating the hat, her condition began to deteriorate.

For nonexperts, Fiona’s tragic death raises several questions: Why and how would a knit hat kill a hippo that weighs more than 2,500 pounds? Why wasn’t surgery possible for Fiona? And for zookeepers, what was the range of treatment scenarios available?

Why Did Fiona Die?

Jan Hawkins, the head of the the clinical science department at North Carolina State University's College of Veterinary Medicine, tells WIRED that—with the caveat that we won’t officially know until doctors conduct a post-mortem analysis—Fiona’s death was likely due to one of a few downstream effects of the hat getting caught somewhere in her intestinal tract.

In a sense, an intestinal blockage in a hippo is like a car crash on an incredibly long one-lane highway. Hawkins said that, estimating, a hippo’s intestinal tract is likely over 100 feet long, with more than 70 feet in the small intestines alone. In humans, the lengths of the small and large intestines are a comparably diminutive 25 feet.

Hawkins says that in a healthy hippo, liquids can take as little as 12 hours to pass, and food takes two to three days. According to zoo officials, Fiona ate the hat on or about Sunday. Zoo officials claimed that Fiona was asymptomatic at first, but began to lose her appetite after a few days. If the hat was going to come out, Hawkins says it likely would have happened within five days. So what happened?

One possibility, Hawkins says, is that when the hat got stuck, it caused a huge amount of swelling and pressure in her abdomen. That swelling could have led to her blood circulation being cut off, and eventually, to tissue death. After becoming green or black, Hawkins says that dead tissue is more likely to leak, and perhaps rupture, releasing the contents of the digestive tract into her blood. This can easily cause toxic shock.

Tech.title: Dudes Online Are So Mad That ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Makes Them Respect Women
Tech.content:
The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”

In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

The concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.)

Tech.title: What’s With All These Outages?
Tech.content:
Sophie Kleeman: You wake up in the morning and you think Anthropic IPO.

Brian Barrett: I think ANT, ANT, ANT. But it's the first, not the first, it's the biggest pure-play AI IPO that we've had and maybe that we're going to have depending on what happens with OpenAI. SpaceX had an IPO recently, but that is a rocket company with an AI company stapled to it. So what do you look for when this company goes public and people can trade on it? How much do we look at it as a bellwether for the industry in general? Not on the first day of trading even, but just in general, how much can we look and say, oh, that's how the AI industry is going?

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, I think it is the bellwether, right? It is the first, it is enormous. It's such a leader in the space. And I think that the interesting thing to me is how much it is connected to the other sort of giants in the space, which is to say Amazon and Google, and a few other companies. I mean, those two firms are themselves going to make a shit ton of money from this IPO. They have, what is it? 15 percent. Amazon will own 15 percent. Google will own nearly 14 percent. Those are huge numbers. So I think just this idea that all the financing is tied together and all of these people are riding on the same rocket ship that may or may not crash onto the surface of the earth.

Brian Barrett: And not just that, but Anthropic, they're like a rent-not-own approach to data centers. So they've got nearly a trillion dollars of data center commitments that is all going to other companies. It is sort of fueling, whether that's SpaceX or Google. So they are such a symbol of the interdependency of this industry. And again, can't stress this enough, they are pretty sure that AI will destroy everything, and think that their best chance to make a trillion dollars is to build the kind of AI that will destroy everything as fast as they can. It's in their prospectus.

Sophie Kleeman: Only they can prevent mass AI destruction. The other thing I would like to sort of cite here: I feel like with these IPO stories, obviously everyone's sort of focused on the money, and the What does it mean? and blah, blah, blah. But one kind of very weird fun fact that I would like to just highlight here is that Sam Bankman-Fried of all of this. He was supposed to make money on this because he was invested in Anthropic, but when he went through his bankruptcy and all of his legal problems, the government clawed back that investment.

Leah Feiger: Wait, so where are his shares now? Love that.

Sophie Kleeman: They got sold to some people for a very little amount of money, and now those people are going to be rich.

Leah Feiger: Oh, that's fun. That's a fun thing to follow.

Sophie Kleeman: Highly recommend checking that out.

Leah Feiger: Yeah. Look, you guys know me. I'm interested in this from a political standpoint. Voters voted against data centers. Politicians won their campaigns by promising that data centers were out across the board. This was bipartisan, this was Republican, this was Democrat. So as Anthropic is entering this space, as other companies, OpenAI, etc., are kind of watching how this goes for them, I'm really curious in the coming months what these investments in data centers is going to mean for them. I wonder if it's going to mean slowdowns. I wonder if any of these newly electeds will actually be able to hold these folks accountable. We're going to see, but there is very much a question mark for me there about what comes next.

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, I think one of the great things for us as journalists too about this IPO is Anthropic will now be a public company. So they are much more accountable and accountable in ways that we can actually dig into and go through their 10-Ks and go through their 10-Qs and all the rest of it. They're going to have to do earnings calls and all the rest of it, which is great for us, because we will have such a better window into how they're actually doing.

Leah Feiger: Oh, it's amazing.

Sophie Kleeman: Such a better window into how they're actually doing.

Leah Feiger: Also, just because they're so tied up, sourcing inside Anthropic is hard. This is a company that is very much kept to themselves, which is why any kernel of information ... When Jacob Coxon, the Anthropic doomer who bounced out and said, "This really is going to all end the world," and he was on, I don't know, every single talk show or podcast available. One, because of what he was saying, but two, because getting information from inside of Anthropic is difficult. So to your point, a hundred percent. The fact that we're going to have more information there is a game change.

Brian Barrett: The one thing I would add, yes, it's great for us as journalists. We're going to get to see and know so much more information. I'm not as excited about Anthropic now being on this quarterly cycle of needing to demonstrate constant growth and earnings, which is a private company you're shielded from a little bit because the incentives that will make AI profitable are not necessarily the incentives that will make humanity more sustainable, but that's fine.

Sophie Kleeman: Who cares about sustainability? Yep.

Brian Barrett: Who cares? We're all going to be podcasting in caves. Speaking of giant AI companies that are having big moments, good or bad, we've got to talk a little bit about Nvidia. If you're sick of it, totally understand. It's been everywhere, but there are some important updates. Some things have happened just in the last day or two that we should touch on at least quickly. On Tuesday, the company reported its most recent earnings, not surprising that they had another big, big quarter, $115.8 billion in revenue. It's more than six billion ahead of expectations. It was Nvidia's first earnings report since Jensen Huang resigned last week after it became public that he had had affairs with a woman suspected of being an asset of Chinese intelligence, and also with at least one of his own direct reports within Nvidia. Over the last few days, we've had a number of Silicon Valley leaders, including, surprise, Elon Musk, campaigning to bring him back. Some have floated the theory that he was set up. Huang himself said in a statement, first statement that he released since this all happened, that he would be honored to return to Nvidia if the board would have him back. Sounds like the board is saying absolutely not. They said that in very clear terms during the earnings call. What do we make of Nvidia in this moment? I should say, too, that we are recording this just after Nvidia's first all hands after Jensen Huang left was led by interim CEO, former CFO, Colette Kress. It's a lot of information. She didn't say much other than, "Hey employees, we're going to give you a lot more money and a lot more stock equity to make you happier so that you don't leave."

Sophie Kleeman: And she kept saying, "We got this," right?

Brian Barrett: She kept saying, “We got this.”

Sophie Kleeman: That was her direct quote, that was her top line, "We're going to be fine. We got this. Do not worry."

Leah Feiger: But so many people just don't think that. I can't stop thinking about what Zoë told us last week, Brian, and the week before. She's been saying this for a while now, just about how Jensen was in such a particular place compared to all of his co-CEOs around Silicon Valley and that he was just not insulated. He was not insulated within his company. He's not the Mark Zuckerberg model at Meta where that guy's not going anywhere. There is just no world where he's getting stripped from his title or responsibilities, which then makes this entire Bring Back Jensen campaign all the more interesting to me, to see Elon Musk and all of these variety of CEOs, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, all of these different people who not even are just kind of quietly commenting on the sidelines, but signing literal petitions saying this. There's an interesting look, at least for me, of the accountability of it all, of is this possible? I guess this is possible. This shouldn't be possible.

Sophie Kleeman: I'm fascinated by this. And Brian, I would love to know what you think is going on here because I sort of though the sharks would be circling in a way, or I thought that they would not want to touch this with a 10-foot pole kind of thing. I mean, I understand that Jensen is just such a sort of crucial part of this ecosystem and Nvidia is such a crucial part of this ecosystem. They've sort of engineered it that way, but I'm curious what you think, what's the vibe? Why are they all coming out so strongly?

Brian Barrett: Oh, because I think that they all see a little bit of themselves in him.

Leah Feiger: He's one of their own.

Brian Barrett: A raconteur, a bad boy about town. And when you are a unique special genius, you should be able to get away with doing whatever else. We talked about this before, it's the idea of separating the art from the artist, but applied to real allegedly scummy behavior, like having sex with a direct report and lying to your board of directors about it. I don't think Jensen's coming back. I'm prepared to be wrong because this industry has done dumber things on shorter timelines, but I do think the board has been so resolute in it. I think Nvidia's going to be fine. This is not a popular take, I think. I think they're going to be fine in the long term. They've got such lock in. They've got customers that don't have anywhere else to turn, and it will be a long time before they do. They may not be as essential a pillar to the US economy and the industry in the long run. Maybe they don't grow quite as fast, but I think that's probably healthy overall. I think a smaller Nvidia with more competition is probably ... I mean, it makes less systemic risk for everybody else. So I think we're going to be OK.

Leah Feiger: One more piece of news before we go to break. President Donald Trump is in Asia this week. He stopped in the Philippines. He's heading to China. He's expected to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday. Right before the trip, the administration said it was moving forward with a new rule that would clamp down on China's ability to access advanced AI chips through the use of data centers outside of China's borders. The rule aims to close what a lot of folks in Washington thought was a loophole, basically, which is that Chinese firms are banned from buying the most advanced AI chips made by companies like Nvidia, but they have continued to legally access the chips by renting them from data centers. And this issue became the entire issue this past week because of Nvidia, because Alice Huang was an executive at one of these companies, Megaspeed. WIRED senior correspondent Hugo Lowell has been reporting on what the administration's response has been throughout all of this. And it's been really interesting, honestly, which is for as much as Trump and co are like, "We have to be ahead of China. This is the whole thing. We can't slow down. We can't have guardrails. We have to beat China." There's also been this undercurrent of figuring out how you cooperate, how you're still making money without stifling innovation. This has played out into disputes within Trump's own cabinet. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent versus Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. I have loved the drama of it all.

Sophie Kleeman: The girls are fighting.

Leah Feiger: The girls are fighting. But frankly, for as much as Bessent spent the last week throwing Lutnick entirely under the rug, it kind of turns out, and Hugo found, that Trump has been really playing that middle and siding with Lutnick in a lot of this. So this new rule is going to be really interesting. I'm very curious about it getting enforced. I'm curious about how it's going to also be talked about and communicated this week on the ground actually in China. Hugo's newsletter that published Wednesday night gets into this, and basically what officials have told him quietly is that there probably isn't going to be a lot of movement on AI as Trump arrives, really because of the Nvidia scandal, because there has been so much consternation of quote, unquote Chinese spies everywhere. And this conversation is a little bit at a standstill. So new rule, conversations happening, maybe no results. I don't know. Is that politics as usual? Perhaps.

Brian Barrett: I have a couple questions. One, this is a dumb one, I'm sorry, but we just heard Donald Trump saying, when asked about outages, that if you're big, then people will go for you, even though that has nothing to do with what's going on. So my question, Leah, the eternal question with Donald Trump, how much do we think he actually knows or cares about any of this versus whoever was in the room with him last has told him a thing that sounds good?

Leah Feiger: Oh, I think that's a huge part of it. Ultimately, and I should have this tattooed on my forehead, which is that similar rules to these already existed. They existed in the Biden era. Trump rolled them back in 2025. Again, unclear how much of that context is memorable to the administration or to Trump himself. But I think the underlying current, really for him, for as far as we've been able to understand from his public statements and his private ones that people have been able to report out, is that he wants the US to be competitive. Fist on table, be competitive. Whether that means we're selling chips or not selling chips, they're not very complicated thoughts. I'm sorry to say. I don't know how else to put it other than I'm not sure that the minutia is that interesting to him. And frankly, the minutia is barely interesting to the rest of us.

Sophie Kleeman: It's deeply unsexy. It's deeply unsexy.

Leah Feiger: It's like every time that we're writing an article on this, and I'm sure that you struggle with this as well, Sophie, I'm like, "And here's our context paragraph where I spell out exactly what Megaspeed meant for chips."

Sophie Kleeman: It reads like a white paper. Yeah.

Leah Feiger: It's horrible. Whereas it's much easier to say, "No, we must be competitive with China. Also, we have to work with China." OK, what does that mean when you're spelling it out?

Sophie Kleeman: I mean, my question too, not to put on my conspiracy theory hat again, but I think-

Brian Barrett: Dit it.

Leah Feiger: This is when we unveil you as our ... This is why you're here.

Sophie Kleeman: Resident conspiracy theorist. I mean, so the reporting about this, it was a little bit hedged. It was like they are moving toward closing a loophole.

Leah Feiger: Yeah.

Sophie Kleeman: So my question is, are they just trying to get out ahead of, they were caught with their pants down in some respects with the Nvidia, the Megaspeed, all that stuff. And so now they're like, "OK, we need to sort of look like we're doing something. So we're just going to say that we're going to do this, and maybe we will or maybe we won't, but we're just going to be like, OK, look, look over here instead of over there."

Leah Feiger: I mean, 100 percent. Back in September, that's when we were told that this Cold War era-style hotline was going to be coming between China and the US, that this was going to be how we were going to address these issues. There was going to be an open dialogue. And look, that's still apparently, Hugo is learning, is still being discussed, is still on the table, but also to me just reads as to exactly what you're saying, which is here's an option, here's another option. I'm not defending anyone here, to be entirely clear, but there is a thin line. I mean, the US and Trump has gone for China hard with trade restrictions. China has not liked that. They've responded with restrictions of their own, rare earth exports et al. So there is this line that they have to draw of, yes, we are anti-China. They have to appease the anti-China hawks in the party while also having to work with the richest nation around. And so it's a very tricky balance.

Brian Barrett: One last politics thing to mention, just because it's significant. It has nothing to do with export controls. On Wednesday, the incoming head of the House Oversight Committee directed Donald Trump Jr. son of Donald Trump, to preserve all records related to his lavish wedding celebrations and his many business ventures. That's not the only records preservation, "Hey, we're going to investigate you" stuff going on this week. We had representative Robert Garcia, incoming head of the House Oversight Committee issuing a similar record preservation request to Eric Trump along with Donald Trump Jr. related to their wildly controversial crypto firm, World Liberty Financial, along with brother-in-law, Jared Kushner, who runs a Saudi backed investment firm while also serving as a presidential envoy to the Middle East. Leah, not a question so much as a statement, but sparks are flying. Or they're about to.

Leah Feiger: Sparks are flying.

Brian Barrett: Not the romantic kind, sorry. I mean more excitement and investigations coming.

Leah Feiger: Look, within hours of Democrats winning the midterms, they immediately started saying that investigations were coming. You're going to be seeing evidence of this really soon. The fact that the Trump family is going to be at the core of this already is expected, but they're coming in hard. Also listed in these record preservation requests was Stephen Miller, now White House chief of staff, for all of his activities regarding ICE invasions of American cities over this past year. We have Susie Wiles, the ex-chief of staff. We have Kristi Noem, we have Corey Lewandowski, former DHS officials. There's a lot here that [Robert] Garcia and the oversight committee are going to be digging into. And regardless of when all of these things kind of begin, at the very least, this is our first official indication that things are coming. They're going to drag people in front of Congress. I can't wait to see this play out. This is going to be huge. They're going for everyone. Everyone in the Trump orbit is going to be called in here.

Brian Barrett: Coming up after the break, we're going to share our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: It is time for our WIRED and TIRED segment. As usual, whatever is new and cool is WIRED and whatever passé thing we're over is TIRED. Brian, can you go first?

Brian Barrett: ... to play Grand Theft Auto VI is totally fine and normal. I'm supportive of this. Again, I don't have a console that can play it. I have a Switch in my house that nobody plays, but I recognize that it's a big cultural moment. So go ahead. Don't feel bad about it. And I'll do the same for March Madness when that comes around. So that's my WIRED. You've got my permission, America, to do that.

I think if you've got it, you don't need to say that you've got it. So saying you've got it is TIRED because it really suggests to me that you probably don't got it.

Brian Barrett: Although are they too on it? I feel like whenever we've tried to sell something on Facebook Marketplace, it's like an inundation of messages and people getting really mad when you don't write back immediately.

Tech.title: The Best Hatch Black Friday Deals (2026)
Tech.content:
If you’re still using your iPhone’s “Radar” sound as an alarm, it might be time for an upgrade. The latest Hatch Sleep Clock is designed to make both falling asleep and waking up a little more pleasant. It combines a sunrise alarm clock, dimmable bedside light, sound machine, and contactless sleep tracking into one bedside gadget. And for the first time, it’s going on sale (early) as a Black Friday deal.

From November 19 through November 20, the Sleep Clock is 25 percent off at Hatch and Amazon. Normally $250, it’s down to $188, which is just $18 more than the Hatch Restore 3’s $170 retail price. And unlike its predecessor, the newer Hatch adds passive sleep monitoring, which is pretty compelling for anyone who hates wearing wearables to bed. Or maybe you’re like me and occasionally forget to wear your Oura Ring to bed, in which case, you wouldn’t have to worry because the Hatch is already quietly tracking your sleep in the background.

Hatch Sleep Clock for $188 ($62 Off)

Photograph: Boutayna Chokrane Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Hatch Sleep Clock $250 $188 (25% off) Hatch

I’ve been testing the Hatch Sleep Clock for over two months, and it’s earned a permanent spot on my nightstand. As someone who already wears a smart ring and smartwatch to bed, I’m not exactly short on sleep-tracking data. But I’ve never owned a sunrise alarm clock, and I instantly became a convert. Unlike my iPhone or Amazon Echo Dot, it doesn’t wake me up by blaring an obnoxious alarm in my pitch-black bedroom. Instead, it gradually illuminates the room within my scheduled wake-up time. You can customize the sunrise's duration and brightness, and pair it with a soundscape of your choosing. It truly makes getting out of bed feel less jarring, especially as the mornings get darker.

Most notably, the Sleep Clock also doubles as a contactless sleep tracker, using a built-in motion sensor to detect your movements and breathing throughout the night. I compared its readings against my Oura Ring 5 and Apple Watch Series 12, and while sleep duration estimates were generally aligned, the sleep-stage readings were less consistent. The device doesn’t measure physiological metrics like heart rate, and it can’t detect snoring or other audio-based sleep disruptions. I also found that placement significantly matters. My nightstand tends to collect clutter, so I had to rearrange my trinkets to make room for the clock.

Each morning, the Hatch app gives you a breakdown of when you went to bed, when you fell asleep, when you woke up, and how much time you spent in different sleep stages. The color-coded reports are easy to understand without burying me in random metrics. Plus, unlike most sleep trackers, Hatch doesn't require a subscription to access your sleep data. (You will need that Hatch+ membership ($6 per month) if you want to access the full audio library, however.)

Overall, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the best all-in-one bedside device. I wouldn’t recommend replacing your dedicated wearable with it if detailed health tracking is your priority. But if you’ve been wanting a sunrise alarm clock that can also offer a little insight into your sleep, do not sleep on this Black Friday deal.

More Hatch Deals

If you don’t care for sleep tracking, Hatch is also offering discounts on several other products across its lineup.

Tech.title: The Jensen Huang Blast Radius Has Hit His Favorite Restaurants
Tech.content:
Few things could generate more buzz for a small restaurant than a visit from Jensen Huang. In recent years, the former Nvidia CEO became known for dining out at street markets and hole-in-the-wall noodle joints across Asia, drawing huge crowds of fans and photographers wherever he went.

But after Huang resigned last week amid revelations of multiple extramarital affairs, some of the food vendors he helped put on the map are wondering whether their most famous customer is still good for business. In Taiwan, where Huang was born and his dining habits have long been a spectator sport, many say they aren't ready to turn against their hometown hero.

Tu Chang-chun, the owner of Ice World, a shaved-ice shop in Taipei, describes Huang as friendly, the kind of person who puts others around him at ease. His impression of the billionaire hasn’t changed since he learned of his affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman accused of spying for China.

“It’s not as if he killed someone or set something on fire. Why blow it all out of proportion?” Tu said on Monday evening, standing beneath the yellow lights of his stall at Linjiang Street Night Market. “Now, a lot of foreigners walk past, see my sign, and laugh. People just love kicking someone when they’re down.”

At the entrance of his shop, Tu continues to proudly display a photo of Huang posing with him and his wife. “I think he’s such a warm and approachable person,” Tu added. “Why are people treating him this way?”

Tech.title: Google Built a Giant ‘Mirror Dimension’ Internet to Test Its Chrome AI Agents
Tech.content:
As the Google Chrome team has worked to develop AI browsing features using the company's Gemini models, they realized they need to go the extra mile to keep things from going haywire. So they did the only thing they could think to do—they built an expansive alternate-universe internet that they completely control.

“Web-use” agents need to be familiar with the open internet, how to navigate real websites and platforms, and how to be hardened against web attacks. So training them in limited test environments is only so effective. Plus, models can develop what's known as “eval awareness,” where they behave differently because they have determined that they are in a test or simulation. On the other hand, setting unrefined agents loose on the open internet is a bad idea. That’s where the alternate-universe internet comes in.

The “Mirror Dimension,” which Google is detailing in a blog post today for the first time, is a sweeping and diverse but isolated web ecosystem that the Chrome team entirely controls. It includes a vast array of websites and platforms—including social media sites, shopping, and bank dashboards—that are built with all the components and attributes of real websites. Browsing assistant agents must interact with the sites and complete tasks in Chrome the way they would on the real internet. And they face resilience tests as they go, like hidden prompt-injection attacks, to test their defenses.

“Agents are not programmed, so you can’t predict every possible thing an agent might see; the exploration space that we have to address is huge, and the web is hostile,” says Charles Qian, a software engineer on the Chrome AI security team. “Any user can ask any prompt on any website, so we really need to explore that space as thoroughly as we can. And we’ve seen the agent start to develop a mature sense of judgment when it comes to knowing what information is actually needed for a task and when to punt back to the user for a confirmation.”

Building out and populating the Mirror Dimension was a challenge in itself, because it needed to be vast and varied enough to represent the scale of the real web while being developed quickly. To construct it, the Chrome team gathered armies of website and web app development agents guided by a purpose-built AI harness to quickly create realistic web services and data flows—down to details like entering promo codes on a shopping site or populating social media pages.

Even though the entire environment is controlled by Google, Chrome is built with so many user protections and validity checks that, in order to allow the agents to use real Chrome (which is crucial for accurate training), the researchers essentially had to hack the browser and take elaborate steps like making forged web certificates for validity checks so the agents could have a normal experience. The team emphasizes, though, that none of these attacks would be possible against regular Chrome users on the open internet. They were all facilitated by the god-mode-type access and privilege the team inherently has because they control the entire environment and network.

The researchers say that while the browsing assistant agents they have been testing are benign and do not have cyber capabilities, their goal is to make the Mirror Dimension available to teams across Google so more researchers have access to the safe and controlled environment for testing.

“We’re sharing this approach so other teams both internally and externally think about doing it this way,” says Doug Turner, Google’s director of engineering. “This is the first step; there’s going to be continued investment in this approach to train models. And I would imagine as they become more sophisticated, we’ll have to continue working on this environment to make it more and more realistic.”
